The principal modern structures are the church of St Peter, and the other churches; the aqueducts and fountains; the Vatican, and the other palaces; the Campidolio, where the Roman senate resides, &c. The principal remains of antiquity are the pila millaria of fine marble; the equestrian brass statue of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; the marble monument of the emperor Alexander Severus; marble busts of the emperors and their consorts; three brick arches of the temple of Peace, built by the emperor Vespasian; the triumphal arch of Septimus Severus and of Gallienus; the circus of Antoninus Caracalla; some parts of the cloaca maxima; the column Antoinina, representing the principal actions of Marcus Aurelius; the columna Trajani, or Trajan's pillar; some fragments of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a> or palace of Antoninus Pius, and of Nerva's forum; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Augustus, in the Strada Pontifici; the remains of the emperor Severus's tomb without St John's gate; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Cestius near St Paul's gate; the porphyry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of St Helen, and the original statue of Constantine the Great, in the church of St John of Lateran: a font of oriental <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, in the chapel of St Giovanni in fonte, said to have been erected by Constantine the Great; an Egyptian obelisk near the church of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Maggiore; the stately remains of Diocletian's baths; the celebrated Pantheon; the obelisks of Sestostris and Augustus by the Clementine college; the church of St Paul fuori della Mura, said to have been built by Constantine the Great; the Farnese <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, of a colossal size and exquisite workmanship, in a court of the Farnese palace, and an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> cut out of one <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of marble, in another court of the same palace. Besides these there are a great many more, which our bounds will not allow us to take any further notice of. Here is a great number of rich and well-regulated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. Near the church of St <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEBASTIANO">Sebastiano</a> alle Catacombe, are the most spacious of the catacombs, where the Christians, who never burned their dead, and such of the Pagan Romans as could not afford the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, were buried. Along the Via Appia, without St Sebastian's gate, were the tombs of the principal families of Rome, which at present are used for cellars and store-houses, by the gardeners and vintners. Rome was entered, in February 1798, by the French, and in consequence of a tumult which ensued, when their general Duphot was killed, they deposed the pope, abolished the papal government, and erected in its stead a republic, to which they gave the designation of the Roman republic. They sent the pope himself to France, where he died on his various removals; they likewise sent away great numbers of the most valuable statues and paintings of antiquity, and compelled the inhabitants to pay heavy contributions. In the month of September 1799, the allies retook this city, and the new French government was overthrown. It was afterwards obliged to yield to the insatiable ambition of Bonaparte, and formed a part of his dominions till the overthrow of his power in 1815, when the pope was replaced.

ISAIAH BY

Pages 835-836

h by means of the antithetic parallelism, without departing from his usual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, adds greatly to the sweetness of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in the following instances: In a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> have I forsaken thee; But with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mercies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> I receive thee again: In a short wrath I hid my <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> for a moment from thee; But with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee. Isaiah liv. 7, 8. Behold my servants shall eat, but ye shall be famished; Behold my servants shall drink, but ye shall be thirsty; Behold my servants shall rejoice, but ye shall be confounded; Behold my servants shall sing aloud, for gladness of heart, But ye shall cry aloud for grief of heart; And in the anguish of a broken spirit shall ye howl. Isaiah lxv. 13, 14. Frequently one line <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> member contains two sentiments: The nations raged; the kingdoms were moved: He uttered a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was dissolved: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted in the nations, I will be exalted in the earth. Ps. xlvii. 6, 10. When thou passest through waters I am with thee; And through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, they shall not overwhelm thee: When thou walkest in the fire thou shalt not be scorched; And the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> shall not cleave to thee. Isaiah xliii. 2. The third sort of parallels is the synthetic or constructive: where the parallelism consists only in the similar form of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>; in which word does not answer to word, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> to sentence, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> or opposite; but there is a correspondence and equality between different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, in respect of the shape and turn of the whole sentence, and of the constructive parts; such as noun answering to noun, verb to verb, member to member, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> to negative, interrogative to interrogative. Lo! he withholdeth the waters, and they are dried up: And he sendeth them forth, and they overturn the earth. With him is strength, and perfect existence; The deceived, and the deceiver are his. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xii. 13—16. Is such then the fast which I choose? That a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should afflict his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>? Is it, that he should bow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his head like a bulrush, And spread sackcloth and ashes for his couch? Shall this be called a fast, And a day acceptable to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a>? Is not this the fast that I choose? To dissolve the bands of wickedness; To loosen the oppressive burdens; To deliver those that are crushed by violence; And that ye should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> asunder every yoke? Is it not to distribute thy <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the hungry? And to bring the wandering <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> into thy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>? When thou seest the naked, that thou clothe him; And that thou hide not thyself from thine own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>? Then shalt thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> break forth like the morning; And thy wounds shall speedily be healed over: And thy righteousness shall go before thee; And the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Jehovah shall bring up thy rear. Isaiah lviii. 5—8. We shall produce another example of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of parallelism from Ps. xix. 8—11. from Dr Lowth: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Jehovah is perfect, restoring the soul; The testimony of Jehovah is sure, making wise the simple: The precepts of Jehovah are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, rejoicing the heart; The commandment of Jehovah is clear, enlightening the eyes: The fear of Jehovah is pure, enduring for ever; The judgments of Jehovah are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, they are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> altogether; More desirable than <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or than much fine gold; And sweeter than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, or the dropping of honeycombs. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">Synonymous</a> parallels have the appearance of art and concinnity, and a studied elegance; they chiefly prevail in shorter poems; in many of the Psalms; in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALAAM">Balaam</a>'s prophecies; frequently in those of Isaiah, which are most of them distinct poems of no great length. The antithetic parallelism gives an acuteness and force to adages and moral sentences; and therefore abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s Proverbs, and elsewhere is not often to be met with. The poem of Job, being on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> and in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tragic style, though very exact in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and in the parallelism, and affording many fine examples of the synonymous kind, consists chiefly of the constructive. A happy mixture of the several sorts gives an agreeable variety; and they mutually serve to recommend and set off one another. The reader will perceive that we have derived everything we have said relating to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> from the elegant Lectures of Dr Lowth, which are beautifully translated by Mr Gregory, a distinguished author as well as translator. The book of Proverbs has always been accounted canonical. The Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of it is Mishli *, which signifies "similitudes." It has always been ascribed to Solomon, whose name it bears, though some have doubted whether he really was the author of every one of the maxims which it contains. Those in chap. xxx., are indeed called the words of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AGUR">Agur</a> the son of Jakel, and the title of the 31st or last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> is the words of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Lemuel. It seems certain that the collection called the Proverbs of Solomon was digested in the order in which we now have it by different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; but it is not, therefore, to be concluded that they are not the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Solomon. Several persons might have made collections of them: Hezekiah, among others, as mentioned chapter xxv. Agur and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> might have done the same. From these several collections the work was compiled which we have now in our hands. The book of Proverbs may be considered under five divisions. 1. The first, which is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, extends to the 10th chapter. This contains general cautions and exhortations from a teacher to his pupil, expressed in elegant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, duly connected in its parts, illustrated with beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, and well contrived to engage and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> extends from the beginning of chap. x. to chap. xxii. 17, and consists of what may strictly and properly be called proverbs, viz. unconnected sentences, expressed with much neatness and simplicity. They are truly, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the language of their sage author "apples of gold in pictures of silver." 3. In the third part, which is concluded between chapter xxii. 16, and chapter xxv. the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> drops the sententious style, addresses his pupil as present, and delivers his advice in a connected manner. 4. The proverbs which are included between chapter xxv. and chapter xxx. are supposed to have been selected by the men of Hezekiah from some larger collection of Solomon, that is, by the prophets whom he employed to restore the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Some of the proverbs which Solomon had introduced into the former part of the book are here repeated. 5. The prudent admonitions which Agur delivered to his pupils Ithiel and Ucail are contained in the 30th chapter, and in the 31st are recorded the precepts which the mother of Lemuel delivered to her son. Several references are evidently made to the book of Proverbs by the writers of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. † The Proverbs of Solomon afford specimens of the didactic poetry of the Hebrews. They abound with antithetic parallels; for this form is peculiarly adapted to that kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to adages, aphorisms, and detached sentences. Indeed, the elegance, acuteness, and force of a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Solomon's wise sayings arise in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> from the antithetic form, the opposition of diction and sentiment. Take the following examples. The blows of a friend are faithful; But the kisses of an enemy are treacherous. The cloyed will trample on an honeycomb; But to the hungry every bitter thing is sweet. There is who maketh himself rich, and wanteth all things; Who maketh himself poor, yet hath much wealth. The rich man is wise in his own eyes, But the poor man that hath discernment to trace him out will despise him.* * Proverbs xviii. 6, 7. The Hebrew title of the book which we call <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTES">Ecclesiastes</a> is Keloth, that is, the Gatherer or Collector; and it is so called, either because the work itself is a collection of maxims, or because it was delivered to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> gathered together to hear them. The Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Ecclesiastes is of the same import, signifying one who gathers together a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, or who discourses or preaches to an assembly convened. That Solomon was the author of this book is beyond all doubt; the beautiful description of the phenomena in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> world, and their causes; of the circulation of the blood, as some think, ‡ and the economy of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frame, § shows it to be the work of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. At what stage of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> it was written may be easily found out. The affecting account of the infirmities of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> which it contains, is a strong indication that the author knew by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> what they were; and his complete conviction of the vanity of all earthly enjoyments proves it to have been the work of a penitent. Some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in it seem, indeed, to express an Epicurean notion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. But it is to be observed, that the author, in an academic way, disputes on both sides of the question; and at last concludes properly, that to "fear God and keep his commandments is the whole duty of man; for God (says he) will bring every work to judgment, and every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil." The general tenor and style of Ecclesiastes is very different from the book of Proverbs, though there are many detached sentiments and proverbs interspersed. For the whole work is uniform, and confined to one subject, namely, the vanity of the world exemplified by the experience of Solomon, who is introduced in the character of a person investigating a very difficult question, examining the arguments on either side, and at length disengaging himself from an anxious and doubtful disputation. It would be very difficult to distinguish the parts and arrangement of this production: the order of the subject, and the connexion of the arguments, are involved in so much obscurity, that scarcely any two commentators have agreed concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the work, and the accurate division of it into parts or sections. The truth is, the laws of methodical composition and arrangement were neither known by the Hebrews nor regarded in their didactic writings. They uniformly retained the old sententious manner, nor did they submit to method, even where the occasion appeared to demand it. The style of this work is, however, singular; the language is generally low; it is frequently loose, unconnected, approaching to the incorrectness of conversation; and possesses very little of the poetical character, even in the composition and structure of the periods: which peculiarity may possibly be accounted

OLD SARUM

Pages 525-526

in Wilts, about one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of New Sarum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, has the ruins of a fort which belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons; and is said also to have been one of the Roman stations. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> intrenchment, with a deep ditch. It is of an orbicular form, and has a very august look, being erected on one of the most elegant plans for a fortress that can be imagined. In the north-west <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> stood the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the bishop, whose see was removed hither from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a> and Sherborn; but the bishop quarrelling with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen, he seized the castle and put a garrison into it, which which was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of its destruction, as the see was soon after removed from hence to Salisbury in 1219. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of this ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is situated on an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> hill, whose walls were three yards thick, the ruins of which in many places in the circumference are still to be seen, and the tracks of the streets and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> may be traced out by the different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the corn growing where once the city stood. Here synods and parliaments have formerly been held, and hither were the states of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> summoned to swear fidelity to William the Conqueror. Here also was a palace of the British and Saxon kings, and of the Roman emperors; which was deserted in the reign of Henry III. for want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so that one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is all that is left of this ancient city; yet it is called the Borough of Old Sarum, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, who are chosen by the proprietors of certain adjacent lands. In February 1795 a subterraneous passage was discovered at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, of which we have the following account in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> dated Salisbury, Feb. 10. "Some persons of Salisbury on Saturday last went to the upper verge of the fortification (the citadel), and on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, after they had reached the summit, discovered a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole. They got a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, and went <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a flight of steps for more than 30 yards. It was an arched way <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet wide, neatly chiselled out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock or chalk. It is probable the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> gave way from the sudden thaw, and fell in. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of rubbish at the entrance. It appears to be between six and seven feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and a circular arch overhead all the way. These particulars I learned from the person who himself explored it; but was afraid to go farther, lest it might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in again and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> him. He thinks it turns a little to the right towards Old Sarum house, and continues under the fosse till it reaches the outer verge. The marks of a chisel, he says, are visible on the side. There are two large pillars of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> at the entrance, which appear to have had a door at foot. They are 18 inches by 27, of good free-stone, and the mason <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is extremely neat. The highest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the archway is two feet below the surface of the ground. "It is all now again filled up by order of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> Whitechurch, who rents the ground of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Camelford, and thinks curiosity would bring so many people there as to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> down his grass whenever grass shall be there. I went into it 30 yards, which was as far as I could get for the rubbish. I measured it with a line, and found it extend full 120 feet inwards from the two pillars supposed to be the entrance; then onwards it appeared to be filled to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> with rubbish. By measuring with the same line on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, I found it must go under the bottom of the outer <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the outer trench; where I think the opening may be found by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> a very little way. Whether it was a Roman or a Norman work it is difficult to say; but it certainly was intended as a private way to go into or out of the castle; and probably a fort or strong castle was built over the outer entrance. I looked for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> or coins, but have not heard of any being found." SASATRAS. See Laurus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

RHODAEAE

Pages 23-23

the name of the 27th order in Linnaeus's fragments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method, consisting of poppy and a few genera which resemble it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and structure. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

RHODES

Pages 12-23

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, the largest and most easterly of the Cyclades, was known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times by the names of Asteria, Ophiusa, Eilithrea, Trinacria, Corymbia, Poesa, Atabyria, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARCIA">Marcia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODESSA">Odessa</a>, Stadia, Telchinis, Pelagia, and Rhodus. In later ages, the name of Rhodus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Rhodes, prevailed, from the Greek word rhodon, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed, signifying a "rose;" the island abounding very much with these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Others, however, give different etymologies, among which it is difficult to find one preferable to another. It is about 20 miles distant from the coasts of Lycia and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, and about 120 miles in compass. Several ancient authors assert, that Rhodes was formerly covered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, but gradually raised its head above the waves, and became an island. Delos and Rhodes (says Pliny), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> which have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been celebrated, sprung at first from the sea. The same fact is supported by such a variety of other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as render it indubitable. Philo ascribes the event to the decrease of the waters of the ocean. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his conjecture be not without foundation, most of the isles of the Archipelago, being lower than Rhodes, must have had a similar origin. But it is much more probable that the volcanic fires, which in the fourth year of the 135th Olympiad, raised Therasia and Thera, known at present by the name of Santorin, from the depths of the sea, and have in our days thrown out several small islands adjacent, also produced in some ancient era Rhodes and Delos. The first inhabitants of Rhodes, according to Diodorus Siculus, were called the Telchinae, who came originally from the island of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. These, by their skill in astrology, perceiving that the island was soon to be drowned with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, left their habitations, and made room for the Heliades, or grandsons of Phœbus, who took possession of the island after that god had cleared it from the water and mud with which it was overwhelmed. These Heliades, it seems, excelled all other men in learning, and especially in astrology; invented <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, &c. In after ages, however, being infested with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> which bred in the island, they had recourse to an oracle in Delos, which advised them to admit Phorbas, a Thessalian, with his followers, into Rhodes. This was accordingly done: and Phorbas having destroyed the serpents, was, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, honoured as a demigod. Afterwards a colony of Cretans settled in some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, and a little before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Tlepolemus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the whole island, and governed with great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and moderation. After the Trojan war, all the ancient inhabitants were driven out by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be masters of the island for many ages. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was at first monarchical; but a little before the expedition... tion of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, a republican form of government was introduced; during which the Rhodians applied themselves to navigation, and became very powerful by sea, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> several colonies in distant countries. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Peloponnesian war, the republic of Rhodes was rent into two factions, one of which favoured the Athenians, and another the Spartans; but at length the latter prevailing, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> was abolished, and an aristocracy introduced. About 351 B.C. we find the Rhodians oppressed by Mausolus king of Caria, and at last reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> his widow. In this emergency, they applied to the Athenians, by whose assistance, probably, they regained their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. From this time to that of Alexander the Great, the Rhodians enjoyed an uninterrupted tranquillity. To him they voluntarily submitted; and were on that account highly favoured by him: but no sooner did they hear of his death, than they drove out the Macedonian garrisons, and once more became a free people. About this time happened a dreadful inundation at Rhodes; which being accompanied with violent storms of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and hailstones of an extraordinary bigness, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> many houses, and killed great numbers of the inhabitants. As the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, and no care had been taken to clear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and conduits which conveyed the water into the sea, the lower parts of the city were in an instant laid under water, several houses quite covered, and the inhabitants drowned before they could get to the higher places. As the deluge increased, and the violent showers continued, some of the inhabitants made to their ships, and abandoned the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, while others miserably perished in the waters. But while the city was thus threatened with utter destruction, the wall on a sudden burst asunder, and the water discharging itself by a violent current into the sea, unexpectedly delivered the inhabitants from all danger. The Rhodians suffered greatly by this unexpected accident, but soon retrieved their losses by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> application to trade. During the wars which took place among the successors of Alexander, the Rhodians observed a strict neutrality; by which means they enriched themselves so much, that Rhodes became one of the most opulent states of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; insomuch that, for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> good of Greece, they undertook the piratic war, and, at their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, cleared the seas of the pirates who had for many years infested the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. However, notwithstanding the neutrality they professed, as the most advantageous branches of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> were derived from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, they were more attached to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, king of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, than to any of the neighbouring princes. When therefore Antigonus, having engaged in a war with Ptolemy about the island of Cyprus, demanded succours of them, they earnestly intreated him not to compel them to declare war against their ancient friend and ally. But this answer, prudent as it was, drew upon them the displeasure of Antigonus, who immediately ordered one of his admirals to sail with his fleet to Rhodes, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> all the ships that came out of the harbour for Egypt. The Rhodians, finding their harbour blocked up by the fleet of Antigonus, equipped a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of galleys, fell upon the enemy, and obliged him, with the loss of many ships, to quit his station. Hereupon Antigonus, charging them as aggressors, and beginners of an unjust war, threatened to besiege their city with the strength of his whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The Rhodians endeavoured by frequent embassies to appease his wrath; but all their remonstrances served rather to provoke than allay his resentment; and the only terms upon which he would hearken to any accommodation were, that the Rhodians should declare war against Ptolemy, that they should admit his fleet into their harbour, and that an hundred of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> citizens should be delivered up to him as hostages for the performance of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The Rhodians sent ambassadors to all their allies, and to Ptolemy in particular, imploring their assistance, and representing to the latter, that their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> had drawn upon them the danger to which they were exposed. The preparations on both sides were immense. As Antigonus was near fourscore years of age at that time, he committed the whole management of the war to his son Demetrius, who appeared before the city of Rhodes with 200 ships of war, 170 transports having on board 40,000 men, and 1000 other vessels laden with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and all sorts of warlike engines. As Rhodes had enjoyed for many years a profound tranquillity, and been free from all devastations, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of booty, in the plunder of so wealthy a city, allured multitudes of pirates and mercenaries to join Demetrius in this expedition; insomuch that the whole sea between the continent and the island was covered with ships: which struck the Rhodians, who had a prospect of this mighty armament from the walls, with great terror and consternation. Demetrius, having landed his troops without the reach of the enemy's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, detached several small bodies to lay waste the country round the city, and cut down the trees and groves, employing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and materials of the houses without the walls, to fortify his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with a strong rampart and a triple palisade; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> were employed, was finished in a few days. The Rhodians, on their part, prepared for a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Many great commanders, who had signalized themselves on other occasions, threw themselves into the city, being desirous to try their skill in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs against Demetrius, who was reputed one of the most experienced captains in the conduct of sieges that antiquity had produced. The besieged began with dismissing from the city all such persons as were useless; and then taking an account of those who were capable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, they found that the citizens amounted to 6000, and the foreigners to 1000. Liberty was promised to all the slaves who should distinguish themselves by any glorious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and the public engaged to pay their masters their full <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was likewise made, declaring, that whoever died in defence of their country should be buried at the expense of the public; that his parents and children should be maintained out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>; that fortunes should be given to his daughters; and his sons, when they were grown up, should be crowned and presented with a complete <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of armour at the great solemnity of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> kindled an incredible ardour in all ranks of men. Demetrius, having planted all his engines, began to batter with incredible fury the walls on the side of the harbour; but was for eight days successively repulsed by the besieged, who set fire to most of his warlike engines. gines, and thereby obliged him to allow them some respite, which they made good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in repairing the breaches, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> new walls where the old ones were either weak or low. When Demetrius had repaired his engines, he ordered a general assault to be made, and caused his troops to advance with loud shouts, thinking by this means to strike terror into the enemy. But the besieged were so far from being intimidated, that they repulsed the aggressors with great slaughter, and performed the most astonishing feats of bravery. Demetrius returned to the assault next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but was in the same manner forced to retire, after having lost a great number of men, and some officers of distinction. He had seized, at his first landing, an eminence at a small distance from the city; and, having fortified this advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, he caused several batteries to be erected there, with engines, which incessantly discharged against the walls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of 150 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. The towers, being thus furiously battered night and day, began to totter, and several breaches were opened in the walls; but the Rhodians, unexpectedly sallying out, drove the enemy from their post, overturned their machines, and made a most dreadful havoc; insomuch that some of them retired on board their vessels, and were with difficulty prevailed upon to come ashore again. Demetrius now ordered a scalade by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> at the same time; and so employed the besieged, that they were at a loss what place they should chiefly defend. The attack was carried on with the utmost fury on all sides, and the besieged defended themselves with the greatest intrepidity. Such of the enemy as advanced first were thrown down from the ladders, and miserably bruised. Several of the chief officers, having mounted the walls to encourage the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> by their example, were there either killed or taken prisoners. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> had lasted many hours, with great slaughter on both sides, Demetrius, notwithstanding all his valour, thought it necessary to retire, in order to repair his engines, and give his men some days rest. Demetrius being sensible that he could not reduce the city till he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the port, after having refreshed his men, he returned with new vigour against the fortifications which defended the entry into the harbour. When he came within the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of a dart, he caused a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torches and firebrands to be thrown into the Rhodian ships, which were riding there; and at the same time galled, with dreadful showers of darts, arrows and stones, such as offered to extinguish the flames. However, in spite of their utmost efforts, the Rhodians put a stop to the fire; and, having with great expedition manned three of their strongest ships, drove with such violence against the vessels on which the enemy's machines were planted, that they were shattered in pieces, and the engines dismounted and thrown into the sea. Exestus the Rhodian <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, being encouraged by this success, attacked the enemy's fleet with his three ships, and sunk a great many vessels; but was himself at last taken prisoner; the other two vessels made their escape, and regained the port. As unfortunate as this last attack had proved to Demetrius, he determined to undertake another; and, in order to succeed in his attempt, he ordered a machine of a new <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to be constructed, which was thrice the height and breadth of those he had lately lost. When the work was finished, he caused the engine to be placed near the port, which he was resolved, at all adventures, to force. But as it was upon the point of entering the harbour, a dreadful storm arising, drove it against the shore, with the vessels on which it had been reared. The besieged, who were attentive to improve all favourable conjunctures, while the tempest was still raging, made a sally against those who defended the eminence mentioned above; and, though repulsed several times, carried it at last, obliging the Demetrians, to the number of 400, to throw down their arms and submit. After this victory gained by the Rhodians, there arrived to their aid 150 Gnostians, and 500 men sent by Ptolemy from Egypt, most of them being natives of Rhodes, who had served among the king's troops. Demetrius being extremely mortified to see all his batteries against the harbour rendered ineffectual, resolved to employ them by land, in hopes of carrying the new machine called helopolis, which was by many degrees larger than any that had ever been invented before. Its basis was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, each side being in length near 50 cubits, and made up of square pieces of timber, bound together with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. In the middle part he placed thick planks, about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> distance from each other; and on these the men were to stand who forced the engine forward. The whole was moved upon eight strong and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, whose fellos were strengthened with strong iron plates. In order to facilitate and vary the movements of the helopolis, casters were placed under it, whereby it was turned in an instant to what side the workmen and engines pleased. From each of the four <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> a large pillar of wood was carried to about the height of 100 cubits, and inclining to each other; the whole machine consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories, whose dimensions gradually lessened in the ascent. The first story was supported by 43 beams, and the last by no more than nine. Three sides of the machine were plated over with iron, to prevent its being damaged by the fire that might be thrown from the city. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of each story were windows of the same size and shape as the engines that were to be discharged from thence. To each window were shutters, to draw up for the defence of those who managed the machines, and to deaden the force of the stones thrown by the enemy, the shutters being covered with skins stuffed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Every story was furnished with two large staircases, that whatever was necessary might be brought up by one, while others were going down by the other, and so every thing may be dispatched without tumult or confusion. This huge machine was moved forwards by 3000 of the strongest men of the whole army; but the art with which it was built greatly facilitated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Demetrius caused likewise to be made several testudoes or pent-houses, to cover his men while they advanced to fill up the trenches and ditches; and invented a new sort of galleries, through which those who were employed at the siege might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass at their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, without the least danger. He employed all his seamen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> the ground over which the machines... machines were to be brought up, to the space of four furlongs. The number of workmen who were employed on this occasion amounted to 30,000. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the Rhodians, observing these formidable preparations, were busy in raising a new wall within that which the enemy intended to batter with the helepolis. In order to accomplish this work, they pulled down the wall which surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, some neighbouring houses, and even some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, after having solemnly promised to build more magnificent structures in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods, if the city were preserved. At the same time, they sent out nine of their best ships to seize such of the enemy's vessels as they could meet with, and thereby distress them for want of provisions. As these ships were commanded by the bravest sea-officers, they soon returned with an immense booty, and a great many prisoners. Among other vessels, they took a galley richly laden, on board of which they found a great variety of valuable furniture, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robe, which Phila herself had wrought and sent as a present to her husband Demetrius, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written with her own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The Rhodians sent the furniture, the royal robe, and even the letter, to Ptolemy; which exasperated Demetrius to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. While Demetrius was preparing to attack the city, the Rhodians having assembled the people and magistrates to consult about the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> they should take, some proposed in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> the pulling down of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of Antigonus and his son Demetrius, which till then had been held in the utmost veneration. But this proposal was generally rejected with indignation, and their prudent conduct greatly allayed the wrath both of Antigonus and Demetrius. However, the latter continued to carry on the siege with the utmost vigour, thinking it would reflect no small dishonour on him were he obliged to quit the place without raking himself master of it. He caused the walls to be secretly undermined; but, when they were ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, a deserter very opportunely gave notice of the whole to the townsmen; who having, with all expedition, drawn a deep trench all along the wall, began to countermine, and, meeting the enemy under ground, obliged them to abandon the work. While both parties guarded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, one Athenagoras a Milesian, who had been sent to the assistance of the Rhodians by Ptolemy with a body of mercenaries, promised to betray the city to the Demetrians, and let them in through the mines in the night-time. But this was only in order to ensnare them; for Alexander, a noble Macedonian, whom Demetrius had sent with a choice body of troops to take possession of a post agreed on, no sooner appeared, but he was taken prisoner by the Rhodians, who were waiting for him under arms.—Athenagoras was crowned by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and presented with five talents of silver. Demetrius now gave over all thoughts of undermining the walls, and placed all his hopes of reducing the city in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> engines which he had contrived. Having therefore levelled the ground under the walls he brought up his helepolis, with four testudoes on each side of it. Two other testudoes of an extraordinary size, bearing battering-rams, were likewise moved forward by a thousand men. Each story of the helepolis was filled with all sorts of engines for discharging of stones, arrows, and darts. When all things were ready, Demetrius ordered the signal to be given; when his men, setting up a shout, assaulted the city on all sides both by sea and land. But, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the attack, when the walls were ready to fall by the repeated strokes of the battering rams, ambassadors arrived from Cnidus, earnestly soliciting Demetrius to suspend all further hostilities, and at the same time giving him hopes that they should prevail upon the Rhodians to submit to an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. A suspension of arms was accordingly agreed on, and ambassadors sent from both sides. But the Rhodians refusing to capitulate on the conditions offered them, the attack was renewed with so much fury, and the machines played off in so brisk a manner, that a large tower built with square stones, and the wall that flanked it were battered down. The besieged, nevertheless, fought in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> with so much courage and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, that the enemy, after various unsuccessful attempts, were forced to abandon the enterprise, and retire. In this conjuncture, a fleet which Ptolemy had freighted with 300,000 measures of corn, and different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> for the use of the Rhodians, arrived very seasonably in the port, notwithstanding the vigilance of the enemy's ships, which cruised on the and set the coasts of the island to surprise them. A few days after came in safe two other fleets, one sent by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDER">Cassander</a>, with 100,000 bushels of barley; the other by Lysimachus, with 400,000 bushels of corn and as many of barley. This seasonable and plentiful supply arriving when the city began to suffer for want of provisions, inspired the besieged with new courage, and raised their drooping spirits. Being thus animated, they formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of setting the enemy's engines on fire; and with this view ordered a body of men to sally out the night ensuing, about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> watch, with torches and firebrands, having first placed on the walls an incredible number of engines, to discharge stones, arrows, darts, and fireballs, against those who should attempt to oppose their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a>. The Rhodian troops, pursuant to their orders, all on a sudden sallied out, and advancing, in spite of all opposition, to the batteries, set them on fire, while the engines from the walls played incessantly on those who endeavoured to extinguish the flames. The Demetrians on this occasion fell in great numbers, being incapable, in the darkness of the night, either to see the engines that continually discharged showers of stones and arrows upon them, or to join in one body and repulse the enemy. The conflagration was so great, that several plates of iron falling from the helepolis, that vast engine would have been entirely consumed, had not the troops that were stationed in it with all possible speed quenched the fire with water, before prepared, and ready in the apartments of the engine against such accidents. Demetrius, fearing lest all his machines should be consumed, called together, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, those whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to move them; and, by their help, brought them off before they were entirely destroyed. When it was day, he commanded all the darts and arrows that had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> by the Rhodians to be carefully gathered, that he might from their numbers form some judgment of the number of machines in the city. Above 800 firebrands were found on the spot, and no fewer than... than 1500 darts, all discharged in a very small portion of the night. This struck the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> himself with no small terror; for he never imagined that they would have been able to bear the charges of such formidable preparations. However, after having caused the slain to be buried, and given directions for the curing of the wounded, he applied himself to the repairing of his machines, which had been dismounted and rendered quite unserviceable. In the mean time, the besieged, improving the respite allowed them by the removal of the machines, built a third wall in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, which took in all that part that was most exposed to the enemy's batteries; and, besides, drew a deep trench behind the breach, to prevent the enemy from entering the city that way. At the same time, they detached a squadron of their best ships, under the command of Amyntas, who made over to the continent of Asia; and there meeting with some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> who were commissioned by Demetrius, took both the ships and the men, among whom were Timoecles the chief of the pirates, and several other officers of distinction belonging to the fleet of Demetrius. On their return, they fell in with several vessels laden with corn for the enemy's camp, which they likewise took, and brought into the port. These were soon followed by a numerous fleet of small vessels loaded with corn and provisions sent them by Ptolemy, together with 1500 men, commanded by Antigonus a Macedonian of great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in military affairs.—Demetrius, in the mean time, having repaired his machines, brought them up anew to the walls; which he incessantly battered till he opened a great breach and threw down several towers. But when he came to the assault, the Rhodians, under the command of Aminias, defended themselves with such resolution and intrepidity, that he was in three successive attacks repulsed with great slaughter, and at last forced to retire. The Rhodians likewise, on this occasion, lost several officers; and amongst others, the brave Aminias their commander. While the Rhodians were thus signalizing themselves in the defence of their country, a second embassy arrived at the camp of Demetrius from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and the other cities of Greece, soliciting Demetrius to compose matters, and strike up a peace with the Rhodians. At the request of the ambassadors, who were in all above 50, a cessation of arms was agreed upon; but the terms offered by Demetrius being again rejected by the Rhodians, the ambassadors returned home without being able to bring the contending parties to an agreement. Hostilities were therefore renewed; and Demetrius, whose imagination was fertile in expedients for succeeding in his projects, formed a detachment of 1500 of his best troops, under the conduct of Alcinus and Mancius, two officers of great resolution and experience, ordering them to enter the breach at midnight, and, forcing the entrenchment behind it, to possess themselves of the posts about the theatre, where it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to maintain themselves against any efforts of the townsmen. In order to facilitate the execution of so important and dangerous an undertaking, and amuse the enemy with false attacks, he at the same time, upon a signal given, ordered the rest of the army to set up a shout, and attack the city on all sides both by sea and land. By this means he hoped that, the besieged being alarmed in all parts, his detachment might find an opportunity of forcing the entrenchments which covered the breach, and afterwards of seizing the advantageous post about the theatre. This feint had all the success the prince could expect; for the troops having set up a shout from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, as if they were advancing to a general assault, the detachment commanded by Alcinus and Mancius entered the breach, and fell upon those who defended the ditch, and the wall that covered it, with such vigour, that, having slain the most part of them and put the rest in confusion, they advanced to the theatre, and seized on the post adjoining to it. This occasioned a general uproar in the city, as if it had been already taken; but the commanding officers dispatched orders to the soldiers on the ramparts not to quit their posts, nor stir from their respective stations. Having thus secured the walls, they put themselves at the head of a chosen body of their own troops, and of those who were lately come from Egypt, and with these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> the enemy's detachment. But the darkness of the night prevented them from dislodging the enemy and regaining the advantageous posts they had seized. Day, however, no sooner appeared, than they renewed their attack with wonderful bravery. The Demetrians without the walls, with loud shouts endeavoured to animate those who had entered the place, and inspire them with resolution to maintain their ground till they were relieved with fresh troops. The Rhodians being sensible that their fortunes, liberties, and all that was dear to them in the world, lay at stake, fought like men in the utmost despair, the enemy defending their posts for several hours without giving ground in the least. At length the Rhodians, encouraging each other to exert themselves in defence of their country, and animated by the example of their leaders, made a last effort, and, breaking into the very heart of the enemy's battalion, there killed both their commanders. After their death the rest were easily put in disorder, and all to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> either killed or taken prisoners. The Rhodians likewise on this occasion lost many of their best commanders; and among the rest Damotetis, their chief <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, a man of extraordinary valour, who had signalized himself during the whole time of the siege. Demetrius, not at all discouraged by this check, was making the necessary preparations for a new assault, when he received letters from his father Antigonus, enjoining him to conclude a peace with the Rhodians upon the best terms he could get, lest he should lose his whole army in the siege of a single town. From this time Demetrius wanted only some plausible pretence for breaking up the siege. The Rhodians likewise were now more inclined to come to an agreement than formerly; Ptolemy having acquainted them that he intended to send a great quantity of corn, and 3000 men to their assistance, but that he would first have them try whether they could make up matters with Demetrius upon reasonable terms. At the same time ambassadors arrived from the Ætolian republic, soliciting the contending parties to put an end to a war which might involve all the east in endless calamities. An accident which happened to Demetrius in this conjuncture, did not a little contribute towards the wished-for pacification. This prince was preparing to advance his helopolis against the city, when a Rhodian less... engineer found means to render it quite useless. He undermined the tract of ground over which the helepolis was to pass the next day in order to approach the walls. Demetrius not suspecting any stratagem of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, caused the engine to be moved forward, which coming to the place that was undermined, sunk so deep into the ground that it was impossible to draw it out again. This misfortune, if we believe Vegetius and Vitruvius, determined Demetrius to hearken to the Ætolian ambassadors, and at last to strike up a peace upon the following conditions: That the republic of Rhodes should be maintained in the full enjoyment of their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and liberties, without any foreign garrison; that they should renew their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Antigonus, and assist him in his wars against all states and princes except Ptolemy king of Egypt; and that, for the effectual performance of the articles stipulated between them, they should deliver 100 hostages, such as Demetrius should make choice of, except those who bore any public employment. Thus was the siege raised, after it had continued a whole year; and the Rhodians amply rewarded all those who had distinguished themselves in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of their country. They also set up statues to Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus; to all of whom they paid the highest honours, especially to the first, whom they worshipped as a god. Demetrius at his departure presented them with the helepolis, and all the other machines which he had employed in battering the city; from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of which, with some additional sums of their own, they erected the famous colossus. After this they applied themselves entirely to trade and navigation; by which means they became quite masters of the sea, and much more opulent than any of the neighbouring nations. As far as lay in their power, they endeavoured to preserve a neutrality with regard to the jarring nations of the east. However, they could not avoid a war with the Byzantines, the occasion of which was as follows: The Byzantines being obliged to pay a yearly tribute of 80 talents to the Gauls, in order to raise this sum, they came to a resolution of laying a toll on all ships that traded to the Pontic Sea. This resolution provoked the Rhodians, who were a trading <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, above all the rest. For this reason they immediately dispatched ambassadors to the Byzantines, complaining of the new tax; but as the Byzantines had no other method of satisfying the Gauls, they persisted in their resolution. The Rhodians now declared war, and prevailed upon Prusias king of Bithynia, and Attalus king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, to assist them; by which confederacy the Byzantines were so intimidated, that they agreed to exact no toll from ships trading to the Pontic sea, the demand which had been the occasion of the war. About this time happened a dreadful earthquake, which threw down the colossus, the arsenal, and great part of the city walls of Rhodes; which calamity the Rhodians improved to their advantage, sending ambassadors to all the Grecian princes and states, to whom their losses were so much exaggerated, that their countrymen obtained immense sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> under pretence of repairing them. Hiero king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> presented them with 100 talents; and, besides, exempted from all tolls and duties such as traded to Rhodes. Ptolemy king of Egypt gave them 100 talents, a million of measures of wheat, materials for building quinqueremes and the like number of triremes; and besides, sent them 100 architects, 300 workmen, and materials for repairing their public buildings, to a great value, paying them moreover 14 talents a-year for the maintenance of the workmen whom he sent them. Antigonus gave them 100 talents of silver, with 10,000 pieces of timber, each piece being 16 cubits long; 7000 planks; 3000 pounds of iron, as many of pitch and rosin, and 1000 measures of tar. Chryseis, a woman of distinction, sent them 100,000 measures of wheat, and 3000 pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. Antiochus exempted from all taxes and duties the Rhodian ships trading to his dominions; presented them with 10 galleys, and 200,000 measures of corn, with many other things of great value. Prusias, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, and all the princes then reigning in Asia, made them proportionable presents; in short, all the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and nations, all the princes of Europe and Asia, contributed, according to their ability, to the relief of the Rhodians on that occasion; insomuch that their city not only soon arose from its ruins, but attained to an higher pitch of splendour than ever. In the year 203 B.C. the Rhodians engaged in a war with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon. This monarch had invaded the territories of Attalus king of Pergamus; and Macedon, because the Rhodians seemed to favour their ancient friend, sent one Heraclides, by birth a Tarentine, to set fire to their fleet; at the same time that he dispatched ambassadors into Crete, in order to stir up the Cretans against the Rhodians, and prevent them from sending any assistance to Attalus. Upon this war was immediately proclaimed. Philip at first gained an considerable advantage in a naval engagement; but the next year was defeated with the loss of 11,000 men, while the Rhodians lost but 60 men and Attalus 70. After this he carefully avoided coming to an engagement at sea either with Attalus or the Rhodians. The combined fleet, in the mean time, sailed towards the island of Ægina in hopes of intercepting him; but having failed in their purpose, they sailed to Athens, where they concluded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with that people; and, on their return, drew all the Cyclades into a confederacy against Philip. But while the allies were thus wasting their time in negotiations, Philip, having divided his forces into two bodies, sent one, under the command of Philocles, to ravage the Athenian territories; and put the other aboard his fleet, with orders to sail to Meronea, a city on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of Thrace. He then marched towards that city himself with a body of forces, took it by assault, and reduced a great many others; so that the confederates would, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, have had little reason to boast of their success, had not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> come to their assistance, by whose help the war was soon terminated to their advantage. In the war which took place between the Romans and Antiochus the Great king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the Rhodians were very useful allies to the former. The best part of their fleet was indeed destroyed by a treacherous contrivance of Polyxenades the Syrian admiral; but they soon fitted out another, and defeated a Syrian squadron commanded by the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, the Carthaginian commander; after which, in conjunction with the Romans, they utterly defeated the whole Syrian fleet commanded by Polyxenades; which together... together with the loss of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, so dispirited Antiochus, that he submitted to whatever conditions the Romans pleased. For these services the Rhodians were rewarded with the provinces of Lycia and Caria; but tyrannizing over the people in a terrible manner, the Lycians applied to the Romans for protection. This was readily granted; but the Rhodians were so much displeased with their interfering in this matter, that they secretly favoured Perses in the war which broke out between him and the Roman republic. For this offence the two provinces above mentioned were taken from them; but the Rhodians, having banished or put to death those who had favoured Perses, were again admitted into favour, and greatly honoured by the senate. In the Mithridatic war, their alliance with Rome brought upon them the king of Pontus with all his force; but having lost the greatest part of his fleet before the city, he was obliged to raise the siege without performing any remarkable exploit. In the war which Pompey made on the Cilician pirates, the Rhodians assisted him with all their naval force, and had a great share in the victories which he gained. In the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, they assisted the latter with a very numerous fleet. After his death they joined Caesar; which drew upon them the resentment of C. Cassius, who advanced to the island of Rhodes with a powerful fleet, after having reduced the greatest part of the continent. The Rhodians, terrified at his approach, sent ambassadors intreating him to make up matters in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner, and promising to stand <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a>, and recall the ships which they had sent to the assistance of the triumviri. Cassius insisted upon their delivering up their fleet to him, and putting him in possession both of their harbour and city. This demand the Rhodians would by no means comply with, and therefore began to put themselves in a condition to stand a siege; but first sent Archelaus, who had taught Cassius the Greek tongue while he studied at Rhodes, to intercede with his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> in their behalf. Archelaus could not, with all his authority, prevail upon him to moderate his demands; wherefore the Rhodians, having created one Alexander, a bold and enterprising man, their prorator or prytanis, equipped a fleet of 33 sail, and sent it out under the command of Mnaseus, an experienced sea-officer, to offer Cassius battle. Both fleets fought with incredible bravery, and the victory was long doubtful; but the Rhodians, being at length overpowered by numbers, were forced to return with their fleet to Rhodes; two of their ships being sunk, and the rest very much damaged by the heavy ships of the Romans. This was the first time, as our author observes, that the Rhodians were fairly overcome in a sea-fight. Cassius, who had beheld this fight from a neighbouring hill, having refitted his fleet, which had been no less damaged than that of the Rhodians, repaired to Loryma, a stronghold on the continent belonging to the Rhodians. This castle he took by assault; and from hence conveyed his land-forces, under the conduct of Fannius and Lentulus, over into the island. His fleet consisted of 80 ships of war and above 200 transports. The Rhodians no sooner <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> this mighty fleet appear, but they went out again to meet the enemy. The second engagement was far more bloody than the first; many ships were sunk, and great numbers of men killed on both sides. But victory anew declared for the Romans; who immediately blocked up the city of Rhodes both by sea and land. As the Rhodians had not had time to furnish the city with sufficient store of provisions, some of the inhabitants, fearing that if it were taken either by assault or by famine, Cassius would put all the inhabitants to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, as Brutus had lately done at Xanthus, privately opened the gate to him, and put him in possession of the town, which he nevertheless treated as if it had been taken by assault. He commanded 50 of the chief citizens, who were suspected to favour the adverse party, to be brought before him, and sentenced them all to die; others, to the number of 25, who had commanded the fleet or army, because they did not appear when summoned, he proscribed. Having thus punished such as had either acted or spoken against him or his party, he commanded the Rhodians to deliver up to him all their ships, and whatever money they had in the public treasury. He then plundered the temples; stripping them of all their valuable furniture, vessels, and statues. He is said not to have left one statue in the whole city, except that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; bragging, at his departure, that he had stripped the Rhodians of all they had, leaving them nothing but the sun. As to private persons, he commanded them, under severe penalties, to bring to him all the gold and silver they had, promising, by a public crier, a tenth part to such as should discover any hidden treasures. The Rhodians at first concealed some part of their wealth, imagining that Cassius intended by this proclamation only to terrify them; but when they found he was in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>, and saw several wealthy citizens put to death for concealing only a small portion of their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, they desired that the time prefixed for the bringing in their gold and silver might be prolonged. Cassius willingly granted them their request; and then through fear they dug up what they had hid under ground, and laid at his feet all they were worth in the world. By this means he extorted from private persons above 8000 talents. He then fined the city in 500 more; and leaving L. Varus there with a strong garrison to exact the fine without any abatement, he returned to the continent. After the death of Cassius, Marc Antony restored the Rhodians to their ancient rights and privileges; bestowing upon them the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>, Tenos, and the city of Myndus. But these the Rhodians so oppressed and loaded with taxes, that the same Antony, though a great friend to the Rhodian republic, was obliged to divest her of the sovereignty over those places, which he had a little before so liberally bestowed upon her. From this time to the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius we find no mention made of the Rhodians. That prince, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> informs us, deprived them of their liberty for having crucified some Roman citizens. However, he soon restored them to their former condition, as we read in Suetonius and Tacitus. The latter adds, that they had been as often deprived of, as restored to, their liberty, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> or reward for their different behaviour, as they had obliged the Romans with their assistance in foreign wars, or provoked them with their seditions at home. Pliny, who wrote in the beginning of Vespasian's reign, style Rhodes a beautiful and free town. But this liberty they did not long enjoy, the island became soon after reduced by by the same Vespasian to a Roman province, and obliged to pay a yearly tribute to their new masters. This province was called the province of the islands. The Roman praetor who governed it resided at Rhodes, as the chief city under his jurisdiction; and Rome, notwithstanding the eminent services rendered her by this republic, thenceforth treated the Rhodians not as allies, but vassals.
