See Botany Index Richardson, Samuel, a celebrated English sentimental sentimental <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a>-writer, born in 1688, was bred to the business of a printer, which he exercised all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> with eminence. Though he is said to have understood no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> but his own, yet he acquired great reputation by his three epistolary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, entitled Pamela, Clarissa, and Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Grandison; which show an uncommon knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. His purpose being to promote virtue, his pictures of moral excellence are by much too highly coloured; and he has described his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> such rather as we might wish them to be, than as they are to be found in reality. It is also objected by some, that his writings have not always the good effect intended; for that, instead of improving natural characters, they have fashioned many <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> ones; and have taught delicate and refined ladies and gentlemen to despise every one but their own self-exalted persons. But after all that can be urged of the ill effects of Mr Richardson's novels on weak minds, eager to adopt characters they can only <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>; a sensible reader will improve more by studying such models of perfection, than of those nearer to the natural standard of human frailty, and where those frailties are artfully exaggerated so as to fix and misemploy the attention on them. A stroke of the palsy carried off Mr Richardson, after a few days illness, upon the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1761. He was a man of fine parts, and a lover of virtue; which, for ought we have ever heard to the contrary, he showed in his life and conversation as well as in his writings. Besides the works above-mentioned, he is the author of an Aesop's Fables, a Tour through <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, 4 vols. and a volume of Familiar Letters upon business and other subjects. He is said from his childhood to have delighted in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; and therefore was the more easily led to throw his romances into that form; which, if it enlivens the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in some respects, yet lengthens it with uninteresting prate, and formalities that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> nothing, and on that account is sometimes found a little tedious and fatiguing. The most eminent writers of our own country, and even of foreign parts, have paid their tribute to the transcendent talents of Mr Richardson, whose works have been published in almost every language and country of Europe. They have been greatly admired, notwithstanding every dissimilitude of manners, or every disadvantage of translation. The celebrated M. Diderot, speaking of the means employed to move the passions, in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, mentions Richardson as a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of that art: "How striking (says he), how pathetic are his descriptions! His personages, though silent, are alive before me; and of those who speak, the actions are still more affecting than the words."—The famous John-James Rousseau, speaking, in his letter to M. d'Alembert, of the novels of Richardson, asserts, "that nothing was ever written equal to, or even approaching them, in any language." —Mr <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill calls his Pamela a "delightful nursery of virtue."—Dr Warton speaks thus of Clementina; "Of all representations of madness, that of Clementina, in the History of Sir Charles Grandison, is the most deeply interesting. I know not whether even the madness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAR">Lear</a> is wrought up, and expressed, by so many little strokes of nature and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> pedantry to prefer and compare the madness of Orestes in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a> to this of Clementina."—Dr John- son, in his Introduction to the 97th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the Rambler, which was written by Mr Richardson, observes, that the reader was indebted for that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s entertainment to an author, "from whom the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> has received greater favours, who has enlarged the knowledge of human nature, and taught the passions to move at the command of virtue;" and, in his life of Rowe, he says, "The character of Lothario seems to have been expanded by Richardson into that of Lovelace; but he has excelled his original in the moral effect of the fiction. Lotario, with gaiety which cannot be hated, and bravery which cannot be despised, retains too much of the spectator's kindness. It was in the power of Richardson alone to teach us at once esteem and detestation; to make virtuous resentment overpower all the benevolence which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and elegance, and courage, naturally excite; and to lose at last the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in the villain."—Dr Young very pertinently observed, that Mr Richardson, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> advantages of nature, improved by a very moderate progress in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, struck out at once, and of his own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, into a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of writing, in which he succeeded to admiration. And what is more remarkable, that he not only began, but finished the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> on which he set out, leaving no room for any one after him to render it more complete; and that not one of the various writers that have ever since attempted to imitate him, have in any respect equalled, or at all approached near him. This kind of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> is peculiarly his own; and "I consider him (continues the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>) as a truly great natural genius; as great and supereminent in his way as Shakespeare and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were in theirs." Richardson, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, a celebrated painter of heads, was born about the year 1665, and against his inclination was placed by his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> apprentice to a scrivener, with whom he lived six years; when obtaining his freedom by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his master, he followed the bent of his disposition, and at 20 years old became the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Riley; with whom he lived four years, whose niece he married, and of whose manner he acquired enough to maintain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and lasting reputation, even during the lives of Kneller and Dahl; and to remain at the head of the profession when they went off the stage. There is strength, roundness, and boldness in his colouring; but his men want <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and his women <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. The good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is characterised in his portraits. You see he lived in an age when neither enthusiasm nor servility were predominant. Yet with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> so firm, possessed of a numerous and excellent collection of drawings, full of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, and profound in reflections on his art, he drew nothing well below the head, and was void of imagination. His attitudes, draperies, and back-grounds, are totally insipid and unmeaning; so ill did he apply to his own practice the sagacious rules and hints he bestowed on others. Though he wrote with fire and judgment, his paintings owed little to either. No man dived deeper into the inexhaustible stores of Raphael, or was more smitten with the native lustre of Vandyck. Yet though capable of tasting the elevation of the one and the elegance of the other, he could never contrive to see with their eyes, when he was to copy nature himself. One wonders that he could comment their works so well, and imitate them so little. He quitted business himself some years before his death; but his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and virtue contributed to protract his life to a great length in the full enjoyment of his understanding, and in the felicity of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> friendship. He had had a paralytic stroke that affected his arm, yet never disabled him from his customary walks and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. He had been in St James's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, and died suddenly at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> on his return home, May 28, 1745, when he had passed the 80th year of his age. He left a son and four daughters, one of whom was married to his disciple Mr Hudson, and another to Mr Grigson an attorney. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and learning of the son, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> in which he lived with his father, are visible in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> works they composed. The father in 1719 published two discourses: 1. An Essay on the whole Art of Criticism as it relates to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>; 2. An Argument in behalf of the Science of a Connoisseur; bound in one volume octavo. In 1722 came forth An Account of some of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, bas-reliefs, drawings, and pictures, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, &c. with Remarks by Mr Richardson, senior and junior. The son made the journey; and from his notes, letters, and observations, they both at his return compiled this valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. As the father was a formal man, with a slow, but loud and sonorous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, with some affectation in his manner; and as there is much singularity in his style and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, these peculiarities (for they were scarcely foibles) struck superficial readers, and between the laughters and the envious the book was much ridiculed. Yet both this and the former are full of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, good sense, and instruction: and the very quaintness of some expressions, and their laboured <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, show the difficulty the author had to convey mere visible ideas through the medium of language. Those works remind one of Cibber's imitable treatise on the stage: when an author writes on his own profession, feels it profoundly, and is sensible his readers do not, he is not only excusable, but meritorious, for illuminating the subject by new metaphors or bolder figures than ordinary. He is the coxcomb that sneers, not he that instructs, in appropriated diction. If these authors were censured when conversant within their own circle, it was not to be expected that they would be treated with milder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> when they ventured into a sister region. In 1734, they published a very thick octavo, containing explanatory notes and remarks on Milton's Paradise Lost, with the life of the author, and a discourse on the poem. Again were the good sense, the judicious criticisms, and the sentiments that broke forth in this work, forgotten in the singularities that distinguish it. The father having said in apology for being little conversant in classic literature, that he had looked into them through his son, Hogarth, whom a quibble could furnish with wit, drew the father peeping through the nether end of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>, with which his son was perforated, at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> aloft on a shelf. Yet how forcibly Richardson entered into the spirit of his author, appears from his comprehensive expression that Milton was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, born two thousand years after his time. Richardson, however, was as incapable of reaching the sublime or harmonious in poetry, as he was in painting, though so capable of illustrating both. Some specimens of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> that he has given us here and there in his works, excite no curiosity for more, though he informs us in his Milton, that Richardson, if <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> was his wife, poetry had been his secret concubine. It is remarkable, that another commentator of Milton has made the same confession. —Sunt et mihi carmina, me quoque dicunt Valentini pastores— says Dr Bently. Neither the doctor nor the painter adds sed non ego credulus illis, though all their readers are ready to supply it for both. Besides his pictures and commentaries, we have a few etchings by his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, particularly two or three of Milton, and his own head. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of his collections of drawings, in February 1747, lasted 18 days, and produced about L2060, his pictures about L700. Hudson his son-in-law bought many of his drawings.

RICHELET

Pages 30-30

CAESAR <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">PETER</a>, a French writer, born in 1631 at Chemin in Champagne. He was the friend of Patru and Ablancourt; and like them applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> with success. He compiled a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of that language, full of new and useful remarks; but exceptionable, as containing many satirical reflections and obscenities. The best edition is that of Lyons, 3 vols. folio, 1728. He also collected a small dictionary of rhymes, and composed some other pieces in the grammatical and critical way. He died in 1698.

RICHES

Pages 30-31

a word used always in the plural <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, means wealth, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, possession, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a splendid sumptuous appearance. When used to express the fortune of private persons, whether patrimonial or acquired, it signifies opulence; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which expresses not the enjoyment, but the possession, of numerous superfluities.—The riches of a state or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> expresses the produce of industry, of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, of different incorporated bodies, of the internal and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> administration of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> members of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is composed, &c. Our Saviour says, that it is more easy for a camel to go through the eye of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, than for a rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to enter the kingdom of heaven; and we find, in fact, that riches frequently bring along with them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of inattention, lukewarmness, and irreligion, such as sufficiently confirms the divine assertion; which is merely a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and which by no means asserts the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> impossibility of being virtuous and rich at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. For as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers wisely taught, riches, considered in themselves, and abstractedly from the bad purposes to which they may be applied, are not necessarily incompatible with virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. They are indeed absolutely indifferent; in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be useful, and promote the cause of truth, virtue, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>; and in bad hands they are the source of much mischief; on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> they confer the power of doing much good, and on the other they are equally powerful in doing ill. To men, however, whose principles of virtue are not sufficiently founded, riches are unquestionably a dangerous and seducing bait; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> rightly taught, they are to the greatest number of men, in an infinite variety of circumstances, a powerful obstacle to the practice of moral virtues, to the progress of truth, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> which prevents them from rising to that degree of knowledge and perfection of which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is capable. They multiply without ceasing the occasions of vice, by the facility which they give to satisfy tisfy a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> passions, and to turn at length those who are attached to them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of virtue, and from the desire of inquiring after truth. It is this which Seneca means to express, when he says, "that riches in a vast number of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> have been a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> obstacle to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and that, to enjoy freedom of mind necessary for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, a man must live in poverty, or as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Every man (adds he) who wishes to live a pleasant, tranquil, and secure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, must avoid, as much as possible, the deceitfulness of riches, which are a bait with which we allow ourselves to be taken as in a snare, without afterwards having the power to extricate ourselves, being so much the more unhappy, that we believe we possess them, while on the contrary, they tyrannize over us." Senec. Epist. 17. and Epist. 8. "The wise man (says the same author in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>) does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> riches to excess, but he would not choose wholly to divest himself of them; he does not receive them into his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, but into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; he is careful of them, and employs them for the purpose of opening a wide field for virtue, and of making it appear in all its splendour. Who can doubt that a wise man has not more occasions of displaying the elevation and greatness of his mind when he is possessed of riches than when he labours under indigence, since, in the last condition, he can <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> only one virtue, namely, resignation; whereas, riches give him an opportunity of displaying, in their greatest lustre, the virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, liberality, diligence, regularity, and magnificence. There is no occasion, then, to prohibit philosophers from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wealth, or to condemn wisdom to poverty. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> may possess the greatest riches, provided he has not employed force or shed blood in acquiring them; provided he has not gained them by unjust or illegal means; in a word, provided the use which he makes of them be as pure as the source from which they were derived, and no person (the envious excepted) regretting his possession; he will not refuse the kindness of fortune, and will enjoy, without shame or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, the wealth acquired by honest means; he will have more reason to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, if, after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his riches to the view of the whole world, he can desire any person to carry away the reward of treachery or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of oppression. If, after these words, his riches continue undiminished, this man is truly great, and worthy to be rich." Senec. de Vila Beata, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21, 22, & 23.

RICHIEU

Pages 31-31

JOHN ARMAND DU PLESSIS DE, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of Richlieu and Fronsac, bishop of Lucon, &c., was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1585. He was of excellent parts; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 22 had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to obtain a dispensation to enjoy the bishopric of Lucon in 1607. Returning into France, he applied himself in a particular manner to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of preaching; and his reputation this way procured him the office of almoner to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis. His abilities in the management of affairs advanced him to be secretary of state in 1616; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> soon gave him the preference to all his other secretaries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the marquis d'Ancre having produced a revolution in state affairs, Richlieu retired to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>; where he employed himself in composing books of controversy and piety. The king having recalled him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he was made a cardinal in 1622; and, two years after, first minister of state, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. In 1626, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rhée was preserved by his care, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> taken, having stopped up the haven by that famous dyke which he ordered to be made there. He accompanied the king to the siege of Cazal, and contributed not a little to the raising of it in 1629. He also obliged the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> to the peace at Alets, which proved the ruin of that party; he took Pameral, and succoured Cazal besieged by Spinola. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> found fault with his conduct, and persuaded the king to discard him. The cardinal, for his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, was unmoved with it; and by his reasonings overthrew what was thought to be determined against him; so that, instead of being disgraced, he from that moment became more powerful than ever. He punished all his enemies in the same manner as they would have had him suffer; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> which produced this event, so glorious to Cardinal Richlieu, was called the day of dupes. This able minister had from thence forwards an ascendancy over the king's mind; and he now resolved to humble the excessive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. For that purpose he concluded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with Gustavus Adolphus king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, for carrying the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> into the heart of Germany. He also entered into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>; secured Lorrain; raised a part of the princes of the empire against the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; treated with the Dutch to continue the war against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; favoured the Catalans and Portuguese till they shook off the Spanish yoke; and, in short, took so many different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, that he accomplished his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and after having carried on the war with success, was thinking of concluding it by a peace, when he died at Paris on the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1642, aged 58. He was interred in the Sorbonne, where a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> is erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> politician made the arts and sciences flourish; formed the botanical garden at Paris, called the king's garden; founded the French academy; established the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-house; erected the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> afterwards called Le Palais Royal, which he presented to the king; and rebuilt the Sorbonne with a magnificence that appears trulry royal. Besides his books of controversy and piety, there go under the name of this minister, A Journal, in 2 vols.; 12mo; and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in 12mo; all treating of politics and state affairs. Cardinal Mazarine pursued Richlieu's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and completed many of the schemes which he had begun, but left unfinished.

RICHMOND

Pages 31-31

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; it is delightfully situated on the north side of James's river at the falls. Vessels of 125 tons come up within a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the town, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> round the falls by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, and to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance farther up the river. In 1817 this town contained 13,000 inhabitants, nearly half of whom were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. The capital, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> where the legislature meets, is one of the handsomest structures in America. Many of the private houses also are elegant, but rents are very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> dear. The trade of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is considerable in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> and flour; of the former the annual exports were estimated in 1817 at 25,000 hogsheads; and of the latter at 200,000 barrels. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 77° 40'. N. Lat. 37° 28'.

RICINUS

Pages 31-31
or Palma Christi, a genus of plants belonging to the monoeia class, and in the natural method ranking under the 35th order, Tricoccce. See Botany and Materia Medica Index.

RICOCHET

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, is when guns, howitzers, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mortars, are loaded with small charges, and elevated from 5 to 12 degrees, so as to fire over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> or shell rolls along the opposite rampart: it is called ricochet-firing, and the batteries are likewise called ricochet-batteries. This method of firing was first invented by M. Belidor, and first used at the siege of Ath in 1697. This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of firing out of mortars was first tried in 1723 at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> school at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, and with success. At the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Rossbach, in 1757, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> had several 6-inch mortars made with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNNIONS">trunnions</a>, and mounted on travelling-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, which fired obliquely on the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and amongst their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, loaded with 8 ounces of powder, and at an elevation of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> 15 minutes, which did <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> execution; for the shells rolling along the lines, with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> fuses, made the stoutest of the enemy not wait for their bursting.

RICOTIA

Pages 32-32

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tradynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order, Siliqueae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

RIDEAU

Pages 32-32

in Fortification, a small elevation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, extending itself lengthwise on a plain; serving to cover a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> give an advantage in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. RIDEAU is sometimes also used for a trench, the earth of which is thrown up on its side, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> for covering the men.

RIDGE

Pages 32-32

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of rising <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> between two furrows. See Agriculture.

RIDGLING

Pages 32-32
or RIDGEL, among farriers, &c. the male of any beast that has been but half gelt.

RIDICULE

Pages 32-33

in matters of literature, is that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> which excites contempt with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>. The ridiculous, however, differs from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RISIBLE">risible</a>, (see Risible). A risible object produceth an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of laughter merely: a ridiculous object is improper as well as risible; and produceth a mixed emotion, which is vented by a laugh of derision <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scorn. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">Burlesque</a>, though a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> engine of ridicule, is not confined to that subject; for it is clearly distinguishable into burlesque that excites laughter merely, and burlesque that provokes derision or ridicule. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> subject in which there is no impropriety, may be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by a certain colouring so as to be risible; which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> Travesie, and also the case of the Secchia Rapita; the authors laugh first, in order to make their readers laugh. The Lutrin is a burlesque poem of the other sort, laying hold of a low and trifling incident, to expose the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, indolence, and contentious spirit of a set of monks. Boileau, the author, gives a ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> to the subject, by dressing it in the heroic style, and affecting to consider it as of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and importance. In a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this kind, no image professedly ludicrous ought to find <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, because such images destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>; and accordingly the author shows always the grave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and never once betrays a smile. Though the burlesque that aims at ridicule produces its effects by elevating the style far above the subject, yet it has limits beyond which the elevation ought not to be carried: the poet, consulting the imagination of his readers, ought to confine himself to such images as are lively and readily apprehended: a strained elevation, soaring above an ordinary reach of fancy, makes not a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>: the reader, fatigued with being always upon the stretch, is soon disgusted; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he persevere, becomes thoughtless and indifferent.—Further, a fiction gives no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> unless it be painted in colours so lively as to produce some perception of reality; which never can be done effectually where the images are formed with labour or difficulty. For these reasons, we cannot avoid condemning the Batrachomyomachia, said to be the composition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>: it is beyond the power of imagination to form a clear and lively image of frogs and mice acting with the dignity of the highest of our species; nor can we form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the reality of such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in any manner so distinct as to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> our affections even in the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">Rape</a> of the Lock is of a character clearly distinguishable from those now mentioned; it is not properly a burlesque performance, but what may rather be termed an heroi-comical poem: it treats a gay and familiar subject with pleasantry, and with a moderate degree of dignity: the author puts not on a mask like Boileau, nor professes to make us laugh like Tassoni. The Rape of the Lock is a gentler species of writing, less strained than those mentioned; and is pleasant or ludicrous without having ridicule for its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> aim; giving way, however, to ridicule, where it naturally arises from a particular character, such as that of Sir Plume. Addison's Spectator*, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, is extremely gay and ludicrous, resembling in its subject the Rape of the Lock. There remains to show, by examples, the manner of treating subjects so as to give them a ridiculous appearance. Il ne dit jamais, je vous donne, mais, je vous prete le bon jour. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. I know him to be valiant. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">Constable</a>. I was told that by one that knows him better than you. Orleans. What's he? Constable. Marry, he told me so himself; and he said, he car'd not who knew it. Henry V. Shakespeare. He never broke any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head but his own, and that was against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> when he was drunk. Ibid. Millamont. Seatentious Mirabel! prithee <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">don</a>'t look with that violent and inflexible wise face, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> at the dividing of the child in an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>-hanging. Way of the World. A true critic, in the perusal of a book, is like a dog at a feast, whose thoughts and stomach are wholly set upon what the guests fling away, and consequently is apt to snarl most when there are the fewest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. Tale of a Tub. In the following instances, the ridicule arises from absurd conceptions in the persons introduced. Mascarille. Te souvient-il, vicomte, de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CETTE">cette</a> demi-lune, que nous emportames sur les ennemis au siege d'Afras? Jodelet. Que veux-tu dire avec <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a> demi-lune! c'etoit bien une lune toute entiere. Moliere, les Precieuses Ridicules, sc. 11. Slender. I came yonder at Eaton to marry Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Page; and she's a great lubberly boy. Page. Upon my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> then you took the wrong— Slander. What need you tell me that? I think so when I took a boy for a girl: if I had been married to him, for all he was in woman's apparel, I would not have had him. Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. Valentine. Your blessing, Sir. Sir Sampson. You've had it already, Sir; I think I sent it you to-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for four thousand pounds; a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Foresight. Foresight. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AY">Ay</a>, indeed, Sir Sampson, a great deal of money for a young man; I wonder what he can do with it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> for Love, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> ii. sc. 7. Millamant. I nauseate walking; 'tis a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> diver- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>; I lothe the country, and every thing that relates to it. Sir Wilfull. Indeed, hah! look ye, look ye, you do! nay, 'tis like you may—here are choice of pastimes here in town, as plays and the like; that must be con- fess'd, indeed. Millamant. Ah l'etourdie! I hate the town too. Sir Wilfull. Dear heart, that's much—hah! that you should hate 'em both! hah! 'tis like you may; there are some cannot relish the town, and others can't away with the country—'tis like you may be one of these, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">Cousin</a>. Way of the World, act iv. sc. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">Froth</a>. I assure you, Sir Paul, I laugh at no- body's jests but my own, or a lady's: I assure you, Sir Paul. Brisk. How? how, my Lord? what, affront my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>? Let me perish, do I never say any thing worthy to be laugh'd at? Lord Froth. O foy, don't misapprehend me, I don't say so, for I often smile at your conceptions. But there is nothing more unbecoming a man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> than to laugh; 'tis such a vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the passions! every body can laugh. Then especially to laugh at the jest of an inferior person, or when any body else of the same quality does not laugh with one; ridiculous! To be pleas'd with what pleases the crowd! Now, when I laugh I always laugh alone. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> Dealer, act i. sc. 4. So sharp-sighted is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> in blemishes, and so willing to be gratified, that it takes up with the very slightest improprieties: such as a blunder by a foreigner in speaking our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, especially if the blunder can bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> that reflects on the speaker: Quickly. The young man is an honest man. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a>. What shall de honest man do in my closet? dere is no honest man dat shall come in my closet. Merry Wives of Windsor. Love speeches are finely ridiculed in the following passage: Quoth he, My <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> as adamantine, As chains of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, I'll maintain; True as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> ever spoke, Or oracle from heart of oak; And if you'll give my <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> but vent, Now in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> hugger-mugger pent, And shine upon me but benignly, With that one and that other pigsney, The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and day shall sooner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> Than love, or you, shake off my heart; The sun, that shall no more dispense His own, but your bright influence: I'll carve your name on barks of trees, With true love notes and flourishes; That shall infuse eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, And everlasting flourishing: Drink every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> on't in stum, And make it brisk champaigne become. Where'er you <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>, your foot shall set The primrose and the violet; All spices, perfumes, and sweet powders Shall borrow from your breath their odours; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> shall renew And take all lives of things from you; The world depend upon your eye, And, when you frown upon it, die. Only our loves shall still survive, New worlds and natures to outlive; And, like to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> moons, remain All crescents, without change or wane. Hudibras, part 2. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> 1. Those who have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for ridicule, which is sel- dom united with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for delicate and refined beau- ties, are quick-sighted in improprieties; and these they eagerly grasp, in order to gratify their favourite propen- sity. Persons galled are provoked to maintain that ri- dicule is improper for grave subjects. Subjects really grave are by no means fit for ridicule; but then it is urged against them, that, when called in question whe- ther a certain subject be really grave, ridicule is the only means of determining the controversy. Hence a celebrated question, Whether ridicule be or be not a test of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. On one side, it is observed, that the objects of ridi- cule are falsehood, incongruity, impropriety, or turpi- tude of certain kinds: but as the object of every exci- ted <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> must be examined by reason, before we can determine whether it be proper or improper; so ridi- cule must apparently at least, establish the truth of the improprieties designed to excite the passion of contempt. Hence it comes into the aid of argument and reason, when its impressions on the imagination are consistent with the nature of things; but when it strikes the fancy and affections with fictitious images, it becomes the in- strument of deceit. But however ridicule may impress the idea of apparent turpitude or falsehood in the im- agination, yet still reason remains the supreme judge; and thus ridicule can never be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> test or touch- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of truth and falsehood. On the other side, it is contended that ridicule is not a subject of reasoning, but of sense or taste: (see and compare the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Risible and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRUITY">Congruity</a>.) Stating the question, then, in more accurate terms, Whether the sense of ridicule be the proper test for distinguishing ridiculous objects from what are not so? they proceed thus: No person doubts that our sense of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> is the true test of what is beautiful; and our sense of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>- eur, of what is great or sublime. It is more doubtful whether our sense of ridicule be the true test of what is ridiculous? It is not only the true test, but indeed the only test; for this subject comes not, more than beauty or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of reason. If any subject, by the influence of fashion or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, have acquired a degree of veneration to which naturally,

RIDING

Pages 33-35

in general, signifies the being carried along on any vehicle. Riding on horseback. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">Horsemanship</a>. Riding, in Medicine. During this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> all the viscera are shaken, and pressed against each other; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the pure <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> acts with a greater force on the lungs. Weakly persons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those whose stomachs are infirm, should, however, be cautious of riding before their meals are somewhat digested. Riding, in naval affairs, is the state of a ship's being retained in a particular station, by means of one or more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> with their anchors, which are for this purpose sunk into the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, &c., in order to prevent the vessel from being driven at the mercy of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or current.—A rope is said to ride, when one of the turns by which it is wound about the capstern or windlass lies over another, so as to interrupt the operation of heaving. Riding Athwart, the position of a ship which lies across the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the wind and tide, when the former is so strong as to prevent her from falling into the current of the latter. Riding between the Wind and Tide, the situation of a vessel at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, when the wind and tide <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon her in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition, in such a manner as to destroy the effort of each other upon her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a>: so that she is in a manner balanced between their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> forces, and rides without the least strain on her cables. When a ship does not labour heavily, or feel a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strain when anchored in an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, she is said to ride easy. On the contrary, when she pitches violently into the sea, so as to strain her cables, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, or hull, it is called riding hard, and the vessel is termed a bad roader. A ship is rarely said to ride when she is fastened at both the ends, as in a harbour or river; that situation being comprehended in the article Mooring. Riding, a district visited by an officer.—<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> is divided into three ridings, viz. the east, west, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> ridings. In all indictments in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, both the town and riding must be expressed. Riding, as connected with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, and susceptible of embellishment. See Gardening. A riding, though in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> differing so widely from a garden, yet agrees with it in many particulars: for, exclusive of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of character which results from their being both improvements, and both destined to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, a closer relation arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a riding, to extend the idea of a seat, and appropriate a whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the mansion; for which purpose it must be distinguished from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, and the marks of distinction must be borrowed from a garden. Those which a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> or a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> can supply are faint and few; but whenever circumstances belonging to a garden occur, they are immediately received as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the domain. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the trees <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> often be decisive: plantations of firs, whether placed on the sides of the way, or in clumps or woods in the view, denote the neighbourhood of a seat; even limes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> chestnuts are not indifferent; for they have always been frequent in improvements, and rare in the ordinary scenes of cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the riding be carried through a wood, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, which for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> or their fragrance have been transplanted from the country into gardens, such as the sweet-fern, the viburnum, the euonymus, and the woodbine, should be encouraged in the underwood; and to these may be added several which are still peculiar to shrubberies, but which might easily be transferred to the wildest coverts, and would require no further care. Where the species are not, the disposition may be particular, and any appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is a mark of improvement. A few trees standing out from a hedge-row, raise it to an elegance above common rusticity: and still more may be done by clumps in a field; they give it the air of a park. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> lane may be decorated with plantations in all the little vacant spaces: and even the groups originally on the spot (whether it be a wood, a field or a lane), if properly selected, and those only left which are elegant, will have an effect: though every beauty of this kind may be found in nature, yet many of them are seldom seen together, and never unmixed. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and the choice are symptoms of design. Another symptom is variety. If the appendages of the riding be different in different fields, if in a lane, or a wood, some distinguishing circumstance be provided for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>: or when, carried over an open exposure, it winds to several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view; if this be the conduct throughout, the intention is evident, to amuse the length of the way: variety of ground is also a characteristic of a riding, when it seems to have proceeded from choice; and pleasure being the pursuit, the changes of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> both compensate and account for the circuitry. But a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> undistinguished from a common road, succeeding to others more adorned, will by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> alone be sometimes agreeable; and there are beauties frequent in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-way, and almost peculiar to it, which may be very acceptable in a riding: a green lane is always delightful; a passage winding between thickets of brambles and briars, sometimes with, and sometimes without a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-wood rising amongst them, or a cut in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> through the furze of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> or the fern of a heath, is generally pleasant. Nor will the character be absolutely lost in the interruption, it will soon be resumed, and never forgotten; when it has been once strongly impressed, very slight means will preserve the idea. Simplicity may prevail the whole length of the way when the way is all naturally pleasant, but especially if it be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between several spots, which in character are raised above the rest of the country: A fine open <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> is unusual, except in a park or a garden; it has an elegance in the disposition which cannot be attributed to accident, and it seems to require a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of preservation beyond the care of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> husbandry. A neat railing on the edge of a steep which commands a prospect, alone distinguishes that from other points of view. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is still more strongly strongly characteristic: it may be only ornamental, or it may be accommodated to the reception of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; for though a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to alight at interrupts the range of a riding, yet, as the object of an airing, it may often be acceptable. A small spot which may be kept by the labour of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, inclosed from the fields, and converted into a shrubbery or any other scene of a garden, will sometimes be a pleasant end to a short excursion from home: nothing so effectually extends the idea of a seat to a distance; and not being constantly visited, it will always retain the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> and variety. When a riding is carried along a high road, a kind of property may in appearance be claimed even there, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> on both sides trees equidistant from each other, to give it the air of an approach; regularity intimates the neighbourhood of a mansion. A village therefore seems to be within the domain, if any of the inlets to it are avenues: other formal plantations about it, and still more trivial circumstances, when they are evidently ornamental, sometimes produce and always corroborate such an effect; but even without raising this idea, if the village be remarkable for its beauty, or only for its singularity, a passage through it may be an agreeable incident in a riding. The same ground which in the fields is no more than rough, often seems to be romantic when it is the site of a village; the buildings and other circumstances mark and aggravate the irregularity. To strengthen this appearance, one cottage may be placed on the edge of a steep, and some winding steps of unhewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> up to the door; another in a hollow, with all its little appurtenances hanging above it. The position of a few trees will sometimes answer the same purpose; a footbridge here and there for a communication between the sides of a narrow dip, will add to the character; and if there be any rills, they may be conducted so as greatly to improve it. A village which has not these advantages of ground, may however be beautiful; it is distinguished by its elegance, when the larger intervals between the houses are filled with open groves, and little clumps are introduced upon other occasions. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> often is, it generally may be, made a picturesque object. Even the cottages may be neat and sometimes grouped with thickets. If the place be watered by a stream, the crossings may be in a variety of pleasing designs; and if a spring rise, or only a well for common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> be sunk by the side of the way, a little covering over it may be contrived which shall at the same time be simple and pretty. There are few villages which may not easily be rendered agreeable. A small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> will sometimes occasion a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the appearance. By the help of a few trifling plantations, the objects which have a good effect may be shown to advantage, those which have not may be concealed, and such as are similar be disguised. And any form which offends the eye, whether of ground, of trees, or of buildings, may sometimes be broken by the slightest circumstances, by an advanced paling, or only by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. Variety and beauty, in such a subject, are rather the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than expense. But if the passage through the village cannot be pleasant; if the buildings are all alike, or stand in un- meaning rows and similar situations; if the place furnishes no opportunities to contrast the forms of dwellings with those of out-houses; to introduce trees and thickets; to interpose fields and meadows; to mix farms with cottages; and to place the several objects in different positions: yet on the outside even of such a village there is certainly room for wood; and by that in a riding alone the whole may be grouped into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, which shall be agreeable when skirted by a riding; and still more so when seen from a distance. The separate farms in the fields, also, by planting some trees about them, or perhaps only by managing those already on the spot, may be made very interesting objects; or if a new one is to be built, beauty may be consulted in the form of the house, and the disposition of its appurtenances. Sometimes a character not their own, as the semblance of a castle or an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, may be given to them; they will thereby acquire a degree of consideration, which they cannot otherwise be entitled to; and objects to improve the views are so important to a riding, that buildings must sometimes be erected for that purpose only; but they should be such as by an actual effect adorn or dignify the scene; not those little slight deceptions which are too well known to succeed, and have no merit if they fail: for though a fallacy sometimes contributes to support a character, or suggests <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to the imagination, yet in itself it may be no improvement of a scene; and a bit of turret, the tip of a spire, and the other ordinary subjects of these frivolous attempts, are so insignificant as objects, that whether they are real or fictitious is almost a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of indifference.

RIDLEY

Pages 37-38

Nicholas, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to the Reformation, was descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and born in the beginning of the 16th century, at Wilmswick in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. From the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> upon Tyne, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in the year 1518, where he was supported by his uncle Dr Robert Ridley, fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. In 1522 he took his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in arts; two years after, was elected fellow; and, in 1525, he commenced <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. In 1527, having taken orders, he was sent by his uncle, for further improvement, to the Sarbonne at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; from there he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> abroad till the year 1529. On his return to Cambridge, he was chosen under-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the university: and, in 1533, was elected senior proctor. He afterwards proceeded bachelor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and was chosen chaplain of the university, orator, and magister glomeria. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was much admired as a preacher and disputant. He lost his kind uncle in 1536; but was soon after patronized by Dr Cramner, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, who made him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain, and presented him to the vicarage of Herne in East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; where, we are told, he preached the doctrine of the Reformation. In 1540, having commenced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chaplain; and in the same year, was elected master of his college in Cambridge. Soon after, Ridley was collated to a prebend in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Canterbury; and it was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he was accused in the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, at the instigation of Bishop Gardiner, of preaching against the doctrine of the Six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">Articles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being referred to Cramner, Ridley was acquitted. In 1545, he was made a prebendary of Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; in 1547 was presented, by the fellows of Pembroke-hall, to the living of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOHAM">Soham</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>; and the same year was consecrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>. In 1550 he was translated to the see of London; in which year he was one of the commissioners for examining Bishop Gardiner, and concurred in his deprivation. In the year 1552, our prelate returning from Cambridge, unfortunately for himself, paid a visit to the Princess, afterwards Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; to whom, prompted by his zeal for reformation, he expressed himself with too much freedom: for she was scarcely seated on the throne when Ridley was doomed a victim to her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. With Cramner and Latimer he was burnt alive at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, on the 16th of October 1555. He wrote, 1. A treatise concerning images in churches. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">Brief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>. 3. Certain godly and comfortable conferences between Bishop Ridley and Mr Hugh Latimer, during their imprisonment. 4. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the comfortable doctrine of the Gospel and the traditions of the Popish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and other works. Ridley, Dr Gloster, was of the same family with the preceding. He was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in the year 1702, on board the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> East Indiaman, from which circumstance he obtained his Christian name. He was educated at Winechester school, and afterwards obtained a fellowship at new College, Oxford. He paid his court to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and laid the foundation of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and elegant acquisitions which afterwards distinguished him so eminently as a divine, historian, and poet. During a vacation in 1728, he joined with four friends in composing a tragedy called "The Fruitless Redress," each undertaking an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> agreeably to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which they had previously concerted. It was offered to Mr Wilkes, but never acted, and is still in manuscript. Dr Ridley in his youth was extremely attached to theatrical performances. The Redress, and another called Jugurtha, were exhibited at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDHURST">Midhurst</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> were chiefly the gentlemen tlemen who assisted him in their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. We are informed that he played Mark Anthony, Jaffier, Horatio, and Moneses, with very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause, which may be readily inferred from his graceful manner of speaking in the pulpit. During a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he had only the small college living of Westow in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and that of Poplar in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence. His college added to these some years after, the donative of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMFORD">Romford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, which left him little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no time for what he considered as the necessary studies of his profession. Yet in this situation he remained in the possession of, and satisfied with domestic felicity, and enjoyed the intimate friendship of some who were equally distinguished for worth and learning. The eight sermons which he preached at Lady Mover's Lecture in 1740 and 1741, were given to the public in 1742. In the year 1756 he was invited to go to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as first chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, but declined to accept of it. In the year 1763 he published the life of Bishop Ridley, in 4to, by subscription, from the profits of which he was enabled to purchase L.800 in the public funds. In the concluding part of his life he lost both his sons, who were young men of considerable abilities. The elder, called James, was author of Tales of the Genii, and some other literary performances; and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Thomas was sent as a writer to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> by the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, where he suddenly died of the smallpox. In the year 1765, Dr Ridley published his review of Phillips's Life of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Pole; and as a reward for his labours in this controversy, he was presented, in 1768, by Archbishop Secker with a rich prebend in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>; the only reward he received from the great during a long and useful life. He was at last worn out with infirmities, and died in 1774, leaving behind him a wife and four daughters. By his elegant epitaph, written by Bishop Lowth, we are informed that the university of Oxford, for his merits, conferred upon him the degree of D.D. the highest literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which that learned body has to bestow.

RIENZI

Pages 38-39

NICHOLAS GABRINI DE, one of the most singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the 14th century, was born at Rome, but it is not certainly known in what year. His father, as some affirm, was a vintner, but a miller according to others, and his mother was a laundress, yet they found means to give their son a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and to a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> understanding he added uncommon application. He was well acquainted with the laws and customs of nations; and had a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, which enabled him to retain much of Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Livy, the two Senecas, and in particular Caesar's Commentaries, which he constantly perused. This extensive erudition proved the foundation of his future rise. He acquired the reputation of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquarian, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he spent among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> which are to be found at Rome, and these inspired him with exalted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. He even persuaded himself, and found means to persuade others, that he should one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> be the restorer of the Roman republic. The credulity of the people was powerfully encouraged and strengthened by his advantageous stature, by the attractions of his countenance, and by that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> which he could assume at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> energy of all these prepossessing qualities made a deep and almost indelible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the minds of his hearers. Nor was his fame merely confined to the vulgar, for he even ingratiated himself into the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of many distinguished personages belonging to the administration. The Romans chose him one of their deputies to Pope Clement VI. then at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>, the purport of whose mission was to persuade his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, that his absence from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was inimical to its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. His commanding eloquence and gay conversation charmed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Avignon, from which Rienza was encouraged to tell the Pope, that the great men of Rome were public thieves, robbers, adulterers, and profligates, by whose example the most horrid crimes were sanctioned. This ill-timed freedom of speech made <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Colonna his enemy, though the friend of genuine merit, because he thought that some of his family were abused by such a thundering philippic, in consequence of which Rienzi was disgraced, and fell into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> misery, vexation, and sickness, which, by being united with indigence, brought him to an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. But as the cardinal was compassionate, the offender was again brought before the Pope, who being informed that Rienza was a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and the strenuous advocate of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and justice, gave him higher proofs of his esteem and confidence than before. He was appointed apostolic nary, and sent back to Rome loaded with the effects of papal munificence. The functions of this office he executed in such a manner as to become the idol of the people, whose affections he laboured to secure by exclaiming against the vices of the great, rendering them as odious as possible; for which imprudent liberties he was dismissed from office. In this situation of his affairs he endeavoured to kindle and keep alive in the minds of the people a zeal for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> liberties, displaying emblems of the ancient grandeur and present decline of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, accompanied with harangues and many expressive predictions. Such an intrepid, and at the same time extraordinary conduct, made some regard him as a lunatic, while others hailed him as their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> and deliverer. When he supposed that the numbers attached to his interest were sufficiently strong, he called them together, and gave them a dismal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the state of the city, overrun with debaucheries, which their governors had no capacity either to correct <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> amend.
