He declared that the Pope could, even at the rate of fourpence, raise 100,000 florins by firing, an equal sum by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and as much more by the customs and other duties, insinuating that he did not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on the revenues without the consent of his Holiness. This artful <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> so powerfully animated his hearers, that they signified their determination to secure these treasures for whatever purposes might be most convenient, and that to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> they would cheerfully devote themselves. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> he caused them confirm by an oath, and it is said that he had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to procure from the Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> the sanction of his authority. On the 20th of May he pretended that he did nothing but in consequence of the particular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of the Holy Ghost, and about 9 o'clock he came out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with his head bare, attended by the Pope's vicar, and about 100 men in armour. Having proceeded directly to the capital, and declared from the rostrum, with even more than his wonted boldness and energy, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of of their emancipation was at length arrived; that he himself was to be their glorious deliverer, and that he poured contempt on the dangers to which he might be exposed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his Holiness, and for the happy deliverance of the people. The laws of the "good establishment" were next ordered to be read; and he rested assured that the Romans would resolve to observe these laws, in consequence of which he pledged himself to re-establish them in a short time in their ancient grandeur and magnificence. Plenty and security were the blessings promised by the good establishment, and the humbling of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, who were regarded as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oppressors. Such ideas filled the people with transport, and they became zealously attached to the fanaticism of Rienzi. The multitude declared him to be sovereign of Rome, to whom they granted the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, of rewards and punishments, of making and repealing laws, of treating with foreign powers, and a full and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority over all the Roman territories. Having thus arrived at the zenith of his ambition, he concealed his artifice as much as possible, and pretended to be extremely averse to accept of their proffered honours, unless they would make choice of the Pope's vicar to be his copartner, and find means to procure the sanction of the Pope himself. His wish to have the vicar (bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a>) as his copartner was readily complied with, while all the honours were paid to Rienzi, the duped bishop enjoying but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nominal authority. Rienzi was seated in his triumphal chariot, and the people were dismissed, overwhelmed with joy and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. This strange <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was ratified by the Pope, although it was impossible that he could inwardly approve of it; and to procure a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of his Holiness, was the next object of Rienzi's ambition. He sought, therefore, and readily obtained the title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, which was conferred on him and his coadjutor, with the additional epithet of deliverers of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The conduct of Rienzi immediately subsequent to this elevation justly procured him esteem and respect, as well from the Romans as from neighbouring states: but as his beginning was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and obscure, he soon became intoxicated with his sudden, his extraordinary elevation, and the incensed nobles having conspired against him, successfully drove him from an authority which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> or address to retain not more than six months. At this critical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his life was only preserved by flight, and disguises to which he had afterwards recourse. Having made an ineffectual effort at Rome to regain his authority, he went afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Romans, in consequence of which rash step he was thrown into prison at Avignon, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for three years. When he procured his enlargement, Pope Innocent IV. who succeeded Clement, well knew that many of the Romans were still attached to Rienzi, and therefore he made choice of him as a fit object for assisting him in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of humbling the other petty tyrants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. In short, he was set at liberty, and appointed governor and senator of Rome. It was hoped that his chastisement would teach him more moderation in future, and that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> would induce him to preserve an inviolable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the holy see during the remainder of his life. He met with considerable opposition in assuming his new authority, but cunning and resolution enabled him to overcome it. But gratifying his passions, which were violent in the extreme, and disgracing his office and character by acts of cruelty; he was murdered on the 8th of October 1354. Thus died Nicolas Rienzi, one of the most extraordinary characters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived; who, having formed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> big with extravagance, and carried it into execution nearly in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the whole world, with such remarkable success as to become sovereign of Rome; having blessed the Romans with plenty, liberty, and justice; having afforded protection to some princes, and proved a terror to others; having become the arbiter of crowned heads, established the ancient majesty and power of the Roman republic, and filled all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with his fame; finally, having procured their sanction whose authority he had usurped in opposition to their interests; he fell at last a sacrifice to the nobles whose ruin he had vowed, and to those vast projects, the execution of which was only prevented by his death.

RIGA

Pages 39-39

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, strong, populous, and rich town of the Russian empire, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. It is a large trading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and has a very considerable fortress; the trade is chiefly in corn, skins, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and naval stores. It was taken by the Russians in 1710, after they had blocked it up a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while, during which the inhabitants were afflicted with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. The castle is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and defended by four towers and six bastions; besides which, it has a fine arsenal. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have still a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> here. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is computed at 27,000. It is seated on a large plain on the river Dvina. E. Long. 24. 25. N. Lat. 57. 0.

RIGADOON

Pages 39-40

a gay and brisk dance, borrowed originally from Provence in France, and performed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and woman. RIGGING of a Ship, a general name given to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> employed to support the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and to extend <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reduce the sails, or arrange them to the disposition of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The former, which are used to sustain the masts, remain usually in a fixed position, and are called standing rigging; such are the shrouds, stays, and backstays. The latter, whose office is to manage the sails, by communicating with various blocks or pulleys, situated in different parts of the masts, yards, shrouds, &c., are comprehended in the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of running rigging; such are the braces, sheets, halyards, clue-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, brails, &c. In rigging a mast, the first thing usually fixed upon its head is a circular wreath or rope, called the gromet, or collar, which is firmly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the top of the hounds. The intent of this is to prevent the shrouds from being fretted or worn by the trestle-trees, or shoulders of the mast; after this are laid on the two pendants, from whose lower ends the main or fore-tackles are suspended; and next, the shrouds of the starboard and larboard side, in pairs, alternately. The whole is covered by the stays, which are the largest ropes of the rigging.—When a yard is to be rigged, a gromet is also driven first on each of its extremities; next to this are fitted on the horses, the braces, and lastly the lifts or top-sail sheet-blocks. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects to be considered in rigging a ship, appear to be strength, convenience, and simplicity; or, the properties of affording sufficient security to the masts, yards, and sails; or arranging the whole machi- RIG very in the most advantageous manner, to sustain the masts, and facilitate the management of the sails; and of avoiding perplexity, and rejecting whatever is super- fluous or unnecessary. The perfection of this art, then, consists in retaining all those qualities, and in preserving a judicious medium between them. See SHIP-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">BUILDING</a>.

RIGHT

Pages 40-44

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, signifies the same with straight; thus, a straight line is called a right one. RIGHT is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> conferred, 1. Together with Rever- end, upon all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. 2. Together with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a>, upon earls, viscounts, and barons. 3. By courtesy, toge- ther with Honourable, upon the sons of dukes, marquises, and the eldest sons of earls. 4. Together with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>- able, to the speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons; but to no other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> excepting those who are members of his majesty's most honourable privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and the three <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayors of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, and the lord provost of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, during their office. See HONOURABLE and PROVOST. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">Hereditary</a> Right. See HEREDITARY. RIGHT is a word which, in the propriety of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is used sometimes as an adjective and sometimes as a substantive. As an adjective it is nearly of the same import with fit, suitable, becoming, proper, and whilst it expresses a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, it indicates a relation*. Thus, when we say that an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is right, we must not only know the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the action, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we speak in- telligibly, must also perceive its relation to the end for which it was performed; for an action may be right with one end in view which would be wrong with ano- ther. The conduct of that general would be right, who, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> that could not be otherwise saved, should <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> in a station where he knew they would all be inevitably cut off; but his conduct would be very wrong were he to throw away the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a single individual for any purpose, however important, which he knew how to accomplish without such a sacrifice. Many philosophers have talked of actions being right and wrong in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> without regard to their natu- ral consequences; and converting the word into a sub- stantive, they have fancied an eternal rule of right, by which the morality of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> conduct is in every partic- ular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> to be tried. But in these phrases we can <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- cover no meaning. Whatever is right must be so on some account <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other; and whatever is fit, must be fit for some purpose. When he who rests the foundation of virtue on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, speaks of an action being right, he must <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that it is such as, through the medium of that sense, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> excite complacency in the mind of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to him the general approbation of mankind. When he who rests moral obligation on the will of God, speaks of some actions as right and of others as wrong, he must mean that the former are agreeable to the di- vine will, however made known to men, and the latter disagreeable to it; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who deduces the laws of virtue from what he calls the fitness of things, must have some end in view, for which things are fit, and denominate actions right or wrong as they tend to pro- mote or counteract that end. But the word right, used as a substantive, has in com- mon as well as in philosophical language a signification which at first view appears to be very different from this. It denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> claim or an honest possession. Thuswise, a father has a right to reverence from his children, a husband to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and fidelity of his wife, and a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> of his subjects. But if we trace these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> to their source, we shall find that they are all laws of moral obligation, and that they are called rights only because it is agreeable to the will of God, to the in- stinctive dictates of the moral sense, or to the fitness of things, if such a phrase has any meaning, that children reverence their parents, that wives love their husbands, and that subjects pay all allegiance to their sovereign. This will be apparent to any man who shall put to himself such questions as these: "Why have parents a right to reverence from their children, husbands to the love of their wives, and sovereigns to the allegiance of their subjects?" As these questions contain in them nothing absurd, it is obvious that they are each capable of a precise answer; but it is impossible to give to any of them an answer which shall have any meaning, and not imply that right and obligation are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a>, or, in other words, that wherever there is a right in one person there is a corresponding obligation upon others. Thus to the question, "Why have parents a right to reverence from their children?" it may be answered, "because, under God, they were the authors of their children's being, and protected them from danger, and furnished them with necessaries, when they were in a state so helpless that they could do nothing for themselves." This answer conveys no other meaning than that there is an obligation upon children, in return for benefits re- ceived, to reverence their parents. But what is the source of this obligation? It can only be the will of God, the moral sense, or the fitness of things. This view of the nature of right will enable us to form a proper judgment of the assertion of a late writer, "that man has no rights." The arguments by which this apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a> is maintained, are not merely in- genious and plausible; they are absolutely conclusive. But then our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who never chooses to travel in the beaten track, takes the word right in a sense ve- ry different from that in which it has been used by all other men, and considers it as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to discretionary power. "By the word right (says he) is understood a right of full and complete power of either doing a thing or man, omitting it, without the person's becoming liable to, animadversion or censure from another; that is, in other words, without his incurring any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of turpitude or guilt." In this sense of the word he affirms, and affirms truly, that a man has no rights, no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>- ary power whatever, except in things of such total in- <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> as, whether "he shall sit on the right or on the left side of his fire, or dine on beef to-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or to- morrow." A proposition so evidently true as this stood not in need of argument to support it; but as his arguments are clearly expressed, and afford a complete <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of some popular errors sanctioned by the respectable phrase rights of man, we shall give our readers an op- portunity of studying them in his own words. "<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is founded on the principles of morality and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. It is impossible for intellectual beings to be brought into coalition and intercourse without a certain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of conduct, adapted to their nature and connection, immediately becoming a duty incumbent on the parties concerned. Men would nev- er have associated if they had not imagined that, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, they would mutually conduce conduce to the advantage and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of each other. This is the real purpose, the genuine basis, of their intercourse; and, as far as this purpose is answered, so far does society answer the end of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. There is only one postulate more that is necessary to bring us to a conclusive mode of reasoning upon this subject. Whatever is meant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> right, there can neither be opposite rights, nor rights and duties hostile to each other. The rights of one man cannot clash with or be destructive of the rights of another: for this, instead of rendering the subject an important branch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and morality, as the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of the rights of man certainly understood it to be, would be to reduce it to a heap of unintelligible jargon and inconsistency. If one man have a right to be free, another man cannot have a right to make him a slave; if one man have a right to inflict chastisement upon me, I cannot have a right to withdraw myself from chastisement; if my neighbour have a right to a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in my possession, I cannot have a right to retain it in my pocket. It cannot be less incontrovertible, that I have no right to omit what my duty prescribes. From hence it inevitably follows that men have no rights. "It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> said, 'that a man has a right to the disposal of his fortune, a right to the employment of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, a right to the uncontrolled choice of his profession or pursuits.' But this can never be consistently affirmed till it can be shown that he has no duties, prescribing and limiting his mode of proceeding in all these respects. "In reality, nothing can appear more wonderful to a careful inquirer, than that two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> so incompatible as man and rights should ever have been associated together. Certain it is, that one of them must be utterly exclusive and annihilatory of the other. Before we ascribe rights to man, we must conceive of him as a being endowed with intellect, and capable of discerning the differences and tendencies of things. But a being endowed with intellect, and capable of discerning the differences and tendencies of things, instantly becomes a moral being, and has duties incumbent on him to discharge: and duties and rights, as has already been shown, are absolutely exclusive of each other. "It has been affirmed by the zealous advocates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, 'that princes and magistrates have no rights;' and no position can be more incontrovertible. There is no situation of their lives that has not its correspondent duties. There is no power intrusted to them that they are not bound to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> exclusively for the public good. It is strange, that persons adopting this principle did not go a step farther, and perceive that the same restrictions were applicable to subjects and citizens." This reasoning is unanswerable; but it militates not against the rights of man in the usual acceptation of the words, which are never employed to denote discretionary power, but a just claim on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, implying a corresponding obligation on the other. Whether the phrase be absolutely proper is not worth the debating: it is authorised by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>—the jus et norma loquendi—and is universally understood except by such as the demons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, in the form of paradoxical writers on political justice, have been able to mislead by sophistical reasonings. Rights, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation of the word, are of various kinds: they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or adventitious, alienable or unalienable, perfect or imperfect, particular or general. See the article Liberty. Natural rights are those which a man has to his life, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, and liberty; to the produce of his personal labour; to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, in common with others, of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. That every man has a natural right or just claim to these things, is evident from their being absolutely necessary to enable him to answer that purpose, whatever it may be, for which he was made a living and a rational being. This shows undeniably, that the Author of his nature designed that he should have the use of them, and that the man who should wantonly deprive him of any one of them, would be guilty of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> inconsistently with the fitness of things in every sense in which that phrase can possibly be understood. Adventitious rights are those which a king has over his subjects, a general over his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, a husband to the person and affections of his wife, and which every man has to the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. That the rights of the king and the general are adventitious, is universally admitted. The rights of property have been considered elsewhere (see Property); and though the human <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> shows sufficiently that men and women have a natural right to the use of each other, yet it is evident that the exclusive right of any one man to any one woman, and vice versa, must be an adventitious right: but the important question is, How are adventitious rights acquired? In answer to this question, the moralist who deduces the laws of virtue from the will of God, observes, that as God appears from his works to be a benevolent Being, who wills the happiness of all his creatures (see <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No 312), he must of course will every thing which naturally tends to promote that happiness. But the existence of civil society evidently contributes in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree to promote the sum of human happiness (see Society); and therefore whatever is necessary for the support of civil society in general, or for the conduct of particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> already established, must be agreeable to the will of God: But the allegiance of subjects to their sovereign, the obedience of soldiers to their leader, the protection of private property, and the fulfilling of contracts, are all absolutely necessary to the support of society: and hence the rights of kings, generals, husbands, and wives, &c., though adventitious, and immediately derived from human appointments, are not less sacred than natural rights, since they may all be ultimately traced to the same source. The same conclusion may easily be drawn by the philosopher, who rests moral obligation on the fitness of things or on a moral sense; only it must in each of these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> partake of the instability of its foundation. To the sacredness of the rights of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, an author already quoted has lately urged some declamatory objections. "It is absurd (says he) to expect, that the inclinations and wishes of two human beings should coincide through any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time. To oblige them to act and to live together, is to subject them to some inevitable portion of thwarting, bickering, and unhappiness. This cannot be otherwise, so long as man has failed to reach the standard of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> perfection. The supposition that I must have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> for life, is the result of a complication of vices. It is the dictate of cowardice, and not of fortitude. It flows from the desire of being loved and esteemed for some- thing that is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. "But the evil of marriage, as it is practised in Eu- ropean countries, lies deeper than this. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is, for a thoughtless and romantic youth of each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> to come together, to see each other for a few times, and under circumstances full of delusion, and then to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> to each other eternal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>. What is the conse- quence of this? In almost every instance they find them- selves deceived. They are reduced to make the best of an irretrievable mistake. They are presented with the strongest imaginable temptation to become the dupes of falsehood. They are led to conceive it their wisest policy to shut their eyes upon realities; happy if by any perversion of intellect they can persuade themselves that they were right in their first crude <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of their companion. "So long as two human beings are forbidden by positive institution to follow the dictates of their own mind, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> is alive and vigorous. So long as I seek to engross one woman to myself, and to prohibit my neighbour from proving his superior desert and reaping the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of it, I am guilty of the most odious of all monopolies. Over this imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> men watch with perpetual jealousy; and one man will find his de- sires and his capacity to circumvent as much excited, as the other is excited to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> his projects and frustrate his hopes. As long as this state of society continues, philanthropy will be crossed and checked in a thousand ways, and the still augmenting stream of abuse will continue to flow. "The abolition of marriage will be attended with no evils. The intercourse of the sexes will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under the same system as any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of friendship. Ex- clusively of all groundless and obstinate attachments, it will be impossible for me to live in the world without finding one man of a worth superior to that of any other whom I have an opportunity of observing. To this man I shall feel a kindness in exact proportion to my <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of his worth. The case will be pre- cisely the same with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> sex; I shall assiduously cultivate the intercourse of that woman whose accomplishments shall strike me in the most powerful manner. But it may happen that other men will feel for her the same preference that I do. This will create no difficulty. We may all enjoy her conversa- tion; and we shall all be wise enough to consider the sensual intercourse as a very trivial object. This, like every other affair in which two persons are concerned, must be regulated in each successive instance by the un- forced consent of either party. It is a mark of the ex- treme depravity of our present habits, that we are in- clined to suppose the sensual intercourse anywise mate- rial to the advantages arising from the purest affection. Reasonable men now eat and drink, not from the love of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, but because eating and drinking are essen- tial to our healthful existence. Reasonable men then will propagate their species, not because a certain sensi- ble pleasure is annexed to this action, but because it is right the species should be propagated; and the man- ner in which they exercise this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> will be regulat- ed by the dictates of reason and duty." It is right then, according to this political innovator, mutual; and thoughtless endearing than assiduities which take their rise from affection, generally procure to the married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> a repose and satisfaction sufficient for their happiness." So differently from our author does this judicious writer reason concerning the effects of a permanent union on the tempers of the married pair. Instead of subjecting them to some inevitable portion of thwarting, bickering, and unhappiness, it lays them, in his opinion, under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of curbing their unruly passions, and acquiring habits of gentleness, forbearance, and peace. To this we may add, that both believing the children propagated during their marriage to be their own, (a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> unattainable by the father in a state of promiscuous concubinage), they come by a natural <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the human passions (see <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">Passion</a>) to love each other through the medium of their offspring. But if it be the duty of man to acquire a spirit first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, it must be agreeable to the will of God, and a branch of the fitness of things, that the sexual union last during the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> lives of the parties; and therefore the exclusive right of marriage, though adventitious, must be equally sacred with those which are natural. But to return from this digression, into which the importance of the subject led us, rights, besides being natural or adventitious, are likewise alienable or unalienable. Every man, when he becomes the member of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, alienates a part of his natural rights. In a state of nature, no man has a superior on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and each has a right to defend his life, liberty, and property by all the means which nature has put in his power. In civil society, however, these rights are all transferred to the laws and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, except in cases of such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> urgency as leave not time for legal interposition. This single consideration is sufficient to show, that the right to civil liberty is alienable; though, in the vehemence of men's zeal for it, and in the language of some political remonstrances, it has often been pronounced to be an unalienable right. "The true reason" (says Mr Paley) why mankind hold in detestation the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those who have sold their liberty to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> is, that, together with their own, they sold commonly or endangered the liberty of others; of which they had certainly no right to dispose." The rights of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> over his people, and of a husband over his wife, are generally and naturally unalienable. Another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of rights is into those which are perfect and those which are imperfect. Perfect rights are such as may be precisely ascertained and asserted by force or in civil society by the course of law. To imperfect rights neither force nor law is applicable. A man's rights to his life, person, and property, are all perfect; for if any of these be attacked, he may repel the attack by instant violence, punish the aggressor by the course of law, or compel the author of the injury to make restitution or satisfaction. A woman's right to her honour is likewise perfect: for if she cannot otherwise escape, she may kill the ravisher. Every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> man has an undoubted right to relief from the rich: but his right is imperfect, for if the relief be not voluntarily given, he cannot compel it either by law or by violence: There is no duty upon which the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> puts a greater value than alms-giving; and every preacher of the gospel has an undoubted right to inculcate the practice of it upon his audience: but even this right is imperfect, for he cannot refuse the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> to a man merely on account of his illiberality to the poor, as he can to another for the neglect of any duty comprehended under the term justice. In elections or appointments to offices, where the qualifications are prescribed, the best qualified candidate has unquestionably a right to succeed; yet if he be rejected, he can neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the office by force, nor obtain redress at law. His right, therefore, is imperfect. Here a question naturally offers itself to our consideration: "How comes a person to have a right to a thing, and yet have no right to use the means necessary to obtain it?" The answer is, That in such cases the object or the circumstances of the right are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a>, that the permission of force, even where the right is real and certain, would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to force in other cases where there exists no right at all. Thus, though the poor man has a right to relief, who shall ascertain the mode, season, and quantum of it, or the person by whom it shall be administered? These things must be ascertained before the right to relief can be enforced by law; but to allow them to be ascertained by the poor themselves, would be to expose property to endless claims. In like manner, the comparative qualifications of the candidate must be ascertained, before he can enforce his right to the office: but to allow him to ascertain his qualifications himself, would be to make him judge in his own cause between himself and his neighbour. Wherever the right is imperfect on one side, the corresponding obligation on the other must be imperfect likewise. The violation of it, however, is often not less criminal in a moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> view than of a perfect obligation. It is well observed by Mr Paley, that greater guilt is incurred by disappointing a worthy candidate of a place upon which perhaps his livelihood depends, and in which he could eminently serve the public, than by filching a book out of a library, or picking a pocket of a handkerchief. The same sentiment has been expressed by Mr Godwin, but in terms by much too strong, and such as show that he was not at the time complete <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of his subject. "My neighbour (says he) has just as much right to put an end to my existence with dagger or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, as to deny me that pecuniary assistance without which I must starve, or as to deny me that assistance without which my intellectual attainments, or my moral exertions, will be materially injured. He has just as much right to amuse himself with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> my house, or torturing my children upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>, as to shut himself up in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, careless about his fellow men, and to hide his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in a napkin." It is certainly true, that the man who should suffer another to starve for want of that relief which he knew that he alone could afford him, would be guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and murder of the cruellest kind; but there is an immense difference between depriving society of one of its members, and withholding from that member what might be necessary to enable him to make the greatest possible intellectual attainments. Newton might have been useful and happy though he had never been acquainted with the elements of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and the late celebrated Mr Fergusson might have been a valuable member of society, though he had never emerged from his original condition of a shepherd. The remainder of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a> is too absurd to require a formal confutation. Had our author, burying his talent in a napkin, shut himself up <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years ago in a cell, careless about his fellow men and political justice, he would have deprived the public of what he doubtless believes to be much useful instruction; but had he at that period amused himself with burning his neighbour's house, and torturing on the rack two or three children, he would have cut off, for any thing he could know, two or three future Newtons, and have himself been cut off by the insulted laws of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Now, without supposing the value of ten Newtons to be equal to that of one Godwin, we are warranted to say, that however great his merits may be, they are not infinite, and that the addition of those of one Newton to them would undoubtedly increase their sum. Rights are particular or general. Particular rights are such as belong to certain individuals or orders of men, and not to others. The rights of kings, of masters, of husbands, of wives, and, in short, all the rights which originate in society, are particular. General rights are those which belong to the species collectively. Such are our rights to the vegetable produce of the earth, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of animals for food, though about the origin of this latter right there has been much diversity of opinion, which we have noticed in another place. (See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, part 1, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 2d.) If the vegetable produce of the earth be included under the general rights of mankind, it is plain that he is guilty of wrong who leaves any considerable portion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> waste merely for his own amusement: he is lessening the common stock of provision which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> intended to distribute among the species. On this principle it would not be easy to vindicate certain regulations respecting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, as well as some other monopolies which are protected by the municipal laws of most countries. Mr Paley, by just reasoning, has established this conclusion, "that nothing ought to be made exclusive property which can be conveniently enjoyed in common." An equal division of land, however, the dream of some visionary reformers, would be injurious to the general rights of mankind, as it may be demonstrated, that it would lessen the common stock of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, by laying every man under the necessity of being his own weaver, tailor, shoemaker, smith, and carpenter, as well as ploughman, miller and baker. Among the general rights of mankind is the right of necessity; by which a man may use or destroy his neighbour's property when it is absolutely necessary for his own preservation. It is on this principle that goods are thrown overboard to save the ship, and houses pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to stop the progress of a fire. In such cases, however, at least in the last, restitution ought to be made when it is in our power; but this restitution will not extend to the original value of the property destroyed, but only to what it was worth at the time of destroying it, which, considering its danger, may be very little.

RIGHTEOUSNESS

Pages 44-44

means <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, honesty, virtue, goodness, and amongst <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> is of exactly the same import with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>, without which, we are told, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall see the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. The doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, has occasioned much disputation, and given rise to many singular notions in the world. The haughty <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, dissatisfied with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, and with the humiliating doctrine of atonement by a crucified Saviour, has made a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> for himself, which he calls rational Christianity; and the enthusiast, by extracting doctrines from Scripture which are not contained in it, and which are repugnant to its spirit, has given too much countenance to this presumption. The doctrine of imputed righteousness, by which the merit of Christ is said to be imputed to us, appears to be of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; and though it has been held by many good, and by some learned men, it is certainly in general unfriendly to virtue, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be readily allowed by all who have conversed with the more ignorant sort of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a> in England <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Seceders in Scotland. That it does not follow from the doctrine of the atonement, and consequently that it has no foundation in Scripture, will appear elsewhere. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> delivered by the lords and commons to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and princess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, 13th February 1688; and afterwards enacted in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, when they became <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. It sets forth, that King James did, by the assistance of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> evil counsellors, endeavour to subvert the laws and liberties of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, by exercising a power of dispensing with and suspending of laws; by levying <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by pretence of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> without consent of parliament; by prosecuting those who petitioned the king, and discouraging petitions; by raising and keeping a standing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of peace; by violating the freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of members to serve in parliament; by violent prosecutions in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; and causing partial and corrupt jurors to be returned on trials, excessive bail to be taken, excessive fines to be imposed, and cruel punishments inflicted; all which were declared to be illegal. And the declaration concludes in these remarkable words: "And they do claim, demand, and insist upon, all and singular the premises, as their undoubted rights and liberties." And the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament itself (1 W. and M. stat. 2, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2,) recognizes "all and singular the rights and liberties, asserted and claimed in the said declaration, to be the true, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, indubitable rights of the people of this kingdom." See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>.

RIGIDITY

Pages 44-44

in Physics, denotes a brittle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>. It is opposed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a>, malleability, and softness.

RIGOLL

Pages 44-45
or REGALS, a kind of musical instrument, consisting of several sticks bound together, only separated by beads. It is tolerably harmonious, being well struck with a ball at the end of a stick. Such is the account which Grassineau gives of this instrument. Skinner, upon the authority of an old English dictionary, represents it as a clavichord, or claricord; possibly founding his opinion on the nature of the office of the tuner of the regals, who still subsists in the establishment of the king's chapel at St James's, and whose business is to keep the organ of the chapel royal in tune; and not knowing that such wind instruments as the organ need frequent tuning, as well as the clavichord and other stringed instruments. Sir Henry Spelman derives the word rigoll from the Italian rigabello, a musical instrument, anciently used in churches instead of the organ. Walther, in his description of the regal, makes it to be a reed-work in an organ, with metal and also wooden pipes and bellows adapted to it. And he adds, that the name of it is supposed to be owing to its having been presented by the inventor to some king.—From an account. count of the regal used in Germany, and other parts of Europe, it appears to consist of pipes and keys on one side, and the bellows and wind-chest on the other. We may add, that Lord Bacon (Nat. Hist. cent. ii. 102.) distinguishes between the regal and organ, in a manner which shows them to be instruments of the same class. Upon the whole, there is reason to conclude, that the regal or rigoli was a pneumatic, and not a stringed instrument. Mersennus relates, that the Flemings invented an instrument, les regales de bois, consisting of 17 cylindrical pieces of wood, decreasing gradually in length, so as to produce a succession of tones and semitones in the diatonic series, which had keys, and was played on as a spinet; the hint of which, he says, was taken from an instrument, in use among the Turks, consisting of 12 wooden cylinders, of different lengths, strung together, which being suspended and struck with a stick, having a ball at the end, produced music. Hawkins's Hist. Mus. vol. ii. p. 449.

RIGOR

Pages 45-45

in Medicine, a convulsive shuddering from severe <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> fit, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other disorder.

RIMINI

Pages 45-45

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, populous, and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Romagna, which is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a bishop's see, an old castle, and a strong tower; as also many remains of antiquity, and very fine buildings. It is famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in 1559, consisting of 400 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, who were all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> except 20. It is seated in a fertile plain, at the mouth of the river Marecchia, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 39. N. Lat. 44. 6.

RING

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for taking an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, &c. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches in diameter, suspended by a small swivel, at the distance of 45°, from the point of which there is a perforation, being the centre of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> of 90° divided in the inner concave surface. It is to be held up by the swivel when used, and turned round to the sun, till his rays, falling through the hole, form a spot among the degrees, by which the required altitude is pointed out. This instrument is deemed preferable to the astrolabe, because the divisions are larger than on that instrument. RINGS. The antiquity of rings is known from Scripture and profane authors. Jehoshaphat left his ring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a> with Tamar (Gen. xxxviii. 18.). When <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> committed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, he took his ring from his finger, and gave it to Joseph (Gen. xli. 42.). After the victory that the Israelites obtained over the Midianites, they offered to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> the rings, the bracelets, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> necklaces, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings, that they had taken from the enemy (Numb. xxxi. 50.). The Israelitish women wore rings not only on their fingers, but also in their nostrils and their ears. St James distinguishes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by the ring of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> that he wore on his finger (James ii. 2.). At the return of the prodigal son, his father orders him to be dressed in a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of clothes, and to have a ring put upon his finger (Luke xv. 22.). When the Lord threatened <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Jeconiah with the utmost effects of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, he tells him, that though he wore the signet or ring upon his finger, yet he should be torn off (Jer. xxii. 24.). The ring was used chiefly to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> with; and the Scripture generally puts it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of princes and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> persons; as the king of Egypt, Joseph, Ahab, Jezebel, King Ahasuerus, his favourite Haman, Mordecai who succeeded Haman in his dignity, King <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> (1 Kings xxi. 8.; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a> iii. 10., &c.; Dan. vi. 17.). The patents and orders of these princes were sealed with their rings or signets; and it was this that secured to them their authority and respect. See the article Seal. RING-Bone. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. RING-Ousel, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Turdus. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

RIO DE JANEIRO

Pages 45-46

the name of one of the provinces into which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, the Portuguese portion of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is divided, and by far the most important in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the discovery and improvement of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> about 300 miles to the northwest. The diamond mines are the exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, as well as a fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the gold. The people have of late begun to manufacture many necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> for their own consumption. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is luxuriant, producing spontaneously most kinds of fruit; and the ground is covered with one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> forest of trees of perpetual verdure, which, from the exuberance of the soil, are so entangled with briars, thorns, and underwood, as to form a thicket absolutely impenetrable, except by some narrow foot-paths, which the inhabitants have made for their own convenience. The woods are extremely fragrant, from the many aromatic trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> with which they abound, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and vegetables of every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> thrive here almost without culture, and are to be procured in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is excellent; and among the ordinary productions of this richest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brazil may be ranked cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, coffee, cocoa, wheat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. Vines are here met with in great perfection, but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> are not pressed for the purpose of obtaining wine. Gold, silver, and precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, are annually exported by the Portuguese, whose indolence has prevented them from giving to the world any satisfactory accounts concerning those remote regions which are subject to their authority. See Brasil Supplement. Rio de Janeiro, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St Sebastian, an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the foregoing province of Brazil, and the see of a bishop. It has a very extensive and commodi- ous harbour, which is defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of forts. The city is built upon ground which is rather low and was at one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of a swampy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; it is environed by hills which exclude in great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the advantages of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, both from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on which account the summers are inimical to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> being almost suffocating. The different <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> carry on their respective branches in distinct parts of the town, particular trades having particular streets assigned to them. The viceroy's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is erected on the side of an extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and there are fountains in different other squares, to which an aqueduct of considerable length conveys water over valleys by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> point are a fort called Santa Cruz, built on a prodigious rock of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, and a Benedictine convent, jutting into the harbour, opposite to which is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">Serpent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, where there are houses for magazines and naval stores, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yard. The warehouses for the reception and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of slaves from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, are in another part of the harbour, known by the name of Val Longo. The city of Rio Janeiro is situated near the mouth of a river of the same name in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. The streets of this city are in general well paved and straight. The houses in general are two stories <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, covered with tiles, and have balconies of wood extending in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the upper stories; but the best of them have that dull and heavy appearance which must necessarily be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> when latticed windows supply the want of glass. The rocks in its vicinity are granite, of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or deep blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the last being of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and hard texture. Females of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and distinction are said to have fine dark eyes, countenances full of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>, and their heads only ornamented with their tresses, which are bound up with ribbons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. There are numerous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and monasteries, and labour is in general performed by slaves, 20,000 of which are said to be annually imported. Rio de Janeiro is a city of very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, including slaves, has been estimated at 60,000; but according to Dr Morss, at no fewer than 200,000, as we find in his American Gazetteer, published in 1798; yet it appears extraordinary, that in such a city there is neither inn, nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a>, nor any sort of accommodation for the reception of strangers. Such accommodation, however, is scarcely necessary, the weak and jealous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> being so inhospitable, as to prohibit strangers from remaining on shore after the going <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and from walking the streets during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> spies. When Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> visited this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he found only two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> shops in it, after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> search, and many inquiries; but they contained nothing useful or interesting to a native of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. A number of old volumes on the subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a> and medicine, many more on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and theological controversy, with a few on the mighty deeds of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a>, were all their catalogues contained. It is said that the inhabitants sometimes go in small parties to the Public Garden, where they take <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, walk, and enjoy themselves with music and fireworks to a very late <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night. Rio de Janeiro may justly be regarded as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> central point on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Brazils, from which every other part of it may be at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> overawed. Its regular force is said to consist of two squadrons of Rio de Janeiro cavalry, two regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, six regiments of infantry, two battalions of disciplined <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, and 200 disciplined free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, making a sum total of more than 10,000 men; but Mr Barrow is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this estimate is much exaggerated, since during his stay in that city he could discover nothing to warrant such a conclusion; and he is inclined to think that the whole force of the Brazils united cannot exceed the number of 10,000 men. This place, which has for a time at least become the residence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family and government of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, no doubt, acquire additional importance, and may perhaps at some future period be the seat of a mighty empire. Rio Janeiro, a river which rises in the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Brazil, and running east through that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, falls into the Atlantic ocean at St Sebastian.

RIO-GRADE

Pages 45-45

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which runs from east to west through Negroland, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, in 11 degrees of latitude. Some take it to be a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, of which there is not the least <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>.

RIOT

Pages 46-47

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. The riotous assembling of 12 persons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more, and not dispersing upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, was first made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> by statute 3 and 4 Edw. VI. c. 5, when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, and a change of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to be effected; but that statute was repealed by statue 1 Mar. c. 1, among the other treasons created since the 25 Edw. III.; though the prohibition was in substance re-enacted, with an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, by statute 1 Mar. st. 2. c. 12, which made the same offence a single felony. These statutes specified and particularized the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the riots they were meant to suppress; as, for example, such as were set on foot with intention to offer violence to the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, or to change the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, or for certain other specific purposes; in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the persons were commanded by proclamation to disperse, and they did not, it was by the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> made felony, but within the benefit of clergy; and also the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> indemnified the peace-officers and their assistants, if they killed any of the mob in endeavouring to suppress such riot. This was thought a necessary security in that sanguinary reign, when <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a> was intended to be re-established, which was like to produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> discontents: but at first it was made only for a year, and was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. And, by statute 1 Eliz. c. 16, when a reformation in religion was to be once more attempted, it was revived and continued during her life also; and then expired. From the accession of James I. to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, it was never once thought expedient to revive it; but, in the first year of George I. it was judged necessary, in order to support the execution of the act of settlement, to renew it, and at one stroke to make it perpetual, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> additions. For, whereas the former acts expressly defined and specified what should be accounted a riot, the statute 1 Geo. I. c. 5, enacts, generally, that if any 12 persons are unlawfully assembled to the disturbance of the peace, and any one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, under-sheriff, or mayor of a town, shall think proper to command them by proclamation to disperse, if they contemn his orders and continue together for one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> afterwards, such contempt shall be felony without benefit of clergy. And farther, if the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the proclamation be by force opposed, or the reader be in any manner manner wilfully hindered from the reading of it, such opposers and hinderers are felons without benefit of clergy; and all persons to whom such proclamation ought to have been made, and knowing of such hindrance, and not dispersing, are felons without benefit of clergy. There is the like indemnifying clause, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> any of the mob be unfortunately killed in the endeavour to disperse them; being copied from the act of Queen Mary. And by a subsequent clause of the new act, if any person, so riotously assembled, begin even before proclamation to pull <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, chapel, meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, dwelling-house, or out-houses, they shall be felons without benefit of clergy. Riots, routs, and unlawful assemblies, must have three persons at least to constitute them. An unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> is, when three, or more, do assemble themselves together to do an unlawful act, as to pull down inclosures, to destroy a warren or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> therein; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> without doing it, or making any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> towards it. A rout is where three or more meet to do an unlawful act upon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> quarrel, as forcibly breaking down fences upon a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> claimed of common, or of way, and make some advances towards it. A riot is where three or more actually do an unlawful act of violence, either with or without a common cause or quarrel; as if they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; or hunt and kill game in another's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, warren, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; or do any other unlawful act with force and violence; or even do a lawful act, as removing a nuisance, in a violent and tumultuous manner. The punishment of unlawful assemblies, if to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 12, we have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now seen, may be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, according to the circumstances that attend it; but, from the number of three to eleven, is by fine and imprisonment only. The same is the case in riots and routs by the common law; to which the pillory in very enormous cases has been sometimes superadded. And by the statute 13 Hen. IV. c. 7, any two justices, together with the sheriff or under-sheriff of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, may come with the possi comitatus, if need be, and suppress any such riot, assembly, or rout, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> the rioters, and record upon the spot the nature and circumstances of the whole transaction; which record alone shall be a sufficient conviction of the offenders. In the interpretation of which statute it hath been holden, that all persons, noblemen and others, except women, clergymen, persons decrepit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> under 15, are bound to attend the justices in suppressing a riot, upon pain of fine and imprisonment; and that any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, wounding, or killing the rioters, that may happen in suppressing the riot, is justifiable. So that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law, previous to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> riot-act, seems pretty well to have guarded against any violent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the public peace; especially as any riotous assembly on a public or general account, as to redress grievances or pull down all inclosures, and also resisting the king's forces if sent to keep the peace, may amount to overt acts of high treason, by levying <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the king.

RIPEN

Pages 47-47

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of the same name, with a bishop's see, a good harbour, a castle, two colleges, and a public library. The tombs of several of the kings of Denmark are in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is a very handsome structure. The harbour, which has contributed greatly to the prosperity of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, is at a small distance, being seated at the mouth of the river Nipsia, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which supplies the best heves in Denmark.
