It is 45 miles north-west of Sleswick and 25 south-west of Wilburg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 94. N. Lat. 55. 25. The diocese is bounded on the north by those of Wilburg and Athuys, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sleswick, and on the east and west by the sea. RIPENING of Grain, means its arriving to maturity. The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, which appeared in the first volume of the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, may be worthy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of farmers in this country; where it frequently happens, from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> rains, that the corn is quite green when the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> sets in; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, the farmers cut it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, without thinking it can possibly arrive at further maturity. "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a> 1782 having been remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and unfavourable, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> was very late, and much of the grain, especially oats, was green even in October. In the beginning of October the cold was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that, in one night, there was produced on ponds near Kinneil, in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BORROWSTOUNNESS">Borrowstounness</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> three-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch thick. It was apprehended by many farmers, that such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cold would effectually prevent the further filling and ripening of their corn. In order to ascertain this point, Dr Roebuck selected several stalks of oats, of nearly equal fulness, and immediately cut those which, on the most attentive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, appeared the best, and marked the others, but allowed them to remain in the field 14 days longer; at the end of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they too were cut, and kept in a dry room for 10 days. The grains of each parcel were then weighed; when 11 of the grains which had been left standing in the field were found to be equal in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to 30 of the grains which had been cut a fortnight sooner, though even the best of the grains were far from being ripe. During that fortnight (viz. from October 7th to October 21st) the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, according to Fahrenheit's thermometer, which was observed every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at eight o'clock in the morning and six in the evening, was a little above 43. Dr Roebuck observes, that this ripening-and-filling of corn in so low a temperature should be the less surprising to us, when we reflect, that seed-corn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> vegetate in the same degree of heat; and he draws an important inference from his observations, viz. That farmers should be cautious of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down their urine corn, on the supposition that in a cold autumn it could fill no more." A writer in the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1792, under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of Agricola, when speaking on this subject, adds the following piece of information, viz. "That grain cut down before it is quite ripe will grow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> equally well as ripe and plump grain, provided it is properly preserved. I relate this from a fact, and also on the authority of one of the most judicious and experienced farmers in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, William Craik of Arbigland, Esq. near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>, who was taught by such a season as this threatens to prove. This being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, every wise economical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> will preserve his ripe and plump grain for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and sow the green and seemingly shrivelled grain, with a perfect conviction that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> proceeding from such seed will yield as strong and thriving corn as what grows from plump seed. By this means the farmer will enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage of having the corn most productive in flour for bread, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> shrivelled grain will go much farther in seed than..."

RIPHATH

Pages 48-48
or Riphat, second son of Gomer, and grandson of Japhet (Gen. x. 3. יְרֵפַת Riphat). In most copies he is called Diploth in the Chronicles (1 Chr. i. 6. יְרֵפַת Diphat). The resemblance of the two Hebrew letters ר Resh and ד Daleth is so much that they are very often confounded. But, to the credit of the translators of our English version be it said, that in this instance, as well as in many others, they have restored the original reading, and rendered it Riphath. The learned are not agreed about the country that was peopled by the descendants of Riphath. The Chaldee and Arabic take it for France; Eusebius for the country of the Samaritans; the Chronicon Alexandrinum for that of the Garamantae; Josephus for Paphlagonia. Mela assures us, that anciently the people of this province were called Riphatei, or Riphases; and in Bithynia, bordering upon Paphlagonia, may be found the river Rhebus, a people called Rhebanites, and a canton of the same name. These reasons have prevailed with Bochart to believe, that Riphath peopled Paphlagonia. Others think he peopled the Montes Rhipei; and this opinion seems the most reasonable to us, because the other sons of Gomer peopled the northern countries towards Scythia, and beyond the Euxine sea.

RIPHOEAN MOUNTAINS

Pages 47-48

are a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in Russia, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the river Obi, where there are said to be the finest sables of the whole empire.

RISIBLE

Pages 48-49

anything capable of exciting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>. Ludicrous is a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying, as may appear from its derivation, what is playsome, sportive, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> jocular. Ludicrous therefore seems the genus, of which risible is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, limited as above to what makes us laugh. However easy it may be, concerning any particular object, to say whether it be risible or not, it seems difficult, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all practicable, to establish any general character, by which objects of that kind may be distinguished from others. Nor is that a singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; for, upon a review, we find the same difficulty in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> already handled. There is nothing more easy, viewing a particular object, than to pronounce that it is beautiful or ugly, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> or little; but were we to attempt general rules for ranging objects under different classes according to these qualities, we should be much gravelled. A separate cause increases the difficulty of distinguishing risible objects by a general character: all men are not equally affected by risible objects, nor the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at all times; for in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirits a thing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make him laugh outright, which will scarcely provoke a smile in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> mood. Risible objects, however, are circumscribed within certain limits. No object is risible but what appears slight, little, or trivial; for we laugh at nothing that is of importance to our own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> or to that of others. A real distress raises pity, and therefore cannot be risible; but a slight or imaginary distress, which moves not pity, is risible. The adventure of the fulling-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, is extremely risible; so is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> where Sancho, in a dark night, tumbling into a pit, and attaching himself to the side by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and foot, hangs there in terrible dismay till the morning, when he discovers himself to be within a foot of the bottom. A nose remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> or short, is risible; but to want it altogether, so far from provoking laughter, raises horror in the spectator. With respect to works both of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art, none of them are risible but what are out of rule; some remarkable defect or excess, a very long visage, for example, or a very short one. Hence nothing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, proper, decent, beautiful, proportioned, or grand, is risible. Even from this slight sketch it will be readily conjectured, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> raised by a risible object is of a nature singular, scarce to find <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> while the mind is occupied with any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> or emotion; and the conjecture is verified by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; for we scarce ever find that emotion blended with any other. One emotion we must except; and that is, contempt raised by certain improprieties: every improper <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> inspires us with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of contempt for the author; and if an improper act be at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> risible to provoke laughter, of which blunders and absurdities are noted instances, the two emotions of contempt and of laughter unite intimately in the mind, and produce externally what is termed a laugh of derision or of scorn. Hence objects that cause laughter may be distinguished into two kinds: they are either risible or ridiculous. A risible object is mirthful only; a ridiculous object is both mirthful and contemptible. The first raises an emotion of laughter that is altogether pleasant: the pleasant emotion of laughter raised by the other, is blended with the painful emotion of contempt; and the mixed emotion is termed the emotion of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. The pain a ridiculous object gives me, is resented and punished by a laugh of derision. A risible object, on the other hand, gives me no pain: it is altogether pleasant by a certain sort of titillation, which is expressed externally by mirthful laughter. See RIMICULE. Risible objects are so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and so well understood, that it is unnecessary to consume <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or time upon them. Take the few following examples: Falstaff: I do remember him at Clement's inn, like a man made after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> of a cheese-paring. When he was naked, he was, for all the world like a forked radish, with a head fantastically carved upon it with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a>, Henry IV, act iii. sc. 5. The foregoing is of disproportion. The following examples are of slight or imaginary misfortunes. Falstaff: Go fetch me a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of sack, put a toast in't. Have I liv'd to be carried in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, like a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">barrow</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s offal, and to be thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>! Well, if I be served such another trick, I'll have my brains <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>'en out and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>'d, and give them to a dog for a new-year's gift. The rogues slighted me into the river with as little remorse as they would have drown'd a bitch's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> puppies, fifteen i'th' litter; and you may know by my size that I have a kind of alacrity in sinking; if the bottom were as deep as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, I should <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. I had been drown'd, but that the shore was shelvy and shallow; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that I abhor: for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> swells a man; and what a thing should I have been when I had been swell'd? I should have been a mountain of mummy. Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, act iii. sc. 15. Falstaff. Fusilaff. Nay, you shall hear, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> Brook, what I have suffer'd to bring this woman to evil for your good. Being thus cram'm'd in the basker, a couple of Ford's knaves, his hinds, were call'd forth by their mistress, to carry me in the name of foul clothes to Datchet-lane. They took me on their shoulders, met the jealous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a> their master in the door, who ask'd them once or twice what they had in their basket. I quak'd for fear, lest the lunatic knave would have search'd it; but Fate, ordaining he should be a cuckold, held his hand. Well, on went he for a search, and away went I for foul clothes. But mark the sequel, Master Brook. I suffer'd the pangs of three egregious deaths: first, an intolerable fright, to be detected by a jealous rotten <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-wether; next, to be compass'd like a good bilbo, in the circumference of a peck, hilt to point, heel to head; and then to be stopt in, like a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, with stinking clothes that fretted in their own grease. Think of that, a man of my kidney; think of that, that am as subject to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> as butter; a man of continual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> and thaw; it was a miracle to 'scape suffocation. And in the height of this bath, when I was more than half stew'd in grease, like a Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, to be thrown into the Thames, and cool'd glowing hot, in that surge, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>; think of that; hissing hot; think of that, Mr Brook. Merry Wives of Windsor, act iii. sc. 17.

or REPEAT, in Music, the burden of a song; or the repetition of the first or other verses of a song at the end of each couplet.

RITTERHUSIUS

Pages 49-49
Conrad, a learned German civilian, born at Brunswick in 1560. He was professor of civil law at Altdorf, and published a variety of works, particularly as a civilian; together with an edition of Oppian in Greek and Latin; he was moreover an excellent critic; his notes upon many eminent authors having been inserted in the best editions of them. He died in 1613.

RITUAL

Pages 49-49

a book directing the order and manner to be observed in performing divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in a particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heathens had also their rituals, which contained their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies to be observed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, consecrating a temple or altar, in sacrificing, and deifying, in dividing the curiae, tribes, centuries, and, in general, in all their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies. There are several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in Cato's books, De re Rustica, which may give us some idea of the rituals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>.

RIVAL

Pages 49-49

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more persons who have the same pretensions; and which is properly applied to a competitor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and figuratively to an antagonist in any other pursuit.

RIVER

Pages 49-81

1 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">Definition</a>. Is a current of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, flowing in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">Bed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Channel from its source to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is appropriated to a considerable collection of waters, formed by the conflux of two or more Brooks, which deliver into its channel the united streams of several Rivulets, which have collected the supplies of many Rills trickling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from numberless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, and the torrents which carry off from the sloping grounds the surplus of every shower. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a> form one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> features of the surface of this globe, serving as voiders of all that is immediately redundant in our rains and springs, and also as boundaries and barriers, and even as highways, and in many countries as plentiful storehouses. They also fertilize our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> by laying upon our warm fields the richest mould, brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, where it would have remained useless for want of genial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Being such interesting objects of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, every branch acquires a proper name, and the whole acquires a sort of personal identity, of which it is frequently difficult to find the principle; for the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of waters which discharges itself into the sea is traced backwards to one of the sources, while all the contributing streams are lost, although their waters form the chief <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the collection. And sometimes the feeder in which the name is preserved is smaller than others which are united to the current, and which like a rich but ignoble <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> lose their name in that of the more illustrious family. Some rivers indeed are respectable even at their birth, coming at once in force from some great lake. Such is the Rio de la Plata, the river St Laurence, and the mighty streams which issue in all directions from the Baical lake. But, like the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, they are all of equal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and should take their name from one of the feeders of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. This is indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with a few, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. These, after having mixed their waters with those of the lake, resume their appearance and their name at its outlet. But in general their origin and progress, and even the features of their character, bear some resemblance (as has been prettily observed by Pliny) to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The river springs from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but its origin, the life of is in heaven. Its beginnings are insignificant, and its man, infancy is frivolous; it plays among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>; it waters a garden, or turns a little mill. Gathering strength in its youth, it becomes wild and impetuous. Impatient of the restraints which it still meets with in the hollows among the mountains, it is restless and fretful; quick in its turnings, and unsteady in its course. Now it is a roaring cataract, tearing up and overturning whatever opposes its progress, and it shoots headlong down from a rock; then it becomes a sullen and gloomy pool, buried in the bottom of a glen. Recovering breath by repose, it again dashes along, till tired of the uproar and mischief, it quits all that it has swept along, and leaves the opening of the valley strewn with the rejected waste. Now, quitting its retirement, it comes abroad into the world, journeying... neying with more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, through cultivated fields, yielding to circumstances, and winding round what would trouble it to overwhelm or remove. It passes through the populous cities and all the busy haunts of man, tendering its services on every side, and becomes the support and ornament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Now increased by numerous alliances, and advanced in its course of existence, it becomes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and stately in its motions, loves peace and quiet; and in majestic silence rolls on its mighty waters, till it is laid to rest in the vast <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the real lover of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, sees much to admire in the economy and mechanism of running waters; and there are few operations of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> which give him more opportunities of remarking the nice adjustment of the most simple means for attaining many purposes of most extensive beneficence. All mankind seems to have felt this. The heart of man is ever open (unless perverted by the habits of selfish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> and arrogant self-conceit) to impressions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. He who ascribes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> principle (debased though it be by the humbling abuses of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>) to the workings of fear alone, may betray the slavish meanness of his own mind, but gives a very unfair and a false <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the hearts of his neighbours. Lucretius was but half a philosopher when he penned his often quoted apophthegm. Indeed his own invocation shows how much the animal was blended with the sage. We apprehend, that whoever <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> read with an honest and candid mind, unbiassed by licentious wishes, the accounts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> superstitions, will acknowledge that the amiable emotions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> have had their share in creating the numerous divinities whose worship filled up their kalendars. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of heaven have in all ages and nations been the objects of a sincere worship. Next to them, the rivers seem to have attracted the grateful acknowledgments of the inhabitants of the adjacent countries. They have everywhere been considered as a sort of tutelar divinities; and each little district, every retired valley, had its river god, who was preferred to all others with a partial fondness. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSTULATION">expostulation</a> of Naaman the Syrian, who was offended with the prophet for enjoining him to wash in the river Jordan, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>. "What! (said he), are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, more excellent than all the waters of Judea? Might I not wash in them and be clean? So he went away wroth." In those countries particularly, where the rural labours, and the hopes of the shepherd and the husbandman, were not so immediately connected with the approach and recess of the sun, and depended rather on what happened in a far distant country by the falls of periodical rains or the melting of collected snows, the Nile, the Ganges, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>, the river of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, were the sensible agents of nature in procuring to the inhabitants of their fertile banks all their abundance, and they became the objects of grateful veneration. Their sources were sought out with anxious care even by conquering princes; and when found, were universally worshipped with the most affectionate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. These remarkable rivers, so eminently and so palpably beneficent, preserve to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, amidst every change of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and every increase of civilization and improvement, the fond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of the inhabitants of those fruitful countries through which they hold their stately course, and their waters are still held sacred. No progress of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> refinement, not all the corruption of luxurious sensuality, has been able to eradicate this plant of native growth from the heart of man. The sentiment is congenial to his nature, and therefore it is universal; and we could almost <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the feelings of every reader, whether he does not perceive it in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. Perhaps we may be mistaken in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the case of the corrupted inhabitants of the populous and busy cities, who are habituated to the fond <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of their own individual exertions as the sources of all their hopes. Give the shoemaker but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and a few tools, and he defies the powers of nature to disappoint him; but the simpler inhabitants of the country, the most worthy and the most respectable part of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, after equal, perhaps greater exertion both of skill and of industry, are more accustomed to resign themselves to the great ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and to look up to heaven for the "early and the latter rains," without which all their labours are fruitless. --- **extrema per illos** Numenque excedens terris vestigia fecit. And among the husbandmen and the shepherds of all nations and ages, we find the same fond attachment to their springs and rivulets. Fortunate senex, hic inter flumina nota Et fontes sacros frigus captabitis opacum, was the mournful ejaculation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Melibœus. We hardly know a river of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in our own country whose source is not looked on with some respect. We repeat our assertion, that this worship was the offspring of affection and gratitude, and that it is giving a very unfair and false picture of the human mind to ascribe these superstitions to the working of fear alone. These would have represented the river gods as seated on ruins, brandishing rooted-up trees, with angry looks, pouring out their sweeping torrents. But no such thing. The lively imagination of the Greeks felt, and expressed with an energy unknown to all other nations, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of the human soul. They figured the Naiads as beautiful nymphs, patterns of gentleness and of elegance. These are represented as partially attached to the children of men; and their interference in human affairs is always in acts of kind assistance and protection. They resemble, in this respect, the rural deities of the northern nations, the fairies, but without their caprices and resentments. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we attend to the descriptions and representations of their River-Gods, beings armed with power, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> which slavish fear never fails to couple with cruelty and vengeance, we shall find the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of affectionate trust and confidence in their kind dispositions. They are generally called by the respectable but endearing name of father. "Da Tyberi pater," says <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Mr Bruce says that the Nile at its source is called the abay or "father." We observe this word, or its radix, blended with many names of rivers of the east; and think it probable that when our traveller got this name from the inhabitants of the neighbourhood, they applied to the stream what is meant to express the tutelar or presiding presiding spirit. The river gods are always represented as venerable old men, to indicate their being coeval with the world. But it is always a cruda viricivque se- nectus, and they are never represented as oppressed with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and decrepitude. Their beards are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and flow- ing, their looks placid, their attitude easy, reclined on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, covered, as they are crowned, with never-fading sedges and bulrushes, and leaning on their urns, from which they pour out their plentiful and fertilizing streams. —Mr Bruce's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the sources of the Nile, and of the respect paid to the sacred waters, has not a frowning feature; and the hospitable old man, with his fair <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Irepone, and the gentle priesthood which peopled the little village of Geesh, form a con- trast with the neighbouring Galla (among whom a mi- litary leader was called the lamb, because he did not <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> pregnant women), which very clearly paints the inspiring principle of this superstition. Pliny says (lib. viii. 8.) that at the source of the Clitumnus there is an ancient temple highly respected. The presence and the power of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> are expressed by the fates which stand in the vestibule.—Around this temple are several little chapels, each of which covers a sa- cred fountain; for the Clitumnus is the father of sev- eral little rivers which unite their streams with him. At some distance below the temple is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> which divides the sacred waters from those which are open to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. No one must presume to set his foot in the streams above this bridge; and to step over any of them is an indignity which renders a person infamous. They can only be visited in a consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. Below the bridge we are permitted to bathe, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is incessantly occupied by the neighbouring vil- lagers. See also Vibius Sequent. Orbelinei, p. 101— 103. and 221—223. also Sueton. Caligula, c. 43. Virg. Georg. ii. 146. What is the cause of all this? The Clitumnus flows (near its source) through the richest pastures, through which it was carefully distributed by numberless <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>; and these nourished cattle of such spotless whiteness and extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, that they were sought for with eagerness over all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, as the most acceptable victims in their sacrifices. Is not this superstition then an ef- fusion of gratitude? Such are the dictates of kind-hearted nature in our breasts, before it has been vitiated by vanity and self- conceit, and we should not be ashamed of feeling the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. We hardly think of making any apology for dwelling a little on this incidental circumstance of the superstitious veneration paid to rivers. We cannot think that our readers will be displeased at having agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> excited in their minds, being always of opinion that the torch of true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> will not only enlighten the understanding, but also warm and cherish the affections of the heart. With respect to the origin of rivers, we have very little to offer in this place. It is obvious to every per- son, that besides the torrents which carry down into the rivers what part of the rains and melted snows is not absorbed by the soil or taken up by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which cover the earth, they are fed either immediately or re- motely by the springs. A few remarkable streams rush at once out of the earth in force, and must be consi- dered as the continuation of subterraneous rivers, whose origin we are therefore to seek out; and we do not know any circumstance in which their first beginnings differ from those of other rivers, which are formed by the union of little streams and rills, each of which has its own source in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or fountain. This question, therefore, What is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of nature, and what are the supplies which fill our springs? will be treated of under the word Spring. Whatever be the source of rivers, it is to be met with in almost every part of the globe. The crust of earth with which the rocky framing of this globe is covered is generally stratified. Some of these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> are extremely pervious to water, having but small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for its particles, and being very porous. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of gravelly strata in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Other strata are much more firm, or attract water more strongly, and refuse it passage. This is the case with firm rock and with clay. When a stratum of the first kind has one of the other immediately under it, the water re- maines in the upper stratum, and bursts out wherever the sloping sides of the hills cut off the strata, and this will be the form of a trickling spring, because the water in the porous stratum is greatly obstructed in its passage towards the outlet. As this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> formation of the earth is very general, we must have springs, and of course rivers or rivulets, in every corner where there are high grounds. Rivers flow from the higher to the low grounds. It is the arrangement of this elevation which distributes from the them over the surface of the earth. And this appears to be accomplished with considerable regularity; and, except the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Kobi on the confines of Chi- nese <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, we do not remember any very extensive tract of ground that is deprived of those channels for voiding the superfluous waters; and even there they are far from being redundant. The courses of rivers give us the best general method Course of for judging of the elevation of a country. Thus it the rivers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, appears that Savoy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> are the highest grounds of Europe, from whence the ground slopes in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> proceed the Danube and the Rhine, whose courses mark the two great val- leys, into which many lateral streams descend. The Po also and the Rhone come from the same head, and with a steeper and shorter course find their way to the sea through valleys of less breadth and length. On the west side of the valleys of the Rhine and the Rhone the ground rises pretty fast, so that few tribu- tary streams come into them from that side; and from this gentle elevation France slopes to the westward. If a line, nearly straight, but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, be drawn from the head of Savoy and Switzer- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> all the way to Solikamskoy in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, it will nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the most elevated part of Europe; for in this tract most of the rivers have their rise. On the left go off the various feeders of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, the Wesel, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIEMEN">Niemen</a>, the Duna, the Neva, the Dwina, the Petzora. On the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, after passing the feeders of the Danube, we see the sources of the Sereth and Pruth, the Dniester, the Bog, the Dnie- per, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>, and the mighty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. The elevation, however, is extremely moderate: and it appears from the levels taken with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> by the Abbé <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPPE">Chappe</a> d'Auteroche, that the head of the Volga is not more than 470 feet above the surface of the ocean. And we may observe here by the bye, that its mouth, where it discharges its waters into the Caspian sea, is undoubtedly lower by many feet, than the surface of the ocean. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, No 277. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, form two detached parts, which have little symmetry with the rest of Europe. A chain of mountains begins in <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a>, and stretches due south to near the Caspian sea, dividing Europe from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. About three or four degrees north of the Caspian sea it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> to the south-east, traverses western Tartary, and passing between the Tengis and Zaizan lakes, it then branches to the east and south. The eastern branch runs to the shores of Korea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>. The southern branch traverses Turkestan and Thibet, separating them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVA">Ava</a> joins an arm stretching from the great eastern branch, and here forms the centre of a very singular radiation. Chains of mountains issue from it in every direction. Three or four of them keep very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, dividing the continent into narrow slips, which have each a great river flowing in the middle, and reaching to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBODIA">Cambodia</a>, and Cochin-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a>. From the same central point proceeds another great ridge due east, and passes a little north of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> in China. We called this a singular centre; for though it sends off so many branches, it is by no means the most elevated part of the continent. In the triangle which is included between the first southern ridge (which comes from between the lakes Tengis and Zaizan), the great eastern ridge, and its branch which almost unites with the southern ridge, lies the Butan, and part of Thibet, and the many little rivers which occupy its surface flow southward and eastward, uniting a little to the north of the centre often mentioned, and then pass through a gorge eastward into China. And it is farther to be observed, that these great ridges do not appear to be seated on the highest parts of the country; for the rivers which correspond to them are at no great distance from them, and receive their chief supplies from the other sides. This is remarkably the case with the great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBY">Oby</a>, which runs almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the ridge from the lakes to Nova Zembla. It receives its supplies from the east, and indeed it has its source far east. The higher grounds (if we except the ridges of mountains which are boundaries) of the continent seem to be in the country of the Calmucs, about 95° east from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and latitude 43° or 45° north. It is represented as a fine though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> country, having many little rivers which lose themselves in the sand, or end in little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> lakes. This elevation stretches north-east to a great distance; and in this tract we find the heads of the Irish, Selenga, and Tunguska (the great feeders of the Oby), the Olenitz, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENA">Lena</a>, the Yana, and some other rivers, which all go off to the north. On the other side we have the great river Amur, and many smaller rivers, whose names are not familiar. The Hoangho, the great river of China, rises on the south side of the great eastern ridge we have so often mentioned. This elevation, which is a continuation of the former, is somewhat of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, being very sandy, and at present is a desert of prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is described, however, as interspersed with vast tracts of rich pasture; and we know that it was formerly the residence of a great nation, who came south, by the name of Turks, and possessed themselves of most of the richest kingdoms of Asia. In the south-western extremity of this country are found remains not only of barbaric magnificence, but even of cultivation and elegance. It was a profitable privilege granted by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great to some adventurers to search these sandy deserts for remains of former opulence, and many pieces of delicate workmanship (though not in a style which we would admire) in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver were found. Vaults were found buried in the sand filled with written papers, in a character wholly unknown; and a wall was discovered extending several miles, built with hewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and ornamented with corniche and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>. But we are forgetting ourselves, and return to the consideration of the distribution of the rivers on the surface of the earth. A great ridge of mountains begins at the south-east corner of the Euxine sea, and proceeds eastward, ranging along the south side of the Caspian, and still advancing unites with the mountains first mentioned in Thibet, sending off some branches to the south, which divide <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, India, and Thibet. From the south side of this ridge flow the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, Tigris, Indus, Ganges, &c. and from the north the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a> and many unknown streams. There is a remarkable circumstance in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe. Although it seems to be nearest to the greatest elevations, it seems also to have places of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>. We have already said that the Caspian sea is lower than the ocean. There is in its neighbourhood another great basin of salt water, the lake Aral, which receives the waters of the Oxus or Gishon, which were said to have formerly run into the Caspian sea. There cannot, therefore, be a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of these two basins; neither have they any outlet, though they receive great rivers. There is another great lake in the very middle of Persia, the Zare or Zara, which receives the river Hindemend, of near 250 miles length, besides other streams. There is another such in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. The sea of Sodom and Gomorrah is another instance. And in the high countries we mentioned, there are many small salt lakes, which receive little rivers, and have no outlet. The lake Zara in Persia, however, is the only one which indicates a considerable hollow of the country. It is now ascertained, by actual survey, that the sea of Sodom is considerably higher than the Mediterranean. This feature is not, however, peculiar to Asia. It obtains also in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, whose rivers we now proceed to mention. Of them, however, we know very little. The Nile of Africa, indeed is perhaps better known than any river out of Europe; and of its source and progress we have given a full account in a separate article. See Nile. By the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> kept by Mr Bruce at Gondar in 1770 and 1771, it appears that the greatest rains are about the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. He says that at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> it doubles its rains. The calish or canal is opened at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> about the 9th of August, when the river has risen 14 peeks (each 21 inches), and the waters begin to decrease about the 10th of September. Hence we may form a conjecture concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> which the latter employs in coming from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. Mr Bruce supposes it 9 days, which supposes a velocity not less than 14 feet in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; a thing past <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, and inconsistent with all our notions. The general slope of the river is greatly diminished by several great cataracts; and Mr Bruce expressly says, that He might have come down from Sennar to the cataract's of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYENE">Syene</a> in a boat, and that it is navigable for boats far above Sennaar. He came from Syene to Cairo by water. We apprehend that no boat would venture down a stream moving even six feet in a second, and none could row up it the velocity was three feet. As the waters begin to decrease about the 10th of September, we must conclude that the water then flowing past Cairo had left Abyssinia when the rains had greatly abated. Judging in this way, we must still allow the stream a velocity of more than six feet. Had the first swell at Cairo been noticed in 1770 or 1771, we might have guessed better. The year that Thevenot was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the first swell of eight peaks was observed Jan. 28. The calash was opened for 14 weeks on Aug. 14, and the waters began to decrease on Sept. 23 having risen to 21½ pks. We may suppose a similar progress at Cairo corresponding to Mr. Bruce's observations at Gondar, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> everything five days earlier. We understand that some of our gentlemen stationed far up the Ganges have had the curiosity to take notes of the swellings of that river, and compare them with the overflowings at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>, and that their observations are about to be made public. Such accounts are valuable additions to our practical knowledge, and we shall not neglect to insert the information in some kindred article of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The same mountains which attract the tropical vapours, and produce the fertilizing inundations of the Nile, perform the same office to the famous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, whose existence has often been accounted fabulous, and with whose course we have very little acquaintance. The researches of the gentlemen of the African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> render its existence no longer doubtful, and have greatly excited the public curiosity. For a farther account of its tract, see NIGER. From the great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the very moderate size, of the rivers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> all the way south of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>, we conclude that the western shore is the most elevated, and that the mountains are at no great distance inland. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the rivers at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELINDA">Melinda</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOFALA">Sofala</a> are of a magnitude which indicates a much longer course. But of all this we speak with much uncertainty. The frame-work (so to call it) of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> is better known, and is singular. A chain of mountains begins, or at least is found, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 110° west of London, and latitude 40° north, on the northern confines of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and stretching southward through that kingdom, forms the ridge of the neck of land which separates North from South America, and keeping almost close to the shore, ranges along the whole western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of South America, terminating at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>. In its course it sends off branches, which after separating from it for a few leagues rejoin it again, inclosing valleys of great extent from north to south, and of prodigious elevation. In one of these, under the equatorial sun, stands the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Quito, in the midst of extensive fields of barley, oats, wheat, and gardens containing apples, pears, and gooseberries, and in short all the grains and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the cooler parts of Europe; and although the vine is also there in perfection, the olive is wanting. Not a dozen miles from it, in the low countries, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and all the fruits of the torrid zone, find their congenial heat, and the inhabitants swelter under a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sun. At a small distance on the other hand tower aloft the Pinnacles of Pichineha, Corambourou, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a>, crowned with never-melting snows. The individual mountains of this stupendous range not only exceed in height all others in the world (if we except the Peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>, Mount Etna, and Mont Blanc); but they are set down on a base incomparably more elevated than any other country. They cut off therefore all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a> and the inland continent; and no rivers are to be found on the west coast of South America which have any considerable length of course or body of waters. The country is drained, like Africa, in the opposite direction. Not 100 miles from the city of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, which lies almost on the sea-shore, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the foot of the high Cordilleras, arises out of a small lake the Maragnon or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a>'s river, which, after running northward for about 100 miles, takes an easterly direction, and crosses nearly the broadest part of South America, and falls into the great western ocean at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARA">Para</a>, after a course of not less than 3500 miles. In the first half of its descent it receives a few middle-sized rivers from the north, and from the south it receives the great river Combos, springing from another little lake not 50 miles distant from the head of the Maragnon, and inclosing between them a wide extent of country. Then it receives the Yuta, the Yuerra, the Cuchivara, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARANA">Parana</a> Mire, each of which is equal to the Rhine; and then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, which has flowed above 1300 miles. At their junction the breadth is so great, that neither shore can be seen by a person standing up in a canoe: so that the united stream must be about six miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. In this majestic form it rolls along at a prodigious rate through a flat country, covered with impenetrable forests, and most of it as yet untrodden by human feet. Mr. Condamine, who came down the stream, says, that all is silent as the desert, and the wild beasts and numberless birds crowd round the boat, eying it as some animal of which they did not seem afraid. The bed was cut deep through an equal and yielding soil, which seemed rich in every part, if he could judge by the vegetation, which was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the extreme. What an addition this to the possible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this globe! A narrow slip along each bank of this mighty river would equal in surface the whole of Europe, and would probably exceed it in general fertility; and although the velocity in the main stream was great, he observed that it was extremely moderate, nay almost still, at the sides; so that in those parts where the country was inhabited by men, the Indians paddled up the river with perfect ease. Boats could go from Para to near the mouth of the Madeira in 38 days, which is near 1200 miles. Mr. Condamine made an observation during his passage down the Maragnon, which is extremely curious and instructive, although it puzzled him very much. He observed that the tide was sensible at a vast distance from the mouth: It was very considerable at the junction of the Madeira; and he supposes that it might have been observed much farther up. This appeared to him very surprising, because there could be no doubt but that the surface of the water there was higher by a great many feet than the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of the Atlantic ocean at the mouth of the river. It was there- fore very natural for him to ascribe the tide in the Maragnon to the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> on its waters; and this explanation was the more reasonable, because the river extends in the direction of terrestrial longitude, which by the Newtonian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is most favourable to the production of a tide. Journeying as he did in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> canoe, we cannot suppose that he had much leisure or conveniency for calculations, and therefore are not surprised that he did not see that even this circumstance was of little avail in so small or shallow a body of water. He carefully noted, however, the times of high and low water as he passed along. When arrived at Para, he found not only that the high water was later and later as we are farther from the mouth, but he found that at one and the same instant there were several points of high water between Para and the confluence of the Madeira, with points of low water intervening. This conclusion was easily drawn from his own observations, although he could not see at one instant the high waters in different places. He had only to compute the time of high water at a particular spot, on the day he observed it at another; allowing, as usual, for the moon's change of position. The result of his observations therefore was, that the surface of the river was not an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INCLINED_PLANE">inclined <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> whose slope was lessened by the tide of flood at the mouth of the river, but that it was a waving line, and that the propagation of the tide up the river was nothing different from the propagation of any other wave. We may conceive it clearly, though imperfectly, in this way. Let the place be noted where the tide happens 12 hours later than at the mouth of the river. It is evident that there is also a tide at the very mouth at the same instant; and, since the ocean tide had withdrawn itself during the time that the former tide had proceeded so far up the river, and the tide of ebb is successively felt above as well as the tide of flood, there must be a low water between these two high waters. Newton had pointed out this curious fact, and observed that the tide at London-Bridge, which is 43 feet above the sea, is not the same with that at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVESEND">Gravesend</a>, but the preceding tide (see Phil. Trans. 67). This will be more particularly insisted on in another place. Not far from the head of the Maragnon, the Cordilleras send off a branch to the north-east, which reaches and ranges along the shore of the Mexican <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, and the Rio Grande de Sta Martha occupies the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> between the ridges. Another ridge ranges with interruption along the east coast of Terra Firma, so that the whole waters of this country are collected into the Oroonoko. In like manner the north and east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> are hemmed in by mountainous ridges, through which there is no considerable passage; and the ground sloping backwards, all the waters of this immense tract are collected from both sides by many considerable rivers into the great river Paraguay, or Rio de la Plata, which runs down the middle of this country for more than 1400 miles, and falls into the sea through a vast mouth in latitude 35°. Thus the whole of South America seems as if it had been formerly surrounded by a mound, and been a great basin. The ground in the middle, where the Parana, the Madeira, and the Plata, take their rise, is an immense marsh, uninhabitable for its exhalations, and quite impervious in its present state. The manner in which the continent of North America is watered, or rather drained, has also some peculiarities. By looking at the map, one will observe first of all a general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the whole of the best known part into two, by the valleys in which the beds of the rivers St Laurence and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> are situated. The head of this is occupied by a singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of fresh water seas or lakes, viz. the lakes Superior and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICHIGAN">Michigan</a>, which empty themselves into Lake Huron by two cataracts. This again runs into Lake Erie by the river Detroit, and the Erie pours its waters into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a> by the famous fall of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NIAGARA">Niagara</a>, and from the Ontario proceeds the great river St Lawrence. The ground to the south-west of the lakes Superior and Erie is somewhat lower, and the middle of the valley is occupied by the Mississippi and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSOURI">Missouri</a>, which receive on both sides a number of smaller streams, and having joined proceed to the south, under the name Mississippi. In latitude 37°, this river receives into its bed the Ohio, a river of equal magnitude, and the Cherokee river, which drains all the country lying at the back of the United States, separated from them by the ranges of the Appalachian mountains. The Mississippi is now one of the chief rivers on the globe, and proceeds due south, till it falls into the Mexican <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> through several shifting mouths, which greatly resemble those of the Danube and the Nile, having run above 1200 miles. The elevated country between this bed of the Mississippi and St Laurence and the Atlantic ocean is drained on the east side by a great number of rivers, some of which are very considerable, and of long course; because instead of being nearly at right <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the coast, as in other countries, they are in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> parallel to it. This is more remarkably the case with Hudson's river, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>, Patomack, Rapahannoc, &c. Indeed the whole of North America seems to consist of ribs or beams laid nearly parallel to each other from north to south, and the rivers occupy the interstices. All those which empty themselves into the bay of Mexico are parallel and almost perfectly straight, unlike what are seen in other parts of the world. The westernmost of them all, the North River, as it is named by the Spaniards, is nearly as long as the Mississippi. We are very little informed as yet of the distribution of rivers on the north-west coast of America, or the course of those which run into Hudson's or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAFFIN_S_BAY">Baffin's bay</a>. The Maragnon is undoubtedly the greatest river in the world, both as to length of run and the vast body of water which it rolls along. The other great rivers succeed nearly in the following order: | Maragnon, | Amur, | |-----------|-------| | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, | Oroonoko, | | Nile, | Ganges, | | St Laurence, | Euphrates, | | Hoangho, | Danube, | | Rio de la Plata, | Don, | | Yenisey, | Indus, | | Mississippi, | Dnieper, | | Volga, | Duina, | | Oby, | &c. | We We have been much assisted in this account of the course of rivers, and their distribution over the globe, by a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANISPHERE">planisphere</a> map of the world published by Mr Bode astronomer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>. The ranges of mountains are there laid down with philosophical discernment and precision; and we recommend it to the notice of our geographers. We cannot divine what has caused Mr Buffon to say that the course of most rivers is from east to west or from west to east. No physical point of his system seems to require it, and it needs only that we look at his own map to see its falsity. We should naturally expect to find the general course of rivers nearly perpendicular to the line of sea-coast; and we find it so; and the chief exceptions are in opposition to Mr Buffon's assertion. The structure of America is so particular, that very few of its rivers have their general course in this direction. We proceed now to consider the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of rivers; a subject which naturally resolves itself into two parts, theoretical and practical. Part I. THEORY OF THE MOTION OF RIVERS AND <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">CANALS</a>. THE importance of this subject needs no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>. Every nation, every country, every city is interested in it. Neither our wants, our comforts, nor our pleasures, can dispense with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of it. We must conduct their waters to the centre of our dwellings; we must secure ourselves against their ravages; we must employ them to drive those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> which, by compensating for our personal weakness, make a few able to perform the work of thousands; we employ them to water and fertilize our fields, to decorate our mansions, to cleanse and embellish our cities, to preserve or extend our demesnes, to transport from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> to county every thing which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, convenience, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, has rendered precious to man; for these purposes we must confine and govern the mighty rivers, we must preserve or change the beds of the smaller streams, draw off from them what shall water our fields, drive our machines, or supply our houses. We must keep up their waters for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, or supply their places by canals; we must drain our fens, and defend them when drained; we must understand their motions, and their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of secret, slow, but unceasing action, that our bridges, our wharfs, our dykes, may not become heaps of ruins. Ignorant how to proceed in these daily recurring <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, how often do we see projects of high <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> and heavy expense fail of their object, leaving the state burdened with works not only useless but frequently hurtful? This has long been a most interesting subject of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in Italy, where the fertility of their fields is not more indebted to their rich soil and happy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, than to their numerous derivations from the rivers which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> them; and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, where their very existence requires unceasing attention to the waters, which are every moment ready to swallow up the inhabitants; and where the inhabitants, having once subdued this formidable enemy, have made those very waters their indefatigable drudges, transporting through every corner of the country the materials of the most extensive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this globe. Such having been our incessant occupations with moving waters, we should expect that while the operative artists are continually furnishing facts and experiments, the man of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> and scientific curiosity, excited by the importance of the subject, would ere now have made considerable progress in the science; and that the professional engineer would be daily acting from established principle, and be seldom disappointed in his expectations. Unfortunately the reverse of this is nearly the true state of the case; each engineer is obliged to collect the greatest part of his knowledge from his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and by many dear-bought <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his future operations, in which he still proceeds with anxiety and hesitation: for we have not yet acquired principles of theory, and experiments have not yet been collected and published by which an empirical practice might be safely formed. Many experiments of inestimable value are daily made; but they remain with their authors, who seldom have either leisure, ability, or generosity, to add them to the public stock. The motion of waters has been really so little investigated as yet, that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRAULICS">hydraulics</a> may still be called a new as yet in study. We have merely skimmed over a few common notions concerning the motions of water; and the mathematicians of the first order seem to have contented themselves with such views as allowed them to entertain themselves with elegant applications of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a>. This, however, has not been their fault. They rarely had any opportunity of doing more, for want of a knowledge of facts. They have made excellent use of the few which have been given them; but it required much labour, great variety of opportunity, and great expense, to learn the multiplicity of things which are combined even in the simplest cases of water in motion. These are seldom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of the mathematician; and he is without blame when he enjoys the pleasures within his reach, and cultivates the science of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> in its most abstracted form. Here he makes a progress which is the boast of human reason, being almost insured from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> by the intellectual simplicity of his subject. But when we turn our attention to material objects, and, without knowing either the size and shape of the elementary particles, or the laws which nature has prescribed for their action, presume to foresee their effects, calculate their exertions, direct their actions, what must be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>? Nature shows her independence with respect to our notions, and, always faithful to the laws which are enjoined, and of which we are ignorant, she never fails to thwart our views, to disconcert our projects, and render useless all our efforts. To wish to know the nature of the elements is vain, Proper and our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> organs are insufficient for the study. To suppose what we do not know, and to fancy shapes and sizes at will; this is to raise phantoms, and will produce a system, but will not prove a foundation for any science. But to interrogate Nature herself, study the laws which she so faithfully observes, catch her, as we say, in the fact, and thus wrest from her the secret; this is the only way to become her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and it is the only procedure consistent with good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. And we see, that soon after Kepler detected the laws of the planetary motions, when Galileo discovered the uniform <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCELERATION">acceleration</a> of gravity, when Pascal discovered the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and Newton discovered the laws of attraction and the track of a ray of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">hydrostatics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, quickly became bodies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> doctrine; and the deductions from their respective theories were found fair representations of the phenomena of nature. Whenever a man has discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature, he has laid the foundation of a science, and he has given us a new <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of subjecting our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> some element hitherto independent: and so long as groups of natural operations follow a route which appears to us whimsical, and will not admit our calculations, we may be assured that we are ignorant of the principle which connects them all, and regulates their procedure. This is remarkably the case with several phenomena in the motions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and particularly in the motion of water in a bed or conduit of any kind. Although the first geniuses of Europe have for this century past turned much of their attention to this subject, we are almost ignorant of the general laws which may be observed in their motions. We have been able to select very few points of resemblance, and every case remains nearly an individual. About 150 years ago we discovered, by experience only, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and velocity of water issuing from a small orifice, and, after much labour, have extended this to any orifice; and this is almost the whole of our confidential knowledge. But as to the uniform course of the streams which water the face of the earth, and the maxims which will certainly regulate this agreeably to our wishes, we are in a manner totally ignorant. Who can pretend to say what is the velocity of a river of which you tell him the breadth, the depth, and the declivity? Who can say what swell will be produced in different parts of its course, if a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> or weir of giving dimensions be made in it, or a bridge be thrown across it; or how much its waters will be raised by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> another stream into it, or sunk by taking off a branch to drive a mill? Who can say with confidence what must be the dimensions or slope of this branch, in order to furnish the water that is wanted, or the dimensions and slope of a canal which shall effectually drain a fenney district?
