But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the centre of gravity is placed higher above the keel, the radius of vibration will not only be diminished, but an additional force to oppose the motion of rolling will be communicated to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship's bottom which is below the centre of gravity. So far as relates to the effect of rolling, when produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stowage of the ballast, and to the manner by which it may be prevented, viz. a change of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or disposition of the ballast, we shall endeavour to explain under the article <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">Trim</a>. It may, however, be necessary to remark, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the ship's bottom may also contribute to diminish this movement considerably. Many fatal disasters have happened to ships arising from violent rollings; as the loss of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, loosening of the cannon, and straining violently on the decks and sides, so as to weaken the ship to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. See Pitching. ROLLING-Press. See Rolling-Press. ROLLING-Tackle, a pulley or purchase fastened to that part of a sail-yard which is to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> of the mast, in order to confine the yard <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the leeward when the sail is furled. It is used to prevent the yard from having a great friction against the mast in a high <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which would be equally pernicious to both.

ROLLO

Pages 124-124

the conqueror of Normandy, was a Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, banished from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by Harold Harfager, who conquered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> in 870, on account of the piracies he exercised. He first retired with his fleet among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Scotland, whither the flower of the Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> had fled for refuge ever since Harold had become <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He was there received with open arms by those warriors, who, eager for conquest and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, waited only for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> to undertake some glorious enterprise. Rollo setting himself at their head, and, seeing his power formidable, sailed towards England, which had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it were a field open on all sides to the violence of the northern nations. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Alfred had some years before established such order in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, that Rollo, after several fruitless attempts, despaired of forming there such a settlement as should make him amends for the loss of his own country. He pretended, therefore, to have had a supernatural dream, which promised him a glorious fortune in France, and which served at least to support the ardour of his followers. The weakness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in that kingdom, and the confusion in which it was involved, were still more persuasive reasons to insure them of success. Having therefore sailed up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, he immediately took that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, then called Neustria, and making it his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of arms, he advanced up to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, to which he laid siege in form. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at length ended in the entire cession of Neustria, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the Simple was obliged to give up to Rollo and his Normans in order to purchase a peace. Rollo received it in perpetuity to himself and his posterity, as a feudal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> dependent on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the interview between Charles and this new duke gives us a curious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the manners of these Normans (as they were called by foreigners); for the latter would not take the oath of fealty to his sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> any other way than by placing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> within those of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; and absolutely refused to kiss his feet, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> then required. It was with great difficulty he was prevailed on to let one of his warriors perform this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in his stead; but the officer to whom Rollo deputed this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, suddenly raised the king's foot so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that he overturned him on his back; a piece of rudeness which was only laughed at; to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> were the Normans feared, and Charles despised. Soon after, Rollo was persuaded to embrace Christianity, and he was baptized with much ceremony by the archbishop of Rouen in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. As soon as he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself in full possession of Normandy, he exhibited such virtues as rendered the province happy, and deserved to make his former outrages forgotten. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a>, wise, and liberal, this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of pirates became, after Alfred, the greatest and most humane <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ROLLOCK

Pages 124-125

ROBERT, the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Rollock of Powis, in the vicinity of Stirling. He was born in the year 1555, and was taught the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin tongue by a person then eminent in his profession. He was sent from school to the university of St Andrews, where his progress was so rapid, that he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> soon after he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. The magistrates of Edinburgh having petitioned the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to found a university in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, they obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, by which they were allowed all the privileges of a university, which was built in 1582, and Mr Rollock was chosen principal and professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He was soon famous in the university on account of his lectures, and among his countrymen at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> for his persuasive <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of preaching. In the year 1593, Principal Rollock and others were appointed by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to confer with the popish lords; and in the following year he was one of those made choice of by the general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, to present his majesty with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, entitled, the dangers which, through the impunity of excommunicated papists, traffickers with the Spaniards, and other enemies of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and state, are imminent to the true religion professed within this realm, his majesty's person, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of this our native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His zeal against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a> was carried to excess, and he seems to have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was incumbent on the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> to punish idolatry with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In the year 1595, he was empowered, along with others, to visit the different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> in Scotland, with a view to enquire into the doctrine and practice of the different masters, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> adopted by them, and the state of their rents and living, which they were ordered to report to the next general assembly. He was chosen moderator of the general assembly in the year 1597, at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he was fortunate enough to obtain the redress of several glaring abuses. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was spent in conducting the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, yet Spottiswood assures us that he would rather have preferred retirement and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. Indeed, indeed, the feebleness of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was not equal to the hurry and bustle of public life, which he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> equal to the retirement of study. He was very much affected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the pains of which he bore with the fortitude and resignation of a Christian. He died at Edinburgh on the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of February 1598, in the 43rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, beseeching his brethren, in his last moments, to be more dutiful and obedient to their gracious sovereign. Short as his life was, he published many works, of which the following is a summary. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the first book of Beza's Questions; on St Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians; on the prophet Daniel; a Logical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of St Paul's Epistle to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; some Questions and Answers concerning the covenant of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> and the Sacraments; a treatise of Effectual Calling; a Commentary on the Epistles of Paul to the Thessalonians and Philemon; on fifteen select psalms; on the Gospel of St John, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of the four Evangelists upon the death, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, and ascension of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; certain Sermons on several places of St Paul's Epistles; a Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians; a Logical Analysis of the Epistle to the Hebrews; of the Epistle to the Galatians; a Commentary upon the first two chapters of the first Epistle of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>; a Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">Justification</a>, and another of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">Excommunication</a>. All these, except the Sermons, were written in Latin. The following epitaph seems to prove that Rollock was much esteemed at the university over which he presided. Te Rolloce, extincto, urbs moesta, academia moesta est; Et tota exequis Scotia moesta tuis. Uno in te nobis dederat Deus omnia, in uno Te Deus eripuit omnia quae dederit.

ROLLS

Pages 121-121

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-works, are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> barrels which serve to bruise the canes, and to express the juice. These are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> hollow, and their cavities are filled up with wood, the cylinders of which are properly the rollers.

ROLLS

Pages 117-117

rolls, except satins, gauzes, and crapes; which are apt to break, and take plait not easy to be got out, if folded otherwise. Ribbons, laces, gallons, and paduas of all kinds, are also thus rolled. A roll of tobacco, is tobacco in the leaf, twisted on the mill, and wound twist over twist about a stick or roller. A great deal of tobacco is sold in America in rolls of various weights; and it is not till its arrival in England, Spain, France, and Holland, that it is cut. A roll of parchment, properly denotes the quantity of 60 skins. The ancients made all their books up in the form of rolls; and in Cicero's time the libraries consisted wholly of such rolls. ROLL, in Law, signifies a schedule or parchment which may be rolled up by the hand into the form of a pipe. In these schedules of parchment, all the pleadings, memorials, and acts of court, are entered and filed by the proper officer; which being done, they become records of the court. Of these there are in the exchequer several kinds, as the great wardrobe roll, the cofferer's roll, the subsidy-roll, &c. Roll is also used for a list of the names of persons of the same condition, or of those who have entered into the same engagement. Thus a court-roll of a manor, is that in which the names, rents, and services, of each tenant are copied and enrolled. Calves-head Roll, a roll in the two temples in which every benchers is taxed yearly at 2s. every barrister at 1s. 6d. and every gentleman under the bar at 1s. to the cook and other officers of the house, in consideration of a dinner of calves' heads provided in Easter-term. Muster-Roll, that in which are entered the soldiers of every troop, company, regiment, &c. As soon as a soldier's name is written down on the roll, it is death for him to desert.

ROLLS-OFFICE

Pages 117-117

ROLLS-Office, is an office in Chancery-lane, London, appointed for the custody of the rolls and records in chancery. Master of the Rolls. See MASTER of the Rolls. Rider-Roll, a schedule of parchment frequently sewed or added to some part of a roll or record. ROLLS of Parchment, are the manuscript registers or rolls of the proceedings of our ancient parliaments, which before the invention of printing were all engrossed on parchment, and proclaimed openly in every county. In these rolls are also contained a great many decisions of difficult points of law, which were frequently in former times referred to the decision of that high court. ROLL, or Roller, is also a piece of wood, iron, brass, &c. of a cylindrical form, used in the construction of several machines, and in several works and manufactures. Thus in the glass manufacture they have a running-roll, which is a thick cylinder of cast brass, which serves to conduct the melted glass to the end of the table on which large looking-glasses, &c. are cast. Founders also use a roll to work the sand which they use in making their mould. The presses called calendars, as serving to calendar stuffs withal, consist, among other essential parts, of two rollers. It is also between the two rollers that the waves are given to silks, mohairs, and other stuffs proper to be tabbed. Impressions from copper-plates are also taken by passing the plate and paper between two rollers. See Rolling-press PRINTING. ROLLS, in fluting-mills, &c. are two iron instruments of a cylindrical form, which serve to draw or stretch out plates of gold, silver, and other metals. ROLLS, in sugar-works, are two large iron barrels which serve to bruise the canes, and to express the juice. These are cast hollow, and their cavities are filled up with wood, the cylinders of which are properly the rollers. ROLLER, in Surgery, a long and broad bandage, usually of linen-cloth, rolled round any part of the body, to keep it in, or dispose it to a state of health. ROLLI, PAUL, an Italian poet, was born at Rome in 1687. He was the son of an architect, and a pupil of the celebrated Gravina, who inspired him with a taste for learning and poetry. An intelligent and learned English lord having brought him to London, introduced him to the royal family as a master of the Tuscan language. Rolli remained in England till the death of Queen Caroline his protector, and the patroness of literature in general. He returned to Italy in 1747, where he died in 1767, in the 80th year of his age, leaving behind him a very curious collection in natural history, &c. and a valuable and well chosen library. His principal works first appeared in London in 1735, in 8vo. They consist of Odes in blank verse, Elegies, Songs, &c. after the manner of Catullus, and a Collection of Epigrams, printed at Florence in 1776, in 8vo, to which is prefixed an account of his life by the abbe Fondini. What Martial said of his own Collection may be said of this, "That there are few good, but many indifferent or bad, pieces in it." Rolli, however, bore the character of one of the best Italian poets of his age. During his stay in London, he procured editions of several authors of his own country. The principal of these were, the Satires of Ariosto, the Burlesque Works of Berni, Varchi, &c. 2 vols, in 8vo, which possess considerable merit. The Decameron of Boccace, 1727, in 4to and folio; in which he has faithfully copied the celebrated and valuable edition published by the Juntes in 1527; and, lastly, of the elegant Lucrezia of Marchetti, which, after the manuscript was revised, was printed at London. in 1717, in 8vo, through the influence and attention of Rollin. This edition is beautiful; but the work is thought to be of a pernicious tendency. He likewise translated into Italian verse the Paradise Lost of Milton, printed at London in folio, in 1735; and the Odes of Anacreon, London 1739, in 8vo. ROLLIN. Charles, a justly celebrated French writer, was the son of a cutter at Paris, and was born there on the 3rd of January 1661. He studied at the college Du Plessis, in which he obtained a bursary through the interest of a Benedictine monk of the White Mantle, whom he had served at table, and who discovered in him some marks of genius. Here he acquired the regard of M. Gobinet, principal of that college, who had a particular esteem for him. After having studied humanity and philosophy at the college of Du Plessis, he applied to divinity three years at the Sorbonne; but he did not prosecute this study, and never rose in the church higher than to the rank of a tonsured priest. He afterwards became professor of rhetoric in the same college; and, in 1688, succeeded Horfan, his master, as professor of eloquence, in the royal college. No man ever exercised the functions of it with greater eclat: he often made Latin orations, to celebrate the memorable events of the times; and frequently accompanied them with poems, which were read and esteemed by everybody. In 1694, he was chosen rector of the university; and continued in that office two years, which was then a mark of distinction. By virtue of his office, he spoke the annual panegyric upon Louis XIV. He made many very useful regulations in the university; and particularly revived the study of the Greek language, which was then much neglected. He substituted academical exercises in the place of tragedies; and introduced the practice which had been formerly observed, of causing the students to get by heart passages of Scripture. He was a man of indefatigable attention; and trained innumerable persons, who did honour to the church, the state, and the army. The first president Portail was pleased one day to reproach Rollin in a jocular strain, as if he exceeded even himself in doing business: to whom Rollin replied, with that plainness and sincerity which was natural to him, "It becomes you well, Sir, to reproach me with this: it is this habit of labour in me which has distinguished you in the place of advocate-general, which has raised you to that of first president: you owe the greatness of your fortune to me." Upon the expiration of the rectorship, Cardinal Noailles engaged him to superintend the studies of his nephews, who were in the college of Laon; and in this office he was agreeably employed, when, in 1699, he was with great reluctance made coadjutor to the principal of the college of Beauvais. This college was then a kind of desert, inhabited by very few students, and without any manner of discipline: but Rollin's great reputation and industry soon re-peopled it, and made it that flourishing society it has ever since continued. In this situation he continued till 1712; when the war between the Jesuits and the Jansenists drawing towards a crisis, he fell a sacrifice to the prevalence of the former. Father le Tellier, the king's confessor, a furious agent of the Jesuits, infused into his master prejudices against Rollin, whose connections with Cardinal de Noailles would alone have sufficed to have made him a Jansenist; and on this account he lost his share in the principality of Beauvais. No man, however, could have lost less in this than Rollin, who had everything left him that was necessary to make him happy; retirement, books, and enough to live on. He now began to be employed upon Quintilian; an author he justly valued, and law neglected not without uneasiness. He retrenched in him whatever he thought rather curious than useful for the instruction of youth; he placed summaries or contents at the head of each chapter; and he accompanied the text with short select notes. His edition appeared in 1715, in 2 vols. 12mo, with an elegant preface, setting forth his method and views. In 1710, the university of Paris, willing to have a head suitable to the importance of their interests in a very critical conjuncture of affairs, chose Rollin again rector: but he was displaced in about two months by a lettre de cachet. The university had presented to the parliament a petition, in which it protested against taking any part in the adjustment of the late disputes; and their being congratulated in a public oration by Rollin on this step, occasioned the letter which ordered them to choose a rector of more moderation. Whatever the university might suffer by the removal of Rollin, the public was probably a gainer; for he now applied himself to compose his Treatise upon the Manner of Studying and Teaching the Belles Lettres, which was published, two volumes in 1726, and two more in 1728, 8vo. This work has been justly esteemed for the sentiments of religion which animate its author, whose zeal for the public good prompted him to select the choicest passages of Greek and Latin authors. The style is sufficiently elegant, but the language on some occasions is not remarkable for delicacy; and in the book altogether, there is neither much order nor depth. The author has indeed spoken of common things agreeably, and has spoken as an orator on subjects which demanded the investigation of the philosopher. One can scarcely reduce anything in him to principles.—For example, the three species of eloquence; the simple, the temperate, and the sublime, can scarcely be understood from him when we read that the one resembles a frugal table; the second a beautiful ruin, with green wood growing on its banks; and the third thunder and an impetuous river which overthrows every thing that opposes it. The work, however, has been exceedingly successful, and justly so; and its success encouraged its author to undertake another work of equal use and entertainment; his Histoire Ancienne, &c., or "Ancient History of the Egyptians, Carthaginians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians, Macedonians, and Greeks," which he finished in 13 vols. 8vo, and published between 1730 and 1738. M. Voltaire, after having observed that Rollin was "the first member of the university of Paris who wrote French with dignity and correctness," says of this work, that "though the last volumes, which were written in too great a hurry, are not equal to the first, it is nevertheless the best compilation that has yet appeared in any language; because it is seldom that compilers are eloquent, and Rollin was remarkably so." This is perhaps saying too much. There are indeed in this work some passages very well handled; but they are only such as he had taken from the ancient authors, in doing justice to whom he was always very happy.

ROMAGNA

Pages 127-127

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the pope's territories, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Ferrarese, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Urbino, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and on the west by the Bolognese and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Tuscany. It is fertile in corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and pastures. It has also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, mineral waters, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, which make its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

ROMAN

Pages 125-125

in general, something belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome. See Rome. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">ROMANS</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> elected to be successor to the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany.

ROMANCE

Pages 125-127

in matters of literature, a fabulous relation of certain adventures designed for the entertainment and instruction of the readers, and differing from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> as it always exhibits actions <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, dangerous, and generally extravagant. Many authors of the first name have written on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> romance. It has exercised the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Hurd, of Warburton, and of some ladies, who have not thought it any derogation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> to unite antiquarian research with the cultivation of the belles lettres. We have not, however, seen anywhere so concise, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and elegant an account of the origin and progress of romances as in D'Israeli's Curiosities of Literature. "Romance (says this writer) has been elegantly defined the offspring of fiction and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Men of learning have amused themselves with tracing the epocha of romances. In this research they have displayed more ingenuity than judgment; and some have fancied that it may have existed as far back as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; Dearchus, one of his disciples, having written several works of this amusing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Let us, however, be satisfied in deriving it from the Theagenes and Chariclea of Heliodorus, a bishop who lived in the 4th century, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been lately translated. This elegant prelate was the Grecian Fene lon (A). Beautiful as these compositions are when the imagination of the writer is sufficiently storcd with accurate observations on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in their birth, like many of the fine arts, they found in the zealots of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> men who opposed their progress. However Heliodorus may have delighted those who were not insensible to the felicities of a fine imagination, and to the enchanting elegancies of style, he raised himself, among his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, enemies; who at length so far prevailed, that it was declared by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, that his performance was dangerous to young persons, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the author did not suppress it, he must resign his bishopric. We are told he preferred his romance to his bishopric. Even so late as in Racine's time, it was held a crime to peruse these unhallowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. He informs us, that the first effusions of his muse were in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of studying that ancient romance, which his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> observing him to devour with the keenness of a famished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he snatched it from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and flung it in the fire; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> copy experienced the same fate. What could Racine do? He bought a third, and took the precaution of devouring it secretly till he got it by heart; after which he offered it to his master with a smile to burn, if he chose, like the others. The decision of these bigots was founded in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the immorality of such works. They alleged, that the writers paint too warmly to the imagination, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> themselves too forcibly to the passions, and, in general, by the freedom of their representations, hover on the borders of indecency. This censure is certainly well-founded. Many of the old romances, and even of the dramas, acted in Scotland two centuries ago, are such as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> prostitutes would in this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> think indecent. But we are at present concerned with the origin of Romance. "The learned Fleury thinks that they were not known till the 12th century, and gives as their original the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Dukes of Normandy. Verdier, whose opinion is of no great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, says the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of romance was owing to the Normans of France; and that these fictions being originally written in the old Norman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, they were entitled Normances; the name was afterwards altered to that of Romances. The Spaniards, who borrowed them from the French, called them Romanzes, which also did the Italians. † P (A) An ingenious and learned friend inquires, 'Is not the romance of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Ass, by Apuleius, to be considered as an earlier specimen than that of Heliodorus?' To this our author has no objection; but he would not warrant any romance to be the first that ever was written. It is thus that some writers, more learned than sagacious, have discovered the first inventor of epistolary correspondence. A lady receives this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>: such learning is desperate! From the Asiatic Researches, and other publications on Oriental literature, we are led to believe, that the native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of romance is the east; where it seems to have flourished in all its extravagant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> from time immemorial. "Dom Rivet, one of the learned associates of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of St Maur, authors of the Literary History of France, fixes their origin in the 10th century. He says, that the most ancient romance known was one which appeared in the middle of that century, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Philomena, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Beloved. This romance contains the pretended exploits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, he tells us, they have preserved a copy of the Philomena in its original language; that is to say, the Romaunt or polished; such as was then spoken at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. They preferred this language to the Latin, which was then that of the common people, but vitiated with their corruptions. "So far have we travelled on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of conjecture: we shall now turn into the path of fact. It is certain that these compositions derive their name from the language in which they were first written. Abbe Irauld has given us the character of the earliest romances, which we shall transcribe; for to add to what is well expressed, however it may please the vanity of a writer, seldom tends to the gratification of the reader. "The first romances were a monstrous assemblage of histories, in which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and fiction were equally blended, but all without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of amorous adventures, and all the extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of chivalry. The incidents are infinitely multiplied; destitute of connection, of order, and art. These are the ancient and miserable romances which Cervantes, in his celebrated satirical romance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, has covered with an eternal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>." "It is, however, from these productions rather in their improved state, that poets of all nations have drawn their richest inventions. The agreeable wildness of that fancy which characterised the eastern nations was caught by the crusaders. When they returned home, they mingled in their own the customs of each country. The Saracens, who were men like themselves, because they were of another religion, and were therefore their enemies, were pictured under the tremendous form of Paynim Giants. The credulous reader of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> followed with trembling anxiety the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a>. It was thus that fiction embellished religion, and religion invigorated fiction. Such incidents have enlivened the cantos of Ariosto, and adorned the epic of Tasso. Spencer is the child of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and it is certain that we are indebted to them for some of the bold and strong touches of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>." Other circumstances however have been assigned as the sources of these extravagant fictions. "Castles were erected to repulse the vagrant attacks of the Normans; and in France (from the year 768 to 987) these places became fatal to the public repose. The petty despots who raised these castles, pillaged whoever passed, and carried off the females who pleased them. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">Rape</a>, of every kind, was the privilege of Lords! Mezeray observes, that it is from these circumstances romancers have invented their tales of knights errant, monsters, and giants. "De Saint Foix, in his Historical Essays on this subject, thus expresses himself: 'Women and girls were not in greater security when they passed by abbeys. The monks sustained an assault rather than relinquish their prey: if they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> themselves losing ground, they brought to their walls the relics of some saint. Then it generally happened that the assailants, seized with awful veneration, retired, and dared not to pursue their vengeance. This is the origin of the enchanters of the enchantments, and of the enchanted castles, described in romances.' "To these may be added what the author of Northern Antiquities, vol. i. p. 243, writes, that 'as the walls of the castles ran winding round them, they often called them by a name which signified <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> or dragons; and in these were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> secured the women and young maids of distinction, who were seldom safe at a time when so many bold warriors were rambling up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in search of adventures. It was this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which gave occasion to ancient romancers, who knew not how to describe any thing simply, to invent so many fables concerning princesses of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, guarded by dragons.' "The Italian romances of the 14th century were spread abroad in great numbers. They formed the polite literature of the day. But if it is not permitted to authors freely to express their ideas, and give full play to the imagination, these works must never be placed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the rigid moralist. They indeed pushed their indelicacy to the verge of grossness, and seemed rather to seek than to avoid scenes which a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> would blush to describe. They (to employ the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of one of their authors) were not ashamed to name what God had created. Cinthio, Bandello, and others, but chiefly Boccacio, rendered libertinism agreeable, by the fascinating charms of a polished style, and a luxuriant imagination. "This however must not be admitted as an apology for immoral works; for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> is still poison, even when it is delicious. Such works were, and still continue to be, the favourites of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> which is stigmatised from being prone to illicit pleasures and impure amours. They are still curious in their editions, and are not parsimonious in their price for what they call an uncastrated copy. There are many Italians, not literary men, who are in possession of an ample library of the old novelists. "If we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the moral irregularities of these romances, we may discover a rich vein of invention, which only requires to be released from that rubbish which disfigures it to become of an invaluable price. The Decameron, the Hecatommiti, and the Novellas of these writers, made no inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the little library of our Shakespeare. Chaucer is a notorious imitator and lover of them; his Knight's Tale is little more than a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> of Boccacio's Teceoide. Fontaine has caught all their charms with all their licentiousness. From such works, these great poets, and many of their contemporaries, frequently borrowed their plots; not uncommonly kindled at their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> the ardour of their genius; but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> too submissively to their own peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, or that of their age, in extracting the ore, they have not purified it of their alloy. "We must now turn our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> to the French romances of the last century. They were then carried to a point of perfection, which as romances they cannot exceed. To this the Astrea of D'Ursé greatly contributed. It was followed by the Illustrious Bassa, the Great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, Clelia, &c., which, though not adapted to the present age, gave celebrity to their authors. Their style, as well as that of the Astrea, is diffuse and insipid. Zside (attributed by some to Segrais, but by Huet It was not surprising that romances have been regarded as pernicious to good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, morals, taste and literature. It was in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> they were considered by Boileau; because a few had succeeded, a crowd imitated their examples. Gomberville and Scudery, and a few more were admired; but the satirist dissolved the illusion. This he did most effectually by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>, in which he ridicules those citizens of a certain district, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> were concealed in these romances, under the names of Brutus, Horace Cocles, Lucretius, and Clelia. This dialogue he only read to his friends, and did not give it for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time to the public, as he esteemed Mademoiselle de Scudery: but when at length it was published, it united all the romance writers against our satirist. "From romances, which had now exhausted the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of the public, sprung <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>. They attempted to allure <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> by this inviting title, and reducing their works from ten to two volumes. The name of romance disgusted; and they substituted those of histories, lives, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and adventures. In these works (observes Iraill) they quitted the unnatural incidents, the heroic projects, the complicated and endless intrigues, and the exertion of noble passions; heroes were not now taken from the throne, they were sought for even amongst the lowest ranks of the people. On this subject, I shall just observe, that a novel is a very dangerous poison in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a libertine; it may be a salutary medicine in that of a virtuous writer." See Novel.

ROMANIA

Pages 127-127

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Bulgaria, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south by the Archipelago and the sea of Marmora, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Bulgaria; being 200 miles in length and 150 in breadth. It was formerly called Thrace, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and largest of all the provinces the Turks possess in Europe. It is a fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in corn and pastures, and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. It is divided into three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> governments <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sangiacates; namely, Kerkel, of which Philippi is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GALIPOLI">Galipoli</a>, whose capital is of the same name; and Byzantium, or Byzia, or Viza, of which Constantinople is the capital. The Turks bestow the name of Romelia on all the territories they possess in Europe.

ROMANO

Pages 127-127

GIULIO, a famous painter, was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Raphael, who had such an affection for him, that he appointed him, with John Francis Penni, his heir. His conceptions were more extraordinary and more elevated than even those of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, but not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. He was wonderful in the choice of attitudes; but did not perfectly understand the lights and shades, and is frequently harsh and ungraceful. The folds of his draperies, says Du Fresnoy, are neither beautiful nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, easy nor natural, but all extravagant, like the fantastical habits of comedians. He was, however, superior to most painters, by his profound knowledge of antiquity; and, by conversing with the works of the most excellent poets, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> he made himself master of the qualifications necessarily required in a great designer. Julio Romano was also well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. He was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Medicis, who was afterwards pope under the name of Clement VII.; and afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, whither he was invited by Frederic Gonzagio, marquis of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in order to avoid his being justly punished for his having drawn at Rome the designs of 20 obscene plates, engraved by Mark Anthony, to which Aretine added the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sonnets. Julio Romano embellished the city of Mantua with many of his performances both in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and architecture; and died in that city in 1545, at 45 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, much regretted by the marquis, who had an extraordinary friendship for him.

ROME

Pages 127-133

a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the river Tiber, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13°. N. Lat. 41. 45. once the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the greatest empire in the world; and famous in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for being the centre of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> tyranny, by which for many ages the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world was held in subjection. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> derived their origin from Æneas the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; and though some historians pretend to treat his voyage into Italy as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, yet no sufficient reasons for rejecting this account have been offered, nor has any more probable history of the origin of the Roman name been given; so that, without entering into the dispute, we shall proceed to the history of Æneas and his successors as they are recorded by the generality of Latin writers. When the Greeks, by the treachery of the sons of Antenor, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by whatever other means it happened, were become masters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, Æneas with the forces under his command retired into the fortress of the city, and defended it bravely for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but yielding at length to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, he conveyed away his gods, his father, wife, and children, with every thing he had that was valuable, and, followed by a numerous crowd of Trojans, fled to the strong places of Mount Ida. Hither all those of his countrymen, who were more anxious than the rest to preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, flocked to him from the several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Troas. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> thus augmented and advantageously posted, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> quiet, waiting for the departure of the Greeks, who it was imagined, would return home as soon as they had pillaged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. But these, after they had enriched themselves with the spoils of Troy and of the neighbouring towns, turned their arms against the fugitives, resolving to attack them in their strong-holds upon the mountain. Æneas, to avoid the hazard of being forced in his last refuge, had recourse to negotiation; and, by his heralds, intricated the enemy not to constrain him to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Peace was granted him, on condition that he with his followers quitted the Trojan territories; and the Greeks, on their part, promised sed not to molest him in his retreat, but to let him safely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through any country within the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their domination. Upon this assurance Æneas equipped a fleet, in order to seek a settlement in some foreign <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. We are told, that at his departure he left his eldest son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a> with the Dasylites, a people of Bithynia, who desired to have him for their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; but that the young <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> did not remain long with them: for when Scamandrius (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYANAX">Astyanax</a>), with the rest of the Hectoridae whom Neoptolemus permitted to return home from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, repaired to him, he put himself at their head, and led them back to their native country. The Trojan, having crossed the Hellespont, arrived in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Pallene, where he built a city, called from him Æneia, and left in it a part of that multitude which had followed him. From thence he sailed to Delos; and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a>, where he erected a temple to Venus. He built another to the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> in Zacynthus, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> he likewise instituted games, called the races of Æneas and Venus: the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of both, says Dionysius, are standing to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In Leucas, where the Trojans landed, was to be seen, in the same author's time, a temple erected to Venus the mother of Æneas. Nor were <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a> and Ambracia without monuments that testified his arrival in those places. At <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> were found brazen vases, upon which the name of the Trojan hero, who had made an offering of them to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, was engraven in old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Not far from Ruthrotos, in Epirus, a Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> which had escaped the injuries of time, retained the name of Troja. All these antiquities, still subsisting in the reign of Augustus, were then looked upon as indisputable proofs of Æneas's voyage to Epirus: "and that he came into Italy (adds the same Dionysius) we have the concurrent testimony of all the Romans; the ceremonies they observe in their sacrifices and festivals bear witness to it, as also the Sibylline books, the Pythian <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>, and many other things which nobody can reasonably reject as invented merely for ornament." The first land of Italy which Æneas made, after crossing the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, in Iapygia; and here he went on shore. Sailing afterwards from hence, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> along the south-east of Italy and the east and south sides of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, he arrived with his fleet either by choice or by stress of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at the port of Drepanum in that island, Elymus and Ægestus, who had escaped from Troy a little before him, had brought a Trojan colony to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Æneas augmented it by a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his followers, whom, pleased to have found a safe resting place after many dangers and fatiguing voyages, he willingly left behind him at their request; though certain authors pretend that he was constrained to it by the difficulty of transporting them, because some Trojan women, weary of the sea, had burnt a considerable part of his ships. Æneas, leaving Drepanum, steered his course for Italy across the Tyrrhenian sea. To the cape where he first landed, he gave the name Palinurus, from one of his pilots who died there. The little island of Leucasia, not far distant, whither he sailed next, got its name in like manner from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Æneas's sister, who there ended her days. The port of Misenum, the island of Procivita, and the promontory of Cajeta, where he successively arrived, were so called from being the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> places, the first of a noble Trojan his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of his kinswoman, and the third of his nurse. At length the Trojan prince and his chosen band finished their tedious and painful voyages on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the since famous Latium. This was a small land territory on the east side of the river Tiber, containing a part of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LATINUS">Latinus</a> was the king of it; his capital town, Laurentum; his subjects, a people who, till his time called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, had from him taken the name of Latins. Here, far removed from their implacable enemies the Greeks, Æneas and his followers undertook to raise a second Troy; they fortified a camp near the mouth of the Tiber, gave it the name of Troy, and flattered themselves with the hopes of a quiet settlement, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to all their unhappy adventures. When Æneas arrived in Italy, Latinus was engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Rutuli, a neighbouring people, in which he was attended but with very indifferent success, when news was brought him that a foreign army had made a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> on his coasts, pillaged the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> part of his dominions, and were fortifying themselves in a camp at a small distance from the sea. Hereupon he marched against them with all his forces, hoping to oblige them to reembark and abandon his dominions, without meeting with any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resistance from a band of vagabonds, as he supposed, or pirates, come only to seek for plunder: but finding them, as he drew near, well-armed, and regularly drawn up, he thought it advisable to forbear engaging troops that appeared so well disciplined; and, instead of venturing a battle, to desire a parley. In this conference Latinus understanding who they were, and being at the same time struck with terror, and touched with compassion for those brave but unfortunate men, entered into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with them, and assigned them a tract of land for a settlement, on condition that they should employ their arms and exert their valour in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his dominions, and look upon the Rutuli as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy. This condition Æneas readily accepted; and complied with his engagement so faithfully, that Latinus came at length to repose an entire confidence in the Trojan; and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of it gave him Lavinia, his daughter and only child, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, securing to him by that means the succession to the throne of Latium. Æneas, to testify his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to Latinus, and affection for Lavinia, gave her name to the camp he had pitched; and instead of Troy called it Laviniun. The Trojans followed the example of their leader; and by making alliances with Latin families, became, in a short time, one and the same people with the Latins. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time Turnus, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s nephew, who had been brought up in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> under the eye of Latinus, and entertained hopes of marrying Lavinia and succeeding to the throne, seeing the princess bestowed on a stranger, and all his views defeated, went over to the Rutuli; and by stirring them up, brought on a battle between them and the Latins, in which both he and Latinus were killed. Thus Æneas, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and by that of a troublesome rival, came into the quiet possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Latium, which he governed with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and transmitted to his posterity. Æneas is said to have reigned three years; during which which time he established the worship of the gods of his own country, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Latins added that of Troy. The two Palladiums, which had been the protectors of that city, became the tutelary deities of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a> and, in after ages, of the whole Roman empire. The worship of Vesta was likewise introduced by Æneas; and virgins, from her called Vestals, were appointed to keep a fire continually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of that goddess. Jupiter, Venus, and many other deities who had been revered in Troy, became in all likelihood, known to the Latins by means of Æneas; which gave occasion to the poets of representing him under the character of a pious hero. While Æneas was thus employed, the Rutuli, ancient enemies of the Latin name, entering into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Mezentius king of the Tyrrhenians, took the field with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to drive out those new-comers, of whose power they began to conceive no small jealousy. Æneas marched out against them at the head of his Trojans and Latins. Hereupon a battle ensued, which lasted till night; when Æneas being pushed to the banks of the Numicus, which ran <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by Lavinium, and forced into that river, was there drowned. The Trojans concealed his body; and pretending that he had vanished away on a sudden, made him pass for a deity among his credulous subjects, who accordingly erected a temple to him under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Jupiter Indiges. Upon the death of Æneas, his son Euryleon, called also Ascanius and Iulus, ascended the throne; but as the young king did not think it advisable to venture a battle in the very beginning of his reign, with a formidable enemy, who promised himself great success from the death of Æneas, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to confine himself within the walls of Lavinium, and to try whether he could, by an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> treaty, put an end to so dangerous a war. But the haughty Mezentius demanding of the Latins, as one of the conditions of a peace, that they should pay him yearly, by way of tribute, all the wine produced in the territory of Latium, Ascanius rejected the proposal with the utmost indignation; and having caused all the vines throughout his dominions to be consecrated to Jupiter, and by that means put it out of his power to comply with the enemy's request, he resolved to make a vigorous sally, and try whether he could, by force of arms, bring the insulting Tyrrhonian to more reasonable terms. The main body of the enemy's army was encamped at some distance from Lavinium; but Lausus, the son of Mezentius, with the flower of their youth under his command, lay entrenched at the very gates of the city. The Trojans, who had been long accustomed to make vigorous sallies, marching out in the night, attacked the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> where Lausus commanded, forced his entrenchments, and obliged the troops he had with him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> themselves by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to the main body of the army encamped on the plain; but the unexpected arrival and overthrow of their advance-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> struck them with such terror, that, instead of stopping the flight of their companions, they fled with them, in great disorder, to the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The Latins pursued them, and in their pursuit Lausus was killed: whose death so discouraged Mezentius, that he immediately sued for peace; which was granted him, upon condition, that for the future the Tiber should be the boundary between the Latin and Hetrurian territories. In the mean time Lavinia, who had been left with child by Æneas, entertaining a strong jealousy of the ambition of her son-in-law, retired to the woods, and was there peaceably delivered of a son, who, from his father was named Æneas, and, from the place of his birth, had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Sylvius: but as the queen's flight, who had disappeared on a sudden, raised suspicions at Lavinium prejudicial to the reputation of Ascanius, he used all possible means to remove them, caused diligent search to be made after Lavinia, calmed her fears, and prevailed upon her to return to the town with her son, whom he ever after treated as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. Lavinium grew every day more populous; but as it was in reality the patrimony of Lavinia, and the inheritance of her son Sylvius, Ascanius resolved to resign it to them, and build elsewhere another city for himself. This he made the place of his residence, and the capital of his new kingdom, calling it <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> Longa; Resigns the kingdom, and founds Alba Longa. Alba, from a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sow, which we are told Æneas had found in the place where it was built; and Longa, to distinguish it from another town of the same name in the country of the Marsi; or rather, because it extended, without having much breadth, the whole length of a lake near which it was built. It was 30 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Lavinium that Ascanius fixed his abode at Alba; and there he died, after a reign of about 38 years, 12 of which he had resided at his new settlement. He left a son called Iulus; so that between him and Sylvius lay the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession to the Latin throne; the latter being the son, and the former the grandson, of Æneas. The Latins not thinking it their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to continue divided, as it were, into two states, resolved to unite Alba and Lavinium into one sovereignty; and as Sylvius was born of Lavinia the daughter of Latinus, and had thereby an undoubted title to the kingdom of his grandfather, whereas the other was but the son of a stranger, the Latins bestowed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on Sylvius; and, to make Iulus some amends, decreed to him the sovereign power in affairs of religion; a power which thenceforth continued in his family. Sylvius was succeeded by 13 kings of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who for near 400 years reigned at Alba; but we scarce know anything of them besides their names, and the years of their respective reigns. Æneas Sylvius died, after a reign of 29 years. His son, called also Æneas Sylvius, governed Latium 31 years. Latinus Sylvius, who succeeded him, swayed the sceptre for the space of 51 years.—Alba reigned 39; Capetus, by Livy named Atys, 26; Capis, 28; and Capetus 13. Tiberinus, who succeeded him, engaged in a war which proved fatal to him; for in a battle which was fought on the banks of the Albula, he was forced into that river and drowned. From him the river took the name of Tiber, which it has borne ever since. Agrippa succeeded Tiberinus the name after a reign of eight years; and left the throne, which he had held 41 years, to Alladius; who reigned 19, and was succeeded by Aventinus, who left his name to the hill Aventinus, where he was interred. Procas, who succeeded him, and reigned 23 years, was the father of Numitor and Amulius; and at his death bequeathed the throne to his elder son Numitor. But Amulius, who surpassed his brother in courage and understanding, drove him from the throne; and, to secure it to himself, murdered Ægestus, Numitor's only son, and consecrated crated his daughter Rhea Sylvia to the worship of Vesta, by which she was obliged to perpetual virginity. But this precaution proved ineffectual; for as the Vestal was going to a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> to fetch <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the performance of a sacrifice to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, she was met and ravished by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, like that in which the god Mars is represented. Some authors think that this counterfeit Mars was a lover come thither by her appointment; others <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> Amulius himself with using this violence to his niece, not so much to gratify his lust, as to have a pretence to destroy her.—For ever after he caused her to be carefully watched, till she was delivered of two sons; and then exaggerating her crime in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people, he prevailed upon them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> her to death, and to condemn the fruit of her criminal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> to be thrown into the Tiber. The sentence against Rhea was, according to some authors, changed by Amulius, at the request of his daughter Antio, into perpetual confinement, but executed against the twins; who being laid in a wooden trough, and carried to the foot of Mount Palatine, were there turned adrift on the Tiber, which at that time overflowed its banks. But the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and stream proved both so favourable, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the water the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> were left safe on the strand, and were there happily found by Faustulus, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the king's shepherds, and suckled by his wife Acca Larentia, who for her disorderly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was called Lupi; and this probably gave rise to the fabulous miracle of their being nursed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>. As Faustulus was probably well acquainted with the birth of the twins, he took more than ordinary care of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and sent them to Gabii to be instructed there in Greek literature. As they grew up, they appeared to have something great in their mien and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> which commanded respect; and the ascendant which they assumed over the other shepherds made them dreaded in the forests, where they exercised a sort of empire. A quarrel happening between the herdsmen of Amulius and those of Numitor, the two brothers took the part of the former against the latter; and some blood being shed in the fray, the adverse party, to be revenged on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Remus (for so the twins were called), on the festival of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUPERCALIA">Lupercalia</a>, surprised Remus, and carried him before Numitor, to be punished according to his deserts. But Numitor feeling himself touched in the prisoner's favour, asked him where he was born, and who were his parents. His answer immediately struck Numitor with a lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his two grandsons; their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, which was about 18 years, agreed with the time when the two infants were exposed upon the Tiber; and there needed no more to change his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> into tenderness. In the mean time Romulus, eager to rescue his brother, and pursue those who had carried him off, was preparing to be revenged on them; but Faustulus dissuaded him from it; and on that occasion, disclosing to him his birth, awakened in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> sentiments worthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. He resolved, at all adventures, to attempt the delivering of his mother and grandfather from oppression. With this view he assembled the country people, over whom he had assumed a kind of sovereignty, and engaged them to come to the city on an appointed day, and enter it by different gates, provided with arms, which they were to conceal. While Remulas was thus disposing every thing for the execution of his design, Numitor made the same discovery to Remus concerning his parents, and the oppressions they groaned under; which so fired him, that he was ready to embark in any enterprise. But Numitor took care to moderate the transports of his grandson, and only desired him to acquaint his brother with what he had heard from him, and to send him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Romulus soon came, and was followed by Faustulus, who took with him the trough or skiff in which the twins had been exposed, to shew it to Numitor: but, as the shepherd betrayed an air of concern and earnestness in his looks, he was stopped at the gate of the city, led before Amulius, and examined concerning his burden. It was easily known by its make and inscription, which was still legible; and therefore Faustulus owned what it was, and confessed that the twins were living; but, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> time, pretended that they were feeding flocks in a remote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. In the mean time, the usurper's death being resolved on, Remus undertook to raise the city, and Romulus to invest the king's palace. The country people came at the time appointed, and formed themselves into companies each consisting of 100 men. They had no other ensigns but bundles of hay hanging upon long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, which the Latins at that time called manipuli; and hence came the name of manipulares, originally given to troops raised in the country. With this tumultuous army Romulus beset the avenues of the palace, forced the guard, and having killed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, after he had reigned 42 years, restored his grandfather Numitor to the throne. Affairs being thus settled at Alba, the two brothers, by the advice of Numitor, undertook the founding of a new colony. The king bestowed on them those lands near the Tiber where they had been brought up, supplied them with all manner of instruments for breaking up ground, with slaves, and beasts of burden, and granted full liberty to his subjects to join them. Hereupon most of the Trojans, of whom there still remained 50 families in Augustus's time, chose to follow the fortune of Romulus and Remus, as did also the inhabitants of Pallantium and Saturnia, two small towns. For the more speedy carrying on of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, it was thought proper to divide those who were to be employed in the building of the city into two companies, one under the command of Romulus, the other of Remus; but this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, which was designed purely with a view to the public welfare, and that the two parties might work by way of emulation, gave birth to two factions, and produced a jealousy between the two brothers, which broke out when they came to choose a place for the building of their new city; for Remus was for the Aventine, and Romulus for the Palatine mount. Upon which, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being referred to their grandfathers, he advised the contending parties to have recourse to the gods, and to put an end to the dispute by augury, to which he was himself greatly addicted. The day appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> being come, the brothers posted themselves each upon his hill; and it was agreed, that whoever should see the first flight, or the greatest number of vultures, should gain his cause. After the two rivals had waited some time for the appearance of a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, Romulus, before any had appeared, sent to acquaint his brother that he had seen some vultures; but Remus, having actually seen six, while his brother's messengers messengers were yet on their way, hastened, on their arrival, to Mount Palatine, to examine the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what they had told him. He had no sooner got thither, than by an unexpected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> twelve vultures appeared to Romulus. These he immediately showed to his brother; and, transported with joy, desired him to judge himself of the truth of what his messengers had told him.
