Some of the ancient writers speak of the roundelay or roundel as a kind of air appropriated to dancing; and in this fentence the term seems to indicate little more than dancing in a circle with the hands joined. ROUND-HOUSE, a kind of prifon for the nightly watch in London to secure disorderly persons till they can be carried before a magistrate. Round-House, in a ship, the uppermost room or cabin on the stern of a ship, where the master lies. ROUNDS, in military matters, a detachment from the main-guard, of an officer or a non-commissioned officer and fix men, who go round the rampart of a garrison, to listen if any thing be stirring without the place, and to see that the sentinels be diligent upon their duty, and all in order. In strict garrisons the rounds go every half-hour. The sentinels are to challenge at a distance, and to rest their arms as the round passes. All guards turn out, challenge, exchange the parole, and rest their arms, &c. Rounds are ordinary and extraordinary. The ordinary rounds are three; the town-major's round, the grand-round, and visiting-round. Manner of going the Rounds. When the town-major goes his round, he comes to the main-guard, and demands a sergeant and four or six men to escort him to the next guard; and when it is dark, one of the men is to carry a light. As soon as the sentry at the guard perceives the round coming, he shall give notice to the guard, that they may be ready to turn out when ordered; and when the round is advanced within about 20 or 30 paces of the guard, he is to challenge briskly; and when he is answered by the sergeant who attends the round, Town-major's round, he is to say, Stand round! and rest his arms; after which he is to call out immediately, Sergeant, turn out the guard, town-major's round. Upon the sentry calling, the sergeant is to turn out the guard immediately, drawing up the men in good order with shouldered arms, the officer placing himself at the head of it, with his arms in his hand. He then orders the sergeant and four or six men to advance towards the round, and challenge: the sergeant of the round is to answer, Town-major's round; upon which the sergeant of the guard replies, Advance, sergeant, with the parole! at the same time ordering his men to rest their arms. The sergeant of the round advances alone, and gives the sergeant of the guard the parole in his ear, that none else may hear it; during which period the sergeant of the guard holds the spear of his halbert at the other's breast. The sergeant of the round then returns to his post, whilst the sergeant of the guard leaving his men to keep the round from advancing, gives the parole to his officer. This being found right, the officer orders his sergeant to return to his men; says, Advance, town-major's round! and orders the guard to rest their arms; upon which the sergeant of the guard orders his men to wheel back from the centre, and form a lane, through which the town-major is to pass (the escort remaining where they were), and go up to the officer and give him the parole, laying his mouth to his ear. The officer holds the spear of his escutcheon at the town-major's breast while he gives him the parole. The design of rounds is not only to visit the guards, and keep the sentinels alert; but likewise to discover what passes in the outworks, and beyond them. ROUSSILLON, a province of France, in the Pyrenees, bounded on the east by the Mediterranean sea, on the west by Cerdagne, on the north by Lower Languedoc, and on the south by Catalonia, from which it is separated by the Pyrenees. It is a fertile country, about 50 miles in length, and 25 in breadth, and remarkable for its great number of olive-trees. Perpignan is the capital town. Vol. XVIII. Part I. he met with much attention and much generosity, as we shall soon mention.—It was there that his disputes with Voltaire commenced, with whom he had become acquainted at the college of Louis the Great, who then much admired his turn for poetry. At that time Voltaire assiduously cultivated the acquaintance of

ROWE

Pages 348-349

Nicholas, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> was born in 1673. He acquired a complete <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the classic authors under the famous Dr Busby in Westminster school; but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was his early and darling <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. His father, who was a lawyer, and designed him for his own profession, entered him a student in the Middle Temple. He made remarkable advances in the study of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the belles lettres, and of poetry in particular, stopt him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. His first tragedy, the Ambitious Stepmother, meeting with universal applause, he laid aside all thoughts of rising by the law. He afterward composed several tragedies; but that which he valued himself most upon, was his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>. The others are, the Fair Penitent, Ulysses, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Convert, Jane Shore, and Lady Jane Grey. He also wrote a poem called the Biter, and several poems upon different subjects, which have been published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Miscellaneous Works in one volume as his dramatic works have been in two. Rowe is chiefly to be considered (Dr Johnson observes) in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a tragic writer and a translator. In his attempt at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, he failed so ignominiously, that his Biter is not inserted in his works; and his occasional poems and short compositions are rarely worthy of either praise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> censure, for they seem the casual sports of a mind seeking rather to amuse its leisure than to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> its powers. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of his dramas there is not much art; he is not a nice observer of the unities. He extends <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and varies <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as his convenience requires. To vary the place is not (in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the learned critic from whom these observations are borrowed) any violation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the change be made between the acts; for it is less easy for the spectator to suppose himself at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, than at Thebes in the first; but to change the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, as is done by Rowe in the middle of an act, is to add more acts to the play, since an act is so much of the business as is transacted without interruption. Rowe, by this licence, easily extricates himself from difficulties; as in Lady Jane Gray, when we have been terrified with all the dreadful pomp of public execution, and are wondering how the heroine or the poet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> proceed, no sooner has Jane pronounced some prophetic rhimes, than—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and be gone—the scene closes, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> and Gardiner are turned out upon the stage. I know not (says Dr Johnson) that there can be found in his plays any deep search into nature, any accurate discriminations of kindred qualities, or nice display of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> in its progress; all is general and undefined. Nor does he much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> or affect the auditor, except in Jane Shore, who is always seen and heard with pity. Alicia is a character of empty noise, with more resemblance to real sorrow or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> madness. Whence then has Rowe his reputation? From the reasonableness and propriety of some of his scenes, from the elegance of his diction, and the suavity of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. He seldom moves either pity or terror, but he often elevates the sentiment; he seldom pierces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, but he always delights the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and often improves the understanding. Being a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admirer of Shakespeare, he gave the public an edition of his plays; to which he prefixed an account of that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But the most considerable of Mr Rowe's performances was a translation of Lucan's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>, which he <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> lived to finish, but not to publish; for it did not appear in print till 1728, ten years after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Meanwhile, the love of poetry and books did not make him unfit for business; for nobody applied closer to it when occasion required. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Queensberry, when secretary of state, made him secretary for public affairs. After the duke's death, all avenues were stopped to his preferment; and during the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s reign he passed his time with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> and his books. A story, indeed, is told of him, which shows that he had some acquaintance with her ministers. It is said, that he went one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, who asked him, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he understood Spanish well?" He answered, "No:" but thinking that his Lordship might intend to send him into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> on some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, he presently added, "that he did not doubt but he could shortly be able both to understand and to speak it." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> approving what he said, Rowe took his leave; and, retiring a few weeks to learn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, waited again on the Earl to acquaint him with it. His Lordship asked him, "If he was sure he understood it thoroughly?" and Rowe affirming that he did, "How happy are you, Mr Rowe," said the Earl, "that you can have the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> and understanding the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote in the original?" On the accession of George I., he was made poet laureat, and one of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> surveyors of the customs in the port of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> conferred on him the clerkship of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and the Lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Parker made him his secretary for the presentations. He did not enjoy these promotions <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for he died Dec. 6, 1718, in his 45th year. Mr Rowe was twice married, had a son by his first wife, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> by his second. He was a handsome, genteel man; and his mind was as amiable as his person. He lived beloved; and at his death had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be lamented by Mr Pope, in an epitaph which is printed in Pope's works, although it was not affixed on Mr Rowe's monument in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, where he was interred in the poet's corner, opposite to Chaucer. Rowe, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, an English lady, eminent for her excellent writings both in prose and verse, born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILCHESTER">Ilchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in 1647, was the daughter of worthy parents, Mr Walter Singer and Mrs Elisabeth Portnel. She received the first serious impressions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> as soon as she was capable of it. There being a great <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and poetry, this lady, who had a vein for the one, naturally had a taste for the other. She was also very fond of music; chiefly of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and solemn kind, as best suited to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of her sentiments and the sublimity of her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. But poetry was her favourite employment, her distinguishing excellence. So prevalent was her genius this way, that her prose is all poetical. In 1696, a collection of her poems was published at the desire of two friends. Her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on the xxxviith <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> was written at the request of Bishop Ken. She had no other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> for the French and Italian languages than the honourable Mr Thynne, who willingly took the task upon himself. Her shining merit, with the charms of her person and conversation, had procured her a great many admirers. Among others, it is said, the famous Mr <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> made his addresses to her. But Mr Thomas Rowe was to be the happy man. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> was honourably descended; and his superior genius, and insatiable thirst after knowledge, were conspicuous in his earliest years. He had formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to compile the lives of all the illustrious persons in antiquity omitted by Plutarch; which, indeed, he partly executed. Eight lives were published since his decease. They were translated into French by the abbé Bellanger in 1734. He spoke with ease and fluency; had a frank and benevolent temper, an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and a communicative disposition. Such was the man who, charmed with the person, character, and writings, of our authoress, married her in 1710, and made it his study to repay the felicity with which she crowned his life. Too intense an application to study, beyond what the delicacy of his frame would bear, broke his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and threw him into a consumption, which put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his valuable life in May 1715, when he was but just past the 38th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Mrs Rowe wrote a beautiful elegy on his death; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the last moments of her life to express the highest veneration and affection for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. As soon after his decease as her affairs would permit, she indulged her inclination for solitude, by retiring to Frome, in Somersetshire, in the neighbourhood of which place the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of her estate lay. In this recess it was that she composed the most celebrated of her works, Friendship in Death, and the Letters Moral and Entertaining. In 1736, she published the History of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>; a poem which she had written in her younger years. She did not long survive this publication; for she died of an apoplexy, as was supposed, Feb. 20, 1736-7. In her cabinet were found letters to several of her friends, which she had ordered to be delivered immediately after her decease. The Rev. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Watts, agreeably to her request, revised and published her devotions in 1737, under the title of Devout Exercises of the Heart in Meditation and Soliloquy, Praise and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>; and, in 1739, her Miscellaneous Works, in prose and verse, were published in 2 vols. 8vo, with an account of her life and writings prefixed. As to her person, she was not a regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, yet possessed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of the charms of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. She was of a moderate stature, her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, her eyes of a darkish gray inclining to blue, and full of fire. Her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> was very fair, and a natural blush glowed in her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. She spoke gracefully; her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was exceedingly sweet and harmonious; and she had a softness in her aspect which inspired love, yet not without some mixture of that awe and veneration which distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and virtue, apparent in the countenance, are wont to create.

ROWEL

Pages 349-349

among farriers, a kind of issue answering to what in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SETON">seton</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARRIER">Farrier</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. v.

ROWLEY

Pages 349-349

William, who stands in the third class of dramatic writers, lived in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but whether he took any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> there, is not evident; there being but few particulars preserved in regard to him more than his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> intimacy and connection with all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wits and poetical geniuses of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, by whom he was well beloved, and with some of whom he joined in their writings. Wood styles him "the ornament, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and ingenuity, of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in Cambridge." In a word, he was a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> benefactor to the English stage, having, exclusive of his aid <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to Middleton, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>, Heywood, Webster, &c. left us five plays of his own composing, and one in which even the immortal Shakespeare afforded him some assistance.

ROWNING

Pages 349-349

John, an English mathematician and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of considerable ingenuity, was fellow of Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and afterwards rector of Ansdery in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, in the gift of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. He constantly attended the meetings of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALDING">Spalding</a> society, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an extraordinary philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and turn of mind, while at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his dispositions were social and cheerful. His genius was peculiarly fitted for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> contrivances <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inventions. He published a compendious system of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> at Cambridge, in the year 1738, in two vols. 8vo.; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of much ingenuity, which has gone through several editions. He likewise inserted two pieces in the Philosophical Transactions, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> may be increased at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; vol. xxxviii. p. 29.; and directions for making a machine for finding the roots of equations universally, together with the manner in which it is to be used; vol. lx. p. 240. He died at his lodgings in Carey street, near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s

ROXBURGHSHIRE

Pages 349-351

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, which is also known by the name of Teviotdale, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> about 40 miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and in breadth about 36 miles in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> between east and west; containing 472,320 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> acres. The centre of the county is computed to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in 55° 25' N. Lat. and in 2° 37' W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. from the meridian of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The counties of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> form its boundary on the south; it is also bounded by the former county on the east, by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a> on the north, and on the west by the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>, Selkirk, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance of this county is regarded as upon the whole extremely beautiful, exhibiting an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> succession of hills and dales, through which flow a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the hills are covered with a fine sward, producing valuable grasses for the feeding of sheep; and the county is divided into four different districts, the most mountainous part of it being denominated the district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAWICK">Hawick</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEDBURGH">Jedburgh</a>; the third is the district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a>, and the fourth is known by the name of the district of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELROSE">Melrose</a>, being composed of that part of the county which is situated to the northward of the rest. The most remarkable hills in the county of Roxburgh are Minto, 858 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; Dunion 1021; Eldon 1330; Ruberslaw 1419; Carterfell 1602, Wisp 1803. These constitute a part of that extensive range generally known by the appellation of Cheviot, which is distant not above a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the most easterly point of Roxburgh. Whinstone is their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> constituent, in which veins of Scotch pebbles are usually interspersed. They are often covered with whinstone reduced to the state of powder by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The hills towards their summits are in general of a conical form, a circumstance which some think is favourable to the volcanic system;—that the globe at some remote <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> has suffered the most dreadful convulsions from the irresistible action of fire. The county of Roxburgh is intersected by a multitude of streams, the most important of which are the Teviot, Jed, Tweed, Rule, Kale, Oxnam, Gala, Slitrig, Ale, Caster, Borthwick, Ednam, Bowmont, Allan, Leader, Ettrick, Hermitage, Liddel. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> river is rarely applied to any of these streams, except to the three first, viz. the Teviot, the Jed, and the Tweed, none of which are navigable but for small ferry boats. Some rivers in England, such as the Tyne, the Cocket, &c. have their origin in the more elevated parts of the county of Roxburgh. In an agricultural point of view, Roxburghshire may be divided into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> under tillage and under pasture, although a considerable portion of the latter may be reduced to arable land. The soils under tillage may be divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and clayey, the former of which is usually denominated green, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, because it is best adapted to the rearing of oats, wheat, and other white grains. What is called till in Roxburghshire, generally consists of a hard clay intermixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, by which it resembles coarse gravel. Most Roxburghshire of the different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of till may be changed into a fertile soil in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by being exposed to the action of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and mixed with lime and manure. Sweet, sour, and healthy, are the terms by which lands under pasture are usually distinguished, and these are conferred from a consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soil, its grasses, and such other circumstances as indicate them to be favourable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> unfavourable for the rearing of sheep. Much of these lands was, at a remote period, under wood and heath, the existence of the former being pointed out by the roots of trees still remaining in the ground. The soil in general is sharp and dry upon the hills; but some of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> moors and the grounds in the vicinity of rivers are wet and marshy. There are different tracts of land in this county which still continue in a state of nature, a portion of which kind, measuring about four miles long and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, runs through part of the parishes of Ancrum and Roxburgh, chiefly of a light gravelly nature, covered with heath, bent, and other coarse grasses. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> district of Liddesdale is wholly under sheep-pasturage, with the exception of a few stripes on the banks of the Liddel and Hermitage. Indeed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> wet soil, and exposed situation, and unfriendly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, hold out few incentives to improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times this must have been very different from what it is at present. The marks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> can still be traced on the summits of lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, where the production of crops at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> is wholly impracticable. The counties on the borders were not, at a remote period, possessed by individuals in large detached portions, but the people of a whole neighbourhood had their alternate ridges, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they became interested in defending the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of each other against invaders and plunderers. The wars of the border, however, were happily terminated by the union of England and Scotland under one sovereign, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the holding of property in what was denominated runrigs, no longer possessed its ancient advantages, but was rather a disadvantage, as it created constant quarrels and disputes among farmers, and greatly retarded the improvement of the soil. Each individual, therefore, became anxious to have his lands detached from those of his neighbours, an advantageous change which was very soon and very generally adopted. A Mr Dawson, the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in Roxburghshire, having resided four years in the west riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and a year in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, thereby made himself well acquainted with the most approved methods of husbandry practised in England, and returned to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the full assurance of being able to introduce into the agriculture of Scotland the most essential improvements. On his arrival in Roxburghshire in the year 1753, he immediately introduced the turnip husbandry, which he sowed in drills, and was certainly the first Scots farmer who introduced the cultivation of turnip into the open field. His neighbours being wholly ignorant of the agricultural knowledge which this young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> had acquired in England, began to predict his ruin as wholly inevitable; but he was not to be intimidated by their prophetic sentiments, and he went on resolutely in bringing his lands into the very best condition, which he fully effected by means of the turnip husbandry. husbandry, by the sowing of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> grasses, a practice then unknown in Scotland, and by the free and extensive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lime. By such a procedure his neighbours <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him becoming rapidly opulent, and having followed his example with the most flattering success, they were constrained to alter their sentiments respecting his conduct as a farmer, and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> him the father of the agriculture of the south of Scotland. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of crops now followed in this county has nothing in it of a peculiar nature, the arrangement on a dry soil being generally oats, turnips, barley with grasses, hay or pasture for one year, then barley as before. Where the soil is good and properly prepared, it is not uncommon with farmers to adopt the following rotation, viz. oats, turnips, oats, turnips, wheat or barley with grasses, and hay or pasture for one year. A part of Roxburghshire has been long celebrated for a species of oats which produce early crops, and which are known by the appellation of Blainsly oats, because they have been produced at Blainsly from time immemorial, which is a district in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Melrose, and northern extremity of the county. These are often five shillings a boll dearer than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oats, and in no situation whatever are they known to degenerate. In some rich soils the produce is 16 or 18 for 1, and the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> produce is at least six for one. The general practice of feeding cattle with turnip has diminished the culture of pease and beans in this county, and there are so few potatoes reared that they cannot be regarded as forming a part of the farmer's crop. Extensive crops of hay are not in general cultivated in this county, there being but few cities in which an advantageous market could be found; and the use of it is in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> supplanted by that of turnip. Little more <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> is reared than what is necessary for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> purposes. There is a circumstance worthy of observation, that the rearing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> was, at one period, attempted in this county with remarkable success. It was introduced by a Mr Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, who had been for some time in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Soon after the first experiments were made, a single <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of land produced a crop worth L70 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; and the crop of 13 acres was sold on the ground for L320; but in consequence of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> prohibiting the culture of it, the purchaser could not implement his bargain, and the farmer was obliged to sell it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at the rate of fourpence a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, in consequence of which it brought him no more than L104 instead of L320. Great quantities of cattle are fed in this county, and about 260,000 sheep of the Cheviot breed in general, which are found to thrive remarkably in every part of the county. The horses are either of the English breed, or from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARKSHIRE">Lanarkshire</a>, which latter are deemed preferable for steady <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the plough. Although swine are not kept by the farmers as a part of their stock, yet great numbers of them are reared by tradesmen, cottagers, hinds, and others, the small breed being chiefly preferred, not exceeding eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stones English each. Roxburghshire is also famous for the rearing of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and immense quantities of eggs are sent from it to Berwick, to be shipped for the London market. Crows are here so numerous, that they frequently darken the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in their flight, and are extremely destructive to every species of grain. A great part of the county is uninclosed, and the fences made use of are the hedge and ditch, although in some places upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> dykes have the decided preference, where stones can be readily procured. The orchards of Roxburgh county have been long celebrated for different kinds of fruit, and there are here two extensive nurseries for the rearing of trees. These last are at Hassendean burn in the parish of Min- to, and at Hawick. The whole county, however, like that of Berwick, is extremely defective in mineral productions, and coal has nowhere been found. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">Limestone</a> is no doubt met with in different places of it, but the want of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> requisite for its calcination, induces farmers to bring it from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALKEITH">Dalkeith</a> or Edinburgh in their corn carts, which might otherwise return empty. In the vicinity of Jedburgh there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with indications of more in different parts of the parish, which have not yet been subjected to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, although the waters of Tuddhope well have been regarded as antiscorbutic, and of use also in rheumatic disorders. In this county there are many remains of antiquity, such as ancient strong buildings, and vestiges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>. Different remains of encampments and fortifications are to be met with in the parish of Roberton, which in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> have been the work of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Hermitage castle is situated upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river of the same name, and is nearly 100 feet square, defended by a strong rampart and ditch. The inner part of it is a heap of ruins, but the walls are almost entire. This is probably the very castle mentioned by Smollet, which was built in Liddesdale by Alexander II., and which gave such offence to Henry III. of England that he made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on Alexander in the year 1240. There are several caves or recesses on the banks of the Ale water, not fewer than fifteen of which, it is said, may be still pointed out, in some of which the vestiges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> or fire-places are very discernible. Although at first used by plunderers as places of safe retreat, they were no doubt afterwards employed by the poorer classes of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> as their ordinary habitations. Perhaps the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Melrose is the most distinguished monument of antiquity to be met with in this county. See the article MELROSE. Roxburghshire has given birth to some of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> who have adorned the republic of letters, among whom we find Dr John Armstrong, a distinguished physician and poet; James Thomson, the far-famed author of the Seasons; the poet Gavin Douglas, at one time rector of Hawick, afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a>; and the celebrated George Augustus Eliot, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Heathfield. Notwithstanding the difficulty of procuring fuel in this county, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> have been carried on with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of spirit and determined perseverance, the chief of which are carpets, inkle, cloth and stockings, in the manufacture of which nearly 300 packs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> (each 12 stones) have been annually consumed. About 4000 pairs of stockings have been made in the same time, and 10 tons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> yarn consumed in the making of inkle. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this county in 1801, amounted to 38,682, and in 1811 to 37,280. The following is the population according to the parishes, taken from the Statistical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. See ROXBURGHSHIRE SUPPLEMENT.

ROXENT-CAPE
