RUDBECK

Pages 357-357

Olaus, a learned Swedish physician, born of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family in 1630. He became professor of medicine at Upsal, where he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause by his extensive knowledge; and died in 1702. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Exercitatio anatomica, exhibens ductus novos hepaticos aquosos, et vasorum glandularum serosis, in 4to. He there asserts his claim to the discovery of the lymphatic vessels, against the pretensions of Thomas Bartholin. 2. Athlantica, sive Manheim, vera Japhetii posteriorum sedes ac patria, 4 vols. folio, is full of strange paradoxes supported with profound learning; he there endeavours to prove, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whence all the ancient Pagan divinities and our first parents were derived; and that the Germans, English, French, Danes, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, with all other nations, originally came from thence.

RUDDER

Pages 357-358

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on hinges in the stern of the ship, and which, opposing sometimes one side in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and sometimes another, turns <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> directs the vessel this way or that. See Helm. In the seventh volume of the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> instituted at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for the Encouragement of Arts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, there is explained a method of supplying the loss of a ship's rudder at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, which is Capt. Pakenham's of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, has been approved by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Cornwallis, the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, by the society in whose transactions the account of it was first published, and who presented to Capt. Pakenham their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal, by the Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, by the managing owners of East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> shipping, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Sudermania then regent of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and by the society for the improvement of naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The substitute here recommended for a lost rudder, says the inventor, is formed of those materials without which no ship goes to sea, and its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is simple and speedy. Capt. Pakenham, however, did not give a particular account of his invention to the society whom he addressed, and to whom he sent a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of his invention, till such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as he had an opportunity of reducing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> he had conceived to practice. On the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1758, he made this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> with the Merlin of Newfoundland; and he declares that, during the different manoeuvres of tacking and wearing, he could not discover the least <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> between the operation of the machine and that of the ship's rudder; she was steered with the same ease by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and answered the helm in every situation fully as quick. Admiral Cornwallis certifies the same with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a> of 64 guns, which lost her rudder on the Kentish Knock, when with the substitute she was steered to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> with the utmost ease in a heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a>, and, as the admiral asserts, it would have taken her to the East Indies. The materials and construction are thus described in the Transactions. "N° 1. A topmast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; the fid-hole to ship the tiller in, and secured with hoops from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> stocks; the heel forming the head of the rudder. N° 2. The inner half of a jibboom. N° 3. The outer half of a jibboom. N° 4. A fish; the whole of these materials well bolted together;—in a merchantman her ruff-tree. N° 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> cut out to fit the stern-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and acting as a lower gudgeon, secured to the stern-post with hawsers, leading from the bolts of the cap, under the ship's bottom, into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAWSE">hawse</a>-holes, and hove well taut. N° 6. A plank, or, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> none on board, the ship's gangboards. N° 7. Anchor-stocks, made to fit the topmast as partners, secured to the deck, and supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the upper gudgeon, and in a merchant ship the clamps of her windlass. N° 8. A stern-post. N° 9. Hoops from the anchor-stocks. N° 10. Pigs of ballast, to sink the lower part. The head of the rudder to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through as many decks as you wish." On this the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> makes the following remarks: "It might probably be supposed, that a difficulty would occur in bringing the jaws of the cap to embrace the stern-post; but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at once be obviated, when it is remembered that the top-chains, or hawsers, leading from each end of the jaws, under the ship's bottom, are in fact a continuance of the jaws themselves. Nor can it be apprehended that the cap, when fixed, may be impelled from its station, either by the efforts of the sea, or the course of the ship through the water, though even the hawsers, which confine it in the first instance, should be relaxed:—the experiment proves, that the partners must be first torn away, or the main-piece broken off. "Since the improved state of navigation, notwithstanding remedies have been found in general for the most disastrous accidents at sea, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has evinced that nothing complete had been hitherto invented to supply the loss of a rudder. The first expedient within my knowledge were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> veered astern, with tackles leading from them to the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. This practice was superseded by the invention of the machine usually called the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a> machine; but the construction of it is complex and unwieldy, and vessels are seldom found in possession of the materials which forms it. Commodore Byron, in the Journal of his Voyage round the World, says, that the Tamer, with every assistance from his own ship, was five days in constructing it. Besides, like the before-mentioned scheme, it can only operate to steer a ship..." ship <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> (and that but very wildly), and of course, under the circumstance of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-shore, defeat the most skilful exertions of a seaman. Several other expedients have been adopted, which I shall not mention here, as the same defects equally appear in all. "Thus it was apparent, that ample room was left for the discovery of some more certain resource than any of the former; and the scheme which has suggested itself to me, will, I trust, be found fully to answer the purpose intended. The materials are such as scarcely any ship can venture to sea without; and the construction so speedy, easy, and simple, that the capacity of the meanest sailor will at once conceive it. I need not, from mathematical principles, show the certainty of its effect, as it is formed and managed in the same manner as a ship's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rudder: and as the common rudder is certainly of all inventions the best calculated for guiding a vessel through the water, it will of course follow, that whatever substitute the nearest resembles that, must be best adapted to supply its loss."

RUDDIMAN

Pages 358-361

Thomas, one of the most eminent grammarians which Scotland has produced, was born in October 1674 at Raggel, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Boyndie and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Banff. His father James Ruddiman was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, and strongly attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Stuart. Mr Ruddiman was instructed in the principles of Latin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> at the parish school of Boyndie, where his application was so vigorous, and his progress so rapid, that he quickly surpassed all his class fellows. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> George Morrison, who was a skilful and attentive teacher, being unwilling to check his ardour for learning, permitted him to follow the impulse of his genius, and to advance without waiting the slow progress of the other boys. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which the youthful mind receives from vivid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, though wild and romantic, approaches to ecstasy, and often makes an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> which remains indelible. While at school, the first book which charmed the opening mind of Ruddiman was Ovid's Metamorphoses; nor did he cease to relish the beauties of this author when his judgment was mature, for during the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> Ovid was his favourite poet. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixteen he became anxious to pursue his studies at the university; but his father thinking him too young, opposed his inclination. Hearing of the competition <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, which was annually held at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, Aberdeen, for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bursaries on the foundation of that university, Ruddiman's ambition was kindled. Without the knowledge of his father, and with only a single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> in his pocket, which his sister had privately given him, he set out for that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> he was met by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, who robbed him of his coat, his shoes, his stockings, and his guinea. This misfortune did not damp his enterprising spirit: He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his journey to Aberdeen, presented himself before the professors as a candidate; and, though he had neither clothes to give him a decent appearance nor friend to recommend him, he gained the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. After attending the university four years, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of master of arts; an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of which he was always proud. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> says, the disputation on this occasion lasted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> usque <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> vesperum, i.e. "from morning till night." Though Ruddiman was only 20 years of age when he left the university, it appears from Ruddiman's book entitled Rhetoricorum Libri tres, composed before this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, but never published, that he had then read the Roman classics with uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and advantage. He was soon after engaged as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the son of Robert Young, Esq. of Auldbar, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandson of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Young, who under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Buchanan had been preceptor of James VI. His income here must have been very small, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his situation unpleasant; for within a year he accepted the office of schoolmaster in the parish of Laurencekirk. The profession of schoolmaster in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> parish at that period could open no field for ambition, nor prospect of great emolument; for by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> passed in 1683, the salary appropriated to this office could not be increased above 200 merks Scots, or L.11, 2s. 2½d. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. In discharging the duties of this humble but important station, it is probable that he used Simson's Rudimenta Grammatica, which was then generally taught in the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and by which he himself had been instructed in the principles of Latin grammar. When Ruddiman had spent three years and a half in this employment, the celebrated Dr Pitcairne happening to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through Laurencekirk, was detained in that village by a violent storm. Pitcairne wanting amusement, inquired at the hostess <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she could procure any agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> to bear him company at dinner. She replied, that the schoolmaster, though young, was said to be learned, and, though modest, she was sure could talk. Pitcairne was delighted with the conversation and learning of his new companion, invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and promised him his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>. When Ruddiman arrived in Edinburgh, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> library, which had been founded 18 years before by Sir George Mackenzie, attracted his curiosity and attention, and he was soon after appointed assistant-keeper under Mr Spottiswoode the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> librarian. His salary for executing this laborious office was L.8, 6s. 8d. He had besides a small honorary present from those who were admitted advocates for correcting their theses: he was also paid for copying <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the library. And the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, before he had held the office two years, were so highly pleased with his conduct, that they made him a present of 50 pounds Scots, or L.4, 3s. 4d. sterling. During the sitting of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session he attended the library from ten till three. But this confinement did not prevent him from engaging in other laborious duties: A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was occupied in teaching young gentlemen the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Some he attended at their lodgings, some waited upon him, and some resided in his own house. An exact <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the names of those who attended him, expressing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of their entry, and the sums which he was to receive from each, has been found in his pocket-book; a curious relic, which is still preserved. When Ruddiman's merit as a scholar became better known, his assistance was anxiously solicited by those who were engaged in literary publications. Freebairne, a respectable bookseller of that period, prevailed upon him to correct and prepare for the press Sir Robert Sibbald's Introductio ad historiam rerum d Romanis gestarum in ea Borealis Britanniae parte qua ultra murum Picticum est. He received for his labour L.3 sterling. At the request of Mr Spottiswoode librarian, for 5l. sterling he contributed his aid to the publication of Sir Robert Spottiswoode's Practiques of the Laws of Scotland. In 1707 he commenced auctioneer, an employment not very suitable to the dignified character of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters; but to this occupation he was probably impelled by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>; for upon balancing his accounts at the end of the preceding year, the whole surplus was 28l. 2s. with prospects of 236l. 7s. 6d. Scots. Ruddiman had a family; and seems to have been a stranger to that foolish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> which has seduced some literary men into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it is more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to starve than have recourse to an occupation which men of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and opulence are accustomed to despise. The same year he published an edition of Voluseni de Anima Tranquilitate Dialogus, to which he prefixed the life of Volusenus. Volusenus or Wilson was a learned Scotsman, and had the honour to be patronised by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey (See Wilson). In 1709 he published Johnstoni Cantici Solomonis Paraphrasis Poetica, and Johnstoni Cantica with notes, which he dedicated in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> to his friend and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Dr Pitcairne. The edition consisted of 200 copies. The expense of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> amounted to 5l. 10s. sterling, and he sold them at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> each copy. The philological talents of Ruddiman were next directed to a more important object, in which they became more conspicuous and useful. Freebairn the bookseller proposed to publish a new edition of the Scottish translation of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Aeneid by Gavin Douglas bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a>. Of the contributions which some eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the age presented, the most valuable were supplied by Ruddiman. Freebairn acknowledged in general terms this obligation, but has not done him the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to inform the reader what these valuable contributions were, and Ruddiman's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> restrained him from publicly asserting his claim. From the pocket-book which has been already mentioned, it appears that Ruddiman corrected the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and wrote the glossary; and there is strong reason to believe that he was the author of the 42 general rules for assisting the reader to understand the language of Douglas. To those who wish to be acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> language of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, the glossary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, as it forms a compendious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of the Anglo-Saxon. For this elaborate work Ruddiman was allowed 8l. 6s. 8d. sterling. The reputation of Ruddiman had now extended to a distance. He was invited by the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a> to be rector of the grammar school of that town; but the faculty of advocates, anxious to retain him, augmented his salary to 30l. 6s. 8d. sterling, and he declined the offer. In 1711 he assisted Bishop Sage in publishing Drummond of Hawthornden's works; and performed the same favour to Dr Abercrombie, who was then preparing for the press his Martial Achievements. In 1713 he was deprived of his friend Dr Pitcairne. Ruddiman. On this occasion he testified all the respect which friendship could inspire to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his deceased patron and surviving family. He composed Pitcairne's epitaph, and conducted the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of his library, which was disposed of to Peter the Great of Russia. In 1714 the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">Rudiments</a> of the Latin tongue were published. Eighteen or nineteen Latin grammars, composed by Scotchmen, had appeared before this period; yet such is the intrinsic value of this little treatise, that it soon superseded all other books on the subject, and is now taught in all the grammar schools in Scotland. It has also been translated into other languages. He was next called upon to publish the works of Buchanan. The value of these he enhanced much by an elaborate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, his Tabula Regum Scotiae Chronologica and Proprietorum Nominum Interpretatio. The interpretation of proper names was highly requisite; for Buchanan has so disguised them in the Roman dress, that the original name is scarcely discernible; and the preface puts the reader on his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the chronological errors and factious spirit of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Ruddiman also added a learned dissertation, intitled De Metris Buchananae Libellus, and subjoined annotations critical and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> on the History of Scotland. As he espoused the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, he raised against himself a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of enemies, and gave occasion to that celebrated controversy which has been carried on with much keenness and animosity, and with little intermission, even to the present times. For this work Ruddiman was promised 40l. sterling. He had now been so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> accustomed to superintend the press, that he was led to form the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of erecting a printing-office himself (a). Accordingly, in the year 1715, he commenced printer in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Walter, who had been regularly bred to the business. Some years after he was appointed printer to the university, along with James Davidson bookseller. The first literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> formed in Scotland was instituted in the year 1718. It probably derived its origin from the factions and turbulent spirit of the times. The learned, anxious perhaps to find some respite from the political dissensions of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, endeavoured to procure it in elegant amusement; for one of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> was, that the "affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state should not be introduced." Ruddiman and the masters of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-school had the honour to found this society. They were afterwards joined by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames. In 1725, the first part of his Grammaticae Latinae Institutiones, which treated of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, was published. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part, which explained the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and principles of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a>, appeared in 1731. He also wrote a third part on prosody, which is said to be more copious and correct than any other publication on the subject. When urged to give it to the public, he said drolly, "The age has so little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the sale would not pay (a) It has long been an object of curiosity to ascertain the time at which the art of printing was introduced into Scotland. Mr Robertson, the late keeper of the records, discovered a patent of King James IV. which renders it certain that a printing-press was first established at Edinburgh during the year 1507, 30 years after Caxton had brought it into England. See Printing. Ruddiman, the expense." Of this work he published an abridgement, to which he subjoined an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his pro- Ruddiman next engaged in the management of a newspaper, an employment for which his genius and industry seemed to render him well qualified. But those who should expect either much information or amusement from this publication, would perhaps be greatly disappointed. The newspaper which he conducted was the Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and was established in 1720 by William <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROLLAND">Rolland</a> a lawyer. Ruddiman acted only in the capacity of printer for five years; but upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Rolland in 1729, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> was transferred to him, or to his brother Walter and him conjunctly. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> continued in the family of Ruddiman till the year 1772, when it was sold by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-children. The Caledonian Mercury was at first printed three times a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, in a small 4to of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, with two columns in each page, and 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; so that the whole paper contained only 400 lines. It now contains in its folio size 2480 lines. Mr Ruddiman, after the death of Mr Spottiswoode librarian, remained for some time in his former station; but was at length appointed keeper of the library; though without any increase of salary; and some years after Mr Goodal, the defender of Queen Mary, succeeded him in the office of sub-librarian. The assiduous application of Ruddiman, supported by such learning, was intitled to wealth, which now indeed flowed upon him in what was at that period deemed great abundance. On the first of October 1735, it appeared from an exact statement of his affairs, that he was worth L.1882 5s. 2d. sterling; and on the 20th of May, the ensuing year, his wealth had increased to L.1985 6s. 3d. sterling. In 1710 he valued his effects at L.24 14s. 9d. sterling. In 1737 the schoolmasters and teachers in Edinburgh formed themselves into a society, in order to establish a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the support of their wives and children. Of this scheme Ruddiman was an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> promoter, and was chosen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. Perhaps it was this association which in 1742 gave the idea to the Scots clergy of forming their widows fund. In 1739 he published Selectus Diplomatum et Numismatum Scotiae Thesaurus. This work was projected and begun by Anderson (hence called Anderson's Diplomata), but was finished by Ruddiman. The preface, which is an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on Anderson's performance, was written by Ruddiman, and displays a greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of knowledge than any of his other productions. As Ruddiman had imbibed from his father those political principles which attached him to the family of Stuart, he probably did not remain an unconcerned spectator of the civil commotions which in 1745 agitated Scotland. He did not, however, take any active part in the rebellion. His principles, he has been heard to say, induced him to be a quiet subject and a good citizen. He retired to the country during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1745; and while his fellow-citizens were spilling each other's blood, he was more happily engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Critical Observations on Burnan's Commentaries on Lucan's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>. The Caledonian Mercury was in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time marked with a jealous eye. His son, Ruddiman who had for some time been the principal manager of that newspaper, having copied a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a> which was reckoned seditious from an English paper, was imprisoned. The solicitation of his father procured his release; but it was too late; for the unhappy young man had contracted a distemper in the tolbooth of Edinburgh which brought him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. During the last seventeen years of his life Ruddiman was almost incessantly engaged in controversy. To this he was in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> compelled by the violent attacks which some critics of the times had successively made upon his works. He was first called upon by Benson, auditor in the exchequer, to determine the comparative merit of Buchanan and Johnston as poets. He gave a decided preference to Buchanan in perspicuity, purity, and variety of style; but, like a candid critic, allowed Johnston to be superior in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of his numbers. His next antagonist was Logan, one of the ministers of Edinburgh, a weak illiterate man, but an obstinate polemic. The subject of contest was, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Scotland was strictly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, and whether the birth of Robert III. was legitimate? Ruddiman maintained the affirmative in both <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and certainly far surpassed his antagonist in the powers of reasoning. He proved the legitimacy of Robert by the public records of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> with a force of argument which admits of no reply; but in discussing the first question (by which he was led to consider the contest between Bruce and Baliol) he was not so successful: for there are many instances in the history of Scotland in which the brother succeeded to the crown in preference to the son. He showed, however, that the Scottish crown was at no period properly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>; and that, according to the old licentious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the kingdom, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of Bruce, who was the nearest in blood to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> stock, was preferable to the claim of Baliol though descended from the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. But the labours of Ruddiman did not end when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> dropt from the feeble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of Logan. He was soon called upon to repel the attacks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> schoolmaster of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALKEITH">Dalkeith</a>, who maintained, in opposition to him, that Buchanan had neither repented of his treatment of Queen Mary, nor had been guilty of ingratitude to that princess. That Buchanan ever repented there is reason to doubt. Whether he was guilty of ingratitude, let the unbiased determine, when they are assured by authentic records that Mary conferred on him a pension for life of 500 pounds Scots. When Ruddiman had arrived at his eightieth year, and was almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, he was assailed by James Man, master of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Aberdeen, with a degree of rancour and virulence, united with some learning and ability, which must have touched him in a sensible manner, and alarmed his fears for his reputation after his decease. He was called a finished pedant, a furious columnator, and a corrupter of Buchanan's works. The venerable old man again put on his armour, entered the lists, and gained a complete victory. Man, with all his acuteness, could only point out twenty errors in two folio volumes. Some of these were typographical, some trifling, and some doubtful. Ruddiman, with much pleasantry, drew up against Man an account of 469 errors, consisting of 14 articles, of which two or three may be produced as a specimen. 1. Falsehoods and prevarications. The triumph which he gained over this virulent adversary he did not long enjoy; for he died at Edinburgh on the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1757, in the 83rd year of his age, and was buried in the Grey Friars <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> without any monument to distinguish his grave. He was three times married, but left behind him only one daughter, Alison, who was married in 1747 to James Stewart, Esq. He is supposed to have died worth £3000 sterling. He was of the middle size, of a thin and straight make, and had eyes remarkably piercing. Of his talents and learning his works afford the most satisfactory proofs. His memory was tenacious and exact. He could repeat long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of his favourite poet Ovid, to the amount of 60 lines, and without omitting a word. He was so great a master in the Latin language, that he has perhaps been equalled by none since the days of Buchanan. Ruddiman has left a character unstained by vice, and distinguished by many virtues. His piety was exemplary. He spent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> employment; and we are informed had prayers read to him every morning by his amanuensis when the infirmities of age required such an assistant. He was frugal of his time, neither indolent nor fond of amusement; and so remarkably temperate, that it is said he was never intoxicated. Though often forced into controversy, and treated with insolence, he never descended to scurrility and abuse, nor cherished resentment against his enemies. His candour was much admired in one instance in the favourable character which he published in the Caledonian Mercury of his antagonist Love (b), after his decease. Upon the whole, it must be allowed that Ruddiman has been of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to classical literature, and an honour to his native country.

RUDESHEIM

Pages 361-361

a rich village of the Rhinegau, situated about five miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, contains about 2500 inhabitants. The wine of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is looked upon as without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> the best of the Rhinegau, and consequently of all Germany. Baron Riesbeck says, he found it much more fiery than that of Hochheim; but that for pleasanness of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> there is no comparison betwixt them. The best Rudesheim, like the best Hochheimer, sells upon the spot for three guilders the bottle. "You can (says our author) have no tolerable wine here for one guilder, nor any very good for two; at least I should prefer the worst <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> I ever tasted to any Rudesheimer I met with either here <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at Mentz for these prices. Indeed the wine of our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> (a rich ecclesiastic) was far better than any we could get at the inn. It stands to reason, that the same vintage furnishes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> of very different degrees of goodness; but besides this, it is in the Rhinegau as everywhere else. The best wines are generally sent abroad by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and middling inhabitants, and the worst kept for internal consumption; for the expense of carriage being the same in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, strangers had much rather pay a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> price for the good than have the bad. It is only rich people, such as our host was, who can afford to keep the produce of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for their own drinking. Upon this principle, I have eaten much better Swiss cheeses out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> than in it, and have drank much better Rhenish in the inns of the northern parts of Germany than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where the wine grows. The position of the country also contributes to render the wine dearer than it would otherwise be. As the best wine grows in its more northern parts, the easy transport by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and all parts of the world, raises its price above its real value. The place where the flower of the Rudesheim wine grows is precisely the neck of the land, formed by the winding of the Rhine to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, after it has run to the westward from Mentz hither. This neck, which is a rock almost perpendicular, enjoys the first rays of the rising and the last of the setting <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. It is divided into small low terraces, which are carried up to the utmost top of the hill like steep stairs; these are guarded by small walls and earthen mounds, which are often washed away by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. The first vine was brought hither from France, and they still call the best grape the Orleannois. They plant the vine stocks very low, scarce ever more than four or five feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. This way of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the vine is favourable to the production of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wine, but not to its goodness, as the phlegmatic and harsh parts of it would certainly evaporate more, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the sap were refined through higher and more numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. This is undoubtedly the reason why every kind of Rhenish has something in it that is harsh, sour, and watery. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> of the best vineyards, which are the lower ones, in the above mentioned neck of land, is often bought before-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, at the advanced price of some ducats, by Dutch and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. It must be a very rich stock to yield above four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of wine.—You may easily imagine, that the cultivation of vineyards must be very expensive in this country, as the dung, which is extremely dear, must be carried up to the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the peasants shoulders."

RUDIMENTS

Pages 361-362

the first principles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grounds of any art or science, called also the elements thereof. RUE. See Ruta, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Rue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> de la, a French orator and poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1643. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits, where he afterwards became a professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. At an early <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> disclosed itself. In 1667, when he was only 24 years old, he composed a Latin poem on the conquests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. which was so much esteemed by (b) The following character of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> was published in the Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> of the 24th of September 1750. "On Thursday morning died at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALKEITH">Dalkeith</a>, after a lingering illness, in the 55th year of his age, Mr John Love, rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school there; who, for his uncommon knowledge in classical learning, his indefatigable diligence, and strictness of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> without severity, was justly accounted one of the most sufficient masters in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>." This character is doubtless <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>; though Love is now known to have been the schoolmaster satirized by Smollet in the beginning of his Roderick Random. the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Corneille, that he translated it into French, presented it to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> passed so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> encomiums on the superior merit of the original, that the author was received into the favour of that monarch, and ever after treated by him with singular respect. De la Rue, anxious to preach the gospel to the Canadians, requested leave of absence from his superiors; but having destined him for the pulpit, they refused to comply with his request. Accordingly he commenced preacher, and became one of the most eminent orators of his age. In his discourses he would probably have been too lavish of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not been cautioned against it by a judicious courtier. "Continue (said he) to preach as you do. We <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hear you with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as you reason with us; but avoid wit. We value the wit contained in two verses of a song more than all that is contained in most of the sermons in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>." Respecting the delivery of sermons, he entertained an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> quite opposite to the established practice of his countrymen. In France it was customary not to read sermons from the pulpit, but to recite them from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. This he considered as a laborious task, not compensated by any advantages. On the contrary, he was of opinion that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> sermons was preferable.—The preacher, with his discourse before him, could read it with ease, free from that timidity and embarrassment which frequently attends the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of recollection; and he would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a considerable time which is usually spent in committing it to memory. In these sentiments many will not be disposed to acquiesce: but, without pretending to determine the question, it may be asserted, that a sermon, whether read or recited, if spoken in a serious manner, and with proper inflections and tones of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, will produce all the effects for which a sermon is calculated. De la Rue died at Paris on the 27th of May 1725, at the age of 82. He was as amiable in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> as he was venerable in the pulpit. His conversation was pleasant and instructive. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and knowledge enabled him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with ease, and to express himself with propriety on every subject. He charmed his superiors by his wit, and his inferiors by his affability. Though living amidst the bustle of the world, he was always prepared for the solitude of the closet and the retreat of the cloister. In the pulpit he poured forth the finest effusions of eloquence in the most animated and impressive manner.—He published Panegyrics, Funeral Orations, and Sermons. His best sermon is that intitled Des Calamités Publiques, and his most admired funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> was composed on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Luxembourg. There are also tragedies of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, both in Latin and French, which were approved by Corneille. He was one of those who published editions of the classics for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, which fell to his share, was published with notes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of the Poet, in 1675, 4to, and is a valuable and useful edition.
