The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">Playhouse</a> tells us, that the three first acts were written by Mr Tho. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a>. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Sidney, in his Apology for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, says, "it is full of stately speeches, and well-sounding phrases, climbing to the height of Seneca in his style, &c." Rymer speaks highly in its commendation. Mr Spence, at the instigation of Mr Pope, republished it in 1736, with a pompous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>. It is said to be our first dramatic piece written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of this reign, Mr Sackville was member for Sussex, and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time he made the tour of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in 1566 was imprisoned at Rome, when he was informed of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by which he became possessed of a very considerable fortune. Having now obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he returned to England; and being first knighted, was created Lord Buckhurst. In 1570 he was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to France. In 1586 he was one of the commissioners appointed to try the unfortunate Mary Queen of Scots; and was the messenger employed to report the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, and to see it executed. The year following he went ambassador to the States General, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their complaint against the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>; who, disliking his impartiality, prevailed on the queen to recall him, and confine him to his house. In this state of confinement he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> about 10 months, when Leicester dying, he was restored to favour; and in 1580 was installed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>: but the most incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the queen's partiality for Lord Buckhurst appeared in the year 1591, when she caused him to be elected <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in the university of Oxford, in opposition to her favourite <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In-1598, on the death of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh, Lord Buckhurst succeeded him, and by virtue of his office became in effect prime minister; and when, in 1601, the earls of Essex and Southampton were brought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, he sat as lord <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> on that awful occasion. On the accession of James I. he was graciously received, had the office of lord high treasurer confirmed to him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and was created earl of Dorset. He continued in high favour with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his death, which happened suddenly, on the 19th of April 1608, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> chamber at Whitehall. He was interred with great solemnity in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. He was a good poet, an able minister, and an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. From him is descended the present noble family of the Dorsets. "It were needless (says Mr Walpole) to add, that he was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of genius and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>." Sackville, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, earl of Dorset, a celebrated wit and poet, descended from the foregoing, was born in 1637. He was, like Villiers, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, Sedley, &c., one of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a> of King Charles's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and sometimes indulged himself in inexcusable excesses. He openly discountenanced the violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of James II. and engaged early for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, by whom he was made lord chamberlain of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and taken... SACRAMENT is derived from the Latin word sacramentum, which signifies an oath, particularly the oath taken by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to be true to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and general. The words of this oath, according to Polybius, were, obtemperatus sum et facturus quicquid mandabitur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> imperatoribus justa vires. The word was adopted by the writers of the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and employed, perhaps with no great propriety, to denote those ordinances of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> by which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> came under an obligation, equally sacred with that of an oath, to observe their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the covenant of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and in which they have the assurance of Christ that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fulfil his part of the same covenant. Of sacraments, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, Protestant churches admit of but two; and it is not easy to conceive how a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> can be made out from Scripture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a sacrament be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> which is given by the church of England. By that church, the meaning of the word sacrament is declared to be "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace given unto us, ordained by Christ himself as a means whereby we receive the same, and a pledge to assure us thereof." According to this definition, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a> are certainly sacraments; for each consists of an outward and visible sign of what is believed to be an inward and spiritual grace: both were ordained by Christ himself, and by the reception of each does the Christian come under a solemn obligation to be true to his divine master, according to the terms of the covenant of grace. (See Baptism and Supper of the Lord.) The Romanists, however, add to this number confirmation, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> unction, ordination, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, holding in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sacraments; but two of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> not being peculiar to the Christian church cannot possibly be Christian sacraments, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the sacraments or obligations into which men of all religions enter. Marriage was instituted from the beginning, when God made man <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, and commanded them to be fruitful, and multiply and replenish the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and penance, as far as it is of the same import with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in all religions which teach that God is merciful, and men fallible.—The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> severities imposed upon penitents by the church of Rome (see Penance) may indeed be in some respects peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of that church, though the penances of the Hindoos are certainly as rigid; but none of these severities were ordained by Christ himself as the pledge of an inward and spiritual grace; nor do they, like baptism and the Lord's Supper, bring men under obligations which are supposed to be analogous to the meaning of the word sacramentum. Confirmation has a better <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the appellation of a sacrament than any of the other five popish rites of that name, though it certainly was not considered as such by the earliest writers of the Christian church, nor does it appear to have been ordained by Christ himself, (see Confirmation.) Ordination is by many churches considered as a very important rite; but as it is not administered to all men, nor has any particular form appropriated to it in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, it cannot be considered as a Christian sacrament conferring grace generally necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. It is rather a form of authorising certain persons to perform certain offices, which respect not themselves but the whole church; and extreme unction is a rite which took its rise from the miraculous powers of the primitive church vainly claimed by the succeeding clergy. (See Ordination and Extreme Unction.) These considerations seem to have some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> with the Romish clergy themselves; for they call the eucharist, by way of eminence, the holy sacrament. Thus to expose the holy sacrament, is to lay the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> on the altar to be adored.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of the holy sacrament is that in which this host is carried about the church, or about a town. Numerous as we think the sacraments of the Romish church, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Christians sprung up in England early in the current century who increased their number.—The founder of this sect was a Dr Deacon, we think, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, where the remains of it subsisted very lately, and probably do so at present. According to these men, every rite and every phrase in the book called the Apostolical Constitutions were certainly in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the apostles themselves. Still, however, they make a distinction between the greater and the lesser sacraments. The greater sacraments are only two. Baptism and the Lord's Supper. The lesser are no fewer than ten, viz. five belonging to baptism, exorcism, anointing with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> garment, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and anointing with chrism or ointment. The other five are, the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, unction of the sick, holy orders, and matrimony. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of these lesser sacraments, or the grace which they are supposed to confer, our limits will permit us to give no account.—Nor is it necessary that we should. The sect which taught them, if not extinguished, is certainly in its last wane. It has produced, however, one or two learned men; and its founder's Full, True, and Comprehensive View of Christianity, in two Catechisms, is a work which the Christian antiquary will read with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> for information, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> for the materials which it contains for meditation on the workings of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. It was published in 8vo, in the year 1748. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a> of the Holy Sacrament, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> establishment formed in France, whose founder was Aetherius, bishop of Bethlehem, and which, in 1642, received an order from Urban VIII. to have always a number of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> ready to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their ministry among pagan nations, wherever the pope, or congregation de propaganda, should appoint. Sacramentarians, a general name given to all such as have published or held erroneous doctrines of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly applied among <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, by way of reproach, to the Lutherans, Calvinists, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. Sacramentary, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romish church-book, which contains all the prayers and ceremonies practised at the celebration of the sacraments. It was wrote by Pope Gelasius, and afterwards revised, corrected, and abridged, by St Gregory. Sacre, or Saker, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of falcon, called by authors falco sacer, and differently described by different authors, but by all agreed to be an extremely bold and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. It is a native of of the northern regions of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and a variety, called by some writers the speckled <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a> hawk, is found at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.

SACRED

Pages 461-461

something holy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is solemnly offered and consecrated to God, with benedictions, uncions, &c. Kings, prelates, and priests, are reckoned sacred persons; abbots are only blessed.—The deaconhood, sub-deaconhood, and priesthood, are all sacred orders, and are said to impress a sacred indelible character. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of consecrating kings with holy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is derived (says Gutilingius) from the Hebrews; among whom, he agrees with Grotius, it was never used but to kings who had not an evident <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by succession. He adds, that the Christian emperors never used it before Justin the younger; from whom he takes it to have passed to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, &c. SACRED is also applied to things belonging to God and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Church-lands, ornaments, &c. are held sacred.—The sacred <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> is that of the cardinals. SACRED Majesty, is applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England; yet Loyseau says it is blasphemy. See MAJESTY. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> struck with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> as sacred. In the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, sacred place chiefly denotes that where a person deceased has been interred. SACRED Elixir. See ELIXIR.

SACRIFICE

Pages 466-467

shrine? <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a mother the most engaging and affectionate of her daughters, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> rising to maturity, to be slaughtered at the altar of Ashtaroth or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a>? Justin describes this unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> very pathetically: "Quippe homines, ut victimas, immolabant; et impubes (quae celas hostium misericordiam provocat) aris admovebant; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PACEM">pacem</a> sanguine eorum exposcentes, pro quorum via Dii rogari maxime solent." Such was their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> zeal, that this was continually practised; and so much of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection still left unextinguished, as to render the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> ten times more shocking, from the tenderness which they seemed to express. They embraced their children with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fondness, and encouraged them in the gentlest terms, that they might not be appalled at the sight of the hellish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; begging of them to submit with cheerfulness to this fearful operation. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there was any appearance of a tear rising, or a cry unawares escaping, the mother smothered it with her kisses, that there might not be any show of backwardness or constraint, but the whole be a free-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> offering. These cruel endearments over, they stabbed them to the heart, or otherwise opened the sluices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and with the blood warm, as it ran, besmeared the altar and the grim visage of the idol. These were the customs which the Israelites learned of the people of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, and for which they are upbraided by the Psalmist: "They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> commanded them; but were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works: yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, and shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> was polluted with blood. Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a-whoring with their own inventions." These cruel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, practised in so many nations, made Plutarch debate with himself, "Whether it would not have been better for the Galatee, or for the Scythians, to have had no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of any superior being, than to have formed to themselves notions of gods who delighted in the blood of men; of gods, who esteemed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> victims the most acceptable and perfect sacrifice? Would it not (says he) have been more eligible for the Carthaginians to have had the atheist Critias, or Diagoras, their lawgiver, at the commencement of their polity, and to have been taught, that there was neither god nor demon, than to have sacrificed, in the manner they were wont, to the god which they adored? Wherein they acted, not as the person did whom <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEDOCLES">Empedocles</a> describes in some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, where he exposes this unnatural custom. The sire there with many idle vows offers up unwittingly his son for a sacrifice; but the youth was so changed in feature and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, that his father did not know him. These people used knowingly and wilfully, to go through this bloody <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and slaughter their own offspring. Even they who were childless would not be exempted from this cursed tribute; but purchased children, at a price, of the poorer sort, and put them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> with as little remorse as one would kill a lamb or a chicken. The mother, who sacrificed her child, stood by, without any seeming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of what she was losing, and without uttering a groan. If a sigh did by chance escape, she lost all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which she proposed to herself in the offering, and the child was notwithstanding slain. All the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, while the children were murdered, there was a noise of clarions and tabors set before the idol, that the cries and shrieks of the victims might not be heard. "Tell me now (says Plutarch) if the monsters of old, the Typhons and the giants, were to expel the gods, and to rule the world in their stead; could they require a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> more horrid than these infernal rites and sacrifices?"

SACRILEGE

Pages 467-467

Sacrilegium, the crime of profaning sacred things, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> things devoted to God; or of alienating to laymen, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> purposes, what was given to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> persons and pious uses.

SACRISTY

Pages 467-467

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an apartment in a church where the sacred utensils were kept, being the same with our Vestry.

SADDLE

Pages 467-467

is a seat upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s back, contrived for the conveniency of the rider. A hunting-saddle is composed of two bows, two bands, fore-bolsters, pannels, and saddle-straps; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> saddle has, besides these parts, corks, hind-bolsters, and a troussequin. The pommel is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both.

SADDUCEES

Pages 467-468

were a famous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews, and consisted of persons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and opulence. Respecting their origin there are various accounts and various opinions. Epiphanius, and after him many other writers, contend, that they took their rise from Dositheus a secretary of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, and their name from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word יְדֵי, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, from the great justice and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> which they showed in all their actions; a derivation which neither suits the word Sadducee nor the general character of the sect. They are thought by some too to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>: but this is by no means probable, as they always attended the worship and sacrifices at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and never at Gerizzim. In the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a> we are told that the Sadducees derived their name from Sadoc, and that the sect arose about 260 years before Christ, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Antigonus of Socho, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Sanhedrim at Jerusalem, and teacher of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> school of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He had often in his lectures, it seems, taught his scholars, that they ought not to serve God as slaves do their masters, from the hopes of a reward, but merely out of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for his own sake; from which Sadoc and Baithus inferred that there were no rewards at all after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They therefore separated from their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and taught that there was no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> nor future state. This new doctrine quickly spread, and gave rise to the sect of Sadducees, which in many respects resembled the Epicureans. Dr Prideaux thinks that the Sadducees were at first no more than what the Caraïtes are now; that is, they would not receive the traditions of the elders, but stuck to the written word only: and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a> being great promoters of those traditions, hence these two sects became directly opposite to each other. See Prideaux's Conn. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> 2. book 2. and 3.; and see also Pharisees and Caraïtes. Afterwards the Sadducees imbibed other doctrines, which rendered them a sect truly impious: for they denied the resurrection of the dead, and the existence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, and of the spirits or souls of men departed (Matt.). They held, that there is no spiritual being but God only; that as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, this world is his all. They did not deny but that we had reasonable souls: but they maintained this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> was mortal; and, by a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, they denied the rewards and punishments of another life. They pretended also, that what is said of the existence of angels, and of a future resurrection, are nothing but illusions. St Epiphanius, and after him St Austin, have advanced, that the Sadducees denied the Holy Ghost. But neither Josephus nor the evangelists accuse them of any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> like this. It has been also imputed to them, that they thought God corporeal, and that they received none of the prophecies. It is pretty difficult to apprehend how they could deny the being of angels, and yet receive the books of Moses, where such frequent mention is made of angels and of their appearances. Grotius and M. Le Clerc observe, that it is very likely they looked upon angels, not as particular beings, subsisting of themselves, but as powers, emanations, or qualities, inseparable from the Deity, as the sunbeams are inseparable from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Or perhaps they held angels not to be spiritual but mortal; just as they thought that substance to be which animates us and thinks in us. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> do not tell us how they solved this difficulty, that might be urged against them from so many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, where mention is made of angels. As the Sadducees acknowledged neither punishments nor recompenses in another life, so they were inexorable in their chastising of the wicked. They observed the law themselves, and caused it to be observed by others, with the utmost rigour. They admitted of none of the traditions, explications, or modifications, of the Pharisees; they kept only to the text of the law; and maintained, that only what was written was to be observed. The Sadducees are accused of rejecting all the books of Scripture except those of Moses; and to support this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, it is observed, that our Saviour makes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of no Scripture against them, but passages taken out of the Pentateuch. But Scaliger produces good proofs to vindicate them from this reproach. He observes, that they did not appear in Israel till after the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the holy books was fixed; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been to choose out of the canonical Scriptures, the Pentateuch was less favourable to them than any other book, since it often makes mention of angels and their apparition. Besides, the Sadducees were present in the temple and at other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assemblies, where the books of the prophets were read indifferently, as well as those of Moses. They were in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employments of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, many of them were even priests. Would the Jews have suffered in these employments persons that rejected the greatest part of their Scriptures? Menasseh ben-Israel says expressly, that indeed they did not reject the prophets, but that they explained them in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> very different from that of the other Jews. Josephus assures us, that they denied <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> or fate; alleging that these were only sounds void of sense, and that all the good or evil that happens to us is in consequence of the good or evil side we have taken, by the free choice of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. They said, also, that God was far removed from doing or knowing evil, and that man was the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> master of his own actions. This was roundly to deny a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>; and upon this footing I Sadducees know not, says F. Calmet, what could be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Sadducees, or what influence they could ascribe to God in things here below. However, it is certain they were not only tolerated among the Jews, but that they were admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priesthood itself. John Hircanus, high-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of that nation, separated himself in a signal manner from the sect of the Pharisees, and went over to that of Sadoc. It is said, also, he gave strict command to all the Jews, on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to receive the maxims of this sect. Aristobulus and Alexander Janneaus, son of Hircanus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to favour the Sadducees; and Maimonides assures us, that under the reign of Alexander Janneaus, they had in possession all the offices of the Sanhedrim, and that there only remained of the party of the Pharisees, Simon the son of Scera. Caiaphas, who condemned <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ to death, was a Sadducee (Acts v. 17. iv. 1); as also Ananus the younger, who put to death St James the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the Jews hold as heretics that small number of Sadducees that are to be found among them. See upon this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> Serrar, Trilacres, Menasseh ben-Israel de Resurrectione mortuorum; Basnage's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Jews, &c.; and Calmet's Dissertation upon the Sects of the Jews before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> of St Mark. The sect of the Sadducees was much reduced by the destruction of Jerusalem, and by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the Jews; but it revived afterwards. At the beginning of the third century it was so formidable in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, that Ammonim, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>'s master, when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them propagate their opinions in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, thought himself obliged to write against them, or rather against the Jews, who tolerated the Sadducees, though they denied the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of their religion. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> mentions the Sadducees in one of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>, banishes them out of all places of his dominions, and condemns them to the severest punishments, as people that maintained atheistical and impious tenets, denying the resurrection and the last judgment. Ananus, or Ananus, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Juda, son of Nachman, a famous rabbin of the 8th century, declared himself, as it is said, in favour of the Sadducees, and strenuously protected them against their adversaries. They had also a celebrated defender in the 12th century, in the person of Alpharag, a Spanish rabbin. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> wrote against the Pharisees, the declared enemies of the Sadducees; and maintained by his public writings, that the purity of Judaism was only to be found among the Sadducees; that the traditions avowed by the Pharisees were useless; and that the ceremonies, which they had multiplied without end, were an unsupportable yoke. The rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> ben <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Italieri replied to Alpharag, and supported the sect of the Pharisees by two great arguments, that of their universality and that of their antiquity. He proved their antiquity by a continued succession from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 1167; and their universality, because the Pharisees are spread all the world over, and are found in all the synagogues. There are still Sadducees in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and in several other places. They deny the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the soul, and the resurrection of the body; but they are rarely found, at least there are but few who declare themselves for these opinions.

SADLER

Pages 468-469

JOHN, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>; born in 1615; and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, Cambridge, where he became eminent for his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knowledge in the oriental languages. He removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn, where he made no small progress in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and in 1644 was admitted one of the masters in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, as also one of the two masters of requests. In 1649 he was chosen town-clerk of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the same year published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">Rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a>. He was greatly esteemed by Oliver Cromwell, by whose special warrant he was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in chancery, when their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was reduced to six. By his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> it was that the Jews obtained the privilege of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for themselves a synagogue in London. In 1658 he was made member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a>; and next year was appointed first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> under the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> with Mr Taylor, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-locke, and others, for the probate of wills. In 1660 he published his Ollia. Soon after the restoration, he lost all his employments. In the fire of London in 1666, he was a great sufferer; which obliged him to retire to his seat of Warmwell in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, where he lived in a private manner till 1674, when he died.

SADOC

Pages 469-469

a famous Jewish rabbi, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Sadducees.

SADOLET

Pages 469-469

James, a polite and learned <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in 1477. Leo X. made him and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Bembus his secretaries, an office for which they were both well qualified; and Sadolet was soon after made bishop of Carpentras, near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>: he was made a cardinal in 1536 by Paul III., and employed in several negotiations and embassies. He died in 1547, not without the suspicion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, for corresponding too familiarly with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and for testifying too much regard for some of their doctors. His works, which are all in Latin, were collected in 1607 at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, in one volume 8vo. All his contemporaries spoke of him in the highest terms.

SAFE-GUARD

Pages 469-469

a protection formerly granted to a stranger who feared violence from some of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects for seeking his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Safe-Conduct is a security given by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, to a stranger for his safe-coming into and passing out of the realm; the form whereof is in Reg. Orig. 25. There are letters of safe-conduct which must be enrolled in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>; and the persons to whom granted must have them ready to show; and touching which there are several statutes. See PRE-rogative.

SAFFRON

Pages 469-470

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, is formed of the stigmata of the crocus officinalis, dried on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>, and pressed together into cakes. See Crocus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. There are two kinds of saffron, the English and Spanish; of which the latter is by far the most esteemed. Saffron is principally cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, in a circle of about ten miles diameter. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this tract is an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with few inclosures; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> there is, as in most other places, to crop two years, and let the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> be fallow the third. Saffron is generally planted upon fallow-ground, and, all other things being alike, they prefer that which has borne barley the year before. The saffron ground is seldom above three acres, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less than one; and in choosing, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing they have regard to is, that they be well exposed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, nor a very stiff clay, but a temperate dry mould, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> lies upon chalk, and is of an hazel <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; though, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> every thing else answers, the colour of the mould is pretty much neglected. The ground being made choice of, about Lady-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or the beginning of April, it must be carefully ploughed, the furrows being drawn much closer together, and deeper if the soil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow it, than is done for any kind of corn; and accordingly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> is greater. About five weeks after, during any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May, they lay between 20 and 30 loads of dung upon each <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and having spread it with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> it in as before. The shortest rotten dung is the best: and the farmers, who have the conveniency of making it, spare no pains to make it good, being sure of a proportionable price for it. About midsummer they plough a third time, and between every 16 feet and a half they leave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> furrow or trench, which serves both as a boundary to the several parcels, and for throwing the weeds into at the proper season. The time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> is commonly in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used at this time is a small narrow spade, commonly called a spit-shovel. The method is this: One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with his shovel raises about three or four inches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and throws it before him about six or more inches. Two persons, generally women, follow with roots, which they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the farthest edge of the trench made by the digger, at about three inches from each other. As soon as the digger has gone once the breadth of the ridge, he begins again at the other side; and, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> as before, covers the roots last set, which makes room for another row of roots at the same distance from the first that they are from one another. The only dexterity necessary in digging is, to leave some part of the first stratum of earth untouched, to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> under the roots; and, in setting, to place the roots directly upon their bottom. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of roots planted on an acre is generally about 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, or 128 bushels. From the time of planting till the beginning of September, or sometimes before, there is no more labour required; but at that time they begin to vegetate, and are ready to show themselves above ground, which may be known by digging up a few of the roots. The ground is then to be pared with a sharp hoe, and the weeds raked into the furrows, otherwise they would hinder the growth of the saffron. In some time after, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> appear. They are gathered before they are full blown, as well as after, and the proper time for it is early in the morning. The owners of the saffron-fields get together a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, who pull off the whole flowers, and throw them by handfuls into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>, and so continue till about 11 o'clock. Having then carried home the flowers, they immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to picking out the stigmata or clivies, and together with them a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of the stylus itself, or string to which they are attached: the rest of the flower they throw away as useless. Next morning they return to the field, without regarding whether the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be wet or dry: and so on daily, even on Sundays, till the whole crop is gathered.—The next labour is to dry the clivies on the kiln. The kiln is built upon a thick plank, that it may be moved from place to place. It is supported by four short legs: the outside consists of eight pieces of wood of three inches thick, in form of a quadrangular frame, about 12 inches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the bottom on the inside, and 22 on the upper part; which last last is likewise the perpendicular height of it. On the foreside is left a hole of about eight inches square, and four inches above the plank, through which the fire is put in; over all the rest laths are laid pretty thick, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to one another, and nailed to the frame already mentioned. They are then plastered over on both sides, as are also the planks at bottom, very thick, to serve for a hearth. Over the mouth is laid a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-cloth, fixed to the edges of the kiln, and likewise to two rollers or moveable pieces of wood, which are turned by wedges or screws, in order to stretch the cloth. Instead of the hair-cloth, some people <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-wire, by which the saffron is soon dried, and with less <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>; but the difficulty of preserving it from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> makes the hair-cloth preferred by the best judges. The kiln is placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and they begin with putting five or six sheets of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the hair-cloth, and upon these they lay out the wet saffron two or three inches thick. It is then covered with some other sheets of paper, and over these they lay a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a> five or six times doubled, or, instead of this, a canvas pillow filled with straw; and after the fire has been lighted for some time, the whole is covered with a board having a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> upon it. At first they apply a pretty strong <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to make the chives sweet as they call it: and at this time a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of care is necessary to prevent burning. When it has been thus dried about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, they turn the cakes of saffron upside <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, putting on the coverings and weight as before. If no sinister accident happens during these first two hours, the danger is thought to be over; and nothing more is requisite than to keep up a very gentle fire for 24 hours, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the cake every half hour. That fuel is best which yields the least <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; and for this reason <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> is preferable to all others. The quantity of saffron produced at a crop is uncertain. Sometimes five or six pounds of wet chives are got from one root, sometimes not above one or two; and sometimes not so much as is sufficient to defray the expense of gathering and drying. But it is always observed, that about five pounds of wet saffron go to make one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of dry for the first three weeks of the crop, and six pounds during the last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. When the heads are planted very thick, two pounds of dry saffron may at a medium be allowed to an acre for the first crop, and 24 pounds for the two remaining ones, the third being considerably larger than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. To obtain the second and third crops, the labour of hoeing, gathering, picking, &c., already mentioned, must be repeated; and about midsummer, after the third crop is gathered, the roots must all be taken up and transplanted. For taking up the roots, sometimes the plough is made use of, and sometimes a forked hoe; and then the ground is harrowed once or twice over. During all the time of ploughing, harrowing, &c. 15 or more people will find work enough to follow and gather the heads as they are turned up. The roots are next to be carried to the house in sacks, where they are cleaned and rased. This labour consists in cleaning the roots thoroughly from earth, decayed old pieces, involucra, or excrescences; after which they become fit to be planted in new ground immediately, or they may be kept for some time, without danger of spoiling. The quantity of roots taken up in proportion to those planted is uncertain; but at a medium, 24 quarters of clean roots, fit to be planted, may be had from each acre.—There sometimes happens a remarkable change in the roots of saffron and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. As soon as they begin to shoot upwards, there are commonly two or three large tap-roots sent forth from the side of the old one, which will run two or three inches deep into the ground. At the place where these bulbs first come out from, the old one will be formed sometimes, though not always, and the tap-root then decays. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> increases in bigness, and at last falls quite off; which commonly happens in April. But many times these tap-roots never produce any bulbs, and remain barren for ever after. All such roots therefore should be thrown away in the making a new plantation. This degeneracy in the roots is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> for which no cure is as yet known. When saffron is offered to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, that kind ought to be chosen which has the broadest blades; this being the mark by which English saffron is distinguished from the foreign. It ought to be of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> or fiery-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, and to yield a dark <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tincture. It should be chosen fresh, not above a year old, in close cakes, neither dry nor yet very moist, tough and firm in tearing, of the same colour within as without, and of a strong, acrid, diffusive smell. This drug has been reckoned a very elegant and useful aromatic. Besides the virtues it has in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other substances of that class, it has been accounted one of the highest cordials, and is said to exhilarate the spirits to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, as, when taken in large doses, to occasion immoderate mirth, involuntary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>, and the ill effects which follow from the abuse of spirituous liquors. This medicine is particularly serviceable in hysteric depressions proceeding from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> cause or obstruction of the uterine secretions, where other aromatics, even those of the more generous kind, have little effect. Saffron imparts the whole of its virtue and colour to rectified spirit, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirit, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. A tincture drawn with vinegar loses greatly of its colour in keeping: the watery and vinous tinctures are apt to grow sour, and then lose their colour also: that made in pure spirit keeps in perfection for many years. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">Meadow</a> Saffron. See Colchicum, Botany Index.

SAGAN

Pages 470-470

in scripture <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the suffragan <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. According to some writers, he was only to officiate for him when he was rendered incapable of attending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> through sickness or legal uncleanness on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>; or, according to others, he was to assist the high-priest in the care of the affairs of the temple and the service of the priests.

SAGAPENUM

Pages 470-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, &c. a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-resin which is made up in two forms; the finer and purer is in loose granules <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> single drops; the coarser kind is in masses composed of these drops of various sizes, cemented together by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the same kind; and is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and the East Indies. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SAGE. See Salvia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Sage, Alain Rene, an ingenious French <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>-writer, was born at Ruys in Brittany in the year 1667. He had a fine flow of imagination, was a complete <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the French and Spanish languages, and wrote several admired romances in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Spanish authors. These were, The Bachelor of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, 2 vols 12mo; New Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Quixote, 2 vols 12mo; The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a> on Two Sticks, 2 vols 12mo; and Gil Blas, 4 vols 12mo. He produced also some comedies, and other humorous pieces. This ingenious author died in the year 1747, in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he supported himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Sage, the Reverend John, so justly admired by all who knew him for his classical learning and reasoning powers, was born, in 1652, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Creich and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, where his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had lived for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> generations with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect though with little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. His father was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Duffus's regiment, and fought for his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> when Monk stormed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a> on the 30th of August 1651. The issue of the civil wars, and the loyalty of Captain Sage, left him nothing to bestow upon his son but a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and his own principles of piety and virtue. In those days the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was taught in the parochial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Scotland with great ability and at a trifling expense; and after young Sage had acquired a competent knowledge of that language at one of those useful seminaries, his father, without receiving from an ungrateful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> any recompense for what he had lost in the cause of royalty, was still able to send him to the university of St Andrew's, where having remained in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> the usual <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of terms or sessions, and performed the exercises required by the statutes, he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of master of arts, the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which it appears he ever received from any university. During his residence in St Andrew's he studied the Greek and Roman authors with great diligence, and was likewise instructed in logic, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, and such other branches of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> as then obtained in the schools, which, though we affect to smile at them in this enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he always spoke of as highly useful to him who would understand the poets, historians, and orators of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and even the fathers of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> agree with him, who is at all acquainted with the ancient metaphysics, and has read the writings of Clemens Alexandrinus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Tertullian, Chrysostome, and other fathers of great name; for each of those writers adopted the principles of some one or other of the philosophical sects, reasoned from their notions, and often made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their terms and phrases. When Mr Sage had taken his master's degree, the narrowness of his fortune compelled him to accept of the first literary employment which was offered to him; and that happened to be nothing better than the office of schoolmaster in the parish of Bingry in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a>, whence he was soon removed to Tippermuir in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>. In these humble stations, though he wanted many of the necessaries and almost all the comforts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he prosecuted his studies with great success; but in doing so, he unhappily imbibed the seeds of several diseases which afflicted him through life, and notwithstanding the native vigour of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and shortened his days. From the miserable drudgery of a parish-schoolmaster, he was relieved by Mr Drummond of Cultmalundie, who invited him to superintend the education of his sons, whom he accompanied first to the public school at Perth, and afterwards to the university of St Andrew's. This was still an employment by no means adequate to his merit, but it was not wholly without advantages. At Perth, he gained the friendship and esteem of Dr Rose, afterwards lord bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and at St Andrew's of every man capable of properly estimating genius and learning. The education of his pupils was completed in 1684, when he was left with no determinate object of pursuit. In this moment of indecision, his friend Dr Rose, who had been promoted from the parsonage of Perth to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the university which he was leaving, recommended him so effectually to his uncle, then archbishop of Glasgow, that he was by that prelate admitted into orders and presented to one of the churches in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was then about 34 years of age; had studied the Scriptures with great assiduity; was no stranger to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or the apologies and other writings of the antient fathers; was a thorough master of school-divinity; had examined with great accuracy the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> controversies, especially those between the Romish and Reformed churches, and between the Calvinists and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a>; and it was perhaps to his honour that he did not fully approve of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> subscribed by any one of these contending sects of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. A man so far advanced in life, and so thoroughly accomplished as a scholar, would naturally be looked up to by the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the clergy as soon as he became one of their body. This was in fact the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>: Mr Sage was, immediately on his admission into orders, appointed clerk to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> or presbytery of Glasgow; an office of great trust and respectability, to which we know nothing similar in the church of England. During the establishment of episcopacy in Scotland, from the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. till the year 1690, the authority of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, though they possessed the sole power of ordination, was very limited in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the church. They did every thing with the consent of the presbyters over whom they presided. Diocesan synods were held at stated times for purposes of the same kind with those which employ the meetings of presbyteries at present (see <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>); and the only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> which the bishop seems to have enjoyed was to be permanent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> over the deliberations of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. The acts of each synod, and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> delivered by the bishop at the opening of it, were registered in a book kept by the clerk, who was always one of the most eminent of the diocesan clergy. Mr Sage <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this office, discharging in Glasgow all the duties of a clergyman, in such a manner as endeared him to his flock, and gained him the esteem even of those who were dissenters from the establishment. Many of his brethren were trimmers in ecclesiastical as well as in civil politics. They had been republicans and presbyterians in the days of the covenant; and, with that ferocious zeal which too often characterizes interested converts, had concurred in the severities which, during the reign of Charles II, were exercised against the party whom they had forsaken at his restoration. When that party again raised its head during the infatuated reign of James, and every thing indicated an approaching change of the establishment, those whose zeal for the church had so lately incited them to persecute the dissenters, suddenly became all gentleness and condescension, and advanced towards the presbyterians as to their old friends. The conduct of Mr Sage was the reverse of this. He was an episcopalian and a royalist from conviction; and in all his discourses, public and private, he laboured to instil into the minds of others the principles which to himself appeared to have their foundation in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. To <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> he was at all times an enemy, whilst he never tamely betrayed through fear what he thought it his duty to maintain. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that in the end of the year 1688 he was treated by the rabble, which in the western counties of Scotland rose against the established church, with greater lenity than his more complying brethren. Whilst they, without the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of their danger, were torn from their families by a lawless force, and many of them persecuted in the cruellest manner, he was privately warned to withdraw from Glasgow, and never more to return to that city. So much was consistency of conduct and a steady adherence to principle respected by those who seemed to respect nothing else. Mr Sage retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and carried with him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> book, which was afterwards demanded by the presbytery of Glasgow, but not recovered, till about twenty years ago, that, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a nephew of Dr Rose the last established bishop of Edinburgh, it was found in his possession, and restored to the presbytery to which it belonged. Mr Sage had detained it and given it to his diocesan friend, from the fond hope that episcopacy would soon be re-established in Scotland; and it was doubtless with a view to contribute what he could to the realising of that hope, that immediately on his being obliged to leave Glasgow, he commenced a keen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> writer. At Edinburgh he preached a while, till refusing to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> when required by the government, he was obliged to retire. In this extremity, he found protection in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Sir William Bruce, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of Kinross, who approved his principles and admired his virtue. Returning to Edinburgh, in 1695, he was observed, and obliged to abscond. Yet he returned in 1696, when his friend Sir William Bruce was imprisoned as a suspected person. He was soon forced to seek for refuge in the hills of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, under the name of Jackson. After a while Mr Sage found a safe retreat with the countess of Callendar, who employed him to instruct her family as chaplain, and her sons as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. These occupations did not wholly engage his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> mind; for he employed his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in defending his order, or in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his oppressors. When the countess of Callendar had no longer sons to instruct, Sage accepted the invitation of Sir John Steuart of Garntully, who wanted the help of a chaplain, and the conversation of a scholar. With Sir John he continued till the decency of his manners, and the extensiveness of his learning, recommended him to a higher station. And, on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1705, he was consecrated a bishop by Paterson the archbishop of Glasgow, Rose the bishop of Edinburgh, and Douglas the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>. But this promotion did not prevent sickness from falling on him in November 1706. After lingering for many months in Scotland, he tried the effect of the waters of Bath in 1709, without success. At Bath and at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> he remained a twelve-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, recognised by the great and caressed by the learned. Yet though he was invited to stay, he returned in 1710 to his native country, which he desired to see, and where he wished to die. And though his body was debilitated, he engaged, with undiminished vigour of mind, in the publication of the works of Drummond of Hawthornden, to which the celebrated Ruddiman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> his aid. Bishop Sage died at Edinburgh on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1711, lamented by his friends for his virtues, and feared by his adversaries for his talents. His works are, 1st, Two Letters concerning the Persecution of the Episcopal Clergy in Scotland, which with other two by different authors were printed in one volume at London in 1689. 2dly, An Account of the late Establishment of Presbyterian Government by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> of Scotland, in 1690, London, 1693. 3dly, The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">Fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a> of Presbytery, London, 1695. 4thly, The Principles of the Cyprianick Age with regard to Episcopal Power and Jurisdiction, London, 1695. 5thly, A Vindication of the Principles of the Cyprianick Age, London, 1701. 6thly, Some Remarks on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> from a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a> in the City, to a Minister in the Country, on Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Williamson's Sermon before the General Assembly, Edinburgh, 1703. 7thly, A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">Brief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of some Things in Mr Meldram's Sermon, preached on the 16th of May 1703, against a Toleration to those of the Episcopal Persuasion, Edinburgh, 1703. 8thly, The Reasonableness of a Toleration of those of the Episcopal Persuasion inquired into purely on Church Principles, Edinburgh, 1704. 9thly, The Life of Gawin Douglas, in 1710. 10thly, An Introduction to Drummond's History of the Five James's, Edinburgh, 1711. Of the principles maintained in these publications, different readers will think very differently; and it is probable that the acrimony displayed in some of them will be generally condemned in the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; whilst the learning and acuteness of their author will be universally acknowledged and admired by all who can distinguish merit in a friend or an adversary.

SAGENE

Pages 472-472
or SAJENE, a Russian long measure, 500 of which make a verst: the sagene is equal to seven English feet.

SAGINA

Pages 472-472

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrantha class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAGITTA

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">Trigonometry</a>, the same as the versed sine of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, being so denominated because it is like a dart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, standing on the chord of the arch.

SAGITTARIA

Pages 472-473
Arrow-head, a genus of plants belonging to the monocotyledonous class; and in the natural method ranking under the fifth order, Tripetaloidae. See Botany Index.—A bulb which is formed at the lower part. part of the root of a species of this plant, constitutes a considerable part of the food of the Chinese; and upon that account they cultivate it.

SAGITTARIUS

Pages 473-473

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the name of one of the 12 signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

SAGO

Pages 473-473

a nutritive substance brought from the East Indies, of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in diet as a restorative. It is produced from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of palm-tree (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCOS">Cocos</a> circinalis, Lin.) growing spontaneously in the East Indies without any culture. The progress of its vegetation in the early stages is very slow. At first it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> shrub, thick set with thorns, which make it difficult to come near it; but as soon as its stem is once formed, it rises in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the height of 30 feet, is about six feet in circumference, and imperceptibly loses its thorns. Its ligneous bark is about an inch in thickness, and covers a multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fibres; which, being interwoven one with another, envelop a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of a gummy kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. As soon as this tree is ripe, a whitish dust, which transpires through the pores of the leaves, and adheres to their extremities, proclaims its maturity. The Malays then cut them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near the root, divide them into several sections, which they split into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; they then scoop out the mass of mealy substance, which is enveloped by and adheres to the fibres; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> it in pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it through a straining bag of fine cloth, in order to separate it from the fibres. When this paste has lost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of its moisture by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, the Malays throw it into a kind of earthen vessels, of different shapes, where they allow it to dry and harden. This paste is a wholesome nourishing food, and may be preserved for many years. The Indians eat it diluted with water, and sometimes baked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boiled.
