Through a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, they reserve the finest part of this meal for the aged and infirm. A jelly is sometimes made of it, which is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and of a delicious flavour.

SAGUM

Pages 473-473

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, open from top to bottom, and usually fastened on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> shoulder with a buckle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clasp. It was not different in shape from the chlamys of the Greeks, and the paludamentum of the generals. The only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them was, that the paludamentum was made of a richer stuff, was generally of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and both longer and fuller than the sagum.

SAGUNTUM

Pages 473-473

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, now called Morvedro, where there are still the ruins of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> to be seen. The new town is seated on a river called Morvedro, 15 miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0.10. N. Lat. 39.38. It was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Peterborough in 1706.

SAHARA

Pages 473-473
or Zaara, the Great Desert, is a vast extent of sand in the interior parts of Africa, which, with the lesser deserts of Bornou, Bilma, Barca, Sort, &c. is equal to about one half of Europe. If the sand be considered as the ocean, the Sahara has its gulfs and bays, as also its islands, or Oases, fertile in groves and pastures, and in many instances containing a great population, subject to order and regular government. The great body, or western division of this ocean, comprised between Fezzan and the Atlantic, is no less than 50 caravan journeys across, from north to south; or from 750 to 800 G. miles; and double that extent in length: without doubt the largest desert in the world. This division contains but a scanty portion of islands (or oases), and those also of small extent: but the eastern division has many, and some of them very large. Fezzan, Gadamis, Taboo, Ghanat, Agadez, Augila, Berdoa, are amongst the principal ones: besides which, there are a vast number of small ones. In effect, this is the part of Africa alluded to by Strabo, when he says, from Cneius Piso, that Africa may be compared to a leopard's skin. From the best inquiries that Mr Park could make when a kind of captive among the Moors at Ludamar, the Western Desert, he says, may be pronounced almost destitute of inhabitants; except where the scanty vegetation, which appears in certain spots, affords pasture for the flocks of a few miserable Arabs, who wander from one well to another. In other places, where the supply of water and pasture is more abundant, small parties of the Moors have taken up their residence. Here they live, in independent poverty, secure from the tyrannical government of Barbary. But the greater part of the desert, being totally destitute of water, is seldom visited by any human being; unless where the trading caravans trace out their toilsome and dangerous route across it. In some parts of this extensive waste, the ground is covered with low stunted shrubs, which serve as land-marks for the caravans, and furnish the camels with a scanty forage. In other parts, the disconsolate wanderer, wherever he turns, sees nothing around him but a vast interminable expanse of sand and sky; a gloomy and barren void, where the eye finds no particular object to rest upon, and the mind is filled with painful apprehensions of perishing with thirst. Surrounded by this dreary solitude, the traveller sees the dead bodies of birds, that the violence of the wind has brought from happier regions; and, as he ruminates on the fearful length of his remaining passage, listens with horror to the voice of the driving blast—the only sound that interrupts the awful repose of the desert. The wild animals which inhabit these melancholy regions, are the antelope and the ostrich; their swiftness of foot enabling them to reach the distant watering-places. On the skirts of the desert, where the water is more plentiful, are found lions, panthers, elephants, and wild boars. The only domestic animal that can endure the fatigue of crossing the desert is the camel; and it is therefore the only beast of burden employed by the trading caravans which traverse, in different directions, from Barbary to Nigritia. The flesh of this useful and docile creature, though to our author's taste it was dry and unsavoury, is preferred by the Moors to all others. The milk of the female, he says, is in universal esteem, and is indeed pleasant and nutritive. That the desert has a dip towards the east, as well as the south, seems to be proved by the course of the Niger. Moreover, the highest points of North Africa, that is to say, the mountains of Mandinga and Atlas, are situated very far to the west. The desert, for the most part, abounds with salt. But we hear of salt mines only in the part contiguous to Nigritia, from whence salt is drawn for the use of those countries, as well as of the Moorish states adjoining; there being no salt in the negro countries south of the Niger. There are salt lakes also in the eastern part of the desert.

SAI

Pages 473-474

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, which, according to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, is completely surrounded by two very deep trenches, at about two hundred yards distant from the walls. On the top of the trenches are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> towers; and the whole has the appearance of a regular fortification. Inquiring into the origin of this extraordinary entrenchment, our author learned from two of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>-people the following particulars; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> true, furnish a mournful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the enormities of African wars: About fifteen years before our traveller visited Sai, when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Bambarra desolated Maniana, the Dooty of Sai had two sons slain in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, fighting in the king's cause. He had a third son living; and when the king demanded a further reinforcement of men, and this youth among the rest, the Dooty refused to send him. This conduct so enraged the king, that when he returned from Maniana, about the beginning of the rainy season, and found the Dooty protected by the inhabitants, he sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before Sai with his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and surrounded the town with the trenches which had attracted our author's notice. After a siege of two months, the towns-people became involved in all the horrors of famine; and whilst the king's army were feasting in their trenches, they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> the miserable inhabitants of Sai devour the leaves and bark of the Bentang tree that stood in the middle of the town. Finding, however, that the besieged would sooner perish than surrender, the king had recourse to treachery. He promised, that if they would open the gates, no person should be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, nor suffer any injury, but the Dooty alone. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> determined to sacrifice himself, for the sake of his fellow-citizens, and immediately walked over to the king's army, where he was put to death. His son, in attempting to escape, was caught and massacred in the trenches; and the rest of the towns-people were carried away captives, and sold as slaves to the different Negro traders. Sai, according to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Rennel, is situated in N. Lat. 14°, and in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 7'.

SAICK

Pages 474-474
or SAIQUE, a Turkish vessel, very common in the Levant for carrying merchandise.

SAIL

Pages 474-478

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, an assemblage of several breadths of canvas sewed together by the lists, and edged round with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, fastened to the yards of a ship, to make it drive before the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. See SHIP. The edges of the cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces, of which a sail is composed, are generally sewed together with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> seam; and the whole is skirted round at the edges with a cord, called the bolt-rope. Although the form of sails is extremely different, they are all nevertheless triangular or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> figures; or, in other words, their surfaces are contained either between three or four sides. The former of these are sometimes spread by a yard, as lateen-sails; and otherwise by a stay, as stay-sails; or by a mast, as shoulder-of-mutton sails; in all which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the foremost leech or edge is attached to the said yard, mast, or stay, throughout its whole length. The latter, or those which are four-sided, are either extended by yards, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> yards of a ship; or by yards and booms, as the studding-sails, drivers, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>-tails, and all those sails which are set occasionally; or by gaffs and booms, as the main-sails of sloops and brigantines. The principal sails of a ship (fig. 1.) are the courses or lower sails \(a\); the top-sails \(b\), which are next in order above the courses; and the top-gallant sails \(c\), which are expanded above the top-sails. The courses are the main-sail, fore-sail, and mizen, main stay-sail, fore stay-sail, and mizen stay-sail; but more particularly the three first. The main stay-sail is rarely used except in small vessels. In all quadrangular sails the upper edge is called the head; the sides or skirts are called leeches; and the bottom or lower edge is termed the foot. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the head is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the foot, the two low corners are denominated clues, and the upper corners earings. In all triangular sails, and in those four-sided sails wherein the head is not parallel to the foot, the foremost corner at the foot is called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a>; and the after lower-corner the clue; the foremost perpendicular or sloping edge is called the fore-leech, and the hindmost the after-leech. The heads of all four-sided sails, and the fore-leeches of lateen-sails, are attached to their respective yard or gaff by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small cords called ro-bands; and the extremities are tied to the yard-arms, or to the peak of the gaff, by earings. The stay-sails are extended upon stays between the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, whereon they are drawn up or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> occasionally, as a curtain slides upon its rod, and their lower parts are stretched out by a tack and sheet. The clues of a top-sail are drawn out to the extremities of the lower yard, by two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> called the top-sail sheets; and the clues of the top-gallant sails are in like manner extended upon the top-sail yard-arms, as exhibited by fig. 2. The studding-sails are set beyond the leeches or skirts of the main-sail and fore-sail, or of the top-sails or top-gallant sails of a ship. Their upper and lower edges are accordingly extended by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> run out beyond the extremities of the yards for this purpose. Those sails, however, are only set in favourable winds and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. All sails derive their name from the mast, yard, or stay, upon which they are extended. Thus the principal sail extended upon the mainmast is called the mainsail, \(d\); the next above, which stands upon the main-top mast, is termed the main-top sail, \(e\); and the highest, which is spread across the main-top-gallant mast, is named the main-top-gallant sail, \(f\). In the same manner there is the fore-sail, \(g\); the fore-top sail, \(h\); and the fore-top-gallant sail, \(i\); the mizen, \(k\); the mizen-top sail, \(l\); and mizen-top-gallant sail, \(m\). Thus also there is the main-stay sail, \(o\); main top-mast stay-sail, \(p\); and main-top-gallant stay-sail, \(q\); with a middle stay-sail which stands between the two last. N.B. All these stay-sails are between the main and fore-masts. The stay-sails between the mainmast and mizenmast are the mizen stay-sail, \(r\); and the mizen topmast stay-sail, \(s\); and sometimes a mizen top-gallant stay-sail above the latter. The stay-sails between the foremast and the bowsprit are the fore stay-sail, \(t\); the fore top-mast stay-sail, \(u\); Sail. u; and the jib, x. There is besides two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> sails extended by yards under the bow-sprit, one of which is called the sprit-sail, y; and the other the sprit-sail top-sail, z. The studding-sails being extended upon the different yards of the main-mast and fore-mast, are likewise named according to their stations, the lower, top-mast, or top-gallant studding sails. The ropes by which the lower yards of a ship are hoisted up to their proper height on the masts, are called the jeers. In all other sails the ropes employed for this purpose are called halyards. The principal sails are then expanded by halyards, sheets, and bowlines; except the courses, which are always stretched out below by a tack and sheet. They are drawn up together, or trussed up, by bunt-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, clue-lines, d d; leech-lines, e e; reef-tackles, f f; slab-line, g; and spilling-lines. As the bunt-lines and leech-lines <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on the other side of the sail, they are expressed by the dotted lines in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The courses, top-sails, and top-gallant sails, are wheeled about the mast, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the various directions of the wind, by braces. The higher studding-sails, and in general all the stay-sails, are drawn down, so as to be furled, or taken in, by down-hauls. Some experienced sail-makers contend, that it would be of much advantage if many of the sails of ships were made of equal magnitude; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> required it, they could be interchangeably used. For example, as the mizen top-sail is now made nearly as large as the main top-gallant sail, it would be easy to make the yards, masts, and sails, so as mutually to suit each other. The main and fore-top sails differ about two feet at head and foot, and from one to three feet in depth. Those likewise could be easily made alike, and in some cases they are so. The same may be said of the main and fore top-gallant sails, and of the mizen top-gallant sail, and main fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>. The main-sail and fore-sail might also, with respect to their head, be made alike; but as the former has a gore at the leech, and a larger gore at the foot for clearing it of the gallows, boats, &c. which the latter has not, there might be more difficulty in arranging them. The difficulty, however, appears not to be insurmountable. These alterations, it is thought, would be extremely useful in the event of losing sails by stress of weather. Fewer sails would be thus necessary, less room would be required to stow them, and there would be less danger of confusion in taking them out. But perhaps the utility of these alterations <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be more felt in the merchant-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> than in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, which latter has always a large store of spare sails, and sufficient room to stow them in order. Thus, too, spare yards and masts might be considerably reduced in number, and yet any casual damages more easily repaired at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Top-mast studding sails are occasionally substituted for awnings, and might, by a very little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> in planning the rigging of a ship, be so contrived as to answer both purposes. See Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Sail is also a name applied to any vessel seen at a distance under sail, and is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to ship. To set Sail, is to unfurl and expand the sails upon their respective yards and stays, in order to begin the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of sailing. To Make Sail, is to spread an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sail, so as to increase the ship's velocity. To shorten Sail, is to reduce or take in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sails, with an intention to diminish the ship's velocity. To Strike Sail, is to lower it suddenly. This is particularly used in saluting or doing homage to a superior force, or to one whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations acknowledges as superior in certain regions. Thus all foreign vessels strike to a British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in the British seas. Sailing, the movement by which a vessel is wafted along the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, by the action of the wind upon her sails. When a ship changes her state of rest into that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, as in advancing out of a harbour, or from her station at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, she acquires her motion very gradually, as a body which arrives not at a certain velocity till after an infinite repetition of the action of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the wind greatly affects the velocity, because the resistance of the water might destroy it; since the velocity being but small at first, the resistance of the water which depends on it will be very feeble: but as the ship increases her motion, the force of the wind on the sails will be diminished; whereas, on the contrary, the resistance of the water on the bow will accumulate in proportion to the velocity with which the vessel advances. Thus the repetition of the degrees of force, which the action of the sail adds to the motion of the ship, is perpetually decreasing; whilst, on the contrary, the new degrees added to the effort of resistance on the bow are always augmenting. The velocity is then accelerated in proportion as the quantity added is greater than that which is subtracted; but when the two powers become equal, when the impression of the wind on the sails has lost so much of its force, as only to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in proportion to the opposite impulse of resistance on the bow, the ship will then acquire no additional velocity, but continue to sail with a constant uniform motion. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> weight of the ship may indeed prevent her from acquiring her greatest velocity; but when she has attained it, she will advance by her own intrinsic motion, without gaining any new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of velocity, or lessening what she has acquired. She moves then by her own proper force in vacuo, without being afterwards subject either to the effort of the wind on the sails, or to the resistance of the water on the bow. If at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the impulsion of the water on the bow should destroy any part of the velocity, the effort of the wind on the sails will revive it, so that the motion will continue the same. It must, however, be observed, that this state will only subsist when these two powers act upon each other in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition; otherwise they will mutually destroy one another. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of working ships depends on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> action, and the perfect equality which should subsist between the effort of the wind and the impulsion of the water. The effect of sailing is produced by a judicious arrangement of the sails to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the wind. Accordingly the various modes of sailing are derived from the different degrees and situations of the wind with regard to the course of the vessel. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAMANSHIP">Seamanship</a>. To illustrate this observation by examples, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a number of ships proceeding on various courses is represented by fig. 3, which exhibits the 32 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, of which C is the centre; the direction of the wind, which is northerly, being expressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. It has been observed in the article <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a>-Hauled, that a ship in that situation will sail nearly within six points of the wind. Thus the ships B and y are close-hauled; the former being on the larboard-tack, steering E. N. E. and the latter on the starboard-tack, sailing W. N. W. with their yards a b braced obliquely, as suitable to that manner of sailing. The line of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> on the larboard-tack would accordingly be expressed by CB, and on the starboard by C y. When a ship is neither close-hauled, nor steering afore the wind, she is in general said to be sailing large. The relation of the wind to her course is precisely determined by the number of points between the latter and the course close-hauled. Thus the ships c and x have the wind one point large, the former steering E. b N. and the latter W. b N. The yards remain almost in the same position as in B and y; the bowlines and sheets of the sails being only a little slackened. The ships d and u have the wind two points large, the one steering east and the other west. In this manner of sailing, however, the wind is more particularly said to be upon the beam, as being at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and coinciding with the position of the ship's beams. The yards are now more across the ship, the bowlines are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off, and the sheets more relaxed; so that the effort of the wind being applied nearer to the line of the ship's course, her velocity is greatly augmented. In e and t the ships have the wind three points large, or one point abaft the beam, the course of the former being E. b S. and that of the latter W. b S. The sheets are still more flowing, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the yards make with the keel further diminished, and the course accelerated in proportion. The ships f and s, the first of which steers E. S. E. and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> W. S. W. have the wind four points large, or two points abaft the beam. In g and r the wind is five points large, or three points abaft the beam, the former sailing S. E. b E. and the latter S. W. b W. In both these situations the sheets are still farther slackened, and the yards laid yet more athwart the ship's length, in proportion as the wind approaches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The ships h and q, steering S. E. and S. W. have the wind six points large, or more properly on the quarter; which is considered as the most favourable manner of sailing, because all the sails co-operate to increase the ship's velocity; whereas, when the wind is right aft, as in the ship m, it is evident that the wind in its passage to the foremost sails will be intercepted by those which are farther aft. When the wind is on the quarter, the fore-tack is brought to the cat-head; and the main-tack being cast off, the weather-clue of the main-sail is hoisted up to the yard, in order to let the wind pass freely to the fore-sail; and the yards are disposed so as to make an angle of about two points, or nearly 22°, with the keel. The ships i and p, of which the former sails S. E. b S. and the latter S. W. b S. are said to have the wind three points on the larboard or starboard quarter: and those expressed by k and o, two points; as steering S. S. E. and S. S. W. in both which positions the yards make nearly an angle of 16°, or about a point and a half, with the ship's length. When the wind is one point on the quarter, as in the ships l and n, whose courses are S. b E. and S. b W. the situation of the yards and sails is very little different from the last mentioned; the angle which they make with the keel being somewhat less than a point, and the stay-sails being rendered of very little service. The ship m sails right afore the wind, or with the wind right aft. In this position the yards are laid at right angles with the ship's length; the stay-sails being entirely useless, are hauled down; and the main-sail is drawn up in the brails, that the foresail may operate; a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which considerably facilitates the steerage, or effort of the helm. As the wind is then intercepted by the main-top sail and main-top-gallant sail, in its passage to the fore-top sail and fore-top-gallant sail, these latter are by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> entirely becalmed; and might therefore be furled, to prevent their being fretted by flapping against the mast, but that their effort contributes greatly to prevent the ship from broaching-to, when she deviates from her course to the right or left thereof. Thus all the different methods of sailing may be divided into four, viz. close-hauled, large, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERING">quartering</a>, and afore the wind; all which relate to the direction of the wind with regard to the ship's course, and the arrangement of the sails.

SAILING ALSO

Pages 478-481

g also implies a particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, formed on the principles, and regulated by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>. Hence we say, Plain Sailing, Mercator's, Middle-latitude, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>-circle Sailing. See the article Navigation. Sail-Making, the art of making sails. See Sail and Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Sailor, the same with Mariner and Seaman. Saint, means a person eminent for piety and virtue, and is generally applied by us to the apostles and other holy persons mentioned in Scripture. But the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> make its application much more extensive. Under the word Canonization we have already said something on their practice of creating saints. Our readers, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not, we trust, be displeased with the following more enlarged account, which they themselves give of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The canonization of saints, then, they tell us, is the enrolment of any person in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> catalogue of those who are called saints; or, it is a judgment and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, by which it is declared, that a deceased person was eminent for sanctity during his lifetime, and especially towards the end of it; and that consequently he must now be in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with God, and deserves to be honoured by the church on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with that veneration which she is wont to pay to the blessed in heaven. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> with regard to this matter has varied. It would seem that in the first ages every bishop in his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> was wont to declare what persons were to be honoured as saints by his people. Hence St Cyprian, about the middle of the third century, B. 3. ep. 6. requires that he be informed of those who should die in prison for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, that so he might make mention of them in the holy sacrifice with the martyrs, and and might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> them afterwards on the anniversary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of their happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This veneration <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> sometimes to be confined to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but sometimes it extended to distant provinces, and even became universal all over the church. It was thus that St Laurence, St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, St Augustine, St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, and many others, appear to have been canonized by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and universal persuasion. In those ages none were reckoned saints but the apostles, the martyrs, and very eminent confessors, whose sanctity was notorious everywhere. Afterwards it appears that canonizations were wont to be performed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> synods under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the metropolitan. It was thus that St Isidore of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> was canonized in the 7th century, by the 8th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, 14 years after his death. This manner of canonization continued occasionally <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the 12th century. The last instance of a saint canonized in that way, is that of St Walter <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Pontaise, who was declared a saint by the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in the year 1153. In the 12th century, in order to prevent mistakes in so delicate a matter, Pope Alexander III. judged it proper to reserve this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> to the Holy See of Rome exclusively; and decreed that no one should for the future be honoured by the church as a saint without the express approbation of the pope. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the canonization of saints has been carried on in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>; and there is at Rome a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of cardinals, called the congregation of holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, who are assisted by several divines under the name of consultors, who examine such matters, and prepare them for the decision of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>. When therefore any potentate, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> body, think fit, they apply to the pope for the canonization of any person. The first juridical step in this business must be taken by the bishop in whose diocese the person for whom the application is made had lived and died, who by his own authority calls witnesses to attest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the holiness, the virtues, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, of the person in question. When the deceased has resided in different dioceses, it may be necessary that different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> take such depositions; the originals of which are preserved in the archives of their respective churches, and authentic copies sealed up are sent to Rome by a special messenger, where they are deposited with the congregation of rites, and where they must remain for the space of ten years without being opened. They are then opened, and maturely examined by the congregation, and with their advice the pope allows the cause to go on or not as he thinks proper. The solicitors for the canonization are then referred by his holiness to the said congregation, which, with his authority, gives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to one or more bishops, or other respectable persons, to examine, on the spot and in the places where the person in question has lived and died, into his character and whole behaviour. These commissioners summon witnesses, take depositions, and collect letters and other writings of the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and get all the intelligence they can concerning him, and the opinion generally entertained of him. The report of these commissioners is considered attentively and at length by the congregation, and every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it discussed by the consultors, when the congregation determines whether or not they can permit the process to go on. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it be allowed to proceed, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, who is called ponent, undertakes to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in that affair. The first question then that comes to be examined is, whether or not the person proposed for canonization can be proved to have been in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> endued with the moral virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, fortitude, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; and with the theological virtues of faith, hope, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>? All this is canvassed with great deliberation; and there is a distinguished ecclesiastic called the promoter of the holy faith, who is sworn to make all reasonable objections to the proofs that are adduced in favour of the canonization. If the decision be favourable, then the proofs of miracles done to show the sanctity of the person in question are permitted to be brought forward; when two miracles must be verified to the satisfaction of the congregation, both as to the reality of the facts, and as to their having been truly above the power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. If the decision on this comes out likewise favourable, then the whole is laid before the pope and what divines he chooses (A). Public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting are likewise prescribed, in order to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and direction from heaven. After all this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> procedure, when the pope is resolved to give his approbation, he issues a bull, first of beatification, by which the person is declared blessed, and afterwards another of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANCTIFICATION">sanctification</a>, by which the name of saint is given him. These bulls are published in St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church with very great solemnity. A person remarkable for holiness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, even before he is canonized, may be venerated as such by those who are persuaded of his eminent virtue, and his prayers may be implored; but all this must rest on private opinion. After his canonization, his name is inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">Martyrology</a>, or catalogue of saints, of which the respective portion is read every day in the choir at the divine office. A day is also appointed for a yearly commemoration of him. His name may be mentioned in the public church <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and his intercession with God besought. His relics may be enshrined; he may be painted with rays of glory, and altars and churches may be dedicated to God in honour of him, and in thanksgiving to the divine goodness for the blessings bestowed on him in life, and for the glory to which he is raised in heaven. The affair of a canonization is necessarily very expensive, because so many persons must be employed about it; so many journeys must be made; so many writings for and against it must be drawn out. The expense altogether amounts to about 25,000 Roman crowns, or 6000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. But it is generally contrived (A) His holiness generally appoints three consistories; in the first of which the cardinals only assist, and give their opinion; in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, a preacher pronounces a speech in praise of the candidate before a numerous audience; to the third, not only the cardinals, but all the bishops who are at Rome, are invited, and all of them give their vote by word of mouth. tried to canonize two or three at a time, by which means the particular expense of each is very much lessened, the solemnity being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. It often happens that the solicitors for a canonization are unsuccessful. Thus the Jesuits, even when their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at Rome was greatest, could not obtain the canonization of Bellarmine; and it is remarkable, that the objection is said to have been, his having defended the indirect power of the pope over Christian princes even in temporals. Several authors have written on canonization, and particularly Prosper Lambertini, afterwards pope under the name of Benedict XIV., who had held the office of promoter of the faith for many years. He published on it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in several volumes, in folio, of which there is an abridgement in French. In this learned performance there is a full <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the canonization of saints in general, and of all the particular processes of that kind that are on record: an account is given of the manner of proceeding in these extraordinary trials; and it is shown, that, besides the assistance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, which is implored and expected in what is so much connected with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, all prudent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> means are made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, in order to avoid mistakes, and to obtain all the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of which the matter is susceptible, and which must appear more than sufficient to every impartial judge. See Pope, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, &c. Saint Catharine, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, not far distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. It was visited by La Perouse, who ascertained it to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between 27° 19' 10" and 27° 49' N. Lat. and its most northerly point to lie in 49° 49' W. Long. from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Its breadth from east to west is only six miles, and it is separated from the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> by a channel only about 200 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. On the point stretching farthest into this channel is situated the city of Nostra Senhora del Destero, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the governor's residence. It contains about 400 houses, and 8000 inhabitants, and has an exceedingly pleasant appearance. In the year 1712, this island served as a retreat to vagabonds, who effected their escape from different parts of the Brazils, being only nominal subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. Its whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> has been estimated at 20,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is extremely fertile, producing all sorts of fruit, vegetables, and corn, almost spontaneously. The whale fishery is very successful; but it is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and is farmed by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, which has three considerable establishments upon the coast. Every year they kill about 400 whales, the produce of which, both <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and spermaceti, is sent to Lisbon by the way of Rio Janeiro. The inhabitants are idle spectators of this fishery, from which they derive not the smallest advantage. A very amiable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, however, is given of their hospitality to strangers, by M. La Perouse. Saint Poin, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hedyarum. See Hedyarum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAINTES">Saintes</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of France, in the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>. Before the revolution, it was a bishop's see. It contained likewise several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, a Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> remarkable for its steeple, which is said to be one of the loftiest in France. It is seated on an eminence, 37 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, and 262 south-south-west of Paris. W. Long. 0° 38', N. Lat. 45° 54'. The castle is seated on a rock, and is reckoned impregnable. The population in 1800 was 10,162. This city was a Roman colony; and those conquerors of the earth, who polished the nations they subdued, have left behind them the traces of their magnificence. In a hollow valley between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and almost adjoining to one of the suburbs, are the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. Though now in the last stage of decay, its appearance is august and venerable. In some parts, scarcely any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> are to be seen; but the east end is still in a great degree of preservation. From its situation in a valley, and from the ruins of an aqueduct which conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the town from near three leagues distance, it has been supposed that Naumachiae were represented in it; but this amounts only to conjecture. A triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, on which is an inscription in Roman letters, merits likewise <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It was erected to Germanicus, on the news of his death, so universally lamented throughout the empire. The river Charente surrounds this city, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> does that of Shrewsbury, describing the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>. Except the remains of Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> yet visible at Saintes, the place contains very little to detain or amuse a traveller. It is built with great irregularity; the streets are narrow and winding, the houses <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and almost all of them are some centuries old. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> has been repeatedly defaced and destroyed by Normans and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>, who made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> alike on every monument of art or piety. One tower only escaped their rage, which is said to have been built as early as the year 800 by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. It is of an enormous magnitude, both as to height and circumference. These circumstances have probably conduced more to its preservation during the fury of war, than any veneration for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of its founder, or for the sanctity of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. Saintogne, a province of France, now forming with the province of Aunis the department of Lower Charente, is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a> and Perigord, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Poitou and the territory of Aunis, on the west by the ocean, and on the south by Bourdeois and Giron, about 62 miles in length and 30 in breadth. The river Charente runs through the middle of it, and renders it one of the finest and most fertile provinces in France, abounding in all sorts of corn and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>: and it is said the best <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is made here. The Saints, are three small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, three leagues distant from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a>, which form a triangle, and have a tolerable harbour. Thirty Frenchmen were sent thither in 1648, but were soon driven away by an excessive drought, which dried up their only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> before they had time to make any reservoirs. A second attempt was made in 1652, and permanent plantations were established, which now yield 50,000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of coffee, and 100,000 of cotton. Sajene, a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, equal to about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> English feet. Sakradawendra is the name of one of the Ceylonese deities, who commands and governs all the rest, and formerly answered the prayers of his worshippers; but according to the fabulous account which is given of him, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on which he sat, and the foot of which was made of wax, that was softened by their prayers and tears, and sunk downward, so that he could take notice of their requests and relieve them, being disposed of among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, they no longer derive any benefit from him, or pay him any reverence. See Budun. SAL. See Salt.

SALACIA

Pages 482-482

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALADIN

Pages 481-481

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, equally renowned as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. He supported himself by his valour, and the influence of his amiable character, against the united efforts of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Christian potentates of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who carried on the most unjust wars against him, under the false appellation of Holy Wars. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Egypt and Crusade.

SALAMANCA

Pages 481-481

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and populous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, situated on the river Tormes, about 75 miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. It is said to have been founded by Teucer the son of Telamon, who called it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Salamanica, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the ancient Salamis. Here is an university, the greatest in Spain, consisting of 24 colleges, and perhaps inferior to none in the whole world, in respect at least to its revenues, buildings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scholars, and masters. Here are also many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and magnificent palaces, squares, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, &c. Of the colleges in the university, four are appropriated to young men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and near it is an infirmary for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> sick scholars. In the neighbourhood of this town a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought on the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1812, between the British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WELLINGTON">Wellington</a>, and the French army under Marshal Marmont, in which the latter was defeated with the loss of 7000 prisoners, and a vast number killed and wounded. The British loss amounted to 700 killed, and 4000 wounded. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 10. N. Lat. 41. 0. SALAMANDER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>, Erpetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALAMIS

Pages 481-482

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34. 0. N. Lat. 37. 32.—It was famous in antiquity for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Greek and Persian fleets. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> held among the Persians on this occasion, all the commanders were for engaging, because they knew this advice to be most agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s inclinations. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> was the only person who opposed this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. She was queen of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>; and followed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> in this war with five ships, the best equipped of any in the fleet, except those of the Sidonians. This princess distinguished herself on all occasions by her singular courage, and still more by her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and conduct. She represented, in the council of war we are speaking of, the dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of engaging a people that were far more expert in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs than the Persians; alleging, that the loss of a battle at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> would be attended with the ruin of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; whereas, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> out the war, and advancing into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, they would create jealousies and divisions among their enemies, who would separate from one another in order to defend each of them their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and that the king might, almost without striking a blow, make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Greece. This advice, though very prudent, was not followed, but an engagement unanimously resolved upon. Xerxes, in order to encourage his men by his presence, caused a throne to be erected on the top of an eminence, whence he might safely behold whatever happened; having several scribes about him, to write <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the names of such as should signalize themselves against the enemy. The approach of the Persian fleet, with the news that a strong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> from the army was marching against Cleombrotus, who defended the isthmus, struck such a terror into the Pelopponesians, that they could not by any intrigues be prevailed upon to stay any longer at Salamis. Being therefore determined to put to sea, and sail to the isthmus, Themistocles privately dispatched a trusty friend to the Persian commanders, informing them of the intended flight; and exhorting them to send <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their fleet round the island, in order to prevent their escape. The same messenger assured Xerxes, that Themistocles, who had sent him that advice, designed to join the Persians, as soon as the battle began, with all the Athenian ships. The king giving <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to all he said, immediately caused a strong squadron to sail round the island in the night, in order to cut off the enemy's flight. Early next morning, as the Pelopponesians were preparing to set sail, they found themselves encompassed on all sides by the Persian fleet; and were against their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> obliged to remain in the straits of Salamis and expose themselves to the same dangers with their allies. The Grecian fleet consisted of 380 sail, that of the Persians of 2000 and upwards. Themistocles avoided the engagement till a certain <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which rose regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and which was entirely contrary to the enemy, began to blow. As soon as he found himself favoured by this wind, he gave the signal for battle. The Persians, knowing that they fought under their king's eye, advanced with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resolution; but the wind blowing directly in their faces, and the largeness and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their ships embarrassing them in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so strait and narrow, their courage soon abated; which the Greeks observing, used such efforts, that in a short time breaking into the Persian fleet, they entirely disordered them; some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> towards Phalarus where their army lay encamped; others saving themselves in the harbours of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The Ionians were the first that betook themselves to flight. But Queen Artemisia distinguished herself above all the rest, her ships being the last that fled: which Xerxes observing, cried out that the men behaved like women, and the women with the courage and intrepidity of men. The Athenians were so incensed against her, that they offered a reward of 10,000 drachmas to any one that should take her alive; but she, in spite of all their efforts, got clear of the ships that pursued her, and arrived safe on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. In this engagement, which was one of the most memorable actions we find recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Grecians lost 40 ships; and the Persians 200, besides a great many more that were taken, with all the men and ammunition they carried. The island of Salamis is of a very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape; it was reckoned 70 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 80 stadia, i.e. 8 or 10 miles, long, reaching westward as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called Kerata, or The Horns. Pausanias informs us, that on one side of this island stood in his time a temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and on the other a trophy for a victory obtained by Themistocles, together with the temple of Cythereus, the site of which is now thought to be occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Nicholas. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Salamis was demolished by the Athenians, because in the war with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDER">Cassander</a> it surrendered to the Macedonians, from disaffection. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, when it was visited by Pausanias, some ruins of the Agora or market-place remained, with a temple and image of Ajax; and not far from the port was shown a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, on which, they related, Telamon sat to view the Salaminian ships on their departure to join the Grecian fleet at Aulis. The walls may still be traced, and it has been conjectured were about four miles in circumference. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> space within them was now covered with green corn. The port is choked with mud, and was partly dry. Among the scattered marbles are some with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. One is of great antiquity, before the introduction of the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. On another, near the port, the name of Solon occurs. This renowned lawgiver was a native of Salamis, and a statue of him was erected in the market-place, with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> covered by his vest, the modest attitude in which he was accustomed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the people of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. An inscription on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble was also copied in 1676 near the ruin of a temple, probably that of Ajax. The island of Salamis is now inhabited by a few Albanians, who till the ground. Their village is called Ampelaki, "the Vineyard," and is at a distance from the port, standing more inland. In the church are marble fragments and some inscriptions.

SALARY

Pages 482-482

a recompense <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> consideration made to a person for his pains and industry in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s business. The word is used in the statute 23 Edw. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 1. Salarium at first signified the rents or profits of a sall, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> (and in Gascoigne they now call the seats of the gentry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">sala</a>'s, as we do halls); but afterwards it was taken for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, stipend, or annual allowance.

SALE

Pages 482-482

is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of a commodity for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> permutation, is the exchange of one commodity for another. When the bargain is concluded, an obligation is contracted by the buyer to pay the value, and by the seller to deliver the commodity, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> agreed on, or immediately, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> no time be specified. In this, as well as other mercantile contracts, the safety of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> requires the utmost good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and veracity. Therefore, although by the laws of England, a sale above the value of 10l. be not binding, unless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> be paid, or the bargain confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, a merchant would lose all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> who refused to perform his agreement, although these legal requisites were omitted. When a specific thing is sold, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, even before delivery, is in some respect vested in the buyer; and if the thing perishes, the buyer must bear the loss. For example, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dies before delivery, he must pay the value; but if the bargain only determines the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the goods, without specifying the identical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and the seller's warehouse, with all his goods, be burned, he is intitled to no payment. He must also bear the loss if the thing perish through his fault; or when a particular time and place of delivery is agreed on, if it perish before it be tendered in terms of the bargain. If a person purchase goods at a shop without agreeing for the price, he is liable for the ordinary market-price at the time of purchase. If the buyer proves insolvent before delivery, the seller is not bound to deliver the goods without payment or security. If the importation, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the commodities sold, be prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or if the buyer knows that they were smuggled, no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies for delivery. The property of goods is generally presumed, in favour of commerce, to belong to the possessor, and cannot be challenged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an onerous purchaser. But to this there are some exceptions. By the Scots law, stolen goods may in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> be reclaimed by the proprietor, and also by the English law, unless they were bought <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide in open market; that is, in the accustomed public places, on stated days, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or in a shop in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and horses may be reclaimed, unless the sale be regularly entered by the book-keeper of the market. In all cases, if the goods be evicted by the lawful proprietor, the seller is liable to the purchaser for the value. Actions for payment of shop-accounts, as well as other debts not constituted by writing, are limited in England to six years. The testimony of one witness is admitted; and the seller's books, although the person that kept them be dead, are good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for one year. In Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> books may be proved within three years of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the last article, by one witness, and the creditors books and oath in supplement. After three years, they can only be proved by the oath or writ of the debtor. A merchant's books are in all cases good evidence against him.

SALEP

Pages 482-483

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the dried root of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of orchis. See Orchis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Several methods of preparing salep have been proposed and practised. Geoffroy has delivered a very judicious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for this purpose in the Histoire de l'Academie Royale des Sciences, 1740; and Retmus, in the Swedish Transactions, 1761, has improved Geoffroy's method. But Mr Moult of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCHDALE">Rochdale</a> has lately favoured the public with a new manner of curing the orchis root; by which salep is prepared, at least equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any brought from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The new root is to be washed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> skin which covers it is to be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the root in hot water, and rubbing it with a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. When a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of roots have been thus cleaned, they are to be spread on a tin-plate, and placed in an oven heated to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, where they are to remain six or ten minutes, in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have lost their milky whiteness, and acquired a transparency like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, without any diminution of bulk. Being arrived at this state, they are to be removed, in order to dry and harden in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which will require several days to effect; or by using a very gentle <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they may be finished in a few hours. Salep thus prepared, may be afforded in those parts of England where labour bears a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> value, at about eightpence or tenpence per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; and it might be sold still cheaper, if the orchis were to be cured, without separating from it the brown skin which covers it; a troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the process, and which does not contribute to render the root either more palatable or salutary; whereas the foreign salep is now sold at five or six shillings per pound. Salep is said to contain the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vegetable nourishment in the smallest bulk. Hence a very judicious writer, to prevent the dreadful calamity of famine at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, has lately proposed that the powder of it should constitute part of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of every ship's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. company. This powder and portable soup, dissolved in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, form a rich thick jelly, capable of supporting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for a considerable length of time. An ounce of each of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, with two quarts of boiling water, will be sufficient subsistence for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and as being a mixture of animal and vegetable food, must prove more nourishing than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>-cake, made by boiling rice in water: which last, however, sailors are often obliged solely to subsist upon for several months; especially in voyages to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and flour are exhausted, and the beef and pork, having been salted in hot countries, are become unfit for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. "But as a wholesome nourishment (says Dr Percival*), rice is much inferior to salep. I digested several alimentary mixtures prepared of mutton and water, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up with bread, sea-biscuit, salep, rice-flower, sago-powder, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, old cheese, &c. in a heat equal to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. In 48 hours they had all acquired a vinous smell, and were in brisk <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, except the mixture with rice, which did not emit many air-bubbles, and was but little changed. The third day several of the mixtures were sweet, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to ferment; others had lost their intestine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and were sour; but the one which contained the rice was become putrid. From this experiment it appears, that rice as an aliment is slow of fermentation, and a very weak corrector of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. It is therefore an improper diet for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>-patients; but more particularly for sailors in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages; because it is incapable of preventing, and will not contribute much to check, the progress of that fatal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, the sea scurvy. Under certain circumstances, rice seems disposed, of itself, without mixture, to become putrid; for by long keeping it sometimes acquires an offensive fetor. Nor can it be considered as a very nutritive kind of food, on account of its difficult solubility in the stomach. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> confirms the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this conclusion; for it is observed by the planters in the West Indies, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> grow thin, and are less able to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whilst they subsist upon rice. "Salep has the singular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of concealing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water; a circumstance of the highest importance at sea, when there is a scarcity of fresh water. I dissolved a dram and a half of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt in a pint of the mucilage of salcp, so liquid as to be potable, and the same quantity in a pint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water. The salep was by no means disagreeable to the taste, but the water was rendered extremely unpalatable. This experiment suggested to me the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the orchis root as a corrector of acidity, a property which would render it a very useful diet for children. But the solution of it, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, seemed only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> like an equal proportion of water, and not to cover its sharpness. Salep, however, appears by my experiments to retard the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a> fermentation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and consequently would be a good lithing for milk-pottage, especially in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the cattle being fed upon sour draff must yield accect milk. "Salep in a certain proportion, which I have not yet been able to ascertain, would be a very useful and profitable addition to bread. I directed one ounce of the powder to be dissolved in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of water, and the mucilage to be mixed with a sufficient quantity of flour, salt, and yeast. The flour amounted to two pounds, the yeast to two ounces, and the salt to 80 grains. The loaf when baked was remarkably well fermented, and weighed three pounds two ounces. Another loaf, made with the same quantity of flour, &c., weighed two pounds and 12 ounces; from which it appears that the salep, though used in so small a proportion, increased the gravity of the loaf six ounces, by absorbing and retaining more water than the flour alone was capable of. Half a pound of flour and an ounce of salcp were mixed together, and the water added according to the usual method of preparing bread. The loaf when baked weighed 13 ounces and a half; and would probably have been heavier if the salep had been previously dissolved in about a pint of water. But it should be remarked, that the quantity of flour used in this trial was not sufficient to conceal the peculiar taste of the salep. "The restorative, mucilaginous, and demulcent qualities of the orchis root, render it of considerable use in various diseases. In the sea scurvy it powerfully obtunds the acrimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and at the same time is easily assimilated into a mild and nutritious chyle. In diarrhoeas and the dysentery it is highly serviceable, by sheathing the internal coat of the intestines, by abating irritation, and gently correcting putrefaction. In the symptomatic fever, which arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of pus from ulcers in the lungs, from wounds, or from amputation, salep used plentifully is an admirable demulent, and well adapted to resist the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the crisis of the blood, which is so evident in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. And by the same mucilaginous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, it is equally efficacious in the strangury and dysury; especially in the latter, when arising from a venereal cause, because the discharge of urine is then attended with the most exquisite pain, from the ulceration about the neck of the bladder and through the course of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>.
