I have found it also an useful aliment for patients who labour under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or gravel." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> chemists appear to have entertained a very high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the orchis root, as appears from the secretia secretorum of Raymund Lully, a work dated 1565.

SALERNO

Pages 483-483

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Hierther Principato, with an archbishop's see, a castle, harbour, and an university chiefly for medicine. It is seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 53. N. Lat. 40. 35.

SALET

Pages 483-483

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> covering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> armour for the head, anciently worn by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LIGHT_HORSE">light-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, only different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> in that it had no crest and was little more than a bare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>.

SALIANT

Pages 483-483

SALIENT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> SAILLANT, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to a lion, or other beast, when its fore-legs are raised in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> posture.

SALIC

Pages 483-484
or SALIQUE, LAW, (Lex Salica), an ancient and fundamental law of the kingdom of France, usually supposed to have been made by Pharamond, or at least by Clovis; in virtue of which males only arc to inherit. Some, as Postellus, would have it to have been called *Salic*, q. d. *Gallic*, because peculiar to the Gauls. Fer. Montanus insists, it was because Pharamond was at first called *Salicus*. Others will have it to be so named, as having been made for the salic lands. These were noble fiefs which their first kings used to bestow on the salians, that is, the great lords of their salls or court, without any other tenure than military service; and for this reason, such fiefs were not to descend to women, as being by nature unfit for such a tenure. Some, again, derive the origin of this word from the Salians, a tribe of Franks that settled in Gaul in the reign of Julian, who is said to have given them lands on condition of their personal service in war. He even passed the conditions into a law, which the new conquerors acquiesced in, and called it *salic*, from the name of their former countrymen.

SALICORNIA

Pages 484-484

JOINTED GLASS-WORT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> *Saltwort*; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the nonandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, *Holoraceae*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The inhabitants near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts where these plants grow, cut them up toward the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when they are fully grown; and, after having dried them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they burn them for their ashes, which are used in making glass and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. These herbs are by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people called *kelp*, and promiscuously gathered for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>.

SALII

Pages 484-484

in Roman antiquity, priests of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, whereof there were 12, instituted by Numa, wearing painted, particoloured garments, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> bonnets; with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> cuirasse on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. They were called *salii*, from *saltare*, "to dance;" because, after assisting at sacrifices, they went <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> about the streets, with bucklers in their left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a rod in their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, striking musically with their rods on one another's bucklers, and singing hymns in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods.

SALINO

Pages 484-484

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIPARI_ISLANDS">Lipari <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, consists of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, both in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> state of cultivation. The one lying more towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> than the other is rather the highest of the two, and is called *del Capo*, "the head." The other is called *della Fossa felice*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the "happy valley." One third of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of these hills from the bottom to the summit is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> orchard, consisting of vines, olive, fig, plum, apricot, and a vast diversity of other trees. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> roofs of the houses, which are everywhere interspersed amid this diversity of verdure and foliage, contribute to variegate the prospect in a very agreeable manner. The back <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of almost all the houses is shaded by an arbour of vines, supported by pillars of brick, with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> to sustain the branches and foliage of the vines. Those arbours shelter the houses from the rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of which is quite scorching in these southern regions. The vines are extremely fruitful; the poles <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. The scenes in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> are more interesting to the lover of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> than to the antiquarian. Sec Reticulum. On the south side of the island, however, there are still to be seen some fine ruins of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bath, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. They consist of a wall 10 or 11 fathoms in extent, and terminating in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, of which only a small part now remains. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> seems to have been reduced to its present state rather by the ravages of men than the injuries of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Almost all the houses in the island are built of materials which have belonged to ancient monuments. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of fresh as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in this island; for whenever the present inhabitants have occasion for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of fresh water, they have only to dig a pit on the shore, and pure sweet water flows in great abundance. There were formerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> here, from which the inhabitants drew a very considerable yearly revenue. But whether they are exhausted, or whatever circumstance may have caused them to be given up, they are now no longer known. The island abounds in a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. On the east side it is very populous. There are two places which are both called *Lingua*, "the tongue," and which contain a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants; the one is near Salino, the other is distinguished by the name of *St Marina*: there are, besides these, two other villages. All these places together may contain about 4000 inhabitants: the circumference of the island may be about 14 miles.

SALISBURY

Pages 484-486

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Wiltshire in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 55. N. Lat. 51.3. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> owed its first rise to its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which was begun in 1219, and finished in 1258. According to an estimate delivered in to Henry III., it cost forty thousand merks. It is a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and is certainly the most elegant and regular in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The doors and chapels are equal in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the months, the windows to the days, and the pillars and pilasters to the hours in a year. It is built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>, with a spire in the middle, and nothing but buttresses and glass windows on the outside. The spire is the highest in the kingdom, being 410 feet, which is twice the height of the Monument in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The pillars and pilasters in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of fusile marble; the art of making which is now either entirely lost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> little known. This magnificent church has lately undergone most beautiful alterations; with an addition of two fine windows, and an organ presented by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which is 50 feet in diameter and 150 in circumference, bears entirely upon one slender pillar, which is such a curiosity as can hardly be matched in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> of the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through the city in the reign of Edward III., was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage to it. The chancellorship of the most noble order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>, which is annexed to this see, was first conferred on Bishop Richard Beauchamp. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> of St Michael's, near this city, was founded by one of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. Dr Seth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a>, bishop of this see in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., contributed greatly to the making the river Avon navigable to Christ-church in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. The same prelate, in 1683, built an hospital for the entertainment of the widows of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> clergymen. There are three other churches besides the cathedral, which is without the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the city, and a greater number of boarding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, especially for young ladies, than in any other town in England. Here is a manufacture of druggets, flannels, bonelace, and those cloths called Salisbury whites; in consideration of which, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, assizes, boardings, boarding-schools, and clergy, the city may be justly said to be in a flourishing condition. It was incorporated by Henry III.; and is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, recorder, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-recorder, 24 aldermen, and 30 assistants or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. The number of souls, in 1811, was 8243. A new council chamber, with proper courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, was built here in the year 1794 by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Radnor; to which Mr Hussey was also a great benefactor. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a>, where the canons and prebendaries live, is like a fine city of itself. In this town are several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>-schools; the expense of one of them is entirely defrayed by the bishop. The city gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the noble family of Cecil. **Salisbury Plain.** The extensive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> in Wiltshire, which are thus denominated, form in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> one of the most delightful parts of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It extends 28 miles west of Weymouth, and 25 east to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>; and in some places is near 40 miles in breadth. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> about Salisbury is a chalky <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and is famous for feeding numerous flocks of sheep. Considerable portions of this tract are now enclosing, the advantages of which are so great, that it is hoped the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> undergo so beneficial a change. This plain contains, beside the famous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a>, numerous other remains of antiquity. **Saliva,** is that fluid by which the mouth and tongue are continually moistened in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state; and is supplied by glands which form it, that are called salivary glands. This humour is thin and pellucid, incapable of being concreted by the fire, almost without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell. By chewing, it is expressed from the glands which separate it from the blood, and is intimately mixed with our food, the digestion of which it greatly promotes. In hungry persons it is acid, and copiously discharged; and in those who have fasted long it is highly acid, penetrating, and resolvent. A too copious evacuation of it produces thirst, loss of appetite, bad digestion, and an atrophy. **Salivation,** in Medicine, a promoting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of saliva, by means of medicines, mostly by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of salivation is in diseases belonging to the glands and membrana adiposa, and principally in the cure of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; though it is sometimes also used in epidemic diseases, cutaneous diseases, &c., whose crises tend that way. **Salix,** the Willow, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 50th order, Amentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Willow trees have been frequently the theme of poetical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Horace, and in Ovid, we have many exquisite allusions to them and their several properties; and for a melancholy lover or a contemplative poet, imagination cannot paint a fitter retreat than the banks of a beautiful river, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a drooping willow. The Babylonica, Babylonian pendulous salix, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called weeping willow, grows to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> size, having numerous, long, slender, pendulous branches, hanging down loosely all round in a curious manner, and long, narrow, spear-shaped, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, smooth leaves. This curious willow is a native of the east, and is retained in our hardy plantations for ornament; and exhibits a most agreeable variety, particularly when disposed singly by the verges of any piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or in spacious openings of grass ground. All the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of salix are of the tree kind, very hardy, remarkably fast growers, and several of them attaining a considerable stature when permitted to run up to standards. They are mostly of the aquatic tribe, being generally the most abundant and of most prosperous growth in watery situations; they however will grow freely almost anywhere, in any common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and exposure; but grow considerably the fastest and strongest in low moist <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, particularly in marshy situations, by the verges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, brooks, and other waters; likewise along the sides of watery ditches, &c.; which places often lying waste, may be employed to good advantage, in plantations of willows, for different purposes. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALLEE">Sallee</a>,** an ancient and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, with a harbour and several forts. The harbour of Sallee is one of the best in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and yet, on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> that lies across it, ships of the smallest draught are forced to unload and take out their guns before they can get into it. There are docks to build ships; but they are hardly ever used, for want of skill and materials. It is a large <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, divided by the river Guero into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. It has long been famous for its rovers or pirates, which make prizes of all Christian ships that come in their way, except there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to the contrary. The town of Sallee in its present state, though large, presents nothing worthy the observation of the traveller, except a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of 24 pieces of cannon fronting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and a redoubt at the entrance of the river, which is about a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and penetrates several miles into the interior country. W. Long. 6. 30. N. Lat. 34. 0. **Sallet,** or Salad, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of eatable herbs, ordinarily accompanying roast meat; composed chiefly of crude fresh herbage, seasoned with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>. Menage derives the word from the Latin salata; of sal, "salt;" others from salcedo; Du-Cange from sal-gama, which is used in Ausonius and Columella in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Some add mustard, hard eggs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; others, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and other spices, with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-peel, saffron, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sallet-herbs, and those which ordinarily make the basis of our English sallets, are lettuce, celery, endive, cresses, radish, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>; along with which, by way of furniture, or additional, are used, purslane, spinach, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, tarragon, burnet, corn-sallet, and chervil. The gardeners call some plants small herbs in sallets; these should always be cut while in the seed-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>: as cresses, mustard, radish, turnip, spinach, and lettuce; all which are raised from seeds sown in drills, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, from the middle of February to the end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, under glasses or frames; and thence to the middle of May, upon natural beds, warmly exposed; and during the summer heats in more shady places; and afterwards in September, as in March, &c.; and lastly, in the rigour of the winter, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they chance to be frozen in very frosty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, putting them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>-water two hours before they are used, recovers them. **Sallo,** Denis de, a French writer, famous for being being the projector of literary journals, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1626. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted a counsellor in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Paris in 1652. It was in 1664 he schemed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Journal des Savans; and the year following began to publish it under the name of Sieur de Heronville, which was that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre. But he played the critic so severely, that authors, surprised at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of such attacks, retorted so powerfully, that M. de Sallo, unable to weather the storm, after he had published his third Journal, declined the undertaking, and turned it over to the abbe Gallois; who, without presuming to criticise, contented himself merely with giving titles, and making extracts. Such was the origin of literary journals, which afterwards sprang up in other countries under different titles; and the success of them, under judicious management, is a clear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their utility. M. de Sallo died in 1669.

SALLUSTIUS

Pages 486-486
CAIUS CRISPUS, a celebrated Roman historian, was born at Amiternum, a city of Italy, in the year of Rome 669, and before Christ 35. His education was liberal, and he made the best use of it. His Roman s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history in six books, from the death of Sylla to the conspiracy of Catiline, the great work from which he chiefly derived his glory among the ancients, is unfortunately lost excepting a few fragments; but his two detached pieces of history which happily remain entire are sufficient to justify the great encomiums he has received as a writer.—He has had the singular honour to be twice translated by a royal hand: first by our Elizabeth, according to Camden; and secondly, by the present Infant of Spain, whose version of this elegant historian, lately printed in folio, is one of the most beautiful books that any country has produced since the invention of printing. No man has inveighed more sharply against the vices of his age than this historian; yet no man had fewer pretensions to virtue. His youth was spent in a most lewd and profligate manner; and his patrimony almost squandered away when he had scarcely taken possession of it. Marcus Varro, a writer of undoubted credit, relates, in a fragment preserved by Aulus Gellius, that Sallust was actually caught in bed with Fausta the daughter of Sylla, by Milo her husband; who scourged him very severely, and did not suffer him to depart till he had redeemed his liberty with a considerable sum. A. U. C. 694, he was made quaestor, and in 702 tribune of the people; in neither of which places is he allowed to have acquitted himself at all to his honour. By virtue of his quaestorship, he obtained an admission into the senate; but was expelled thence by the censors in 704, on account of his immoral and debauched way of life. In the year 705 Caesar restored him to the dignity of a senator; and to introduce him into the house with a better grace, made him quaestor a second time. In the administration of this office he behaved himself very scandalously: exposed every thing to sale for which he could find a purchaser; and if we may believe the author of the invective, thought nothing wrong which he had a mind to do: *Nihil non venale habuerit, cujus aliquis emptor fuit, nihil non æquum et verum duxit, quod ipsi facere collibisset.* In the year 707, when the African war was at an end, he was made praetor for his services to Cæsar, and sent to Numidia. Here he acted the same part as Verres had done in Sicily; outrageously plundered the province; and returned with Sallustius, such immense riches to Rome that he purchased a most magnificent building upon Mount Quirinal, with those gardens which to this day retain the name of Sallustian gardens, besides his country house at Tivoli. How he spent the remaining part of his life we have no account from ancient writers. Eusebius tells us that he married Terentia, the divorced wife of Cicero; and that he died at the age of 50, in the year 710, which was about four years before the battle of Actium. Of the many things which he wrote, besides his histories of the Catilinarian and Jugurthine wars, we have some orations or speeches, printed with his fragments.

SALLY PORTS

Pages 486-486

in fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Postern Gates, as they are sometimes called, are those under-ground <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> from the inner works to the outward ones; such as from the higher flank to the lower, or to the tenailles, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> from the middle of the curtain to the ravelin. When they are made for men to go through only, they are made with steps at the entrance and going out. They are about 6 feet wide and 8½ feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. There is also a gutter or shore made under the sally-ports, which are in the middle of the curtains, for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which runs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the streets to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the ditch; but this can only be done when they are wet ditches. When sally-ports serve to carry guns through them for the out-works, instead of making them with steps, they must have a gradual slope, and be 8 feet wide.

SALMASIUS

Pages 486-486

CLAUDIUS, a French writer of uncommon abilities and immense erudition, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near Semur in 1596. His mother, who was a Protestant, infused her notions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into him, and he at length converted his father: he settled at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; and in 1650 paid a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who is reported to have shown him extraordinary marks of regard. Upon the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. of England, he was prevailed on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, then in exile, to write a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; which was answered by our famous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in 1631, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> intitled *Defensio pro Populo Anglicano contra Claudii Salmasii Defensionem Regiam.* This book was read over all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and conveyed such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the writer's abilities, that he was respected even by those who hated his principles. Salmasius died in 1653; and some did not scruple to say, that Milton killed him by the acuteness of his reply. His works are numerous, and of various kinds; but the greatest monuments of his learning are, his *Notæ in Historia Augustæ Scriptores,* and his *Exercitationes Plinianæ in Solium.*

SALMO

Pages 486-486

the SALMON; a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SALMON. See Salmo, Ichthyology Index. Salmon-Fishery. See Salmon-Fishery.

SALON

Pages 486-487
or SALOON, in architecture, a lofty, spacious sort of hall, vaulted at top, and usually comprehending two stories, with two ranges of windows. The saloon is a grand room in the middle of a building, or at the head of a gallery, &c. Its faces, or sides, are all to have a symmetry with each other; and as it usually takes up the height of two stories, its ceiling, Daviler observes, should be with a moderate sweep. The saloon is a state room much used in the palaces in Italy; and from thence the mode came to us. Ambassadors, and other great visitors, are usually received in the saloon. It is sometimes built square, sometimes round or oval, sometimes octagonal, as at Marly, and sometimes in other forms.

SALONA

Pages 487-487

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venetie. It was formerly a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and its ruins show that it was 10 miles in circumference. It is 18 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Spalato, and subject to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. It is now a wretched village, preserving few distinguishable remains of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour. Doubtless the two last ages have destroyed all that had escaped the barbarity of the northern nations that demolished it. In a valuable MS. relation of Dalmatia, written by the senator Giambattista Guistiniani, about the middle of the 16th century, there is a hint of what existed at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, and magnificence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Salona, may be imagined from the vaults and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which are seen at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; from the vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the finest marble, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> scattered on, and buried in the fields; from the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of three pieces of marble, which is still standing in the place where they say the arsenal was, towards the seashore; and from the many arches of surprising <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, supported by very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> marble columns: the height of the arches is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-throw, and above them there was an aqueduct, which reached from Salona to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>. There are to be seen many ruins and vestiges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> palaces, and many ancient epitaphs may be read on fine marble stones; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is increased, has buried the most ancient stones, and the most valuable things." E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 17. 29. N. Lat. 24. 10.

SALONICHI

Pages 487-487

formerly called Thessalonica, a seaport town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, with an archbishop's see. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and rich, being about 10 miles in circumference. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, carried on principally by the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Jews, the former of which have 30 churches, and the latter as many synagogues; the Turks also have a few mosques. It is surrounded with walls flanked with towers, and defended on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-side by a citadel, and near the harbour with three forts. It was taken from the Venetians by the Turks in 1431. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merchandise is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It is seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name, partly on the top, and partly on the side of a hill, near the river Vardar. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 23. 13. N. Lat. 40. 41.

SALSES

Pages 487-487

a very strong castle of France, in Roussillon, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. It was taken from the Spaniards by the French in 1642; and is seated on a lake of the same name, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERPIGNAN">Perpignan</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 0. N. Lat. 43. 35.

SALSETTE

Pages 487-487

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the East Indies, adjacent to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, from which it is in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> divided only by a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> fordable at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is about 26 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is rich, and by a proper cultivation capable of producing anything that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow in tropical climates. It is everywhere well watered, and when in the possession of the Portuguese furnished such quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, that it was called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">Granary</a> of Goa. It abounds also in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and has <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, both of the four-footed and feathered kind. It has pretty <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> that the whole was thrown up from the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of which it is said, that on the top of the highest hill there was found, some years ago, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, such as was anciently used by the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here we meet with the ruins of a place called Canara, where there are excavations of rocks, supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with those of Elephanta. They are much more numerous, but not comparable to the former either in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> or workmanship. The island of Salsette lately formed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Portuguese dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. It ought to have been ceded to the English along with Bombay, as part of the dower of Catharine of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, espoused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The fulfilment of this article, however, being evaded, the island remained in possession of the Portuguese; and notwithstanding the little care they took of it, the revenue of it was valued at 60,000/. Such was the negligence of the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, that they took no care to fortify it against the attacks of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, from whose dominions Salsette was only separated by a very narrow pass fordable at low water. Here they had only a miserable redoubt of no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, till, on the appearance of an approaching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Mahrattas, they began to build another, which indeed would have answered the purpose of protecting the island, provided the Mahrattas had allowed them to finish it. This, however, was not their intention. They allowed them indeed to go on quietly with their works till they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them almost completed, when they came and took possession of them. The Mahrattas thus became dangerous neighbours to the English at Bombay, until it was ceded to the latter by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded with these people in 1780. E. Long. 72. 15. N. Lat. 19. 0.

SALSOLA

Pages 487-487

Glass-wort, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 12th order, Holoracea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. All the sorts of glasswort are sometimes promiscuously used for making the sal kali, but it is the third sort which is esteemed best for this purpose. The manner of making it is as follows: Having dug a trench near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> laths across it, on which they lay the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in heaps, and, having made a fire below, the liquor, which runs out of the herbs, drops to the bottom, which at length thickening, becomes sal kali, which is partly of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and partly of an ash-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, very sharp and corrosive, and of a saltish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. This, when thoroughly hardened, becomes like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and in that state is transported to different countries, for making of glass.

SALT

Pages 487-492

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bodies. The characteristic marks of salt have usually been reckoned its power of affecting the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and of being soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. But this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not distinguish salt from quicklime, which also affects the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of taste, and dissolves in water; yet quicklime has been universally reckoned an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and not a salt. The only distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of salts, therefore, is their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> in water: but this does not belong to all salts; for the nitrous and marine <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, though allowed on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to be salts, are yet incapable of crystallization, at least least by any method hitherto known. Several of the imperfect neutral salts also, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the nitrous, muriatic, and vegetable acids, with some kinds of earths, crystallize with very great difficulty. However, by the addition of spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other substances which absorb <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the water, keeping the liquor in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, &c. all of them may be reduced to crystals of one kind or other. Salt, therefore, may be defined a substance affecting the organs of taste, soluble in water, and capable of crystallization, either by itself or in conjunction with some other body; and, universally, every salt capable of being reduced into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form, is also capable of crystallization per se. Thus the class of saline bodies will be sufficiently distinguished from all others; for quicklime, though soluble in water, cannot be crystallized without addition either of fixed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> or some other acid; yet it is most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in a solid state. The precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, basaltes, &c. though supposed to be formed by crystallization, are nevertheless distinguished from salts by their insipidity and insolubility in water. But acids and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, and combinations of both, when in a concrete form, are salts, and of the purest form. Hence we conclude, that the bodies, to which the name of salts more properly belongs, are the concretions of those substances; which are accordingly called acid salts, alkaline salts, and neutral salts. These last are combinations of acid and alkaline salts, in such proportion as to render the compounds neither sour nor alkaline to the taste. This proportionate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> is called saturation: thus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> salt is a neutral salt, composed of muriatic acid and soda combined together to the point of saturation. The appellation of neutral salts is also extended to denote all those combinations of acids, and any other substance with which they can unite, so as to lose, wholly or in great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, their acid properties. But although this general <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of salts is commonly received, yet there are many writers, especially mineralogists, who confine the denomination of salts in the manner we first mentioned, viz. to those substances only which, besides the general properties of salts, have the power of crystallizing, that is, of arranging their particles so as to form regular shaped bodies, called crystals, when the water superfluous to their concrete existence has been evaporated. Common Salt, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Salt, the name of that salt extracted from the waters of the ocean, which is used in greater quantities for preserving <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c. It is a perfect neutral salt, composed of marine or muriatic acid, saturated with mineral alkali. It has a saline but agreeable flavour. It requires about four times its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water to be dissolved, and nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, according to Macquer. But according to Kirwan, it only requires 2.5 its weight of water to be dissolved in the temperature of sixty degrees of Fahrenheit. This salt always contains some part formed with a calcareous base; and, in order to have it pure, it must be dissolved in distilled water; then a solution of mineral alkali is to be poured in it until no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> precipitation appears; then by filtrating and evaporating the solution, a pure common salt is produced. Its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is perfectly cubic, and those hollow pyramids, or tremies as the French call them, as well as the parallelopipeds formed sometimes in its crystallization, consist all of a quantity of small cubes, disposed in those forms. Its decrepitation on the fire, which has been reckoned by some as a characteristic of this salt, although the vitriolated tartar, nitrous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and other salts, have the same property, is owing chiefly to the water, and perhaps also to the air of its crystallization. Its specific gravity is 2.120 according to Kirwan. The acid of tartar precipitates nothing from it. One hundred parts of common salt contain thirty-three of real acid, fifty of mineral alkali, and seventeen of water. It is commonly found in salt water, and salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, in the proportion of even thirty-six per cent. It is found also in coals, and in beds of gypsum. This salt is unalterable by fire, though it fuses, and becomes more opaque: nevertheless a violent fire, with the free access of air, causes it to evaporate in white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which adhere to the neighbouring bodies. It is only decomposed, as Macquer affirms, by the sulphuric and nitric acids; and also by the boracic or sedative salt. But although nitre is decomposed very easily by arsenic, this neutral marine salt is nowise decomposed by the same. According to Monge, the fixed vegetable alkali, when caustic, decomposes all this marine salt. It preserves from corruption almost all sorts of animal food much better for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> than any other salt, as it preserves them without destroying their taste and qualities; but when applied in too small a quantity, it then promotes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. Of this most useful commodity there are ample stores on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as well as in the ocean. There are few countries which do not afford vast quantities of rock or fossil salt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> (A) of it have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been discovered and wrought in England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In several parts of the world, there are huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which wholly consist of fossil salt. Of this kind are two mountains in Russia, nigh <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRACAN">Astracan</a>; several in the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> and Algiers, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and several also in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> almost entirely consists of fossil salt. The new world is likewise stored with treasures of this useful mineral, as well as with all other kinds of subterranean productions. Moreover, the sea affords such vast plenty of common salt, that all mankind might thence be supplied with quantities sufficient for their occasions. There are also innumerable springs, ponds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, impregnated with common salt, from which the inhabitants of many countries are plentifully supplied therewith. In some countries which are remote from the sea, and have little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and which are not blessed with mines of salt or salt-waters, the necessities of the inhabitants have forced them to invent a method of extracting (A) Amongst the salt mines of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> are those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NORTHWICH">Northwich</a> in Cheshire, Altemonte in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a> in Tyrol, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a> in Catalonia: also those stupendous mines at Wilieczka in Poland, to be noticed in the sequel of this article, and Soowar in Upper Hungary; of which see accounts in Phil. Trans. No. 61. and 413. ting their common salt from the ashes of vegetables. The muriatic salt of vegetables was described by Dr Grew under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lixiviated marine salt. Leeuwenhoek obtained cubical crystals of this salt from a lixivium of soda or kelp, and also from a solution of the lixivial salt of carduus benedictus; of which he hath given figures in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, published in No 175, of their Transactions. Dr Dagner, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">Act</a>. Acad. N. C. vol. v. obs. 150, takes notice of great quantities of it which he found mixed in potashes. And the ingenious Dr Fothergill extracted plenty of it from the ashes of fern: See Medical Essays, vol. v. article 13. The muriatic salt which the excellent Mr Boyle extracted from sandiver, and supposed to be produced from the materials used in making glass, was doubtless separated from the kelp made use of in that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. Kunckel also informs us, that he took an alkaline salt; and after calcining it with a moderate fire, dissolved it in pure water, and placing the solution in a cool cellar, obtained from it many crystals of a neutral salt. He supposes that the alkaline salt was by the process converted into this neutral salt. But it is more reasonable to believe, that the alkaline salt which he applied was not pure, but mixed with the muriatic salt of vegetables, which by this process was only separated from it. It is doubtless chiefly this muriatic salt which, in some of the inland parts of Asia, they extract from the ashes of duck-weed and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>'s fig-tree, and use for their common salt. That they are able in those countries to make common salt to profit from vegetables, ought not to be wondered at, since in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, capitals of Indostan, salt is so scarce as usually to be sold for half-a-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. We may therefore give some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to Marco <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLO">Polo</a>, when he informs us, that in the inner parts of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the world, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Caindu, lying west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBET">Tibet</a>, the natives used salt instead of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, it being first made up in cakes, and sealed with the stamp of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and that they made great profit of this money by exchanging it with the neighbouring nations for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>. We are also told by Ludolofus, in his Historia Ethiopicla, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Abyssines there are mountains of salt, the which when dug out is soft, but soon grows hard; and that this salt serves them instead of money to buy all things. The same is confirmed by Ramusio. Mr Boyle discovered common salt in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood and urine. "I have observed it (says Mr Brownrigg), not only in human urine, but also in that of dogs, horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. It may easily be discovered in these, and many other liquids impregnated with it, by certain very regular and beautiful starry figures which appear in their surfaces after congelation. These figures I first observed in the great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> in the year 1739. The dung of such animals as feed upon grass or grain, doth also contain plenty of common salt." Naturalists, observing the great variety of forms under which this salt appears, have thought fit to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the several kinds of it under certain general classes; distinguishing it, most usually, into rock or fossil salt, sea-salt, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> or fountain salt. To which classes, others might be added, of those muriatic salts which are found in vegetable and animal substances. These several kinds of common salt often differ from each other in their outward form and appearance, or in such accidental properties as they derive from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> substances with which they are mixed. But when perfectly pure, they have all the same qualities; so that chemists, by the exactest inquiries, have not been able to discover any essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them; for which reason we shall distinguish common salt after a different manner, into the three following kinds, viz. into rock or native salt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> salt, and white salt. By rock salt, or native salt, is understood all salt dug out of the earth, which hath not undergone any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. Under the title of bay salt may be ranked all kinds of common salt extracted from the water wherein it is dissolved, by means of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and the operation of the air; whether the water from which it is extracted be sea water, or natural brine drawn from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and springs, or salt water stagnating in ponds and lakes. Under the title of white salt, or boiled salt, may be included all kinds of common salt extracted by coction from the water wherein it is dissolved; whether this water be sea water, or the salt water of wells, fountains, lakes or rivers; or water of any sort impregnated with rock-salt, or other kinds of common salt. The first of these kinds of salt is in several countries found so pure, that it serves for most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> uses, without any previous preparation (triture excepted); for of all natural salts rock-salt is the most abundantly furnished by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in various parts of the world, being found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, occupying great tracts of land. It is generally found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> under the surface of the earth, as in Hungary, Muscovy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, Poland, Calabria, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, Ethiopia, and the East Indies. In England (says Magellan), the salt mines at Northwich are in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ground, and contain it in layers or strata of various colours, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> are the most plentiful, as I have observed on the spot, which I visited in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1782, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with my worthy and learned friend Mr Volta, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and well known by his great abilities, and many discoveries in that branch of knowledge. The mine into which we descended was excavated in the form of a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a> or vault under ground, supported by various columns of the salt, that were purposely left to support the incumbent weight. And the workmen having lighted a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of candles all round its circumference, it furnished us with the most agreeable and surprising sight, whilst we were descending in the large tub, which serves to bring up the lumps that are broken from the mine," &c. Wraxall gives the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the famous salt mines near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in Poland. "After being let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> (says he) by a rope to the depth of 230 feet, our conductors led us through galleries, which, for loftiness and breadth, seemed rather to resemble the avenues to some subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> cut in a mine. They were perfectly dry in every part, and terminated in two chapels composed entirely of salt, hewn out of the solid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. The images which adorn the altars, as well as the pillars and ornaments, were all of the same transparent materials; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and spars of which reflecting the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from the lamps which the guides held in their hands, produced an effect equally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> and beautiful, Descending lower..." er into the earth by means of ladders, I found myself in an immense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> or cavern of salt, many hundred feet in height, length, and dimensions, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> and sides of which were cut with exact regularity. A thousand persons might dine in it without inconvenience, and the eye in vain attempted to trace or define its limits. Nothing could be more sublime than this vast subterranean apartment, illuminated by flambeaux, which faintly discover its prodigious magnitude, and leave the imagination at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to enlarge it indefinitely. After remaining about two hours and a half under ground, I was drawn up again in three minutes with the greatest facility." See also an account of the same mines by Mr Bernard, Journal de Physique, vol. xvi. for 1780, in which the miraculous tales concerning those subterranean habitations, villages, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, are reduced to their proper magnitude and estimate. The English fossil salt is unfit for the uses of the kitchen, until by solution and coction it is freed from several impurities, and reduced into white salt. The British white salt also is not so proper as several kinds of bay salt for curing fish and such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-meats as are intended for sea provisions, or for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> into hot countries. So that for these purposes we are obliged, either wholly or in part, to use bay salt, which we purchase in France, Spain, and other foreign countries. However, it does not appear that there is any other thing requisite in the formation of bay salt than to evaporate the sea water with an exceedingly gentle heat; and it is even very probable, that our common sea-salt by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> solution and crystallization might attain the requisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity. Without entering into any particular detail of the processes used for the preparation of bay-salt in different parts of the world, we shall content ourselves with giving a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of the best methods of preparing common salt. At some convenient place near the sea-shore is erected the saltern. This is a long, low <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, consisting of two parts; one of which is called the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the other the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>-house, or boiling-house. The fore-house serves to receive the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and cover the workmen; and in the boiling-house are placed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and pan in which the salt is made. Sometimes they have two pans, one at each end of the saltern; and the part appropriated for the fuel and workmen is in the middle. The furnace opens into the fore-house by two mouths, beneath each of which is a mouth to the ash-pits. To the mouths of the furnace, doors are fitted; and over them a wall is carried up to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, which divides the fore-house from the boiling-house, and prevents the dust of the coal and the ashes and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the furnace from falling into the salt pan. The fore-house communicates with the boiling-house by a door placed in the wall which divides them. The body of the furnace consists of two chambers, divided from each other by a brick partition called the midfeather; which from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> base terminates in a narrow edge nigh the top of the furnace; and by means of short pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> erected upon it, supports the bottom of the salt pan; it also fills up a considerable part of the furnace, which otherwise would be too large, and would consume more coals than, by the help of this contrivance, are required. To each chamber of the furnace is fitted a grate, through which the ashes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the ash-pits. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> are made of long bars of iron, supported underneath by strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bars of the same metal. They are not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the farthest part of the furnace, it being unnecessary to throw in the fuel so far: for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> is driven from the fire on the grate to the farthest part of the furnace; and from thence passes, together with the smoke, through two flues into the chimney; and thus the bottom of the salt pan is everywhere equally heated. The salt pans are made of an elongated form, flat at the bottom, with the sides erected at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; the length of some of these pans is 15 feet, in breadth 12 feet, and the depth 16 inches; but at different works they are of different dimensions. They are commonly made of plates of iron, joined together with nails, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> are filled with a strong cement. Within the pan five or six strong beams of iron are fixed to its opposite sides, at equal distances, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other and to the bottom of the pan, from which they are distant about eight inches. From these beams hang down strong iron hooks, which are linked to other hooks or clasps of iron firmly nailed to the bottom of the pan; and thus the bottom of the pan is supported, and prevented from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> down or changing its figure. The plates most commonly used are of malleable iron, about four feet and a half long, a foot broad, and the third of an inch in thickness. The Scots prefer smaller plates, 14 or 15 inches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Several make the sides of the pan, where they are not exposed to the fire, of lead; those parts, when made of iron, being found to consume fast in rust from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> of the pan. Some have used plates of cast iron, five or six feet square, and an inch in thickness; but they are very subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> when unequally heated, and shaken (as they frequently are) by the violent boiling of the liquor. The cement most commonly used to fill the joints is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> made of lime. The pan, thus formed, is placed over the furnace, being supported at the four corners by brick <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but along the middle, and at the sides and ends, by round pillars of cast iron called taplins, which are placed at three feet distance from each other, being about eight inches high, and at the top, where smallest, four inches in diameter. By means of these pillars the heat of the fire penetrates equally to all parts of the bottom of the pan, its four corners only excepted. Care is also taken to prevent the smoke of the furnace from passing into the boiling-house, by bricks and strong cement, which are closely applied to every part of the salt pan. In some places, as at Blyth in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, besides the common salt pans here described, they have a preparing pan placed between two salt pans, in the middle part of the building, which in other works is the fore-house. The sea-water being received into this preparing pan, is there heated and in part evaporated by the flame and heat conveyed under it through flues from the two furnaces of the salt pans. And the hot water, as occasion requires, is conveyed through troughs from the preparing pan into the salt pans. Various other contrivances have been invented to lessen the expense of fuel, and several patents have been obtained for that purpose; but the salt-boilers have found their old methods the most convenient. Between the sides of the pan and walls of the boil- The most convenient instruments for this purpose are skimmers of thin ash boards, six or eight inches broad, and so long that they may reach above half way over the salt pan. These skimmers have handles fitted to them; and the salt-boiler and his assistant, each holding one of them on the opposite sides of the pan, apply them so to each other that they overlap in the middle, and beginning at one end of the pan, carry them gently forward together, along the surface of the boiling liquor, to the other end; and thus, without breaking the scum, collect it all to one end of the pan, from whence they easily take it out. After the water is skimmed, it appears perfectly clear and transparent; and they continue boiling it briskly, till so much of the fresh or aqueous part is evaporated, that what remains in the pan is a strong brine almost fully saturated with salt, so that small saline crystals begin to form on its surface; which operation, in a pan filled 1.5 inches deep with water, is usually performed in five hours. The pan is then filled up a second <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with clear sea-water drawn from the cistern; and about the time when it is half filled, the scratch-pans are taken out, and being emptied of the scratch found in them, are again placed in the corners of the salt pan. The scratch taken out of these pans is a fine white calcareous earth found in the form of powder, which separates from the sea-water during its coction, before the salt begins to form into grains. This subtile powder is violently agitated by the boiling liquor, until it is driven to the corners of the pan, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the liquor being more gentle, it subsides into the scratch-pans placed there to receive it, and in them it remains undisturbed, and thus the greatest part of it is separated from the brine. After the pan hath again been filled up with sea-water, three whites of eggs are mixed with the liquor, by which it is clarified a second time, in the manner before described; and it is afterwards boiled down to a strong brine as at first; which second boiling may take up about four hours. The pan is then filled up a third time with clear sea-water; and after that, a fourth time; the liquor being each time clarified and boiled down to a strong brine, as before related; and the scratch-pans being taken out and emptied every time that the pan is filled up. Then, at the fourth boiling, as soon as the crystals begin to form on the surface of the brine, then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> the fire, and only suffer the brine to simmer, or boil very gently. In this heat they constantly endeavour to keep it all the time that the salt corns or granulates, which may be <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten hours. The salt is said to granulate, when its minute crystals cohere together into little masses or grains, which sink down in the brine, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at the bottom of the salt pan. When most of the liquor is evaporated, and the salt thus lies in the pan almost dry on its surface, it is then time to draw it out. This part of the process is performed by raising the salt to one side of the pan into a long heap, where it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> a while from the brine, and is then filled out into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> or other proper vessels, and carried into the store-house, and delivered into the custody of his majesty's officers. And in this manner the whole process is performed in 24 hours; the salt being usually drawn every morning. In the store-house the salt is put hot into drabs, which are partitions like stalls for horses, lined on three sides and at the bottom with boards, and having a sliding-board on the fore-side to put in or draw out as occasion requires. The bottoms are made shelving, being highest at the back-side, and gradually inclining forwards; by which means the saline liquor, which remains mixed with the salt, easily drains from it; and the salt, in three or four days, becomes sufficiently dry; and is then taken out of the drabs, and laid up in large heaps, where it is ready for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The saline liquor which drains from the salt is not a pure brine of common salt, but hath a sharp and bitter taste, and is therefore called bittern: this liquor, at some works, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> for particular uses, at others throw away. A considerable quantity of this bittern is left at the bottom of the pan after the process is finished; which, as it contains much salt, they suffer to remain in the pan, when it is filled up with sea-water. But at each process this liquor becomes more sharp and bitter, and also increases in quantity: so that, after the third or fourth process is finished, they are obliged to take it out of the pan; otherwise it mixes in such quantities with the salt, as to give it a bitter taste, and disposes it to grow soft and run in the open air, and renders it unfit for domestic uses. After each process there also adheres to the bottom and sides of the pan, a white stony crust, of the same calcareous substance with that before collected from the boiling liquor. This the operators call <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-scratch, distinguishing the other found in the lead-pans by the name of powder-scratch. Once in eight or ten days they separate the stone-scratch from their pans with iron picks, and in several places find it a quarter of an inch in thickness. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this stony crust is suffered to adhere to the pan much longer, it grows so thick that the pan is burnt by the fire, and quickly wears away. In M. de Pagés's Travels round the World, we find the following important fact. "I had been anxious (says that author) to ascertain by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, whether sea-water contains salt in greater quantity under the torrid than under the other zones; and my experiments on this subject served to show, contrary to what I expected, that sea-water is impregnated with salt in less quantity within than without the tropics." These experiments were made on a hundred pounds of sea-water, taken at the depth of ten fathoms, and weighed in water-scales.
