M. de Pagés has given a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of these experiments, from which it appears that 100lb. of sea-water in 46° 12' S. lat. gave 4½ lb. of salt, and in 1° 16" only 3½ lb.; and that in 74° N. lat. it gave 4½ lb. and in 4° 22' only 3½ lb. these being the highest and lowest latitudes in which the experiments were made, and also the greatest and least quantities of salt. Duty on Salt, is a distinct branch of his majesty's extraordinary revenue, and consists in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> of 3s. 4d. per bushel imposed upon all salt, by several statutes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William and other subsequent reigns. This is not generally called an excise, because under the management of different commissioners: but the commissioners of the salt-duties have, by statute I Ann. c. 21. the same powers, and must observe the same regulations, as those of other excises. This tax had usually been only temporary; but by statute 26 Geo II. c. 3. was made perpetual.

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Cornwall in England, situated on the river Tamar, having sufficient depth of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships. Saltash is a borough town, sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and contained 1478 inhabitants in 1811. It is distant 5 miles N.W. from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, 220 miles W.S.W. from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and is in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 6. N. Lat. 50. 24.

SALTIER

Pages 495-495

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> ordinaries—See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. This, says G. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, in his Accedence of Arms, p. 70, was anciently made of the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and driven full of pins, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which was to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> walls, &c. Upton says it was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to catch wild beasts, whence he derives this word from salius, i.e. "a forest." The French call this ordinary sautoir, from sauter, "to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>;" because it may have been used by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to leap over walls of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, which in former times were but low; but some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors think it is borne in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>.

SALTING MEAT FOR THE USE OF THE NAVY

Pages 495-496

The following is the method recommended by the late <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> SAL Admiral Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Knowles. When the ox is killed, let it be skinned and cut up into pieces fit for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as quick as possible, and salted while the meat is hot. For which purpose we must have a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> pounded together and made hot in an oven, of each equal parts; with this sprinkle the meat at the rate of about two ounces to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; then lay the pieces on shelving boards to drain for 24 hours; which done, turn them and repeat the same operation, and let them <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for 24 hours longer. By this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the salt <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be all melted, and have penetrated the meat, and the pieces be drained off; each piece must then be wiped dry with clean coarse cloths. A sufficient quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> salt must then be made hot likewise in an oven, and mixed when taken out with about one third of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; then the casks being ready, rub each piece well with this mixture, and pack them well <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, allowing about half a pound of the salt and sugar to each pound of meat, and it will keep good several years. It is best to proportion the casks to the quantity used at one time, as the less it is exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> the better. The same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> does for pork, only a larger quantity of salt and less sugar must be used; but the preservation of both depends equally upon the meat being hot when first salted. One pound of beef requires two ounces of saltpetre and two ounces of bay-salt, because it is to be sprinkled twice; an ounce of each to a pound of beef both times. The saltpetre requisite for 100 lb. of beef is $12\frac{1}{2}$ lb., which at 12d. per lb. is 12s. 6d.; and the same quantity of bay-salt (for 100 lb. of beef), at three half-pence per lb. is 1s. 6d.; of brown sugar and common salt mixed together half a pound is required, the former in the proportion of one-third, the latter of two-thirds, to a pound of beef. The brown sugar at 8d. per pound. A hundred pounds of beef will take 250 ounces of it, which costs 10s. 5d. The quantity of common salt requisite for 100 lb. of beef is 533 ounces, which at 2d. per lb. amounts to 5s. 6d. The expense therefore will stand thus. | Item | Quantity | Cost | |-----------------------|----------|------| | Saltpetre | 12\(\frac{1}{2}\) lb. | L.0 12 6 | | Bay-salt | 12\(\frac{1}{2}\) lb. | 0 1 6 | | Brown sugar | 250 oz. | 0 10 5 | | Beef, 100 lb. | 6d. per pound | 2 10 0 | | Three casks for it | 1s. 6d. each | 0 4 6 | | Labour, and heating | | 0 4 0 | | Common salt | 533 oz. | 0 5 6 | L.4 8 5 These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> are taken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> beef costs 6d. per pound, meat cured thus will cost less than 1s. per pound; and therefore comes much cheaper than livestock in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> voyages.

SALTOATS

Pages 492-492

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a> in Scotland, and on the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, at the end of the 17th century consisted of only four houses, but contained 1684 inhabitants in 1811. It is now a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of strangers in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> as a watering-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, has a considerable trade in coal and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, with a rope-yard, the manufacture of sail-cloth and ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. It is 30 miles from Glasgow, and 18 from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, and in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 37. N. Lat. 55. 41.

SALTPETRE

Pages 496-497
or Nitre, (nitrate of potash), a compound of nitric acid and potash. See Potash, Chemistry Index. The importance of this salt in various manufactures renders every information relative to its production valuable. The following method has been long practised by the farmers of Appenzell in Switzerland. In so hilly a country, most houses and stables are built on slopes, one side of the edifice resting on the hill, and the other being supported by two strong posts, elevated two or three feet above the ground; so that the air has a free current under the building. Immediately under the stable a pit is dug, usually occupying both in breadth and length the whole space of ground covered by the building; and instead of the clayey earth which is dug out, the pit is filled up with sandy soil. This is the whole process, and all the rest is done by nature. The animal water, which is continually oozing through the planks of the floor, having drenched the earth contained in the pit for the space of two or three years, the latter is emptied, and the saltpetre is refined and prepared in the usual manner. That manner, however, is not the best; and the French chemists, during the incessant wars occasioned by the revolution, have, for the sake of supplying their armies with gunpowder, turned their attention to the best method of refining saltpetre. The following are directions given for this purpose by Chaptal, Champany, and Bonjour. The crude saltpetre is to be beaten small with mallets, in order that the water may more easily attack every part of the mass. The saltpetre is then to be put into tubs, five or six hundred pounds in each tub. Twenty per cent. of water is to be poured into each tub, and the mixture well stirred. It must be left to macerate or digest until the specific gravity of the fluid ceases to augment. Six or seven hours are sufficient for this first operation, and the water acquires the density of between 25 and 35 degrees. (Sp. gr. 1.21, and 1.306, ascertained by Baume's hydrometer.) The first water must then be poured off; and a second portion of water must be poured on the same saltpetre amounting to 10 per cent.; after which the mixture must be stirred up, suffered to macerate for one hour, and the fluid drawn or poured off. Five per cent. of water must then be poured on the saltpetre; and after stirring the whole, the fluid must be immediately drawn off. When the water is drained from the saltpetre, the salt must be thrown into a boiler containing 50 per cent. of boiling water. When the solution is made, it will mark between 66 and 68 degrees of the hydrometer. (Sp. gr. 1.848, and 1.898). The solution is to be poured into a proper vessel, where it deposits, by cooling, about two thirds of the saltpetre originally taken. The precipitation begins in about half an hour, and terminates in between four and six hours. But as it is of importance to obtain the saltpetre in small needles, because in this form it is more easily dried, it is necessary to agitate the fluid during the whole time of the crystallization. A slight motion is communicated to this liquid mass by a kind of rake; in consequence of which the crystals are deposited in very slender needles. In proportion as the crystals fall down, they are scraped to the borders of the vessel, whence they are taken with a skimmer, and thrown to drain in baskets placed on trestles, in such a manner that the water which passes through may either fall into the crystallizing vessel, or be received in basins underneath. The saltpetre is afterwards put into wooden vessels in the form of a mill-hopper or inverted pyramid with a double bottom. The upper bottom is placed two inches above the lower on wooden ledges, and has many small perforations through which water may pass to The lower bottom, which likewise affords a passage by one single aperture. A reservoir is placed beneath. The crystallized saltpetre is washed in these vessels with 5 per cent. of water; which water is afterwards employed in the solution of saltpetre in subsequent operations. The saltpetre, after sufficient draining, and being dried by exposure to the air upon tables for several hours, may then be employed in the manufacture of gunpowder. But when it is required to use the saltpetre in the speedy and immediate manufacture of gunpowder, it must be dried much more strongly. This may be effected in a stove, or more simply by heating it in a flat metallic vessel. For this purpose the saltpetre is to be put into the vessel to the depth of five or six inches, and heated to 40 or 50 degrees of the thermometer (or about 135° of Fahrenheit). The saltpetre is to be stirred for two or three hours, and dried so much that, when strongly pressed in the hand, it shall acquire no consistence, nor adhere together, but resemble a very fine dry sand. This degree of dryness is not required when the powder is made by pounding. From these circumstances, we find that two saline liquids remain after the operation; (1) the water from the washing; and (2) that from the crystallizing vessels. We have already remarked, that the washing of the saltpetre is performed in three successive operations, in which, upon the whole, the quantity of fluid made use of amounts to 3.5 per cent. of the weight of the crude saltpetre. These washings are established on the principle, that cold water dissolves the muriates of soda, and the earthy nitrates and muriates, together with the colouring principle, but scarcely attacks the nitrate of potash. The water of these three washings therefore contains the muriate of soda, the earthy salts, the colouring principle, and a small quantity of nitrate of potash; the amount of which is in proportion to that of the muriate of soda, which determines its solution. The water of the crystallizing vessels contains a portion of the muriates of soda, and of the earthy salts which escaped the operation of washing, and a quantity of nitrate of potash, which is more considerable than that of the former solution. The waters made use of at the end of the operation, to whiten and wash the crystals deposited in the pyramidal vessel, contain nothing but a small quantity of nitrate of potash. These waters are therefore very different in their nature. The water of the washings is really a mother water. It must be collected in vessels, and treated with potash by the known processes. It must be evaporated to 66 degrees (or 1,848 sp.gr.), taking out the muriate of soda as it falls. This solution is to be saturated with 2 or 3 per cent. of potash, then suffered to settle, decanted, and poured into crystallizing vessels, where 20 per cent. of water is to be added to keep the whole of the muriate of soda suspended. The waters which are thus obtained by treatment of the mother water may be mixed with the water of the first crystallization. From these the marine salt may be separated by simple evaporation; and the nitrate of potash, which they hold in solution, may be afterwards obtained by cooling. The small quantity of water made use of to wash and whiten the refined saltpetre, contains nothing but the nitrate of potash; it may therefore be used in the solution of the saltpetre when taken from the tubs. From this description it follows, that a manufactory for the speedy refining of saltpetre ought to be provided with mallets or rammers for pounding the saltpetre; tubs for washing; a boiler for solution; a crystallizing vessel of copper or lead, in which the saltpetre is to be obtained by cooling; baskets for draining the saltpetre; scales and weights for weighing; hydrometers and thermometers, to ascertain densities and temperatures; rakes to agitate the liquor in the crystallizing vessel; skimmers to take out the crystals, and convey them to the baskets; syphons or hand-pumps to empty the boilers. The number and dimensions of these several articles must vary according to the quantity of saltpetre intended to be refined.

SALUTATION

Pages 498-500

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of saluting, greeting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paying respect and reverence to any one. When men (writes the compiler of L'Esprit des Usages salute each other in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner; it signifies little whether they move a particular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, or practise a particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. In these actions there must exist different customs. Every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> imagines it employs the most reasonable ones; but all are equally simple, and none are to be treated as ridiculous. This infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ceremonies may be reduced to two kinds; to reverences or salutations; and to the touch of some part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> and prostrate one's self to express sentiments of respect, appears to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; for terrified persons throw themselves on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> when they adore invisible beings. The affectionate touch of the person they salute, is an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of tenderness. As nations decline from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> simplicity, much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> and grimace are introduced. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a>, the manners of a people, and their situation, influence the modes of salutation; as may be observed from the instances we collect. Modes of salutation have sometimes very different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and it is no uninteresting speculation to examine their shades. Many display a refinement of delicacy, while others are remarkable for their simplicity or for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. In general, however, they are frequently the same in the infancy of nations, and in more polished <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. Respect, humility, fear, and esteem, are expressed much in a similar manner; for these are the natural consequences of the organization of the body. These demonstrations become, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, only empty civilities, which signify nothing. We shall notice what they were originally, without reflecting on what they are. The first nations have no peculiar modes of salutation; they know no reverences, or other compliments, or they despise and disdain them. The Greenlanders laugh when they see an European uncover his head and bend his body before him whom he calls his superior. The islanders, near the Philippines, take the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or foot of him they salute, and with it they gently rub their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The Laplanders apply their nose strongly against that of the person they salute. Dampier says, that at New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> they are satisfied in placing on their heads the leaves of trees, which have ever passed for symbols of friendship and peace. This is at least a picturesque salute. Other salutations are very inconvenient and painful; it requires <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> practice to enable a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be polite in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated in the straits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a>. Houtman tells us, they saluted him in this odd way: "They raised his left foot, which they passed gently over the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> leg, and from hence over his face." The inhabitants of the Philippines bend their body very low, in placing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, and raising at the same time one foot in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, with their knee bent. An Ethiopian takes the robe of another, and ties it about his own waist, so that he leaves his friend half naked. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of undressing on these occasions takes other forms; sometimes men <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> themselves naked before the person whom they salute; it is to show their humility, and that they are unworthy of appearing in his presence. This was practised before Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, when he received the visit of two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> Otaheitans. Their innocent simplicity, no doubt, did not appear immodest in the eyes of the virtuoso. Sometimes they only undress partially. The Japanese only take off a slipper; the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRACAN">Arracan</a>, their sandals in the Salutation street, and their stockings in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the progress of time, it appears <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to uncover one's self. The grandees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> claim the right of appearing covered before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, to show that they are not so much subjected to him as the rest of the nation; and (this writer observes) we may remark, that the English do not uncover their heads so much as the other nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In a word, there is not a nation (observes the humorous Montaigne), even to the people who, when they salute, turn their backs on their friends, but that can be justified in their customs. It must be observed of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, that they are lovers of ludicrous actions, and thus make all their ceremonies farcical. The greater part pull the fingers till they crack. Snelgrave gives an odd representation of the embassy which the king of Dahomy sent to him. The ceremonies of salutation consisted in the most ridiculous contortions. When two negro monarchs visit, they embrace in snapping three times the middle finger. Barbarous nations frequently imprint on their salutations the dispositions of their character. When the inhabitants of Carnena (says Athenzeus) would show a peculiar mark of esteem, they breathed a vein, and presented for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERAGE">beverage</a> of their friend the blood as it issued. The Franks tore <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from their head, and presented it to the person they saluted. The slave cut off his hair, and offered it to his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The Chinese are singularly affected in their personal civilities; they even calculate the number of their reverences. These are their most remarkable postures. The men move their hands in an affectionate manner, while they are joined together on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and bow their head a little. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they respect a person, they raise their hands joined, and then lower them to the earth in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the body. If two persons meet after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> separation, they both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and bend the face to the earth; and this ceremony they repeat two or three times. Surely we may differ here with the sentiment of Montaigne, and confess this ceremony to be ridiculous. It arises from their national affectation. They substitute <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> ceremonies for natural actions. Their expressions <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> as little as their ceremonies. If a Chinese is asked how he finds himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>? he answers, Very well; thanks to your abundant felicity. If they would tell a man that he looks well, they say, Prosperity is painted on your face; or Your air announces your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. If you render them any service, they say, My thanks should be immovable. If you praise them, they answer, How shall I dare to persuade myself of what you say of me? If you dine with them, they tell you at parting, We have not treated you with sufficient distinction. The various titles they invent for each other it would be impossible to translate. It is to be observed, that all these answers are prescribed by the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, or academy of compliments. There are determined the number of bows; the expressions to be employed; the genuflexions, and the inclinations which are to be made to the right or left hand; the salutations of the master before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> where the stranger is to be seated, for he salutes it most profoundly, and wipes the dust away with the skirts of his robe; all these and other things are noticed, even to the silent gestures, by which you are entreated to enter the house. The lower class of people are equally Salutation, nice in these punctilios; and ambassadors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> 40 days in practising them before they are enabled to appear at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. A tribunal of ceremonies has been erected, and every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> very odd decrees are issued, to which the Chinese most religiously submit. The marks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> are frequently arbitrary; to be seated, with us, is a mark of repose and familiarity; to stand up, that of respect. There are countries, however, in which princes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only be addressed by persons who are seated, and it is considered as a favour to be permitted to stand in their presence. This custom prevails in despotic countries. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> cannot suffer without disgust the elevated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of his subjects: he is pleased to bend their bodies with their genius: his presence must lay those who behold him prostrate on the earth: he desires no eagerness, no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; he would only inspire terror. The pope makes no reverence to any mortal except the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, to whom he stoops a very little when he permits him to kiss his lips.

SALUTE

Pages 500-501

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, a testimony of deference <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> homage rendered by the ships of one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to another, or by ships of the same nation to a superior or equal. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is variously performed, according to the circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, or situation, of the parties. It consists in firing a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cannon, or volleys of small arms; in striking the colours or top-sails; or in one or more general shouts of the whole ship's crew, mounted on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> or rigging for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> regulations with regard to salutes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> navy are as follows. "When a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>-officer salutes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the fleet, he is to give him fifteen guns; but when captains salute him, they are to give him seventeen guns. The admiral and commander in chief of the fleet is to return two guns less to flag-officers, and four less to captains. Flag-officers saluting their superior or senior officer, are to give him thirteen guns. Flag-officers are to return an equal number of guns to flag-officers <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> their flags on the same mast, and two guns less to the rest, as also to captains. "When a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> salutes an admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or blue, he is to give him fifteen guns; but to vice and rear admirals, thirteen guns. When a flag-officer is saluted by two or more of his majesty's ships, he is not to return the salute till all have finished, and then to do it with such a reasonable number of guns as he shall judge proper. "In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the meeting of two squadrons, the two chiefs only are to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> salutes. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> single ships meet a squadron consisting of more than one flag, the principal flag only is to be saluted. No salute shall be repeated by the same ships, unless there has been a separation of six months at least. "None of his majesty's ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, commanded only by captains, shall give or receive salutes from one another, in whatsoever <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world they meet. "A flag-officer commanding in chief shall be saluted upon his first hoisting his flag, by all the ships present, with such a number of guns as is allowed by the first, third, or fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. "When any of his majesty's ships shall meet with any ship or ships belonging to any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state, within his majesty's seas (which extend to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>), it is expected, that the said foreign ships do strike their top-sail, and take in their flag, in acknowledgement of his majesty's sovereignty in those seas; and if any shall refuse or offer to resist, it is enjoined to all flag-officers and commanders to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours to compel them thereto, and not suffer any dishonour to be done to his majesty. And if any of his majesty's subjects shall so much forget their duty, as to omit striking their top-sail in passing by his majesty's ships, the name of the ship and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and from whence, and whither bound, together with affidavits of the fact, are to be sent up to the secretary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, in order to their being proceeded against in the admiralty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. And it is to be observed, that in his majesty's seas, his majesty's ships are in nowise to strike to any; and that in other parts, no ship of his majesty's is to strike her flag or top-sail to any foreigner, unless such foreign ship shall have first struck, or at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> strike, her flag or top-sail to his majesty's ship. "The flag-officers and commanders of his majesty's ships are to be careful to maintain his majesty's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon all occasions, giving protection to his subjects, and endeavouring, what in them lies, to secure and encourage them in their lawful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and they are not to injure, in any manner, the subjects of his majesty's friends and allies. "If a foreign admiral meet with any of his majesty's ships, and salutes them, he shall receive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for gun. If he be a vice-admiral, the admiral shall answer with two guns less. If a rear-admiral, the admiral and vice-admiral shall return two less. But if the ship be commanded by a captain only, the flag-officer shall give two guns less, and captains an equal number. "When any of his majesty's ships come to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in a foreign port or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, within cannon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of its forts, the captain may salute the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with such a number of guns as have been customary, upon good assurance of having the like number returned, but not otherwise. But if the ship bears a flag, the flag-officer shall first carefully inform himself how flags of like rank, belonging to other crowned heads, have given or returned salutes, and to insist upon the same terms of respect. "It is allowed to the commanders of his majesty's ships in foreign parts, to salute the persons of any admirals, commanders in chief, or captains of ships of war of foreign nations, and foreign noblemen, or strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as also the factories of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects, coming on board to visit the ship; and the number of guns is left to the commander, as shall be suitable to the occasion and the quality of the persons visiting; but he is nevertheless to remain accountable for any excesses in the abuse of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. If the ship visited be in com- pany with other ships of war, the captain is not to make use of the civilities allowed in the preceding articles but with leave and consent of the commander in chief or the senior captain. "Merchant-ships, whether foreigners or belonging to his majesty's subjects, saluting the admiral of the fleet, shall be answered by six guns less; when they salute any other flag-ships, they shall be answered by four guns less; and if they salute men of war commanded by captains, they shall be answered by two guns less. If several merchant-ships salute in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, no return is to be made till all have finished, and then by such a number of guns as shall be thought proper; but though the merchant-ships should answer, there shall be no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> return. "None of his majesty's ships of war shall salute any of his majesty's forts or castles in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, on any pretence whatsoever."

SALUZZO

Pages 501-501

called by the French Saluces, a town and castle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a marquisate of the same name, with a bishop's see. It is situated on an eminence at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> near the river Po, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 29. N. Lat. 44. 33, and is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. Saluzzo, the marquisate of, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Piedmont in Italy, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Dauphiny, and the province of the Four Valleys, on the east by those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAVIGLIANO">Savigliano</a> and Fossano, on the south by that of Cona and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, and on the west by Barcelonetta. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in 1601.

SALVADORA

Pages 498-498

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the Salutation, tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALVAGE-MONEY

Pages 498-498

a reward allowed by the civil and statute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> for the saving of ships <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goods from the danger of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, pirates, or enemies.—Where any ship is in danger of being stranded, or driven on shore, justices of the peace are to command the constables to assemble as many persons as are necessary to preserve it; and, on its being preserved by their means, the persons assisting therein shall, in 30 days after, be paid a reasonable reward for their salvage; otherwise the ship or goods shall remain in the custody of the officers of the customs as a security for the same.

SALVATION

Pages 498-498

means the safety <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> preservation of any thing which is or has been in danger, and is generally used in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, when it means preservation from eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or reception to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of heaven, which is now offered to all men by the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> upon certain conditions. The Hebrews but rarely make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of concrete terms as they are called, but often of abstracted. Thus, instead of saying that God saves them and protects them, they say that God is their salvation. Thus the word of salvation, the joy of salvation, the rock of salvation, the shield of salvation, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> of salvation, &c. is as much as to say, The word that declares deliverance; the joy that attends the escaping a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger; a rock where anyone takes refuge, and where he may be in safety from his enemy; a buckler, that secures him from the arm of the enemy; a horn or ray of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, of happiness and salvation, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, &c. SALVATOR ROSA. See Rosa.

SALVE REGINA

Pages 498-498

among the Romanists, the name of a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, addressed to the Virgin, and sung after complines, as also upon the point of executing a criminal. Durandus says, it was composed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of singing the salve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the office was begun by order of St Dominic, and first in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, about 1237. Gregory IX. first appointed it to be general. St Bernard added the conclusion, O dulcis! O pia, &c.

SALVIA

Pages 498-498

SAGE, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dignya class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SALVIANUS

Pages 498-498

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> father of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who flourished in the 5th century, and was well skilled in the sciences. It is said he lived in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> with his wife Palladia, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she had been his sister; and that he was so afflicted at the wickedness of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that he was called the Jeremiah of the fifth century. He acquired such reputation for his piety and learning, that he was named the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. He wrote a Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>; another on Avarice; and some epistles, of which Baluze has given an excellent edition; that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Rittershusius, in 2 vols octavo, is also esteemed.

SALZBURG

Pages 497-498

an archbishopric of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, bounded on the east by Styria, and the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tyrol, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bavaria, and on the south by the duchy of Carinthia and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIXEN">Brixen</a>. It is said to be about 100 miles from east to west, and upwards of 60 from north to south. With respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is very mountainous, yielding, however, excellent pasturage, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of that, abounding in cattle, and horses remarkable for their mettle and hardiness. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is particularly noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it produces, and its strong passes and castles. Here are also considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lamariaris, with quarries of marble, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> hot-bath. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Salza, the Inn, the Ens, and Muer; which, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and other streams, are well stored with fish. The peasants here are all allowed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of arms, and trained to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> duty. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> in the country, and most of the lands belong to the clergy. The states consist of the prelates, the cities, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Notwithstanding this country is under the power of a Popish ecclesiastic, and the violent, arbitrary, and oppressive manner in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have always been treated, great numbers of them still remained in it till the year 1732, when no less than 30,000 of them withdrew from it, dispersing themselves in the several Protestant states of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and some of them were even sent from Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to the American colonies. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares, and all sorts of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of coarse cloth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> here. The archbishop had many and great prerogatives: he was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire, and perpetual legate of the holy see in Germany, of which he is also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>. He had the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diet of this circle, and next to the electors in that of the empire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes, in which he and the archduke of Austria presided by turns. But his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> as a sovereign prince were lost when the territory was united to Austria in 1805. He had also the nomination to several bishoprics; and the canonicates that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> vacant in the months in which the popes, by virtue of the concordat, are allowed to nominate, are all in his gift. His suffragans are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Freisingen, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATISBON">Ratisbon</a>, Brixen, Gurk, Chiemsee, Seckan, and Lavant; and of these, the four last are nominated, and even confirmed by him and not by the pope. His revenue was SALTSBURG said to amount to near 200,000l. a year, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it arising from the salt-works. He was able to raise 25,000 men; but kept in constant pay, besides his guards, only one regiment, consisting of 1000 men. At his accession to the see, the archbishop paid 100,000 crowns to Rome for the pall. There is an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> here, instituted in 1711, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St Rupert, who was the first bishop of Salzburg, about the beginning of the 8th century. This territory, which formerly was an independent principality, was united to Austria at the peace with France in 1805. At the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBURG">Presburg</a> in 1809, she was compelled to cede Salzburg to Bavaria; but she regained it in 1815, and it now forms an integrant part of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. Salzburg, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a German archbishopric of the same name, and which takes its own from the river Salza, on which it stands, and over which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is a very handsome <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, well fortified, and the residence of the archbishop. The houses are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and all built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; the roofs are in the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and you may walk upon them. The castle here is very strong, and as strongly garrisoned, and well provided with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and warlike stores. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is magnificent; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> before it, is a fountain, esteemed the largest and grandest in Germany. The stables are very lofty; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the horses usually kept by the archbishop is said to be upwards of 200. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of which one part stands on a steep rock, is well built, but the streets are narrow and badly paved. Besides the above mentioned, there are two other stately palaces belonging to the archbishop, one of which is called the Nuebau, and the other Mirabella. The latter of these has a very beautiful garden; and the number of trees in the orangerie is so great, that Mr Keysler tells us, 20,000 oranges have been gathered from them in one year. The river Salza runs <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the walls of this garden. There are a great many other fine structures in the city, public and private, such as palaces, monasteries, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and churches. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to St Rupert (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of Bavaria, and a Scotchman by birth), all the altars are of marble of different kinds, and one of the organs has above 3200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The whole structure is extremely handsome. It is built of freestone in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s at Rome. The portico is of marble, and the whole is covered with copper. Before the portico there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quadrangular place, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> and galleries, in which is the prince's residence; and in the middle of this place there is a statue of the Virgin in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>; it is a fine piece of art, but of an unnatural size. There are large areas encompassed with handsome buildings on both sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the middle of that which is to the left, there is a most magnificent fountain of marble, and some valuable figures of gigantic size. There is likewise a fountain in that to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, but it is not to be compared with the former one, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> of it makes but a very pitiful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. This town contains many more excellent buildings and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, which remind one that the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> are not far distant. The winter and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> riding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> here are noble structures. The university was founded in 1629, and committed to the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>. Besides it, there are two colleges, in which the young noblemen are educated. Salzburg E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 0. Lat. 47. 45.

SAMA

Pages 501-501

a town and fort in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, stands on an eminence, the fort being watered by the pleasant river of St George, that discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The town contains above 200 houses, which seem to form three distinct villages, one of which is immediately under the cannon of the Dutch fort St Sebastian. Des Marchais deems this town to be one of the largest on the whole coast, Barbot likewise agreeing with him in its situation, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants. The sole employment of the natives is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; a circumstance which easily accounts for their poverty. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is republican, the magistrates having the supreme power, being subject to periodical changes, and under the authority of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Gavi, who seldom however interferes in the affairs of the state. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> resides some leagues distant from the sea, is rich, and much respected by his neighbours.

SAMANEANS

Pages 501-501

in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> philosophers, have been confounded by some with the Bramins. They proceeded from Ariana, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the neighbouring countries, spread themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and taught new doctrines. The Bramins, before their arrival, it is said, were in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, were the only <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of India, and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence was on the banks of the Ganges, and in the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; while the Samaneans were settled towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. Others say, that the Bramins acquired all their knowledge from the Samaneans, before whose arrival it would be difficult to prove that the Bramins were the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> teachers of the Indians. The most celebrated and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the Samanean doctors was Boutta, or Budda, who was born 683 years before Christ. His scholars paid Samaneans him divine honours; and his doctrine, which consisted chiefly in the transmigration of souls, and in the worship of cows, was adopted not only in India, but also in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. It was propagated according to M. de Sainte Croix, in Thibet, in the 8th century, and succeeded there the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Zamolxis. The Samaneans, or Buddhists, were entirely destroyed in India by the jealous rage of the Bramins, whose absurd practices and fables they affected to treat with contempt; but several of their books are still preserved and respected on the coasts of Malabar. We are told, too, that several of the Bramin orders have adopted their manner of living, and openly profess the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their doctrines. L'Ézour Vedam, ou Ancien Comment du Vedam, published by M. de S. Croix, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1779. See Bramins.

SAMAR

Pages 501-501

a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> not far from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a> in the East Indies, is called Samar on the side which looks towards the other isles, and Ibabao on that next the ocean. Its greatest length, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Baliquaton, which, with the point of Manilla, makes the strait of St Bernardino, in 18 deg. 30 min. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, extends to that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUIGNAN">Guignan</a> in 11 deg. towards the south. The other two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, making the greatest breadth of the island, are Cabo de Spirito Santo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cape of the Holy Ghost, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of which are the first discovered by ships from New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and that which lying opposite to Leyte westward, makes another strait, scarce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>'s throw over. The whole compass of the island is about 130 leagues. Between Guignan and Cape Spirito Santo is the port of Borognon, and not far from thence those of Palapa and Catubig, and the little island of Bin, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Catarman. Vessels from countries not yet discovered are very frequently <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away on the before-mentioned coast of Palapa. Within the straits of St Bernardino, and beyond Baliquaton, is the coast of Samar, on which are the villages of Ibatan, Bangahon, Cathalogan, Paranos, and Calviga. Then follows the strait of St Juanillo, without which, standing eastward, appears the point and little island of Guignan, where the compass of the island ends. It is mountainous and craggy, but the few plains which it contains are very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are much the same as those of Leyte; but there is one particular sort, called by the Spaniards chicoy, and by the Chinese, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value on it, seyzu, without kernels.

SAMARA

Pages 501-501

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the te-trandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAMARCAND

Pages 501-502
or Sarmacand, an ancient and famous town of Asia, capital of the kingdom of the same name in the country of the Usbeck Tartars, with a castle and a famous university. The houses are built with stones, and it carries on a trade in excellent fruits. It is pleasantly seated near the river Sogde, a branch of the Amu. E. Long. 69. 0. N. Lat. 39. 50. This town was the capital of the kingdom of Sogdia in the time of Alexander the Great, when it was called Maracanda. It was afterwards the capital of the empire of Tamurlane the Great. In the time of Jenghis Khan, it was forced to yield to the arms of that cruel conqueror; by whom the garrison, amounting to 30,000 men, were butchered; 30,000 of the inhabitants, with their wives, Samaria, and children, were presented to his generals; the rest were permitted to live in the city, on paying a tribute of 300,000 dinars or crowns of gold.

SAMARIA

Pages 502-504

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Samaria, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the ten tribes. It was built by Omri <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, who began to reign in the year of the world 3079, and died 3086 (1 Kings xvi. 24.). He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver or for the sum of 654l. 7s. 6d. It took the name of Samaria from Shemer the owner of the hill; though some think there were already some beginnings of a city, because, before the reign of Omri, there is mention made of Samaria (1 Kings xiii. 32.) in the year of the world 3030. But others take this for a prolepsis, or an anticipation, in the discourse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of God, who speaks of Samaria under the reign of Jeroboam. However this be, it is certain that Samaria was no considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and did not become the capital city of the kingdom of Israel till after the reign of Omri. Before him, the kings of Israel dwelt at Shechem, or Tirzah. Samaria was situated upon an agreeable and fruitful hill, in an advantageous situation, and was 12 miles from Dothaim, 12 from Merom, and four from Atharoth. Josephus says, it was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Besides, though it was built upon an eminence, yet it must have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in abundance: since we find medals struck in this city, whereon is represented the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Astarte treading a river under foot; which proves it to have been well watered. And Josephus observes, that when it was taken by John Hircanus the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Jews, he entirely demolished it, and caused even the brook to flow over its ruins, to obliterate all the footsteps of it. The kings of Samaria omitted nothing to make this city the strongest, the finest, and the richest that was possible. Ahab built there a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> (1 Kings xxii. 39.), that is, in which there were many ornaments of ivory. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a> describes Samaria under Jeroboam II, as a city sunk into all the excesses of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and effeminacy (Amos iii. 15. and iv. 1, 2.). Ben-hadad king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> built public places or streets in Samaria (1 Kings xx. 34.) probably for traffic, where his people dwelt to promote trade. His son Ben-hadad besieged this place under the reign of Ahab (1 Kings xx. 1, 2, 3., &c.) in the year of the world 3103. The following year, Ben-hadad brought an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into the field, probably with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against Samaria; but his army was again cut in pieces. Some years after this, Ben-hadad came a third <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before Samaria, and reduced it to such necessities by famine, that a mother was there forced to eat her own child; but the city was relieved by a sensible effect of the protection of God. Lastly, it was besieged by Salmaneser king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, in the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel (2 Kings xvii. 6, 7, &c.), which was the fourth of Hezekiah king of Judah. It was taken three years after, in the year of the world 3283. The prophet Hosea speaks of the cruelties exercised by Salmaneser against the besieged (Hos. x. 4, 8, 9. xiv. i.); and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a> says, that this city was reduced to a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> (Mic. i. 6.). The Cuthites that were sent by Esar-haddon to inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Samaria, did not think it worth their while to repair the ruins of this city; they dwelt at Shechem, which they made the capital city of their state. They were still upon this footing when Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> came into Phoenicia and Judea. However, the Cuthites had rebuilt some of the houses of Samaria, even from the time of the return from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, since <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> then speaks of the inhabitants of Samaria (Ezra iv. 17. Nehem. iv. 2.); and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, being jealous of the favours that Alexander the Great had conferred on the Jews, revolted from him while this prince was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and burnt Andromachus alive, whom Alexander had left governor of Syria. Alexander marched against them, took Samaria, and put in Macedonians to inhabit it; giving the country round it to the Jews; and to encourage them to cultivate it, he granted them an exemption from tribute. The king of Egypt and Syria, who succeeded Alexander, deprived them of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this country. But Alexander Balas king of Syria restored to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Maccabeus the cities of Lydda, Ephrem, and Ramatha, which he cut off from the country of Samaria (1 Mac. x. 30, 38; and xi. 28, 34.). Lastly, the Jews re-entered into the full possession of this whole country under John Hircanus the Asmonæan, who took Samaria, and ruined it in such a manner, according to Josephus, that he made the river run through its ruins. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this condition to the year of the world 3947; when Aulus Gabinius, the proconsul of Syria, rebuilt it, and gave it the name of Gabiniiana. But it was yet but very inconsiderable, till Herod the Great restored it to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> lustre, and gave it the Greek name of Sebaste, which in Latin is Augusta, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus, who had given him the property of this place. The sacred authors of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> speak but little of Samaria; and when they do mention it, it is rather in respect of the country about it, than of the city itself. (See Luke xvii. 11. John iv. 4, 5.)—It was there our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> had the conversation with the woman of Samaria, that is, with a Samaritan woman of the city of Sychar. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of St Stephen, (Acts viii. 1, 2, 3.), when the disciples were dispersed through the cities of Judea and Samaria, St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the deacon withdrew into the city of Samaria, where he made several converts. When the apostles heard that this city had received the word of God, they sent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and John thither, to communicate the Holy Ghost to such as had been baptized. It was there they found Simon Magus, who offered <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the apostles, being in hopes to buy this power of communicating the Holy Ghost. Samaria is never called Sebaste in the books of the New Testament, though strangers hardly knew it but by this name. St Jerome says, that it was thought Obadiah was buried at Samaria. They also showed there the tombs of Elisha and of St John the Baptist. There are Samaritans. We have already spoken of the Samaritans under the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTH">Cuth</a>. The Samaritans are the people of the city of Samaria, and the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of which Samaria was the capital city. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it should seem that we might give the name of Samaritans to the Israelites of the ten tribes, who lived in the city and territory of Samaria. However, the sacred authors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> give the name of Samaritans only to those strange people whom the kings of Assyria sent from beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> to inhabit the kingdom of Samaria, when they took away captive the Israelites that were there before. Thus we may fix the epoch of the Samaritans at the taking of Samaria by Salmaneser, in the year of the world 3283. This prince carried away captive the Israelites that he found in the country, and assigned them dwellings beyond the Euphrates, and in Assyria, (2 Kings xvii. 24.) He sent other inhabitants in their stead, of which the most considerable were the Cuthites, a people descended from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSH">Cush</a>, and who are probably of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> knew by the name of Scythians. After Salmaneser, his successor Esar-haddon was informed, that the people which had been sent to Samaria were infested by lions that devoured them, (2 Kings xvii. 25.) ; this he imputed to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the people in the manner of worshipping the god of the country. Therefore Esar-haddon sent a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the God of Israel that he might teach them the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Hebrews. But they thought they might blend this religion with that which they professed before; so they continued to worship their idols as before, in conjunction with the God of Israel, not perceiving how absurd and incompatible these two religions were. It is not known how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> they continued in this state; but at the return from the captivity of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, it appears they had entirely quitted the worship of their idols; and when they asked permission of the Israelites that they might labour with them at the rebuilding of the temple of Jerusalem, they affirmed, that from the time that Esar-haddon had brought them into this country they had always worshipped the Lord, (Ezra iv. 1, 2, 3.) And indeed, after the return from the captivity, the Scripture does not anywhere reproach them with idolatrous worship, though it does not dissemble either their jealously against the Jews, nor the ill offices they had done them at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, by their slanders and calumnies, or the stratagems they contrived to hinder the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem.—(Nehem. ii. 10, 19. iv. 2. &c. vi. 1, 2, &c.). It does not appear that there was any temple in Samaria, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all these people who came thither from beyond the Euphrates, before the coming of Alexander the Great into Judea. Before that time, every one was left to his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, and worshipped the Lord where he thought fit. But they presently comprehended, from the books of Moses which they had in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and from the example of the Jews their neighbours, that God was to be worshipped in that place only which he had chosen. So that since they could not go to the temple of Jerusalem which the Jews would not allow of, they bethought themselves of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a temple of their own upon Mount Gerizim, near the city Samaritans of Shechem, which was then their capital. Therefore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANBALLAT">Sanballat</a> the governor of the Samaritans, applied himself to Alexander, and told him he had a son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, called Manasses, son to Jaddus the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priest of the Jews, who had retired to Samaria with a great number of other persons of his own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; that he desired to build a temple in this province, where he might <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the high-priesthood; that this undertaking would be to the advantage of the king’s affairs, because in building a temple in the province of Samaria, the nation of the Jews would be divided, who are a turbulent and seditious people, and by such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> would be made weaker, and less in a condition to undertake new enterprises. Alexander readily consented to what Sanballat desired, and the Samaritans presently began their building of the temple of Gerizim, which from that time they have always frequented, and still frequent to this day, as the place where the Lord intended to receive the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of his people. It is of this mountain and of this temple, that the Samaritan woman of Sychar spoke to our Saviour, (John iv. 20). See Gerizim. The Samaritans did not long continue under the obedience of Alexander. They revolted from him the very next year, and Alexander drove them out of Samaria, put Macedonians in their room, and gave the province of Samaria to the Jews. This preference that Alexander gave to the Israelites contributed not a little to increase that hatred and animosity that had already obtained between these two people. When any Israelite had deserved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for the violation of some important point of the law, he presently took refuge in Samaria or Shechem, and embraced the way of worship according to the temple of Gerizim. When the Jews were in a prosperous condition, and affairs were favourable to them, the Samaritans did not fail to call themselves Hebrews, and pretended to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>. But no sooner were the Jews fallen into discredit or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, but the Samaritans immediately disowned them, would have nothing in common with them, acknowledged themselves to be Phoenicians originally, or that they were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> his son. This used to be their practice in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes. The Samaritans, having received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, or the five books of Moses, from the priest that was sent by Esar-haddon, have preserved it to this day, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and character it was then, that is, in the old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> or Phoenician character, which we now call the Samaritan, to distinguish it from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Hebrew character, which at present we find in the books of the Jews. These last, after their captivity, changed their old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and took up those of the Chaldee, which they had been used to at Babylon: and which they continue still to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It is wrong, says P. Curtius, to give this the name of the Hebrew character, for that can be said properly only of the Samaritan text. Th critics have taken notice of some variations between the Pentateuch of the Jews and that of the Samaritans; but these varieties of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> chiefly regard the word Gerizim, which the Samaritans seem to have purposely introduced to favour their pretensions, that Mount Gerizim was the place in which the Lord was to be adored. The religion of this people were at first the Pagan. Every one worshipped the deity they had been used to in their own country (2 Kings xvii. 25, 30, 31.) The Babylonians worshipped Succoth-benoth; the Cuthites, Nergal; the Hamathites, Ashima; the Avites, Nibhaz and Tartak; the Sepharvites, Adrammelech and Anammelech. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we would enumerate all the names of false gods to whom the Samaritans have paid a sacrilegious worship, we should have enough to do. This <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is sufficiently perplexed, by reason of the different names by which they were adored by different nations, insomuch that it would be almost impossible to clear up this affair. See Succoth-benoth, &c. Afterwards, to this profane worship the Samaritans added that of the Lord, the God of Israel, (2 Kings xvii. 29, 30, 31, 32.) They gave a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their little regard to this worship of the true God, when under Antiochus Epiphanes they consecrated their temple at Gerizim to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Argivus. In the time of Alexander the Great, they celebrated the sabbatical year, and consequently the year of jubilee also. We do not know whether they did it exactly at the same time with the Jews, or whether they observed any other epoch; and it is to little purpose that some critics have attempted to ascertain the first beginning of it. Under the kings of Syria they followed the epoch of the Greeks, or that of the Seleucidae, as other people did that were under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Seleucidae. After that Herod had re-established Samaria, and had given it the name of Sebastae, the inhabitants of this city, in their medals, and all public acts, took the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of this new establishment.
