But the inhabitants of Samaria, of which the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> were Pagans or Jews, were no rule to the other Samaritans, who probably reckoned their years according to the reigns of the emperors they were subject to, till the time they fell under the jurisdiction of the Mahometans, under which they live at this day; and they reckon their year by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, or, as they speak, according to the reign of Ishmael, or the Ishmaelites. Such of our readers as desire to be further acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the ancient Samaritans, we refer to the works of Josephus, where they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find that subject largely treated of. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, it is objected to them, that they receive only the Pentateuch, and reject all the other books of Scripture, chiefly the prophets, who have more expressly declared the coming of the Messiah.—They have also been accused of believing God to be corporeal, of denying the Holy Ghost, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ reproaches them (John iv. 22,) with worshipping they know not what; and in the place already referred to he seems to exclude them from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, when he says, that "Salvation is of the Jews." True it is, that these words might only signify, that the Messiah was to proceed from the Jews; but the crime of schism alone, and a separation from the true <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was sufficient to exclude them from salvation. The Samaritan woman is a sufficient testimony that the Samaritans expected a Messiah, who they hoped would clear up all their doubts (John iv. 25.) Several of the inhabitants of Shechem believed at the preaching of Jesus Christ, and several of Samaria believed at that of St Philip; but it is said, they soon fell back to their former errors, being perverted by Simon Magus. The Samaritans at present are very few in number. Joseph Scaliger, being curious to know their usages, wrote to the Samaritans of Egypt, and to the high-priest of the whole <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who resided at Neapolis in Syria. They returned two answers to Scaliger, dated in the year of the Hegira 998. These were preserved in the French king's library, and were translated into Latin by Father Morin, and printed in England in the collection of that father's letters, in 1682, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Antiquitates Ecclesiae Orientalis. By these letters it appears, that they believe in God, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, the holy law, the mountain Gerizim, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God, the day of vengeance and of peace; that they value themselves upon observing the law of Moses in many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> more rigidly than the Jews themselves.—They keep the sabbath with the utmost strictness required by the law, without stirring from the place they are in, but only to the synagogue. They go not out of the city, and abstain from their wives on that day. They never delay circumcision beyond the eighth day. They still sacrifice to this day in the temple on Mount Gerizim, and give to the priest what is enjoined by the law. They do not marry their own nieces, as the Jews do, nor do they allow themselves a plurality of wives. Their hatred for the Jews may be seen through all the history of Josephus, and in several places of the New Testament. The Jewish historian informs us, that under the government of Coponius, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a> night, when they opened the gates of the temple, some Samaritans had scattered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of dead men there, to insult the Jews, and to interrupt the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of the festival. The evangelists show us, that the Jews and Samaritans held no correspondence together. (John iv. 9.) "The Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." And the Samaritan woman of Sychar was much surprised that Jesus talked with her, and asked drink of her, being a Samaritan. When our Saviour sent his apostles to preach in Juden, he forbade them to enter into the Samaritan cities, (Matt. x. 5;) because he looked upon them as schismatics, and as strangers to the covenant of Israel. One day when he sent his disciples to provide him a lodging in one of the cities of the Samaritans, they would not entertain him, because they perceived he was going to Jerusalem. (Luke ix. 53.) "Because his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> was as though he would go to Jerusalem." And when the Jews were provoked at the reproaches of Jesus Christ, they told him he was a Samaritan (John viii. 48.) thinking they could say nothing more severe against him. Josephus relates, that some Samaritans having killed several Jews as they were going to the feast at Jerusalem, this occasioned a kind of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between them. The Samaritans continued their fealty to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, when the Jews revolted from them; yet they did not escape from being involved in some of the calamities of their neighbours. There are still at this day some Samaritans at Shechem, otherwise called Naplouse. They have priests there, who say they are of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>. They have a high-priest, who resides at Shechemi, or at Gerizim, who offers sacrifices there, and who declares the feast of the passover,

SAMBUCUS

Pages 504-505

Elder, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 43d order, Dumosae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. All the sorts of elder are of the deciduous tribe, very hardy, and grow freely anywhere; are generally free shooters, but particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> elder and varieties, which make remarkably strong, jointed shoots, of several feet in length, in one season; and they flower mostly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, except the racemose elder, which generally begins flowering in April; and the branches being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, spreading, and very abundant, are exceedingly conspicuous; but they emit a disagreeable odour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are succeeded in most of the sorts by large bunches of ripe berries in autumn, which, although very unpalatable to eat, are in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation for making that well known cordial liquor called elder wine, particularly the common <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-berried elder. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, the elder is both useful and ornamental, especially in extensive grounds.

SAMIAN EARTH

Pages 505-505

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, the name of two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> used in medicine, viz. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> kind, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> collyrium samium, being astringent, and therefore good in diarrhoeas, dysenteries, and hemorrhages; they also used it externally in inflammations of all kinds. 2. The brownish white kind, called aster samius by Dioscorides; this also stands recommended as an astringent.

SAMIELS

Pages 505-505

the Arabian name of a hot <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. It blows over the desert in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, and sometimes it continues with all its violence to the very gates of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, but never affects any body within the walls. Some years it does not blow at all, and in others it appears six, eight, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten times, but seldom continues more than a few minutes at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It often passes with the apparent quickness of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. The Arabians and Persians, who are acquainted with the appearance of the sky at or near the time this wind arises, have warning of its approach by a thick haze, which appears like a cloud of dust arising out of the horizon; and they immediately upon this appearance throw themselves with their faces to the ground, and continue in that position till the wind is passed, which frequently happens almost instantaneously; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, on the contrary, they are not careful or brisk enough to take this precaution, which is sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and they get the full force of the wind, it is instant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The above method is the only one which they take to avoid the effects of this fatal blast; and when it is over, they get up and look round them for their companions; and if they see any one lying motionless, they take hold of an arm or leg, and pull or jerk it with some force; and if the limb thus agitated separates from the body, it is a certain sign that the wind has had its full effect; but if, on the contrary, the arm or leg does not come away, it is a sure sign there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> remaining, although to every outward appearance the person is dead; and in that case they immediately cover him or them with clothes, and administer some warm diluting liquor to cause a perspiration, which is certainly, but slowly, brought about. The Arabs themselves can say little or nothing about the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this wind, only that it always leaves behind it a very strong sulphureous smell, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> at these times is quite clear, except about the horizon, in the north-west quarter, before observed, which gives warning of its approach. We have not been able to learn whether the dead bodies are scorched, or dissolved into a kind of gelatinous substance; but from the stories current about them, there has been frequent reason to believe the latter; and in that case such fatal effects may be attributed rather to a noxious vapour than to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. The story of its going to the gates of Bagdad and no farther, may be reasonably enough accounted for, if the effects are attributed to a poisonous vapour, and not an excessive heat. The above mentioned wind, Samiel, is so well known in the neighbourhood of Bagdad and Bassora, that the very children speak of it with dread.

SAMOGITIA

Pages 505-505

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, on the east by Lithuania, on the west by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the south by Regal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, being about 175 miles in length and 125 in breadth. It is full of forests and very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which feed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, and produce a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. There are also very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> horses, in high esteem. The inhabitants are clownish, but honest; and they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not allow a young woman to go out in the night without a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and two bells at her girdle. Rosenna and Worma are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places.

SAMOJEDA

Pages 505-505

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Russian empire, between Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a> and Archangel, lying along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The inhabitants are extremely rude and barbarous. They travel on the snow on sledges, drawn by an animal like a rein-deer, but with the horns of a stag. Their stature is short; their shoulders and faces are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with flat broad noses, hanging lips, and staring eyes; their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> is dark, their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and they have very little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they have any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at all, it is idolatry, though there have been some attempts of late to convert them. Their huts are made of birch bark sewed together, and laid upon stakes set in the ground; at the top is a hole to let out the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; the fire is made in the middle, round which they repose in the night.—Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment is hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>.

SAMOLUS

Pages 505-505
Water Pimpernel, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria class, and in the natural method ranking under the 21st order, Preciae. See Botany Index.

SAMOS

Pages 505-506

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the promontory Mycale, on the continent of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and opposite to Ephesus; the distance only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stadia (Strabo); a free island, in compass 87 miles (Pliny); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 (Isidorus); with a cognominal town (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Horace); famous for the worship and temple of Juno, with a noted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Strabo, Tacitus); and hence their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> exhibited a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a> (Athenæus): The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who, to avoid the oppression of tyrants, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of freedom. Samos, though not so happy in producing wine, which Strabo wonders at, all the adjoining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> yielding a generous sort, yet abounds in all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Vasa Samia, among earthenware, were held in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute. Samii, the people The island is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. It is about 32 miles in length, and 22 in breadth, and extremely fertile. The inhabitants live at their ease, their <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> by the Turks being moderate. The women are very nasty and ugly, and they never shift above once a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. They are clothed in the Turkish manner, except a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> coif, and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their backs, with plates of silver or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>-tin fastened to the ends.—They have abundance of melons, lentils, kidney-beans, and excellent muskadine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>. They have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> figs four times as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort, but not so well tasted. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is very fine, and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax admirable; besides which, their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> are excellent: They have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of a rusty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: they have also <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are of white marble. The inhabitants are about 12,000; who are almost all Greeks; and the monks and priests occupy most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island. They have a bishop who resides at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORA">Cora</a>. See POLYCRATES.

SAMPAN

Pages 506-506

is a Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> without a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, looking almost like a trough; they are made of different dimensions, but are mostly covered. These boats are as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as sloops, but broader, almost like a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> trough; and have at the end one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more decks of bamboo sticks: the cover or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is made of bamboo sticks, arched over in the shape of a grater; and may be raised or lowered at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: the sides are made of boards, with little holes, with shutters instead of windows: the boards are fastened on both sides to posts, which have notches like steps on the inside, that the roof may be let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and rest on them: on both ends of the deck are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> two little doors, at least there is one at the hindmost end. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> smooth carpet, spread up as far as the boards, makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which in the middle consists of loose boards; but this carpet is only made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on. As these boats greatly differ from ours in shape, they are likewise rowed in a different manner: for two rowers, posting themselves at the back end of the sampan, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it forwards very readily by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of two oars; and can almost turn the vessel <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they please: the oars, which are covered with a little hollow quadrangular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, are laid on iron swivels, which are fastened in the sides of the sampan: at the iron the oars are pierced, which makes them look a little bent: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, a rower sits before with a short oar; but this he is forced to lay aside when he comes near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> throng of sampans; and this inconvenience has confirmed the Chinese in their old way of rowing. Instead of pitch, they make use of a cement like our putty, which we call chianam, but the Chinese call it kiang. Some authors say that this cement is made of lime and a resin exuding from the tree tong yea, and bamboo ockam. Besides a couple of chairs, they have the following furniture: two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> tables or boards on which some Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are drawn; a lanthorn for the night <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and a pot to boil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> in. They have also a little cover for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> god, decorated with gilt <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and other ornaments: before him stands a pot filled with ashes, into which the tapers are put before the idol. The candles are nothing else than bamboo chips, to the upper end of which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a>-wood is stuck on with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>. These tapers are everywhere lighted before the idols in the pagodas, and before the doors in the streets; and, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities, occasion a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> very pernicious to the eyes. Before this idol stands some samsos, or Chinese brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. We ought to try whether the Chinese would not like to use juniper-wood instead of sandalwood; which latter comes from Suratte, and has almost the same smell with juniper.

SAMSON

Pages 506-506

one of the judges of Israel, memorable for his supernatural strength, his victories over the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and his tragic end, as related in the book of Judges.

SAMSON'S POST

Pages 506-506

a sort of pillar erected in a ship's hold, between the lower deck and the kelson, under the edge of a hatchway, and furnished with several notches that serve as steps to mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> descend, as occasion requires. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> being firmly driven into its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, not only serves to support the beam and fortify the vessel in that place, but also to prevent the cargo or materials contained in the hold, from shifting to the opposite side, by the rolling of the ship in a turbulent and heavy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Books of SAMUEL, two canonical books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, as being usually ascribed to the prophet Samuel. The books of Samuel and the books of Kings are a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah; for which reason the books of Samuel are likewise styled the first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> books of Kings. Since the first 24 chapters contain all that relates to the History of Samuel, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the first book and all the second include the relation of events that happened after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that prophet, it has been supposed that Samuel was author only of the first 24 chapters, and that the prophets Gad and Nathan finished the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first book of Samuel comprehends the transactions under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELI">Eli</a> and Samuel, and under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; and also the acts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> while he lived under Saul; and is supposed to contain the space of 101 years. The second book contains the history of about 40 years, and is wholly spent in relating the transactions of David's reign.

SAMYDA

Pages 506-506

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decidandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>

SAN FERNANDO

Pages 516-516

near the entrance of the Golfo Dolce, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a>, in 15 degrees 18 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, has lately been fortified by the Spaniards, for the purpose of checking the Musquito-nien, logwood-cutters, and bay-men. It is a very good harbour, with safe anchorage from the north and east winds, in eight fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

SANAA

Pages 506-507
or SANAA, a large, populous, and handsome town of Asia, capital of Arabia Felix, is situated in Proper Yemen, at the foot of Mount Nikkum, on which are still to be seen the ruins of a castle, which the Arabs suppose to have been built by Shem. Near this mountain stands the castle; a rivulet runs upon the other side; and near it is the Bustan el Metwokkel, a spacious garden, which was laid out by Imam Metwokkel; and has been embellished with a fine garden by the reigning imam. The walls of the city, which are built of bricks, exclude this garden, which is inclosed within a wall of its own. The city, properly so called, is not very extensive: one may walk round it all in an hour. The city-gates are seven. Here are a number of mosques, some of which have been built by Turkish pachas. Sana has the appearance of being more populous than it actually is; for the gardens occupy a part of the space within the walls. In Sana are only 12 public baths; but many noble palaces, three of the most splendid of which have been built by the reigning imam. The palace of the late imam El Manzor, with some others, belong to the royal family, who are very numerous. The Arabian palaces are built in a style of architecture different from ours. The materials are, however, burnt bricks, and sometimes even hewn stones; but the houses of the common people are of bricks which have been dried in the sun. There are no glass windows, except in one palace, near the citadel. The rest of the houses have, instead of windows, merely shutters, which are opened in fair weather, and shut when it is foul. In the last case, the house is lighted by a round wicket, fitted with a piece of Muscovy glass; some of the Arabs use small panes of stained glass from Venice. At Sana, and in the other cities of the East, are great simseras or caravanseras for merchants and travellers. Each different commodity is sold in a separate market. In the market for bread, none but women are to be seen; and their little shops are portable. The several classes of mechanics work, in the same manner, in particular quarters in the open street. Writers go about with their desks, and make out briefs, copy-books, and instruct scholars in the art of writing, all at the same time. There is one market where old clothes are taken in exchange for new. Wood for the carpenter's purpose is extremely dear through Yemen; and wood for the fire at Sana is no less so. All the hills near the city are bleak and bare, and wood is therefore to be brought hither from the distance of three days' journey; and a camel's burthen commonly costs two crowns. This scarcity of wood is partially supplied by the use of a little pit-coal. Peats are burnt here; but they are so bad, that straw must be intermixed to make them burn. Fruits are, however, very plenteous at Sana. Here are more than 20 different species of grapes, which, as they do not all ripen at the same time, continue to afford a delicious refreshment for several months. The Arabs likewise preserve grapes, by hanging them up in their cellars, and eat them almost through the whole year. The Jews make a little wine, and might make more if the Arabs were not such enemies to strong liquors. A Jew convicted of conveying wine into an Arab's house is severely punished; nay, the Jews must even use great caution in buying and selling it among themselves. Great quantities of grapes are dried here; and the exportation of raisins from Sana is considerable. One sort of these grapes is without stones, and contains only a soft grain, the presence of which is not perceptible in eating the raisin. In the castle, which stands on a hill, are two palaces. "I saw (says Niebuhr) about it some ruins of old buildings, but, notwithstanding the antiquity of the place, no remarkable inscriptions. There is the mint, and a range of prisons for persons of different ranks. The reigning imam resides in the city; but several princes of the blood-royal live in the castle. The battery is the most elevated place about these buildings; and there I met with what I had no expectation of, a German mortar, with this inscription, Jorg Selos Goswick, 1513. I saw also upon the same battery seven iron cannons, partly buried in the sand, and partly set upon broken carriages. These seven small cannons, with six others near the gates, which are fired to announce the return of the different festivals, are all the artillery of the capital of Yemen."

SANADON

Pages 507-507

NOLL ETIENNE, a Jesuit, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1676, and was a distinguished professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a>. He there became acquainted with Huet, bishop of Avranches, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was similar to his own. Sanadon afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and was entrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Conti, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Du Morceau. In 1728 he was made librarian to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV, an office which he retained to his death. He died on the 21st September 1733, in the 58th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His works are, 1. Latin Poems, in 12mo, 1715, and reprinted by Barbou, in 8vo, 1754. His style possesses the graces of the Augustan age. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is pure and nervous; his verses are harmonious, and his thoughts are delicate and well chosen; but sometimes his imagination flags. His Latin poems consist of Odes, Elegies, Epigrams, and others, on various subjects. 2. A translation of Horace, with Remarks, in 2 vols. 4to, printed at Paris in 1727; but the best edition of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1735, in 8 vols. 12mo, in which are also inserted the versions and notes of M. Dacier. Sanadon translated with elegance and taste; but he has not preserved the sublimity of the original in the odes, nor the energy and precision in the epistles and satires. In general, his version is rather a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> than a faithful translation. Learned men have justly censured him for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> which he has taken in making considerable changes in the order and structure of the odes. He has also given offence by his uncout orthography. 3. A Collection of Discourses delivered at different times, which afford strong proofs of his knowledge of oratory and poetry. 4. A book entitled Prieres et Instructions Chretiennes.

SANBALLAT

Pages 507-508

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor of the Cuthites or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, was always a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy to the Jews. He was a native of Horon, or Horonaim, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> beyond Jordan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Moabites. He lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Nehemiah, who was his great opponent, and from whose book we learn his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There is one circumstance related of him which has occasioned some dispute among the learned; and the state of the question is as follows: When Alexander the Great came into Phœnicia, and sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before the city of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, Sanballat quitted the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and went at the head of 8000 men to offer his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to Alexander. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> readily entertained him, and being much solicited by him, gave him leave to erect a temple upon Mount Gerizim, where he constituted his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. But this story carries a flagrant anachronism: for 120 years before this, that is, in the year of the world 3550, Sanballat was governor of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>; wherefore the learned Dr Prideaux (in his Connexion of the Histories of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>) supposes two Sanballats, and endeavours to reconcile it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, by showing it to be a mistake of Josephus. This author makes Sanballat to flourish in the time of Darius Codomannus, and to build his temple upon Mount Mount Gerizim by license from Alexander the Great; whereas it was performed by leave from Darius Nothus, in the 15th year of his reign. This takes away the difficulty arising from the great <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Sanballat, and brings him to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Nehemiah, as the Scripture history requires.

SANCHEZ

Pages 508-508

François, called in Latin Sanctius, was of Las Brocas in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and has been dignified by his own countrymen with the pompous titles of le Pére de la Langue Latine, et le Docteur de tous les Gens de lettres. He wrote, 1. An excellent treatise intitled <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> de Causis Linguae Latinae, which was published at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1714, in 8vo. The authors of the Port-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Méthode de la Langue Latine have been much indebted to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. 2. The Art of Speaking, and the Method of translating Authors. 3. Several other learned pieces on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>. He died in the year 1600, in his 77th year. We must be careful to distinguish him from another François Sanchez, who died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> in 1632. This last was a Portuguese physician who settled at Toulouse, and, though a Christian, was born of Jewish parents. He is said to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. His works have been collected under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> Medica. His juncti sunt tractatus quidam philosophici non insubtiles. They were printed at Toulouse in 1636.

SANCHONIATHO

Pages 508-510

a Phenician <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian, who is said to have flourished before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Semiramis. Of this most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writer, the only remains extant are sundry fragments of cosmogony, and of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the gods and first mortals, preserved by Eusebius and Theodore; both of whom speak of Sanchoniatho as an accurate and faithful historian; and the former adds, that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which was translated by Philo-Byblius from the Phenician into the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, contains many things relating to the history of the Jews which deserve <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, both because they agree with the Jewish writers, and because the author received these particulars from the annals of Hjerombalus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the god Jao. Several <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers, however, of great learning, have called in question the very existence of Sanchoniatho, and have contended, with much plausibility, that the fragments which Eusebius adopted as genuine upon the authority of Porphyry, were forged by that author <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the pretended translator Philo, from enmity to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and that the Pagans might have something to show of equal antiquity with the books of Moses. These opposite opinions have produced a controversy that has filled volumes, and of which our limits would hardly admit of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>. We shall therefore in few words state what to us appears to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and refer such of our readers as are desirous of fuller information to the works of the authors (A) mentioned at the bottom of the page. The controversy respecting Sanchoniatho resolves itself into two questions. 1. Was there in reality such a writer? 2. Was he of the very remote antiquity which his translator claims for him? That there was really such a writer, and that the fragments preserved by Eusebius are indeed parts of his history, interpolated perhaps by the translator (B), we are compelled to believe by the following reasons. Eusebius, who admitted them into his work as authentic, was one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and a diligent searcher into antiquity. His conduct at the Nicaene <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> shows, that on every subject he thought for himself, neither biased by authority to the one side, nor carried over by the rage of innovation to the other. He had better means than any modern writer can have of satisfying himself with respect to the authenticity of a very extraordinary work, which had then but lately been translated into the Greek language, and made generally known; and there is nothing in the work itself, or at least in those parts of it which he has preserved, that could induce a wise and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to obtrude it upon the public as genuine, had he himself suspected it to be spurious. Too many of the Christian fathers were indeed very credulous, and ready to admit the authenticity of writings without duly weighing the merits of their claim; but then such writings were always believed to be favourable to the Christian cause, and inimical to the cause of Paganism. That no man of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> could suppose the cosmogony of Sanchoniatho favourable to the cause of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, a farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> cannot be requisite than what is furnished by the following extract. "He supposeth, or affirms, that the principles of the universe were a dark and windy <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> made of dark air, and a turbulent evening <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>; and that these things were boundless, and for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time had no bound or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. But when this wind fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with his own principles, and a mixture was made, that mixture was called desire or cupid (πάθος)." "This mixture completed, was the beginning of the (πρώτων) making of all things. But that wind did not know its own production; and of this, with that wind was begotten Mot, which some call Mua, others the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of a watery mixture. And of this came all the seed of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of the universe. "But there were certain animals, which had no sense, out of which were begotten intelligent animals, and were called Zophesemin, that is, the spies or overseers of Heaven; and were formed alike in the shape of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. Thus shone out Mot, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, the less and the greater stars. "And the air shining thoroughly with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, by its fiery --- (A) Bochart, Scaliger, Vossius, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, Dodwell, Stillingfleet, Mosheim's Cudworth, and Warburton. (B) Of these there are indeed several proofs. Philo makes Sanchoniatho speak of Byblus as the most ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Phenicia, which, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, it was not. We read in the book of Judges of Berith or Berytus, the city where Sanchoniatho himself lived; but not of Byblus, which was the native city of Philo, and to which he is therefore partial. He makes him likewise talk of the Greeks at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> long before any of the Grecian states were known or probably peopled. ficacy influence on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, winds were begotten, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> and great defluxions of the heavenly waters. And, when all these things first were parted, and were separated from their proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the sun, then all met again in the air, and dashed against one another, and were broken to pieces; whence thunders and lightnings were made: and at the stroke of these thunders the fore-mentioned intelligent animals were awakened, and frighted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> stirred in the earth and in the sea: This is the generation of animals. "After these things our author (Sanchoniatho) goes on saying: 'These things are written in the Cosmogony of Taautus, and in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>; and out of the conjectures and surer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> signs which his mind <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and found out, and wherewith he hath enlightened us.'" "Afterwards declaring the names of the winds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south and the rest, he makes this epilogue. 'But these first men consecrated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the earth, and judged them gods, and worshipped them; upon whom they themselves lived, and all their posterity and all before them: to these they made their meat and drink offerings.' Then he concludes: 'these were the devices of worship agreeing with the weakness and want of boldness in their minds.'" Let us suppose Eusebius to have been as weak and credulous as the darkest monk in the darkest age of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, a supposition which no man <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make who knows anything of the writings of that eminent historian; what could he see in this senseless jargon, which even a dreaming monk would think of employing in support of Christianity? Eusebius calls it, and calls it truly, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> atheism; but could he imagine that an ancient system of atheism would contribute so much to make the Pagans of his age admit as divine revelations the books of the Old and New Testaments, that he should be induced to adopt, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, an impudent forgery, not 200 years old, as genuine remains of the most remote antiquity? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this Phenician cosmogony be a fabrication of Porphyry, or of the pretended translator, it must surely have been fabricated for some purpose; but it is impossible for us to conceive what purpose either of these writers could have intended to serve by forging a system so extravagantly absurd. Porphyry, though an enemy to the Christians, was not an atheist, and would never have thought of making an atheist of him whom he meant to obtrude upon the world as the rival of Moses. His own principles were those of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> Platonists; and had he been the forger of the works which bear the name of Sanchoniatho, instead of the incomprehensible jargon about dark wind, evening chaos, Mot, the overseers of heaven in the shape of an egg, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> proceeding from the sound of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, we should doubtless have been amused with refined speculations concerning the operations of the Demiurgus and the other persons in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> Triad. See PLATONISM and PORPHYRY. Father Simon of the oratory imagines* that the purpose for which the history of Sanchoniatho was forged, was to support Paganism, by taking from it its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> and allegories, which were perpetually objected to it by the Christian writers; but this learned man totally mistakes the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The primitive Christians were too much attached to allegories themselves to rest their objections to Paganism on such a foundation: what they objected to that system was, the immoral stories told of the priests. To this the Pagan priests and philosophers replied, that these stories were only mythologic allegories, which veiled all the great truths of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, Ethics, and Physics. The Christians said, this could not be; for that the stories of the gods had a substantial foundation in fact, these gods being only dead men deified, who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, had like passions and infirmities with other mortals. This then was the objection which the forger of the works of Sanchoniatho had to remove, if he really forged them in support of Paganism; but, instead of doing so, he gives the genealogy and history of all the greater gods, and shows, that they were men deified after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for the exploits, some of them grossly immoral, which they had performed in this world. We have elsewhere (POLYTHEISM, No. 17.) given his account of the deification of Chrysor, and Ouranos, and Ge, and Hypsistos, and Muth; but our readers may not perhaps be ill pleased to accompany him through the history of Ouranos and Cronus, two of his greatest gods; whence it will appear how little his writings are calculated to support the tottering cause of Paganism against the objections which were then urged to it by the Christian apologists. "Ouranos (says he), taking the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of his father, married Ge his sister, and by her had four sons: Ilos, who is called Cronus; Betylus; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>, who is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, or the god of corn; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. But by other wives Ouranos had much issue, wherefore Ge being grieved at it and jealous, reproached Ouranos, so as they parted from each other. But Ouranos, though he parted from her, yet by force invading her, and lying with her when he listed, went away again; and he also attempted to kill the children he had by her. Ge also often defended or avenged herself, gathering auxiliary powers unto her. But when Cronus came to man's age, using Hermes Trismegistus as his counsellor and assistant (for he was his secretary), he opposed his father Ouranos, avenging his mother. But Cronus had children, Persephone and Athena; the former died a virgin, but by the counsel of the latter Athena, and of Hermes, Cronus made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> a scymitar and a spear. Then Hermes, speaking to the assistants of Cronus with enchanting words, wrought in them a keen desire to fight against Ouranos in the behalf of Ge; and thus Cronus warring against Ouranos, drove him out of his kingdom, and succeeded in the imperial power or office. In the fight was taken a well-beloved concubine of Ouranos big with child. Cronus gave her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to Dagon, and she brought forth at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> what she had in her womb by Ouranos, and called him Demaroon. After these things Cronus builds a wall round about his house, and founds Byblos the first city in Phoenicia. Afterwards Cronus, suspecting his own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Atlas, with the advice of Hermes, throwing him into a deep hole of the earth, there buried him, and having a son called Sadid, he despatched him with his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, having a suspicion of him, and deprived his own son of life with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He also cut off the head of his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, so that all the gods were amazed at the mind of Cronus. But in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, Ouranos being in flight, or banishment, sends his daughter Astarte, with two other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> Rhea and Dione, to cut off Sanchotho off Cronus by deceit, whom Cronus taking, made wives of these sisters. Ouranos, understanding this, sent Eimarmene and Hore, Fate and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a>, with other auxiliaries, to war against him: but Cronus, having gained the affections of these also, kept them with himself. Moreover, the god Ouranos devised Bastulia, contriving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that moved as having life. But Cronus begat on Astarte <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> daughters called Titanides or Artemides; and he begat on Rhea seven sons, the youngest of whom, as soon as he was born, was consecrated a god. Also by Dione he had daughters, and by Astarte moreover two sons, Pothos and Eros, i.e. Cupid and Love. But Dagon, after he had found out <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> corn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, was called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ZEUS">Zeus</a> Aratrus. To Sydye, or the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, one of the Titanides bare Asclepius. Cronus had also in Persea three sons, 1. Cronus his father's namesake. 2. Zeus Belus. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. Is it conceivable, that a writer so acute as Porphyry, or indeed that any man of common sense, either in his age or in that of Philo, would forge a book filled with such stories as these, in order to remove the Christian objections to the immoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the Pagan divinities? The very supposition is impossible to be made. Nor let any one imagine that Sanchoniatho is here <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> allegorically, and by his tales of Ouranos, and Ge and Cronus, is only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSONIFYING">personifying</a> the heaven, the earth, and time. On the contrary, he assures us, that Ouranos, or Epigeus, or Autokthon (for he gives him all these names), was the son of one Eliaun or Hypsistos, who dwelt about Byblus, and that from him the element which is over us was called heaven, on account of its excellent beauty, as the earth was named Ge after his Apul Eu- sister and wife. And his translator is very angry *with the Neoteric Greeks, as he calls them, because that seb. Prep. Evang. lib. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. "by a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of force and straining, they laboured to turn all the stories of the gods into allegories and physical discourses." This proves unanswerably, that the author of this book, whoever he was, did not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to veil the great truths of religion under the cloak of mythologic allegories; and therefore, if it was forged by Porphyry in support of Paganism, the forger so far mistook the state of the question between him and his adversaries, that he contrived a book, which, if admitted to be ancient, totally overthrew his own cause. The next thing to be inquired into with respect to Sanchoniatho is his antiquity. Did he really live and write at so early a period as Porphyry and Philo pretend? We think he did not; and what contributes not a little to confirm us in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is that mark of national vanity and partiality, common to after-times, in making the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> original, and conveyed from Phenicia into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. This, however, furnishes an additional proof that Porphyry was not the forger of the work; for he well knew that the mysteries had their origin in Egypt (see Mysteries), and would not have fallen into such a blunder. He is guilty, indeed, of a very great anachronism, when he makes Sanchoniatho <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Semiramis, and yet pretends that what he writes of the Jews is compiled from the records of Hierombalus the priest of the god Jao; for Bochart has made it appear in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> probable, † that Hierombalus or Jeromb-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">baal</a> is the Jerub-baal or Gideon of Scripture. Between the reign of Semiramis and the Trojan war a period elapsed of near 800 years, whereas Gideon flourished not above seventy years before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. But supposing Sanchoniatho to have really consulted the records of Gideon, it by no means follows that he flourished at the same period with that judge of Israel. He speaks of the building of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> as an ancient thing, while our best chronologers ‡ place it in the time of Gideon. Indeed, were we certain that any writings had been left by that holy man, we should be obliged to conclude, that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract of time had intervened between the death of their author and their falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Sanchoniatho; for, surely, they could not, in a short period, have been so completely corrupted as to give any countenance to his impious absurdities. His atheistic cosmogony he does not indeed pretend to have got from the annals of the priest of Jao, but from records which were deposited in his own town of Berytus by Thoth a Phoenician philosopher, who was afterwards made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Egypt. But surely the annals of Gideon, if written by himself, and preserved pure to the days of Sanchoniatho, must have contained so many truths of the Mosaic religion, as must have prevented any man of sense from adopting so impossible a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> as Thoth's, though sanctioned by the greatest name of profane antiquity. Stillingfleet indeed thinks it most probable that Sanchoniatho became acquainted with the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the life of Jerub-baal from annals written by a Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>. He observes, that immediately after the death of Gideon, the Israelites, with their usual propensity to idolatry, worshipped Baal-berith, or the idol of Berytus, the town in which Sanchoniatho lived; and from this circumstance he concludes that there must have been such an intercourse between the Hebrews and Berytians, that in process of time the latter people might assume to themselves the Jerub-baal of the former, and hand <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his actions to posterity as those of a priest instead of a great commander. All this may be true; but if so, it amounts to a demonstration that the antiquity of Sanchoniatho is not so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> by many ages as that which is claimed for him by Philo and Porphyry, though he may still be more ancient, as we think Vossius has proved him to be, * than any other profane historian whose writings have come down to us either entire or in fragments. But granting the authenticity of Sanchoniatho's history, what, it may be asked, is the value of his fragments, that we should be at any trouble to ascertain whether they be genuine remains of high antiquity, or the forgeries of a modern impostor? We answer, with the illustrious Stillingfleet, that though these fragments contain such absurdities as it would be a disgrace to reason to suppose credible; though the whole cosmogony is the grossest sink of atheism; and though many persons make a figure in the history, whose very existence may well be doubted; yet we, who have in our hands the light of divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, may in this dungeon discover many excellent relics of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, which throw no feeble light upon many passages of holy scripture, as they give us the origin and progress of that idolatry which was so long the opprobrium of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They furnish too a complete refutation of the extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, and show, if they be genuine, that the world is indeed not older than it is said to be by Moses. We shall conclude the article by earnestly recommending to our readers...

SANCRUFT

Pages 510-511

WILLIAM, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was born at Fresingfield in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> in 1616; and admitted into Emanuel <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in 1633. In 1642 he was elected a fellow; and, for refusing to take the covenant, was ejected from his fellowship. In 1660 he was chosen one of the university preachers; and in 1668 was nominated to the deanship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. In 1664 he was installed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of St Paul's. In this station he set himself with unwearyed diligence to repair the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, till the fire of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1666 employed his thoughts on the more noble undertaking of rebuilding it, toward which he gave 1400l. He also rebuilt the deanery, and improved its revenue. In 1668 he was admitted archdeacon of Canterbury, on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s presentation. In 1677, being now prolocutor of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, he was unexpectedly advanced to the archbishopric of Canterbury. In 1687 he was committed to the Tower, with six other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, for presenting a petition to the king against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. Upon King James II.'s withdrawing himself, he concurred with the lords in a declaration to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> for a free <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and due indulgence to the Protestant dissenters. But when that prince and his consort were declared king and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> refusing to take the oath to their majesties, he was suspended and deprived — He lived in a very private manner till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1693. His learning, integrity, and piety, made him an exalted ornament of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He published a volume in 12mo, entitled <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Politics, taken from Machiavel, Borgia, and other select authors; Familiar Letters to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, an 8vo pamphlet; and three of his sermons were printed together after his death.

SANCTIFICATION

Pages 511-511

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sanctifying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rendering a thing holy. The reformed divines define sanctification to be an act of God's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, by which a person's desires and affections are alienated from the world; and by which he is made to die to sin, and to live to righteousness; or, in other words, to feel an abhorrence of all vice, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and virtue.

SANCTION

Pages 511-511

the authority given to a judicial <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by which it becomes legal and authentic.

SANCTORIUS

Pages 511-511
or SANCTORIO, a most ingenious and learned physician, was professor in the university of Padua, in the beginning of the 17th century. He contrived a kind of statical chair, by means of which, after estimating the aliments received, and the sensible discharges, he was enabled to determine with great exactness the quantity of insensible perspiration, as well as what kind of victuals and drink increased or diminished it. On these experiments he erected a curious system, which he published under the title of De Medicina Statica; which is translated into English by Dr Quincy. Sanctorius published several other treatises, which showed great abilities and learning.

SANCTUARY

Pages 511-511

in the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, is also used for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the church in which the altar is placed, encompassed with a rail <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ballustrade.

SAND

Pages 511-511

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, properly denotes small particles of siliceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sands are subject to be variously blended, both with different substances, as that of tales, &c.; and hence, as well as from their various colours, are subdivided into, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> sands, whether pure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mixed with other arenaceous or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> particles; of all which there are several kinds, differing no less in the fineness of their particles than in the different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from a bright and shining white, to a brownish, yellowish, greenish, &c. white. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and reddish sands, both pure and impure. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> sands, whether pure or mixed, are also very numerous. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> sands, distinguished in the same manner. 5. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sands, of which there are only two varieties, viz. a fine shining grayish-black sand, and another of a fine shining reddish-black colour. 6. The green kind: of which there is only one known <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. a coarse variegated dusky green sand, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. Sand is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the glass manufacture; a white kind of sand being employed for making of the white glass, and a coarse greenish-looking sand for the green glass. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> it seems to be the office of sand to render unctuous or clayey earths fertile, and fit to support vegetables, by making them more open and loose.

See AMMODYTES, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAND-FLOODS

Pages 511-512

a name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of sand so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. Mr Bruce gives the following accurate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of some that he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in travelling through that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and dreary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. "At one o'clock (says he) we alighted among some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a> trees at Waadi el Halboub, having gone twenty-one miles. We were here at once surprised and terrified by a sight surely one of the most magnificent in the world. In that vast expanse of desert from west and to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of us, we saw a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prodigious pillars of sand at different distances, at times moving with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celerity, at others stalking on with a majestic slowness; at intervals we thought they were coming in a few minutes to overwhelm us; and small quantities of sand did actually more than once reach us. Again they would retreat so as to be almost out of sight, their tops reaching to the very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. There the tons often separated from the bodies; and these, once disjoined, dispersed in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and did not appear more. Sometimes they were broken near the middle, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> struck with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cannon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. About noon they began to advance with considerable swiftness upon us, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> being very strong..." strong at north. Eleven of them ranged alongside of us about the distance of three miles. The greatest diameter of the largest appeared to me at that distance as if it would <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> ten feet. They retired from us with a wind at south-east, leaving an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon my mind to which I can give no name, though surely one ingredient in it was fear, with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wonder and astonishment. It was in vain to think of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, the swiftest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fastest sailing ship could be of no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to carry us out of this danger; and the full persuasion of this rivetted me as if to the spot where I stood, and let the camels <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> on me so much in my state of lameness, that it was with some difficulty I could overtake them." "The same appearance of moving pillars of sand presented themselves to us this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in form and disposition like those we had seen at Waadi Halhouib, only they seemed to be more in number and less in size. They came several times in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> upon us, that is, I believe, within less than two miles. They began immediately after sunrise, like a thick wood, and almost darkened the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: his rays shining through them for near an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, gave them an appearance of pillars of fire. Our people now became desperate: the Greeks shrieked out, and said it was the day of judgment; Ismael pronounced it to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; and the Tucorories, that the world was on fire. I asked Idris, if ever he had before seen such a sight? He said he had often seen them as terrible, though never worse; but what he feared most was that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> redness in the air, which was a sure <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a> of the coming of the simoom." See SIMOOM. The flowing of sand, though far from being so tremendous and hurtful as in Arabia, is of very bad consequences in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as many valuable pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> have thus been entirely lost; of which we give the following instances from Mr Pennant, together with a probable means of preventing them in future. "I have more than once (says he), on the eastern coasts of Scotland, observed the calamitous state of several extensive tracts, formerly in a most flourishing condition, at present covered with sands, unstable as those of the deserts of Arabia. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Purvie, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Aberdeen, is now reduced to two farms, and above 500l. a year lost to the Errol family, as appears by the oath of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> in 1600, made before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session, to ascertain the minister's salary. Not a vestige is to be seen of any buildings, unless a fragment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. "The estate of Coubin, near Forres, is another melancholy instance. This tract was once worth 300l. a year, at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> overwhelmed with sand. This strange inundation was still in motion in 1769, chiefly when a strong wind prevailed. Its motion is so rapid, that I have been assured, that an apple-tree has been so covered with it in one season, that only the very summit appeared. This distress was brought on about ninety years ago, and was occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some trees, and pulling up the bent or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> which grew on the sand hills; which at last gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of 15 George III. c. 33. to prohibit the destruction of this useful plant. "I beg leave to suggest to the public a possible means of putting a stop to these destructive ravages. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> hath kindly formed this plant to grow only in pure sand. Mankind was left to make, in after-times, an application of it suitable to their wants. The sand-hills, on a portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a> shores, in the parish of Llanasa, are covered with it naturally, and kept firm in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The Dutch perhaps owe the existence of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> at least of their country to the sowing of it on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOBILE">mobile</a> solum, their sand-banks. "My humane and amiable friend, the late Benjamin Stillington, Esq. recommended the sowing of this plant on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> wilds of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, that its matted roots might prevent the deluges of sand which that country experiences. It has been already remarked, that wheresoever this plant grows, the salutary effects are soon observed to follow. A single plant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fix the sand, and gather it into a hillock; these hilloeks, by the increase of vegetation, are formed into larger, till by degrees a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> is made often against the encroachments of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and might as often prove preventive of the calamity in question.
