I cannot, therefore, but recommend the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to the inhabitants of many parts of North <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The plant grows in most places near the sea, and is known to the Highlanders by the name of murrah; to the English by that of bent-star, mat grass, or marram. Linnaeus calls it arundo arenaria. The Dutch call it helm. This plant hath stiff and sharp-pointed leaves, growing like a rush, a foot and a half long: the roots both creep and penetrate deeply into their sandy beds: the stalk bears an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> five or six inches long, not unlike rye: the seeds are small, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and roundish. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, as old Gerard observes, no cattle will eat or touch this vegetable, allotted for other purposes, subservient to the use of mankind." SAND-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIPER">Piper</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRINGA">TRINGA</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">SAND-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> stone, of which there are numerous varieties, arising not only from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, but also in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and proportions of the constituent parts. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> Index. There is a singular variety of sand-stone, which consists of small grains of hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> which strike fire with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> united with some micaceous particles. This variety is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, the flexibility depending on the micaceous part and softness of the gluten with which the particles are cemented. This elastic stone is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>. There are also two tables of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Borghese at Rome, which have the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. But the sparry particles of their substance, though transparent, are rather soft, and may be easily separated by the nail. They effervesce with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and there is a small mixture of minute particles of talc or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a>. Sand-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are of great use in buildings which are required to resist air, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and fire. Some of them are soft in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, but become hard when exposed to the air. The loose ones are most useful, but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and hard ones crack in the fire, and take a polish when used as grindstones. Stones of this kind ought therefore to be nicely examined before they are employed for valuable purposes.

SANDAL

Pages 512-514

in antiquity, a rich kind of slipper worn on the feet by the Greek and Roman ladies, made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other precious stuff; consisting of a sole, with an hollow at one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> to embrace the ankle, but leaving the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foot bare. Sandal, is also used for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> or slipper worn by the pope and other Romish prelates when they officiate. It is also the name of a sort of slipper worn by several congregations of reformed monks. This last consists of no more than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> leathern sole, fastened with latches or buckles, all the rest of the foot being left bare. The Capuchins wear sandals; the Recollects, clogs; the former are of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and the latter of wood. **Sandal-Wood.** See **SAUNDERS.** **SANDARACH,** in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>,* a very beautiful native fossil, though too often confounded with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> factitious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> arsenic, and with the red <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> formed by melting the common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>. It is a pure substance, of a very even and regular structure, is throughout of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> which our dyers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> scarlet, and is considerably transparent even in the thickest pieces. But though, with respect to colour, it has the advantage of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> while in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, it is vastly inferior to it when both are reduced to powder. It is moderately hard, and remarkably heavy; and, when exposed to a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, melts and flows like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> set on fire, it burns very briskly. It is found in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and is sold to the painters, who find it a very fine and valuable red; but its virtues or qualities in medicine are no more ascertained at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> than those of the yellow orpiment. **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">Gum</a>-Sandarach,** is a dry hard resin, usually in the form of loose granules, of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-bean, or larger; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> whitish, yellow colour, transparent, and of a resinous smell, brittle, very inflammable, of an acrid and aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and diffusing a very pleasant smell when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. It was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this gum was obtained from the *juniperus communis*; but this plant does not grow in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> only sandarach is produced; for the gum sandarach of the shops is brought from the southern provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. About six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred quintals of it are exported every year from Santa Cruz, Mogador, and Safy. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the country it is called *el grassa.* The tree which produces it is a *Thuia,* found also by M. Vahl in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. It was made known several years ago by Dr Shaw, who named it *Cypressus fructu quadrivalvis,* *Equiseti instar articulatis,* but neither of these learned men was acquainted with the economical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this tree; probably because, being not common in the northern part of Barbary, the inhabitants find little advantage in collecting the resin which exudes from it. M. Schousboe (A), who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of *thuo* in question, says that it does not rise to more than the height of 20 or 30 feet at most, and that the diameter of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> does not exceed ten or twelve inches. It distinguishes itself, on the first view, from the two other species of the same genus, cultivated in gardens, by having a very distinct trunk, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a real tree; whereas in the latter the branches rise from the root, which gives them the appearance rather of bushes. Its branches also are more articulated and brittle. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are not very apparent, show themselves in April; and the fruit, which are of a spherical form, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in September. When a branch of this tree is held to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it appears to be interspersed with a multitude of transparent vesicles which contain the resin. When these vesicles burst in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, a resinous juice exudes from the trunk and branches, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in other coniferous trees. This resin is the sandarach, which is collected by the inhabitants of the country, and carried to the ports, from which it is transported to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It is employed in making some kinds of sealing-wax, and in different sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>. In 1793 a hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of it cost in Morocco from 13 to 13½ piastres, which make from about £L 5s. to 3L 7s. 6d. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The duty on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> was about 7s. 6d. sterling per quintal. Sandarach, to be good, must be of a bright yellow colour, pure and transparent. It is an article very difficult to be adulterated. Care, however, must be taken, that the Moors do not mix with it too much sand. It is probable that a tree of the same kind produces the gum sandarach of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, which is exported in pretty considerable quantities. **Pounded Sandarach.** See **POUNCE.** **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDEMANIANS">SANDEMANIANS</a>,** in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> that originated in Scotland about the year 1728; where it is at this time distinguished by the name of *Glassites,* after its founder Mr John Glass, who was a minister of the established <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in that kingdom; but being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of subverting the national covenant, and sapping the foundation of all national establishments by the kirk judicatory, was expelled by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> from the church of Scotland. His sentiments are fully explained in a tract published at that time, intitled, "The Testimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of Martyrs," and preserved in the first volume of his works. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of Mr Glass's expulsion, his adherents formed themselves into churches, conformable in their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> to what they apprehended to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the first churches recorded in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Soon after the year 1755, Mr Robert Sandeman, an elder in one of these churches in Scotland, published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters addressed to Mr Hervey, occasioned by his Theron and Aspasio; in which he endeavours to show, that his notion of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is contradictory to the scripture account of it, and could only serve to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> men, professedly holding the doctrines <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Calvinistic, to establish their own righteousness upon their frames, inward feelings, and various acts of faith. In these letters Mr Sandeman attempts to prove, that faith is neither more nor less than a simple assent to the divine testimony concerning <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, recorded in the New Testament; and he maintains, that the word *faith,* or *<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>,* is constantly used by the apostles to signify what is denoted by it in common discourse, viz. a persuasion of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of any proposition, and that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between believing any common testimony, and believing the apostolic testimony, except that which results from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the testimony itself. This led the way to a controversy among those who were called Calvinists, concerning the nature of justifying faith; and those who adopted Mr Sandeman's no- (A) Phys. Med. and Econom. Library, (a Danish Journal) for 1799. tion of it, and who took the denomination of Sandemanians, formed themselves into church order, in strict fellowship with the churches in Scotland, but holding no kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with other churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> opinions and practices in which this sect differs from other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, are, their weekly administration of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">Supper</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-feasts, of which every member is not only allowed but required to partake, and which consist of their dining together at each other's houses in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the morning and afternoon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; their kiss of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> used on this occasion, at the admission of a new member, and at other times, when they deem it to be necessary or proper; their weekly collection before the Lord's Supper, for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and defraying other expenses; mutual exhortation; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from blood and things strangled; washing each other's feet, the precept concerning which, as well as other precepts, they understand literally; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of goods, so far as that every one is to consider all that he has in his possession and power as liable to the calls of the poor and church; and the unlawfulness of laying up treasures on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, by setting them apart for any distant, future, and uncertain use. They allow of public and private diversions; so far as they are not connected with circumstances really sinful; but apprehending a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to be sacred, disapprove of playing at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, dice, &c. They maintain a plurality of elders, pastors, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, in each church; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the presence of two elders in every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of discipline, and at the administration of the Lord's Supper. In the choice of these elders, want of learning, and engagements in trade, &c. are no sufficient objection; but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages disqualify for the office; and they are ordained by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and fasting, imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and giving the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of fellowship. In their discipline they are strict and severe; and think themselves obliged to separate from the communion and worship of all such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> as appear to them not to profess the simple truth for their only ground of hope, and who do not walk in obedience to it. We shall only add, that in every church transaction, they esteem unanimity to be absolutely necessary. From this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the account which they have published of their tenets and practices, it does not seem to be probable that their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> should be very considerable.

SANDIVER

Pages 514-514

an old name for a whitish substance which is thrown up from the metal, as it is called, of which glass is made; and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on its surface, is skimmed off. Sandiver is also plentifully ejected from volcanoes; some is of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and others tinged bluish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. Sandiver is said to be detergent, and good for foulnesses of the skin. It is also used by gilders of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>.

SANDIX

Pages 514-514

a kind of minium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, made of ceruse, but much inferior to the true minium.

SANDOMIR

Pages 514-514

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the same name, in Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>. The Swedes blew up the castle in 1656; and here, in 1659, was a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> between the Tartars and Russians. It is 84 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>. Lat. 49. 26. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20. 10.

SANDORICUM

Pages 514-514

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order, Trililiaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SANDPU

Pages 514-514
or SANPOO, the vulgar name of a river in the East Indies, which is one of the largest in the world; but it is better known by that of Burrampooter. Of this most majestic body of waters we have the following very animated account in Maurice's Indian Antiquities. "An object equally novel and grand now claims our attention; so novel, as not to have been known to Europeans in the real extent of its magnificence before the year 1765, and so awfully grand, that the astonished geographer, thinking the language of prose inadequate to convey his conception, has had recourse to the more expressive and energetic language of poetry: but scarce the Muse herself Dares stretch her wing o'er this enormous mass Of rushing waters; to whose dread expanse, Continuous depth, and wond'rous length of course, Our floods are rills. This stupendous object is the Burrampooter, a word which in Shanscrit signifies the son of Brahma; for no meaner origin could be assigned to so wonderful a progeny. This supreme monarch of Indian rivers derives its source from the opposite side of the same mountain from which the Ganges springs, and taking a bold sweep towards the east, in a line directly opposite to the course of that river, washes the vast country of Tibet, where, by way of distinction, it is denominated Sanpoor, or the river. Winding with a rapid current through Tibet, and, for many a league, amidst dreary deserts and regions remote from the habitations of men, it waters the borders of the territory of Lassa, the residence of the grand Lama; and then deviating with a cometary irregularity, from an east to a south-east course, the mighty wanderer approaches within 200 miles of the western frontiers of the vast empire of China. From this point its more direct path to the ocean lay through the gulf of Siam; but with a desultory course peculiar to itself, it suddenly turns to the west through Assam, and enters Bengal on the north-east quarter. Circling round the western point of the Garrow mountains, the Burrampooter now takes a southern direction; and for 60 miles before it meets the Ganges, its sister in point of origin, but not its rival in point of magnitude, glides majestically along in a stream which is regularly from four to five miles wide, and, but for its freshness, Mr Rennel says, might pass for an arm of the sea. About 40 miles from the ocean these mighty rivers unite their streams; but that gentleman is of opinion that their junction was formerly higher up, and that the accumulation of two such vast bodies of water, scooped out the amazing bed of the Megna lake. Their present conflux is below Luckipoor; and by that confluence a body of fresh running water is produced, hardly equalled, and not exceeded, either in the old or the new hemisphere. So stupendous is that body of water, that it has formed a gulf of such extent as to contain islands that rival our Isle of Wight in size and fertility; and with such resistless violence does it rush into the ocean, that in the rainy season the sea itself, or at least its surface, is perfectly fresh for many leagues out."

SANDS

Pages 514-515

Goodwin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Godwin, are dangerous sand banks banks lying off the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England. See Kent.

SANDWICH

Pages 515-516

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, and one of the cinque ports, having the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an earldom. It consisted of 1398 houses in 1801, most of them old, and built with wood, though there are a few new ones built with brick and flints. The town is walled round, and also fortified with ditches and ramparts; but the walls are much decayed, on account of the harbour being so choked up with sand that a ship of 100 tons burden cannot get in. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, according to the census of 1801, was 6506; but in the census for 1811, the number given is 2735, which is probably an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 51. 20. Sandwich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of islands in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lying near <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NEW_IRELAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, were among the last discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, who so named them in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sandwich, under whose administration these discoveries were made. They consist of 11 islands, extending in latitude from 18. 54. to 22. 15. N. and in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from 150. 54. to 160. 24. W. They are called by the natives Owhyhee, Mowee, Ranai, Morotoi, Tahoorowa, Woahoo, Atoo, Neecheeheow, Orechoua, Morotinne, and Tahoorra, all inhabited except the two last. An account of the most remarkable of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in their alphabetical order, in their proper places in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of these islands differs very little from that of the West Indies in the same latitude, though perhaps more temperate; and there are no traces of those violent winds and hurricanes, which render the stormy months in the West Indies so dreadful. There is also more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> at the Sandwich isles, where the mountainous parts being generally enveloped in a cloud, successive showers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the inland parts, with fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and a clear sky, on the sea shore. Hence it is, that few of those inconveniences, to which many tropical countries are subject, either from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moisture, are experienced here. The winds, in the winter months, are generally from east-south-east to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east. The vegetable productions are nearly the same as those of the other islands in this ocean; but the taro root is here of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit trees thrive not in such abundance as in the rich plains of Otaheite, but produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fruit. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes are of a very unusual size, some of them measuring 11 inches and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> in circumference, and having 14 feet eatable. There is also a root of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, shaped like a yam, and from six to ten pounds in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the juice of which is very sweet, of a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and is an excellent substitute for sugar. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> are confined to the three usual sorts, hogs, dogs, and rats. The fowls are also of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort; and the birds are beautiful and numerous, though not various. Goats, pigs, and European seeds, were left by Captain Cook; but the possession of the goats soon gave rise to a contest between two districts, in which the breed was entirely destroyed. The inhabitants are undoubtedly of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> that possesses the islands south of the equator; and in their persons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, customs, and manners, approach nearer to the New Zealanders than to their less distant neighbours, either of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> or Friendly Islands. They are in general about the middle size, and well made; they walk very gracefully, run nimbly, and are capable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fatigue. Many of both sexes have fine open countenances; and the women in particular have good eyes and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, with a sweetness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of look, that render them very engaging. There is one peculiarity, characteristic of every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of these islands, that even in the handsomest faces there is a fulness of the nostril, without any flatness or spreading of the nose. They suffer their beards to grow, and wear their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> after various fashions. The dress of both men and women nearly resemble those of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and both sexes wear necklaces of small variegated shells. Tattowing the body is practised by every colony of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and arms of the women are also very neatly marked, and they have the singular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of tattowing the tip of the tongue. Like the New Zealanders, they have adopted the method of living together in villages, containing from 100 to 200 houses, built pretty closely together, without any order, and having a winding path between them. They are generally flanked, towards the sea, with detached walls, which are meant both for shelter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. These walls consist of loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inhabitants are very dexterous in shifting them suddenly to such places as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the attack may require. In the sides of the hills, or surrounding eminences, they have also little holes, or caves, the entrance to which is also secured by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of the same kind. They serve for places of retreat in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of extremity, and may be defended by a single person against several assailants. Their houses are of different sizes, some of them being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and commodious, from 40 to 50 feet long, and from 20 to 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; while others are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> hovels. The food of the lower class consists principally of fish and vegetables, to which the people of higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> add the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of dogs and hogs. The manner of spending their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> admits of little variety. They rise with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and, after enjoying the cool of the evening, retire to rest, a few hours after sunset. The making of canoes, mats, &c. forms the occupations of the men; the women are employed in manufacturing cloth, and the servants are principally engaged in the plantations and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. Their idle hours are filled up with various amusements, such as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">boxing</a>, wrestling, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> bear a great resemblance to those of the Southsea islands. Their plantations, which are spread over the whole sea-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, consist of the taro, or eddy-root, and sweet potatoes, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the cloth-trees set in rows. The bottoms of their canoes are of a single piece of wood, hollowed out to the thickness of an inch, and brought to a point at each end. The sides consist of three boards, each about an inch thick, neatly fitted and lashed to the bottom part. Some of their double canoes <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 70 feet in length, three and a half in depth, and twelve in breadth. Their cordage, fish-hooks, and fishing-tackle, differ but little from those of the other islands. Among their arts must not be forgotten that of making <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which they have in great abundance, and of a good quality. Their instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> are spears, daggers, clubs, and slings; and for defensive armour they wear strong mats, which are not easily penetrated by such weapons as theirs. As the islands are not united under one sovereign, wars are frequent among them, which, no doubt, contribute greatly to reduce the number of inhabitants, which, according to the proportion assigned to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, does not exceed 400,000. The same system of subordination prevails here as at the other islands, the same <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority on the part of the chiefs, and the same unresisting submission on the part of the people. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is likewise monarchical and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. At Owhyhee there is a regular society of priests living by themselves, and distinct in all respects from the rest of the people. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> sacrifices are here frequent; not only at the commencement of a war, or any signal enterprise, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of every considerable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> calls for a repetition of these horrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. Notwithstanding the irreparable loss in the death of Captain Cook, who was here murdered through sudden resentment and violence, they are acknowledged to be of the most mild and affectionate disposition. They live in the utmost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and friendship with each other; and in hospitality to strangers they are not exceeded even by the inhabitants of the Friendly Islands. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> capacity seems, in no respect, below the common standard of mankind; and their improvements in agriculture, and the perfection of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, are certainly adequate to the circumstances of their situation, and the natural advantages which they enjoy.

SANDYS

Pages 516-516

George, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the foregoing Sir Edwin, and youngest son of Archbishop Sandys, was born in 1577. He was a very accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; travelled over several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and the East; and published a relation of his journey in folio, in 1615. He made an elegant translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses; and composed some poetical pieces of his own, that were greatly admired in the times of their being written. He also paraphrased the Psalms; and has left behind him a Translation, with notes, of one Sacred Drama, written originally by Grotius, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Christus Patiens; on which, and Adamus Exul, and Masenius, is founded Lauder's impudent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of plagiarism against our immortal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>. Our author became one of the privy chamber to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., and died in 1643.

SANGUIFICATION

Pages 516-516

in the animal economy, the conversion of the chyle into true blood. See Blood.

SANGUINARIA

Pages 516-516

Blood-wort, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> Sanguinaria method ranking under the 27th order, Rhodocoea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The Indians paint themselves <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> with the juice of these plants.

SANGUISORBA

Pages 516-516

Greater wild Burnet, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Miscellaneous. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The cultivation of this plant has been greatly recommended as food for cattle. See Burnet, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index.

SANHEDRIM

Pages 516-517
or Sanhedrin, from the Greek word συνέδριον, which signifies a council or assembly of persons sitting together, was the name whereby the Jews called the great council of the nation, assembled in an apartment of the temple of Jerusalem to determine the most important affairs both of their church and state. This council consisted of seventy senators. The room they met in was a rotunda, half of which was built without the temple, and half within; that is, one semicircle was within the compass of the temple; the other semicircle, they tell us, was built without, for the senators to sit in; it being unlawful for any one to sit down in the temple. The Nasi, or prince of the sanhedrim, sat upon a throne at the end of the hall, having his deputy at his right hand, and his sub-deputy on his left. The other senators were ranged in order on each side. The rabbins pretend, that the sanhedrim has always subsisted in their nation from the time of Moses down to the destruction of the temple by the Romans. They date the establishment of it from what happened in the wilderness, some time after the people departed from Sinai (Numb. xi. 16.), in the year of the world 2514. Moses, being discouraged by the continual murmurings of the Israelites, addressed himself to God, and desired to be relieved, at least, from some part of the burden of the government. Then the Lord said to him, "Gather unto me 70 men of the elders of Israel, whom thou knowest to be the elders of the people, and officers over them; and bring them unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they may stand there with thee: And I will come down and talk with thee there; and I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone." The Lord, therefore, poured out his spirit upon these men, who began at that time to prophesy, and have not ceased from that time. The sanhedrim was composed of 70 counsellors, or rather 72, six out of each tribe; and Moses, as president, made up the number 73. To prove the uninterrupted succession of the judges of the sanhedrim, there is nothing unattempted by the partisans of this opinion. They find a proof where others cannot so much as perceive any appearance or shadow of it. Grotius may be consulted in many places of his commentaries, and in his first book De jure belli et pacis, c. 3. art. 20. and Selden de Synedris veterum Hebraeorum. Also, Calmet's Dissertation concerning the polity of the ancient Hebrews, printed before his Comment upon the Book of Numbers. As to the personal qualifications of the judges of this bench, their birth was to be untainted. They were often taken from the race of the priests or Levites, or out of the number of the inferior judges, or from the lesser They were to be skilful in the law, as well traditional as written. They were obliged to study magic, divination, fortune-telling, physic, astrology, arithmetic, and languages. The Jews say, they were to know to the number of 70 tongues; that is, they were to know all the tongues, for the Hebrews acknowledged but 70 in all, and perhaps this is too great a number. Eunuchs were excluded from the sanhedrim because of their cruelty, usurers, decrepid persons, players at games of chance, such as had any bodily deformities, those that had brought up pigeons to decoy others to their pigeon-houses, and those that made a gain of their fruits in the sabbatical year. Some also exclude the high-priest and the king, because of their too great power; but others will have it, that the kings always presided in the sanhedrim, while there were any kings in Israel. Lastly, it was required, that the members of the sanhedrim should be of a mature age, a handsome person, and of considerable fortune. We speak now, according to the notions of the rabbins, without pretending to warrant their opinions. The authority of the great sanhedrim was vastly extensive. This council decided such causes as were brought before it by way of appeal from the inferior courts. The king, the high-priest, the prophets, were under its jurisdiction. If the king offended against the law; for example, if he married above 18 wives, if he kept too many horses, if he hoarded up too much gold and silver, the sanhedrim had him stripped and whipped in their presence. But whipping, they say, among the Hebrews was not at all ignominious; and the king bore this correction by way of penance, and himself made choice of the person that was to exercise this discipline over him. Also the general affairs of the nation were brought before the sanhedrim. The right of judging in capital cases belonged to this court, and this sentence could not be pronounced in any other place, but in the hall called Laschat-haggazith, or the hall paved with stones, supposed by some to be the Atebopoleos, or pavement, mentioned in John xix.13. From whence it came to pass, that the Jews were forced to quit this hall when the power of life and death was taken out of their hands, 40 years before the destruction of their temple, and three years before the death of Jesus Christ. In the time of Moses this council was held at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony. As soon as the people were in possession of the land of promise, the sanhedrim followed the tabernacle. It was kept successively at Gilgal, at Shiloh, at Kirjath-jearim, at Nob, at Gibeon in the house of Obed-edom; and, lastly, it was settled at Jerusalem, till the Babylonish captivity. During the captivity it was kept up at Babylon. After the return from Babylon, it continued at Jerusalem to the time of the Sicarii, or Assassins. Then finding that these profligate wretches, whose number increased every day, sometimes escaped punishment by favour of the president or judges, it was removed to Hanoth, which were certain abodes situated, as the rabbins tell us, upon the mountain of the temple. From thence they came down into the city of Jerusalem, withdrawing themselves by degrees from the temple. Afterwards they removed to Jamia, thence to Jericho, to Uzzah, to Sepharvaim, to Bethsanin, to Sephoris, last of all to Tiberias, where they continued to the time of their utter extinction. And this is the account the Jews themselves give us of the sanhedrim. But the learned do not agree with them in all this. Father Petau fixes the beginning of the sanhedrim not till Gabinius was governor of Judea, who, according to Josephus, erected tribunals in the five principal cities of Judea; at Jerusalem, at Gadara, at Amathus, at Jericho, and at Sephora or Sephoris, a city of Galilee. Grotius places the origin of the sanhedrim under Moses, as the rabbins do; but he makes it determine at the beginning of Herod’s reign. Mr Basnage at first thought that the sanhedrim began under Gabinius; but afterwards he places it under Judas Maccabeus, or under his brother Jonathan. We see, indeed, under Jonathan Maccabeus, (1 Macc. xii. 6.), in the year 3860, that the senate with the high-priest sent an embassy to the Romans. The Rabbins say, that Alexander Janneaus, king of the Jews, of the race of the Assoneans, appeared before the sanhedrim, and claimed a right of sitting there, whether the senators would or not. Josephus informs us, that when Herod was but yet governor of Galilee, he was summoned before the senate, where he appeared. It must be therefore acknowledged, that the sanhedrim was in being before the reign of Herod. It was in being afterward, as we find from the Gospel and from the Acts. Jesus Christ in St Matthew (v. 22.) distinguishes two tribunals— “Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment;” this, they say, is the tribunal of the 23 judges. “And whosoever shall say to his brother Raca, shall be in danger of the council;” that is, of the great sanhedrim, which had the right of life and death, at least generally, and before this right was taken away by the Romans. Some think that the jurisdiction of the council of 23 extended to life and death also; but it is certain that the sanhedrim was superior to this council. See also Mark xiii. 9. xiv. 55. xv. 1.; Luke xxii. 52, 66.; John xi. 47.; Acts iv. 15. v. 21. where mention is made of the syndrion or sanhedrim. From all this it may be concluded, that the origin of the sanhedrim is involved in uncertainty; for the council of the 70 elders established by Moses was not what the Hebrews understand by the name of sanhedrim. Besides, we cannot perceive that this establishment subsisted either under Joshua, the judges, or the kings. We find nothing of it after the captivity, till the time of Jonathan Maccabeus. The tribunals erected by Gabinius were very different from the sanhedrim, which was the supreme court of judicature, and fixed at Jerusalem; whereas Gabinius established five at five different cities. Lastly, It is certain that this senate was in being in the time of Jesus Christ; but the Jews themselves inform us that they had no longer then the power of life and death (John xviii. 31.)

SANICULA

Pages 518-518

Sanicle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Self-heal, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SANIES

Pages 518-518

in Medicine, a serous putrid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, issuing from wounds. It differs from pus, which is thicker and whiter.

SANJACKS

Pages 517-518

a people inhabiting the Curdistan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, subsisting chiefly by plunder, and the scanty pittance afforded by their own mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. “They were much reduced (says Mr Ives) by the late <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> Achmet of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, who pursued them in person to their subterranean retreats, and destroyed many by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and carried off <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of prisoners, who were sold for slaves.” Notwithstanding this check, in the year 1758, they again became so daring that they would attack <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of 700 men, San Juan de Puerto Rico, usually called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, one of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, is situated in about 18° N. Lat. and between 65° 36' and 67° 45' W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., and is about 40 leagues long and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is beautifully diversified with woods, valleys, and plains, and is extremely fertile. It is well watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, abounds with meadows, is divided by a ridge of mountains running from east to west, and has a harbour so spacious that the largest ships may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in it with safety. Before the arrival of the Spaniards it was inhabited by 400,000 or 500,000 people, who, in a few years, were exterminated by its merciless conquerors. Raynal says, that its whole inhabitants amount at present only to 1500 Spaniards, Mestoes, and Mulattoes, and about 3000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Thus one of the finest islands in the West Indies has been depopulated by the cruelty, and left uncultivated by the indolence, of its possessors. But it is the appointment of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, who seldom permits flagrant crimes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unpunished, that poverty and wretchedness should be uniform consequences of oppression.

SANNAZARIUS

Pages 518-518

James, in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIUS">Actius</a> Cincenis Sannazzarius, a celebrated Latin and Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1458. He by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> ingratiated himself into the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Frederic; and, when that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was dethroned, attended him into France, where he stood with him till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1504. Sannazarius then returned into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he applied himself to polite literature, and particularly to Latin and Italian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His gay and facetious humour made him sought for by all companies; but he was so afflicted at the news that Phillipert prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, had demolished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, that it threw him into an illness, of which he died in 1530. It is said, that being informed a few days before his death, that the prince of Orange was killed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, he called out, "I shall die contented, since <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> has punished this barbarous enemy of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>." He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Italian and Latin poems; among those in Latin, his De Partu Virginis and Eclogues are chiefly esteemed; and the most celebrated of his Italian pieces is his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>.

SANSANDING

Pages 518-518

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated near the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, in N. Lat. 14° 24', and 2° 23' W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. It is inhabited by Moors and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of from eight to ten thousand. The Negroes are kind, hospitable, and credulous; the Moors are, at Sansanding, as everywhere else in the interior parts of Africa, fanatical, bigotted, and cruel.

SANTA CRUZ

Pages 518-520

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and one of the most considerable of those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, being about 250 miles in circumference. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 130° O. S. Lat. 10° 21'. Santa Cruz, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St Croix, a small and unhealthy island, situated in about 6° degrees west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> and 18° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It is about eighteen leagues in length, and from three to four in breadth. In 1643 it was inhabited by Dutch and English, who soon became enemies to each other; and in 1650 were both driven out by 1200 Spaniards, who arrived there in five ships. The triumph of these lasted but a few months. The remains of that numerous body, which were left for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the island, surrendered, without resistance to 160 French, who had embarked in 1651, from St Christopher's, to make themselves masters of the island. These new inhabitants lost no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in making themselves acquainted with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> so much disputed. On a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, in other respects excellent, they found only one river of a moderate size, which, gliding gently almost on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the sea through a flat country, furnished only a brackish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which they found in the innermost parts of the island, made but feeble amends for this defect. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> were for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> dry. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of reservoirs required time. Nor was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> more inviting to the new inhabitants. The island being flat, and covered with old trees, scarcely afforded an opportunity for the winds to carry off the poisonous vapours with which its marshes clogged the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. There was but one remedy for this inconvenience; which was to burn the woods. The French set fire to them without delay; and, getting on board their ships, became spectators from the sea, for several months, of the conflagration they had raised in the island. As soon as the flames were extinguished, they went on shore again. They found the soil fertile beyond <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>, cotton, arnott, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, flourished equally in it. So rapid was the progress of this colony, that in 11 years from its commencement there were upon it 822 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> persons, with a proportionable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of slaves. It was rapidly advancing to prosperity, when such obstacles were thrown in the way of its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> as made it decline again. This decay was as sudden as its rise. In 1696 there were no more than 147 men, with their wives and children, and 623 blacks remaining; and these were transported to St Domingo. Some obscure individuals, some writers unacquainted with the views of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, with their secret negotiations, with the character of their ministers, with the interests of the protectors and the protected; who flatter themselves that they can discern the reason of events amongst a multitude of important or frivolous causes, which may have equally occasioned them; who do not conceive, that among all these causes the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> may possibly be the farthest from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; who after having read the news, or journal of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, with profound <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, decide as peremptorily as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been placed all their lifetime at the helm of the state, and had assisted at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of kings; who are never more deceived than in those circumstances in which they display some share of penetration; writers as absurd in the praises as in the blame which they bestow upon nations, in the favourable or unfavourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> they form of ministerial operations: these idle dreamers, in a word, who think they are persons of importance, because their attention is always engaged on matters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, being convinced that courts are always governed in their decisions by the most comprehensive views of profound policy, have supposed that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> had neglected Santa Cruz, merely because they wished to abandon the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in order to unite all their strength, industry and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, in the large ones; but this is a mistaken notion. This determination arose from the farmers of the revenue, who found that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> trade of Santa Cruz with St Thomas was detrimental to their interests. The spirit of finance hath in all times been injurious to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; it hath destroyed the source from whence it sprang. Santa Cruz <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> without inhabitants, and without cultivation, till 1738, when it was sold by France to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> for 30,750l. Soon after, the Danes built there the fortress of Christianstad. Then it was that this northern power seemed likely to take deep root in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Unfortunately, she laid her plantations under the yoke of exclusive privileges. Industrious people of all sects, particularly Moravians, strove in vain to overcome this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty. Many attempts were made to reconcile the interests of the colonists and their oppressors, but without success. The two parties kept up a continual struggle of animosity, not of industry. At length the government, with a moderation not to be expected from its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, purchased, in 1754, the privileges and effects of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The price was fixed at 412,500l. part of which was paid in ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the remainder in bills upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. From this time the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to the islands was opened to all the subjects of the Danish dominions. Of 345 plantations, which were seen at Santa Cruz, 150 were covered with sugar canes, and every habitation is limited to 3000 Danish feet in length, and 2000 in breadth. It is inhabited by 2136 white men, by 22,244 slaves, and by 155 freedmen. Santa Cruz, in Tenerife. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. Santa Cruz, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, with a harbour and a fort. The Moors took it from the Portuguese in 1536. It is seated at the extremity of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Aguier. W. Long. 10° 7'. N. Lat. 30° 38'. Santa Cruz de la Sierra, a town of South America, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a province of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and in the audience of Los Charcas, with a bishop's see. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, in a country abounding in good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, on the river Guapay. W. Long. 59° 35'. S. Lat. 20° 40'. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a> de Bogota, a town of South America, and capital of New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, with an archbishop's see, a supreme court of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and an university. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is situated at the foot of a steep and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> mountain, at the entrance of a vast and superb plain. In 1774 it contained 1770 houses, 3246 families, and 16,233 inhabitants. Population must necessarily increase there, since it is the seat of government, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> is stricken, the staple of trade; and lastly, since it is the residence of an archbishop, whose immediate jurisdiction extends over 31 Spanish villages, which are called <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; over 195 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> colonies, anciently subdued; and over 28 missions, established in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. This archbishop hath likewise, as metropolitan, a sort of inspection over the dioceses of Quito, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>, of Caracas, of St Martha, and of Cartagena. It is by this last place, though at the distance of 100 leagues, and by the river <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>, that Santa Fe keeps up its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. There are silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> about the city. W. Long. 60° 5'. N. Lat. 3° 58'. Santalum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class; and in the natural method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Santaren, a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in Extremadura, seated on a mountain near the river Taio, 55 miles N. E. from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, in a country very fertile in wheat, wine, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. They get in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> here two months after they have sown their corn. It was taken from the Moors in 1447. The population is estimated at 8000. W. Long. 8° 48'. N. Lat. 39° 15'. Santa Augustine. See Augustine. Santen, a town of Germany, in the Prussian territories in Westphalia. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, 15 miles S. E. from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. It has a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, wherein is an image of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, which it is pretended performs a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. Here the fine walks begin that run as far as Wesel, from which it is five miles distant to the north-west. E. Long. 6° 33'. N. Lat. 51° 38'. Santerre, the former name of a small territory of France, in Picardy; bounded on the north by Cambresis, on the east by Vermandois, on the west by Amiens, and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>. It is very fertile, and the capital town is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERONNE">Peronne</a>. Santeuil, or rather Santeuil, John Baptist de, in Latin Santolius Victorinus, an excellent Latin poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1630. Having finished his studies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the Great's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, he applied himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and celebrated in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> the praises of several great men; by which he acquired universal applause. He enriched Paris with a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, which are to be seen on the public fountains, and the monuments consecrated to posterity. At length, some new hymns being to be composed for the Breviary of Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> Santeuil his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and M. Bossuet, persuaded him to undertake that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and he succeeded in it with the greatest applause. On which the order of Clugny desiring him to compose some for their Breviary, he complied with their request; and that order, out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, granted him letters of filiation, with an annual pension. Santeuil was caressed by all the learned men of his time; and had for his admirers the two princes of Condé, the father and son, from whom he frequently received favours. Louis XIV. also gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his esteem, by bestowing a pension upon him. He attended the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> to Dijon, when that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> went thither in order to hold the states of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; and died there in 1697, as he was preparing to return to Paris. Besides his Latin hymns, he wrote a great number of Latin Poems, which have all the fire and marks of genius discoverable in the works of great poets. To Santeuil we are indebted for many fine church-hymns, as above mentioned. Santeuil read the verses he made for the inhabitants of heaven with all the agitations of a demoniac. Despreaux said he was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> whom God compelled to praise saints. He was among the number of poets whose genius was as impetuous as his muse was decent. La Bruyere has painted the character of this singular and truly original poet in the most lively colours. "Image a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great felicity of temper, complaisant and docile, in an instant violent, choleric, passionate, and capricious. A man simple, credulous, playful, volatile, puerile; in a word, a child in gray hairs: but let him collect himself, or rather call forth his interior genius, I venture to say, without his knowledge or privacy, what sallies! what elevation! what images! what latinity! Do you speak of one and the same person, you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ask? Yes, of the same; of Theodas, and of him alone. He shrieks, he jumps, he rolls upon the ground, he roars, he storms; and in the midst of this tempest, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> issues that shines, that rejoices. Without a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, he rattles like a fool, and thinks like a wise man. He utters truths in a ridiculous way; and, in an idiotic manner, rational and sensible things. It is astonishing to find good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> disclose itself from the bosom of buffoonery, accompanied with grimaces and contortions. What shall I say more? He does and he says better than he knows. These are like two souls that are unacquainted with each other, which have each their turn and separate functions."

SANTILLANE

Pages 520-520

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It is seated on the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, 55 miles east of Oviedo, and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 2. N. Lat. 43. 23.

SANTOLINA

Pages 520-520

Lavender-cotton, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SANTORINI

Pages 520-520
or Santorin, an island of the Archipelago, to the north of Candia, and distant from it about 90 leagues, and to the south-west of Nanphio. It is eight miles in length, and nearly as much in breadth, and almost covered with pumice-stone, whence the soil in general must be dry and barren: it is, however, greatly improved by the labour and industry of the inhabitants, who have turned it into a garden. It affords a great deal of barley, plenty of cotton, and large quantities of wine. Fruit is scarce, except almonds and figs; and there is neither oil nor wood. The partridge and the hare, so common in the other islands of the Archipelago, are scarce at Santorin; but quails are met with in abundance. The inhabitants are all Greeks, and are about 10,000 in number. Pyrgos is the capital town, beside which, there are several little towns and villages. There is but one spring of water in the island, for which reason the rain-water is preserved in cisterns. Though subject to the Turks, they choose their own magistrates. E. Long. 25. 36. N. Lat. 36. 38.

SAONE

Pages 520-520

UPPER, a department in the east of France, including the sources of the river Saone. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile in grain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and vines, and the pastures are numerous and good. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, coal, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are chiefly of iron, glass, tinware, tiles, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; and there is some trade in corn, wine, &c. The territorial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this department is 500,220 hectares. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1817 was 300,156. The contributions of this department in 1800 amounted to 2,199,713 francs. Vesoul is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town. SAONE and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">LOIRE</a>, a department in the east of France, forming <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. The canal of the Centre, which joins the Saone and the Loire, and is about 60 miles in length, lies chiefly in this department. The soil of this department is hilly, but fertile. It produces all kinds of grain, hemp, cattle, and fruits. Its wines are in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation. There are mines of iron and coal, and some manufactures of woollens, hosiery, glass, &c. Its territorial extent is 857,678 hectares; its population in 1817 was 471,457. The contributions for 1802 amounted to 4,376,459 francs. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACON">Macon</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town.

SAP

Pages 520-521

the juice found in vegetables. We observed, when treating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, that it has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> disputed whether the sap of plants be analogous to the blood of animals, and circulates in the same manner. We also mentioned the conclusions that Dr Hales drew from his numerous experiments, which were all in opposition to the doctrine that the sap circulates. Dr Walker, late professor of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, has published, in the 1st volume of the Philosophical Transactions of Edinburgh, an account of a course of experiments on this subject, accompanied with some observations and conclusions. It is well known that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, vegetables contain a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sap; and there are some trees, as the birch and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> wounded, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> discharge a great portion of it. Whence is this moisture derived? Whether is it imbibed from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> does it flow from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> through the roots? These are the questions which require first to be answered; and Dr Walker's experiments enable us to answer them with confidence. He selected a vigorous young birch, 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 26 inches in circumference at the ground. He bored a hole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the ground on the 1st of February, and cut one of its branches at the extremity. He repeated this every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but no moisture appeared at either of the places till the 5th of May, when a small quantity flowed on making an incision near the ground. He then cut 21 incisions in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the tree, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side, at the distance of a foot from one another, and reaching from the ground to the height of 20 feet. The incisions were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> triangles, each side being an inch long and an inch deep, and penetrating through the bark and wood. Dr Walker visited the tree almost every day for two months, and marked exactly from which of the incisions the sap flowed. He observed that it flowed from the lowest incision first, and gradually ascended to the highest. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> will show the progress of the sap upwards, and its correspondence with the thermometer.
