The testimony of the early historians among all the ancient nations, indeed, who are avowedly fabulists, is very little to be depended on, and has been called in question by the most judicious writers of Pagan antiquity. (See Plut. Vita Thes. sub mi.; Thucyd. i. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. i.; Strabo, l. ii. p. 507.; Livy Pref. and Varro ap. August. de Civ. Dei.) The more populous and extensive kingdoms and societies were civilized at a period <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the records of profane history; the presumption, therefore, without taking revelation into the account, certainly is, that they were civilized from the beginning. This is rendered further probable from other circumstances. To account for their system, the advocates of savagism are obliged, as we have seen, to have recourse to numerous suppositions. They imagine that since the creation dreadful convulsions have happened which have spread ruin and devastation over the earth, which have destroyed learning and the arts, and brought on savagism by one sudden blow. But this is reasoning at random, and without a vestige of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>: for the only convulsion that can be mentioned is that at Babel, which we have already shown to be inadequate. Further, it does not appear that any people who were once civilized, and in process of time had degenerated into the savage or barbarous state, have ever recovered their pristine condition without foreign aid. From whence we conclude, that man, once a savage, would never have raised himself from that hopeless state. This appears evident from the history of the world; for that it requires strong incitements to keep man in a very high state of knowledge and civilization, is evident from what we know of the numerous nations which were famed in antiquity, but which are now degenerated in an astonishing degree. That man cannot, or, which is the same thing, has not risen from barbarism to civilization and science by his own efforts and natural talents, appears further from the following facts. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of all the learning, religion, laws, arts, and sciences, and other improvements that have enlightened Europe, a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the northern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, were so many rays diverging from two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. In proportion as nations receded from these two sources of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and civilization, in the same proportion were they more and more immersed in ignorance and barbarism. The Greeks had made no progress towards civilization when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a> first, and afterwards colonies from Egypt and Phenicia, taught them the very elements of science and urbanity.* The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> were in the same state prior to the arrival of the Pelasgi, and the colonies from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> was indebted for the first seeds of improvement to the commercial spirit of the Phenicians. The Gauls, the Britons, and the Germans, derived from the Romans all that in the early periods of their history they knew of science, or the arts of civil life, and so on of other nations in antiquity. The same appears to be the case in modern times. The countries which have been discovered by the restless and inquisitive spirit of Europeans have been generally found in the lowest state of savagism; from which, if they have emerged at all, it has been exactly in proportion to their connexion with the inhabitants of Europe. Even western Europe itself, when sunk in ignorance, during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, did not recover by the efforts of its own inhabitants. Had not the Greeks, who in the 15th century took refuge in Italy from the cruelty of the Turks, brought with them their ancient books, and taught the Italians to read them, we who are disputing about the origin of the savage state, and the innate powers of the human mind, had at this day been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and ignorant savages ourselves, incapable of reasoning with accuracy upon any subject. That we have now advanced far before our masters is readily admitted; for the human mind, when put on the right track, and spurred on by emulation and other incitements, is capable of making great improvements: but between improving science, and emerging from savagism, every one perceives there is an immense <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. Lord Kames observes, that the people who inhabit a grateful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, where the necessaries of life are easily procured, are the first who invent useful and ingenious arts, and the first who figure in the exercises of the mind. But the Egyptians and Chaldeans, who are thought to support this remark, appear from what we have seen to have derived their knowledge from their antediluvian progenitors, and not from any advantages of situation or strength of genius. Besides, the inhabitants of a great part of Africa, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and of many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> lately discovered, live in regions equally fertile, and equally productive of the necessaries of life, with the regions of Chaldea and Egypt; yet these people have been savages from time immemorial, and continue still in the same state. The Athenians, on the other hand, inhabited the most barren and ungrateful region of Greece, while their perfection in the arts and sciences has never been equalled. The Norwegian colony which settled in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> about the beginning of the 8th century, inhabited a most bleak and barren soil, and yet the fine arts were eagerly cultivated in that dreary region when the rest of Europe was sunk in ignorance and barbarism. Again, there are many parts of Africa, and of North and South America, where the soil is neither so luxuriant as to beget indolence, nor so barren and ungrateful as to depress the spirits by labour and poverty; where, notwithstanding, the inhabitants still continue in an uncultured state. From all which, and from numerous other instances which our limits permit us not to bring forward, we infer that some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> influence is necessary to impel savages towards civilization; and that in the history of the world, or the nature of the thing, we find no instance of any people emerging from barbarism by the progressive efforts of their own genius. On the contrary, as we find, in societies highly cultivated and luxurious, a strong tendency to degenerate, so in savages we not only find no mark of tendency to improvement, but rather a rooted aversion to it. Among them, indeed, the social appetite never reached beyond their own horde. It is, therefore, too weak and too confined to dispose them to unite in large communities; and of course, had all mankind been once in the savage state, they never could have arrived at any considerable degree of civilization. Instead of trusting to any such natural progress, as is contended for, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> of Heaven, in pity to the human race, appears at different times, and in different countries, to have raised up some persons endowed with superior talents, or, in the language of poetry, some heroes, demi-gods, or god-like men, who having themselves acquired some knowledge in nations already civilized, by useful inventions, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> institutions, and moral arrangements, sowed the first seeds of civilization among the hordes of wandering disunited barbarians. Thus we find the Chinese look up to their Fohee, the Indians to Brahma, the Persians to Zoroaster, the Chaldeans to Oanes, the Egyptians to Thoth, the Phenicians to Melicerta, the Scandinavians to Odin, the Italians to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, and Picus, and the Peruvians to Manco. In later times, and almost within our own view, we find the barbarous nations of Russia reduced to some order and civilization by the astonishing powers and exertions of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great. The endeavours of succeeding monarchs, and especially of Catharine II. have powerfully contributed to the improvement of this mighty empire. In many parts of it, however, we still find the inhabitants in a state very little superior to savagism; and through the most of it, the lower, and perhaps the middling orders, appear to retain an almost invincible aversion to all further progress; * a fact which, when added to numerous others of a similar nature which occur in the history of the world, seems to prove indisputably, that there is no such natural propensity to improvement in the human mind as we are taught by some authors to believe. The origin of savagism, if we allow mankind to have been at first civilized, is easily accounted for by natural means: The origin of civilization, if at any period the whole race were savages, cannot, we think, be accounted for otherwise than by a miracle, or repeated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. To many persons in the present day, especially, the doctrine we have now attempted to establish will appear very humiliating; and perhaps it is this alone that has prevented many from giving the subject so patient a hearing as its importance seems to require. It is a fashionable kind of philosophy to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to the human mind very preeminent powers: which so flatter our pride, as in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, perhaps, to pervert our reason, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> our judgment. The history of the world, and of the dispensations of God to man, are certainly at variance with the popular doctrine respecting the origin of civilization: for if the human mind be possessed of that innate vigour which that doctrine attributes to it, it will be extremely difficult to account for those numerous facts which seem with irresistible evidence to proclaim the contrary—for that unceasing care with which the Deity appears to have watched over us—and for those various and important revelations He has vouchsafed to us. Let us rejoice and be thankful that we are men, and that we are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but let not a vain philosophy tempt us to imagine that we are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> or gods. SAVAGE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of the small islands in the South sea, lying in S. Lat. 19. 1. W. Long. 169. 37. It is about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues in circuit, of a good height, and has deep water <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to its shores. Its interior parts are supposed to be barren, as there was no soil to be seen upon the coast; the rocks alone supplying the trees with humidity. The inhabitants are exceedingly warlike and fierce, so that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook could not have any intercourse with them.

SAVANNA-LA-MAR

Pages 535-535

a town of Jamaica, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>.—It is the county town, where the assize courts are held. This town was almost totally destroyed in 1781 by an earthquake and inundation, when many of the inhabitants perished. It has now an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and contains about one hundred other houses. It belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, in which are 89 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-estates, 106 other estates, and 18,000 slaves.

SAVANNAH

Pages 535-535

formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated on a river of the same name, and 17 miles from its mouth, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 20. N. Lat. 32. 0. This town is regularly built in form of a parallelogram.

SAVARY

Pages 535-536

an eminent French traveller and writer, was born at Vitre, in Brittany, about the year 1748. He studied with applause at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RENNES">Rennes</a>, and in 1776 travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where he remained almost three years. During this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he was wholly engaged in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in searching out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, and in examining the national manners. After making himself acquainted with the knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of Egypt, he visited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Archipelago, where he spent 18 months. On his return to France, in 1780, he published. 1. A Translation of the Koran, with a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mahomet, in 1783, 2 vols. 8vo. 2. The Morality of the Koran, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a collection of the most excellent maxims in the Koran; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> extracted from his translation, which is esteemed both elegant and faithful. 3. Letters on Egypt, in 3 vols. 8vo, in 1785. In these the author makes his observations with accuracy, paints with vivacity, and renders interesting every thing he relates. His descriptions are in general faithful, but are perhaps in some instances too much ornamented. He has been justly censured for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Egypt and its inhabitants in too <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colours. These letters, however, were bought up by the curious public, and read with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and advantage. Encouraged by this flattering reception, he prepared his letters upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. He died soon after at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> of a malady contracted from too intense application. A sensible obstruction in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> tube of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> had made a decisive progress, which the return of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, some simple medicines, a strict regimen, and travelling, seemed to remove. On his return into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> adjacent to Paris, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> however was still doubtful; for it is well known. known that when the organization of one of the viscera has been much deranged, deep traces of it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever remain. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> mind, however, made him regardless of his health, and he conceived it his duty to profit by those appearances of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> which he experienced at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the summer and the beginning of autumn, to put into order his travels into the islands of the Archipelago, intended as a continuation of his letters on Egypt. His warmth of temper was exasperated by some lively criticisms which had been made on his former productions, and he gave himself up to study with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of which the consequences were sufficiently obvious. An obstruction in the liver again took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and made a new progress; his digestion became extremely languid; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> quite forsook him, both by night and by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; a dry and troublesome cough came on; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> appeared bloated, and his legs more and more inflamed. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BARLEY_WATER">barley-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and cream of tartar still however promoted, in some degree, the urinary secretions, and afforded some little glimmering of hope. In this situation he returned to Paris in the beginning of the year 1788, to attend to the publication of his new work concerning the islands of the Archipelago, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Candia. He had then all the symptoms of a dangerous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>, which became still more alarming from the very exhausted state of the viscera. The right lobe of the liver was extremely hard and sensible. The patient had shiverings without any regular returns, and his strength was undermined by a hectic fever. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> still more uneasy symptoms took place, those of a dropsy in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>; but the circumstances which destroyed all hope, and announced his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, were a severe pain in the left side, with a very troublesome cough, and a copious and bloody expectoration (in hepaticis, says <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, sputum cruentum mortiferum); his respiration became more and more difficult; his strength was exhausted, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> took place on the 4th of February 1788, attended with every indication of the most copious overflowing in the chest, and of an abscess in the liver.—Thus was destroyed, in the vigour of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, an author whose character and talents rendered him worthy of the happiest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Mr Savary's genius was lively and well cultivated; his heart warm and benevolent; his imagination vigorous; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> retentive. He was cheerful and open; and had so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for telling a story, that his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was not less agreeable than instructive. He did not mingle much with the world, but was satisfied with performing well the duties of a son, of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and of a friend.

SAVENDROOG

Pages 536-536

a strong fortress of Hindostan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSORE">Mysore</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is situated on the summit of a vast rock, measuring about half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in perpendicular height, its base being upwards of eight miles in circumference, and divided by a chasm at the top, by which it is formed into two hills, each having a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. They answer the purpose of two citadels which are capable of being maintained independent of the lower works, which are remarkably strong. It was, however, taken by the gallantry of British troops in the year 1791, after a siege of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days continuance. It is 18 miles west of Bangalore. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, No. 167. SAVER-KROUT. See Kroute. SAVERNAKE-Forest, is situated near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> in Wiltshire, and is 12 miles in circumference, well stocked with deer, and delightful from the many vistas cut through the woods and coppices with which it abounds. Eight of these vistas meet, like the rays of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>, in a point near the middle of the forest, where an octagon tower is erected to correspond with the vistas; through one of which is a view of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTTENHAM">Tottenham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Ailesbury's seat, a stately edifice erected after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, and under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Vitruvius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, who to the strength and convenience of the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> has added the elegance of the Italian.

SAVILLE

Pages 536-537

Sir Henry, a learned Englishman, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Henry Saville, Esq. and was born at Bradley, near <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, November the 30th, 1549. He was entered of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1561, where he took the degrees in arts, and was chosen fellow. When he proceeded <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in 1570, he read for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> on the Almagest of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, which procured him the reputation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> eminently skilled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; in the former of which he voluntarily read a public lecture in the university for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In 1578 he travelled into France and other countries; where, diligently improving himself in all useful learning, in languages, and the knowledge of the world, he became a most accomplished <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. At his return, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in the Greek tongue to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, who had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for him. In 1585 he was made warden of Merton College, which he governed 36 years with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and improved it by all the means in his power.—In 1596 he was chosen provost of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> College; which he filled with many learned men.—James I. upon his accession to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, expressed a great regard for him, and would have preferred him either in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state; but Saville declined it, and only accepted the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> in 1604. His only son Henry dying about that time, he thenceforth devoted his fortune to the promoting of learning. Among other things, in 1619, he founded, in the university of Oxford, two lectures, or professorships, one in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the other in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>; which he endowed with a salary of 160l. a year each, besides a legacy of 600l. to purchase more lands for the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. He also furnished a library with mathematical books, near the mathematical school, for the use of his professors; and gave 100l. to the mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> of his own appointing; adding afterwards a legacy of 40l. a year to the same chest, to the university, and to his professors jointly. He likewise gave 120l. towards the new <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, beside several rare <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> and printed books to the Bodleian library; and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of Greek types to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> press at Oxford. After a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> thus spent in the encouragement and promotion of science and literature in general, he died at Eton College the 19th of February 1622, in the 73rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and was buried in the chapel there. On this occasion, the university of Oxford paid him the greatest honours, by having a public speech and verses made in his praise, which were published soon after in 4to, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Ultima Linæa Savilli. The highest encomiums were bestowed on Saville by all the learned of his time: by Casaubon, Mercerus, Melibonius, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger, and especially the learned Bishop Montague; who, in his Diatribe upon Selden's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Tythes, styles him, "that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of learning, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> shall be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> amongst not only the learned, but the righteous, for ever." His works are, 1. Four Books of the Histories of Cornelius Tacitus, and the Life of Agricola; with Notes upon them, in folio, dedicated to Queen Elizabeth, 1581.—2. A View of certain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Matters, or Commentaries concerning Roman Warfare, 1598.—3. Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> Bedam, &c. 1596. This is a collection of the best writers of our English history; to which he added chronological tables at the end, from Julius Caesar to William the Conqueror.—4. The Works of St Chrysostom, in Greek, in 8 vols folio, 1613. This is a very fine edition, and composed with great cost and labour. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> he says, "that having himself visited, about 12 years before, all the public and private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and copied out thence whatever he thought useful to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he then sent some learned men into France, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the East, to transcribe such parts as he had not already, and to collate the others with the best manuscripts." At the same time, he makes his acknowledgements to several eminent men for their assistance; as Thuanus, Velserus, Schottus, Casaubon, Duceus, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRUTER">Gruter</a>, Hoeschelius, &c. In the 8th volume are inserted Sir Henry Saville's own notes, with those of other learned men. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of this edition, including the several sums paid to learned men, at home and abroad, employed in finding out, transcribing, and collating the best manuscripts, is said to have amounted to no less than 8000l. Several editions of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> were afterwards published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.—5. In 1618 he published a Latin work, written by Thomas Bradwardin, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, against <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELAGIUS">Pelagius</a>, entitled De Causa Dei contra Pelagium, et de virtute causarum; to which he prefixed the life of Bradwardin.—6. In 1621 he published a collection of his own Mathematical Lectures on Euclid's Elements, in 4to.—7. Oratio <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORAM">coram</a> Elisabetha <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REGINA">Regina</a> Oxonia habita, anno 1592. Printed at Oxford in 1658, in 4to.—8. He translated into Latin King James's Apology for the Oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">Allegiance</a>. He also left several manuscripts behind him, written by order of King James; all which are in the Bodleian library. He wrote notes likewise upon the margin of many books in his library, particularly Eusebius's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> History; which were afterwards used by Valesius, in his edition of that work in 1659.—Four of his letters to Camden are published by Smith, among Camden's Letters, 1691, 4to.

SAVIOUR

Pages 537-538

an appellation peculiarly given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, Christ, as being the Messiah and Saviour of the world. See Jesus. Order of St Saviour, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, founded by St Bridget, about the year 1345, and so called from its being pretended that our Saviour himself declared its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and rules to the foundress. According to the constitutions, this is principally founded for religious women who pay a particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the holy virgin; but there are some monks of the order, to administer the sacrament and spiritual assistance to the nuns. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">SAUL</a> the son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, was the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Israelites. On account of his disobedient conduct, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was taken from his family, and given to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. See the First Book of Samuel.

SAVONA

Pages 540-540

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, with two castles, and a bishop's see, and containing about 6000 inhabitants in 1800. It contains several handsome churches. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in 1746, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it had a capacious harbour; but the people of Genoa, being afraid that it would hurt their own trade, choked it up. It is seated on the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in a well-cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and all kinds of good fruit. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 14. N. Lat. 44. 21.

SAVONAROLA

Pages 540-542

Jerome, a famous Italian monk, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> in 1452, and descended of a noble family. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 22 he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a Dominican friar, without the knowledge of his parents, and distinguished himself in that order by his piety and ability as a preacher. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> where he chose to appear; there he preached, confessed, and wrote. He had <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> enough to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> which opposed the family of the Medici. He explained the Apocalypse, and there found a prophecy which foretold the destruction of his opponents. He predicted a renovation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and declaimed with much severity against the clergy and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome. Alexander VI. excommunicated him, and prohibited him from preaching. He derided the anthemas of the pope; yet he forbore preaching for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and then resumed his employment with more applause than before. The pope and the Medici family then thought of attacking him with his own weapons, Savonarola having posted up a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">thesis</a> as a subject of disputation, a Franciscan, by their instigation, offered to prove it heretical. The Franciscan was seconded by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> friars, and Savonarola by his; and thus the two orders were at open <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with each other. To <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the dispute, and to convince their antagonists of the superior sanctity of Savonarola, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> offered to walk through a fire, and in order to prove his wickedness, a Franciscan agreed to the same experiment. The multitude, eager to witness so extraordinary a spectacle, urged both parties to come to a decision; and the magistrates were constrained to give their consent. According'y, Saturday the 7th of April 1498 was fixed for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. On that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the champions appeared; but when they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one another in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood, and beheld the wood in flames, they were seized with fear, and were very anxious to escape by any subterfuge the immi- Savonarola's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was a result of his refusal to recant his beliefs. The Dominican order, which he had joined, demanded that he renounce his heretical views. Savonarola refused, citing his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in the word of God. He was tried by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a> and found guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. Despite his conviction, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to preach and teach until his execution. The Dominican order, which he had joined, demanded that he renounce his heretical views. Savonarola refused, citing his belief in the word of God. He was tried by the Inquisition and found guilty of heresy. Despite his conviction, he continued to preach and teach until his execution. Savoy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, lying between France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and which takes its name from the Latin Sabaadia, altered afterwards to Saboia, and Soboja. This country was anciently inhabited by the Celtes, whose descendants therein were subdivided into the Allobroges, Nantuates, Veragri, Seduni, Salassi, Centrones, Garocelli, and some others of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Of all these the Allobroges were the most considerable. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of these tribes, in which Julius Caesar had made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress, was completed under Augustus. Afterwards this country shared the fate of the rest of the western empire, and was overrun by the northern barbarians. The Burgundians held it a considerable time; but when <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> how it first became a distinct earldom under the present family, is what historians are not agreed about: thus much, however, is certain, that Amadeus I., who lived in the 12th century, was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of it. In 1416, Amadeus VIII. was created by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy; and Victor Amadeus first took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and afterwards of Sardinia. See SARDINIA. Savoy was lately conquered by the French, and added to the republic as the 80th department. As this arrangement, though decreed by the convention to last for ever, may probably be of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, we shall write of the dutchy as of an independent state. Savoy, then, is bounded to the south by France and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; to the west by France; and to the east by Piedmont, the Milanese, and Switzerland; its greatest length being about 88 miles, and breadth about 76. As it lies among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, it is full of lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which in general are very barren; many of the highest of them are perpetually covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snow. The summit of those called Montagnes Maudites, "the cursed mountains," are said to be more than two English miles in perpendicular height above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the lake of Geneva, and the lake itself is much higher than the Mediterranean. In some few of the valleys there is corn <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and pasture, and a good breed of cattle and mules; and along the lake of Geneva, and in two or three other places, a tolerable wine is produced. Mount Semis or Cenis, between Savoy and Piedmont, over which the highway from Geneva to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> lies, is as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not higher, than the Montagnes Maudites; but of all the mountains of the Alps, the highest is Mount Rochmelon, in Piedmont, between Fertiere and Novalese. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> over these mountains are very tedious, disagreeable, and dangerous, especially as huge masses of snow, called by the Italians avalanches, and fragments of rocks, frequently roll <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into them from the impending precipices. The way of travelling is either in sledges, chairs, or on the backs of mules: in some places the path on the brink of the precipices is so narrow, that there is but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> room for a single person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. It begins to snow on these mountains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> about the beginning of October. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, August, and September, many of them yield very fine grass, with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and herbs; and others boxwood, walnuts, chestnuts, and pines. The height and different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these mountains, their towering summits rising above one another and covered with snow, the many cataracts or falls of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the noise and rapidity of the river Arc, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> and green tincture of its water, the echoes of its numerous streams tumbling from cliff to cliff, form altogether a very romantic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. These mountainous tracts, notwithstanding their height, are not altogether free from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> in summer, and are also much expos- Savoy, ed to thick <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which sometimes settle unexpectedly on them, and continue several days. There are some wolves among the thickets; and they abound with hares, rupicapras or chamois, and marmottes. In the lower parts of Savoy, there are also bears, wild boars, deer, and rabbits; and among the desolate mountains are found great quantities of rock-crystal. In the glaciers or ice-valleys, between the high mountains, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is extremely cold, even in the months of July and August. The surface of these ice-valleys looks like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or lake, which, after being agitated by fierce and contrary winds, has been frozen all at once, interspersed with hideous cracks and chasms. The noise of these cracks, when first made by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the noon-day <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and reverberated by the surrounding rocks and mountains, is astonishing. The height of the impending mountains is such, that the sun's rays seldom reach the ice-valleys, except a few hours in the middle of summer. The avalanches or snow-balls, which the least concussion of the air <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> occasion, tumble down the mountains with amazing rapidity, continually increasing, and carrying all before them. People have been taken out alive, after being buried several days under them. The mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this dutchy renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> an useless <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. The peasants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> up the hungry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> with the pickaxe and spade, and to improve it carry up mould and dung in baskets. For the purpose of preserving it from drought in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and summer, they cut small reservoirs above it, the water of which may be let out at will; and to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from giving way, break the declivity of the mountains by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> walls on the side for its support, which frequently assume the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fortifications, and are a very pleasing deception to travellers. The Savoyards carry their better sort of cheese into Piedmont, as the flavour is much esteemed there; but they <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> more by their skins of bears, chamois, and bouquetins (a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the wild goat), or by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of grouse and pheasants, which they carry in great numbers to Turin. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, which, on the side of Geneva, separates Savoy from France; the Arve, which has some particles of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in its sands; the Isere, the Seran, the Siers, and the Arc. There are also a great many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in this country, which yield plenty of fish, but none of them are very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, together with medicinal and reciprocating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people is a corrupt French; but the better sort, and those that live in the great cities, speak as good French as they do in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> itself. In their temper, however, and disposition, the Savoyards resemble the Germans more than the French, retaining still much of the old German honesty and simplicity of manners, which no doubt is partly owing to the poverty and barrenness of the country. To this also, joined to their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> and the fruitfulness of their women, which are the effects of their cheerful disposition, healthy air, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and sobriety, it is owing that great numbers of them are obliged to go abroad in quest of a livelihood, which they earn, those at least who have no trades, by showing marmottes, cleaning shoes, sweeping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, and the like. It is said, that there are generally about 18,000 of them, young and old, about Paris. In summer they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the streets, and in winter, 40, 50, or 60 of them lodge together in a room: they are so honest that they may be trusted to any amount. The children are often carried abroad in baskets before they are able to walk. In many villages of Savoy there is hardly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be seen throughout the year, excepting a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or two. Those that have families generally set out and return about the same season, when their wives commonly lie in; and they never fail to bring home some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their small earnings. Some of them are such consummate masters of economy, that they set up shops and make fortunes, and others return home with a competency for the rest of their days. An old man is often despatched with letters, little presents, and some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, from the younger sort, to their parents and relations, and brings back with him fresh colonies, letters, messages, and news. The cultivation of their grounds, and the reaping and gathering in of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> and vintage, are generally left to the women and children; but all this is to be understood of the mountainous parts of Savoy. Great numbers of the mountaineers of both sexes are said to be lame and deformed; and they are much subject to a kind of wens, which grow about their throats, and very much disfigure them, especially the women; but that is the only inconvenience they feel from them. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Savoy, and the other dominions of the king of Sardinia, labour under great hardships and restrictions, unheard of in other countries. A minute account of them will be found in Mr Keyser's Travels. In short, the king has left neither <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, power, nor much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, to any but himself and the clergy, whose overgrown wealth he has also greatly curtailed. No other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is professed or tolerated in Savoy but that of the church of Rome. The decrees, however, of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> are not admitted; nor are the churches asylums for malefactors. This country was annexed to France in 1792, and remained in her possession till the peace of 1814. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> in 1805, the lordships of Chablais, Faucigny, and Genevrino, were separated from the Sardinian dominions.

SAW

Pages 545-547

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which serves to cut into pieces several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> matters; as wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, &c. The best saws are of tempered <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> ground bright and smooth; those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are only hammer-hardened: hence the first, besides their being stiffer, are likewise found smoother than the last. They are known to be well hammered by the stiff <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of the blade; and to be well and evenly ground, by their bending equally in a bow. The lapidaries, too, have their saw, as well as the workmen in mosaic; but of all <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, none have so many saws as the joiners, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are the following. The pit-saw, which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> two-handed saw, employed for sawing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> in pits, and chiefly used by the sawers. The whip-saw, which has likewise two handles, used in sawing such large pieces as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-saw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not easily reach. The hand-saw is made to be used by an individual, of which there are different kinds, as the frame-saw, which is furnished with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. By the twisted cords which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from the upper parts of these cheeks, and the tongue in the middle of them, the upper ends are drawn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, and the lower set further asunder. The tenon-saw, which being very thin, has a back to keep it from bending. The compass-saw, which is very small, and its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> usually not set; its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to cut a round, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other compass-kert, on which account the edge is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and the back thin, that it may have a compass to turn in. At an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the trunks of trees were split with wedges into as many and as thin pieces as possible; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were necessary to have them still thinner, they were hewn on both sides to the proper size. This simple and wasteful manner of making boards has been still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in some places to the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> of Russia endeavoured to put a stop to it, by forbidding hewn deals to be transported on the river Neva. The saw, however, though so convenient and beneficial, has not been able to banish entirely the practice of splitting timber used in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, or in making furniture and utensils; for we do not here speak of firewood; and indeed it must be allowed that this method is attended with peculiar advantages which that of sawing can never possess. The wood-splitters perform their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> more expeditiously than sawers, and split timber is much stronger than that which has been sawn; for the fissure follows the grain of the wood, and leaves it whole; whereas the saw, which proceeds in the line chalked out for it, divides the fibres, and by these means lessens its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> and solidity. Split timber, indeed, turns out often crooked and warped; but for many purposes to which it is applied this is not injurious, and these faults may sometimes be amended. As the fibres, however, retain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> length and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, thin boards particularly, can be bent much better. This is a great advantage in making pipe staves, or sieve frames, which require still more art, and in forming various implements of a similar kind. Our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> saw, which requires only to be guided by the hand, however simple it may be, was not known to the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> when they were subdued by the Europeans. The inventor of this instrument has been inserted in their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> by the Greeks, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, place, in which, among their gods, they honoured the greatest benefactors of the earliest ages. By some he is called Talus, and by others Perdix. None except Pliny make Daedalus the inventor; but Hardouin, in the passage where this occurs, reads Talus for Daedalus. Talus is the name of the inventor according to Diodorus Siculus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, and others. He was the son of Daedalus's sister, and was by his mother placed under the tuition of her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, to be instructed in his art. Having found the jaw-bone of a snake, he employed it to cut through a small piece of wood; and by these means was induced to fabricate a similar instrument of iron, that is, to make a saw. This <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, by which labour is greatly facilitated, excited the envy of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and prompted him to put Talus privately to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Being asked, when burying the body, what he was depositing in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, he replied, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. This ambiguous answer discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>; and thus a snake was the cause of the invention of the murder, and of its being brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. By others the inventor is called Perdix, who is supposed to have been the son of a sister of Daedalus. Perdix did not employ the jaw-bone of a snake for a saw, but the back-bone of a fish, as is mentioned by Ovid. The saws of the Greek carpenters had the same form, and were made with equal ingenuity as the same instruments at present. This appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> preserved among the antiquities of Herculaneum. Two genii are represented at the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> resting on two four-footed stools; and the piece of wood to be sawn through is secured by cramps. The saw with which the genii are at work bears a striking resemblance to our frame-saw. It consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> frame, having a blade in the middle, the teeth of which are perpendicular to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the frame. The piece of wood to be sawn extends beyond the end of the bench, and one of the workmen appears standing, and the other sitting on the ground. The arms in which the blade is fastened, have the same form as that given to them at present. In the bench are seen holes, in which the cramps holding the timber are stuck. They are shaped like the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 7; and the ends of them reach below the boards which form the top of it. Saw-fish. See Pristis, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Saw-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">Mills</a>. The most beneficial improvement of the operation of sawing was the invention of saw mills, which are driven either by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Mills of the first kind were erected so early as the fourth century, in Germany, on the small river Ruer. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> marble with a saw is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. According to Pliny, it was invented in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">Stones</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-rock kind, which are softer than marble, were sawn at that period; but it appears that the harder kinds of stone were also then sawn; for we are informed respecting the discovery of a building which was encrusted with cut <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, carnelian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli, and amethysts. There is, however, no account in any of the Greek or Roman writers of a mill for sawing wood; and as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors speak of saw-mills as new and uncommon, it appears that the oldest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of them has been forgotten, or that some interesting improvement has made them appear entirely new. Becher says that saw-mills were invented in the 17th century, which is a mistake; for when the infant Henry sent people to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, discovered Saw-mill in 1420, he gave orders for saw-mills to be erected, for the purpose of sawing into deals the various <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of excellent timber with which the island abounded, and which were afterwards exported to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. There was a saw-mill in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> about the year 1427, producing a yearly rent of three merks; and in 1490, the magistrates of Erfurth purchased a forest, in which they erected a saw-mill, besides renting another in the neighbourhood. The first saw-mill in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> was erected about the year 1530. In the year 1552 there was a saw-mill erected at Joachimsthal, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a mathematician called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Geusen. In 1555, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of England to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, having seen a saw-mill in the vicinity of Lyons, the writer of his travels gave a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. The first saw-mill was erected in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> at Saardam in 1596, the invention of which is ascribed to Cornelius Cornelissen. The first mill of this kind in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> was erected in the year 1653. At present, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> possesses the largest perhaps ever constructed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, where a water-wheel, 12 feet broad, drives at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> 72 saws. In England, saw-mills had at first a similar fate with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, the ribbon-loom in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a> at Strasburg. When attempts were made to introduce them, they were violently opposed, because it was apprehended that the sawers would thus be deprived of the means of procuring subsistence. An opulent merchant in 1767 or 1768, by desire of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Arts, caused a saw-mill to be erected at Limehouse, driven by wind; but it was demolished by the mob, and the damage was sustained by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, while some of the rioters were punished. This, however, was not the only mill of the kind then in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; for at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a> there was one driven by wind, some years before. Saw-mills are very common in America, where the moving power is generally water. Some have been constructed on a very extensive <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; one in particular, we have been informed, has been erected in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, in British America, for the purpose of cutting planks for the English market. This machine works 15 saws in one frame, and is capable, it is said, of cutting annually not fewer than 8,000,000 feet of timber. The mechanism of a sawing-mill may be reduced to three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> things: the first, that the saw is drawn up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as long as is necessary, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> communicated to the wheel by water; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, that the piece of timber to be cut into boards is advanced by an uniform motion to receive the strokes of the saw; for here the wood is to meet the saw, and not the saw to follow the wood, therefore the motion of the wood and that of the saw ought immediately to depend the one on the other; the third, that where the saw has cut through the whole length of the piece, the whole machine stops of itself, and remains immovable; lest having no obstacle to surmount, the moving power should turn the wheel with too great velocity, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the machine. Saw-mills have been distinguished into two kinds, viz. those which have a reciprocating and those which have a rotatory motion. Fig. 1 represents the elevation of a reciprocating saw-mill. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a> is the shaft or axle, upon which is fixed the wheel BB (of 17½ or 18 feet diameter), containing 40 buckets to receive the water by which it is impelled. CC a wheel fixed upon the same shaft containing 96 teeth, to drive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> No. 2, having 32 teeth, which is fastened upon an iron axle or spindle, having a coupling box on each end that turns the cranks, as DD, round: one end of the pole E is put on the crank, and its other end moves on a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> or iron bolt at F, in the lower end of the frame GG. The crank DD being turned round in the hole E, moves the frames GG up and down, and these having saws in them, by this motion cut the wood. The pinion, No. 2, may work two, three, or more cranks, and thus move as many frames of saws. No. 3, an iron wheel having angular teeth, which one end of the iron K takes hold of, while its other end rolls on a bolt in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> HH. One end of this lever moves on a bolt at I, the other end may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a notch in the frame GG so as to be pushed up and down by it. Thus the catch K pulls the wheel round, while the catch L falls into the teeth and prevents it from going backwards. Upon the axle of No. 3, is also fixed the pinion No. 4, taking into the teeth the under edge of the iron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, that is fastened upon the frame TT, on which the wood to be cut is laid: by this means the frame TT is moved on its rollers SS, along the fixed frame UU; and of course the wood fastened upon it is brought forward to the saws as they are moved up and down by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round of the crank DD.

SAXE

Pages 548-552

Maurice <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of, was born the 13th Oc- tober 1693. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Frederic Au- gustus II, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and of the countess of Konigsmarc, a Swedish lady, cele- brated both for her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. He was educat- ed along with Frederic Augustus the electoral <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, afterwards king of Poland. His infancy announced the future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. Nothing could prevail on him to apply to his studies but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of being allowed, after he had finished his task, to mount on horseback, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> himself with arms. He served his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> commanded by prince Eugene and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, when only twelve years old. He signalized himself at the sieges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a> and Mons, and particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALPLAQUET">Malplaquet</a>. In the evening of that memo- rable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was heard to say, "I'm content with my day's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." During the campaign of 1710, Prince Eugene and the duke of Marlborough made many public encomiums on his merit. Next year the young count accompanied the king of Poland to the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STRALSUND">Stralsund</a>, the strongest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Pomerania, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- played the greatest intrepidity. He swam across the river in sight of the enemy, with a pistol in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. His valour shone no less conspicuously on the bloody day of Gaedelbusch, where he commanded a regiment of cavalry. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> killed under him, after he had three times rallied his regiment, and led them on to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. Soon after that campaign, his mother prevailed on him to marry the countess of Lubin, a lady both rich and beautiful. This union lasted but a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In 1721, the count procured a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; a step of which he afterwards repented. The countess left him with regret; but this did not prevent her from marrying soon after. The count of Saxe was too fond of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and variety to submit to the duties which marriage imposes. In the midst, however, of the pleasures in which he sometimes indulged, he never lost sight of his profession. He carried along with him wherever he went a library of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> books; and even when he seemed most taken up with his pleasures, he never failed to spend an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or two in private <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In 1717 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> had an army of 15,000 men under the command of Prince Eugene. Young Count Saxe was present at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, and at a battle which the prince gained over the Turks. On his return to Poland in 1718, he was made a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Eagle. The wars in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> being concluded by the treaties of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> and Passarowitz, Count Saxe went to France. He had always professed a partiality for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. French, indeed, was the only foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which during his infancy he was willing to learn. He spent his whole time during the peace in studying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, fortification, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, sciences which exactly suited his genius. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of exercising troops had struck his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> when very young. At 16 he invented a new exercise, which was taught in Saxony with the greatest success. Having obtained a regiment in France in 1722, he formed it himself according to his new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. From that moment the Chevalier Folard, an excellent judge of military talents, predicted that he would be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. In 1726 the states of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a> chose him for their sovereign. But both Poland and Russia rose in arms to oppose him. The Czarina wished to bestow the dutchy on Menzikoff, a happy adventurer, who from a pastry-cook's boy, became a general and a prince. Menzikoff sent 800 Russians to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, where they besieged the new-chosen duke in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Count Saxe, who had only 60 men, defended himself with astonishing intrepidity. The siege was raised, and the Russians obliged to retreat. Soon after he retired to Usmaiz, and prepared to defend his people against the two hostile nations. Here he remained with only 300 men, till the Russian general approached at the head of 4000 to force his retreat. That general invited the count to a conference, during which he intended to surprise him, and take him prisoner. The count, informed of the plot, reproached him for his baseness, and broke up the conference. About this time he wrote to France for men and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Mademoiselle le Couvreur, a famous actress, pawned her jewels and plate, and sent him the sum of 40,000 livres. This actress had formed his mind for the fine arts. She had made him read the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the French poets, and given him a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which he retained even in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The count, unable to defend himself against Russia and Poland, was obliged in the year 1729 to leave his new dominions, and retire into France. It is said that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Iwanowa, duchess dowager of Courland, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the tsar Ivan Alexiowitz, had given him hopes of marriage, and abandoned him at that time because she despaired of fixing his wavering <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>.—This inconstancy lost him not only Courland, but the throne of Russia itself, which that princess afterwards filled. Count Saxe, thus stript of his territories, devoted himself for some time to the study of mathematics. He composed also, in 13 nights, and during the intervals of anague, his Reveries, which he corrected afterwards. This book is written in an incorrect but forcible style; it is full of remarks both new and profound, and is equally useful to the soldier and the general. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the king of Poland his father in 1733, kindled a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Europe. His <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, the elector of Saxony, offered him the command of all his forces, but he preferred the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and repaired to the marechal of Berwick's army, which was encamped on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. "Count," said that general, who was preparing to attack the enemy's entrenchments at Ethlinghen, "I was going to send for 3000 men, but your arrival is of more value than theirs." When the attack began, the count, at the head of a regiment of grenadiers, forced the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and by his bravery decided the victory. He behaved at the siege of Philipburgh with no less intrepidity. For these services he was, in 1734, rewarded with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general. Peace was concluded in 1736; but the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI., emperor of Germany, kindled a new war almost immediately. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> was besieged by the Count of Saxe in 1741, near the end of November, and taken the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> by assault. The conquest of Egra followed that of Prague. It was taken a few days after the trenches were opened.
