This success gave so much joy to the emperor Charles VII., that he wrote a congratulatory <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the conqueror with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. In 1744 he was made marechal of France, and commanded a part of the French army in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. During that campaign he displayed the greatest military conduct. Though the enemy was superior in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, he observed their motions so skilfully that they could do nothing. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1745, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> was concluded at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Hungary, the king of England, and the States of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> of the States General, meeting Marechal Saxe one day at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, asked his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. "I think (says he), that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the king my <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> would give me an unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, I would read the original at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> before the end of the year." This answer was not a bravado; the marechal was capable of performing it. He went soon after, though exceedingly ill, to take the command of the French army in the Low Countries. A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> seeing the feeble condition in which he left <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, asked him how he could in that situation undertake so great an enterprise. "The question (replied he) is not about living, but setting out."—Soon after the opening of the campaign, the battle of Fontenoy was fought. Marechal Saxe was at the point of death, yet he caused himself to be put into a litter, and carried round all the posts. During the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he mounted on horseback, though he was so very weak that his attendants dreaded every moment to see him expire. The victory of Fontenoy, owing entirely to his vigilance and capacity, was followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Tournay, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, Ghent, Oudenard, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, Ath, and... and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>: This last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken on the 28th February 1746; and very soon after the king sent to the marechal a letter of naturalization conceived in the most flattering terms. The succeeding campaigns gained him additional honours. After the victory of Raucoix, which he gained on the 11th October 1746, the king of France made him a present of six pieces of cannon. He was, on the 12th of January of the following year, created marechal of all the French armies, and, in 1748, commander-general of all those parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a> which were lately conquered. Holland now began to tremble for her safety. Maastricht and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom had already fallen, and nothing but misfortunes seemed to attend the further prosecution of the war. The States General, therefore, offered terms of peace, which were accepted, and a treaty concluded on the 18th October 1748. Marechal Saxe retired to Chambord, a country seat which the king of France had given him. Some time after, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, where the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> received him as Alexander would have received Caesar.—On his return to France, he spent his time among men of learning, artists, and philosophers. He died of a fever, on the 30th November 1750, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 54. Some days before his death, talking to M. Senac his physician about his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, “It has been (says he) an excellent dream.” He was remarkably careful of the lives of his men. One day a general officer was pointing out to him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> which would have been of great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, “It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only cost you (says he) a dozen grenadiers,” “That would do very well,” replied the marechal, “were it only a dozen lieutenant-generals.” It was impossible for Marechal Saxe, the natural brother of the king of Poland, elected sovereign of Courland, and possessed of a vigorous and restless imagination, to be destitute of ambition. He constantly entertained the notion that he would be a king. After losing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Russia by his inconstancy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, he formed, it is said, the project of assembling the Jews, and of being the sovereign of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> which for 1700 years had neither possessed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> nor country. When this chimerical idea could not be realized, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his eyes upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Corsica. After failing in this project also, he was busily employed in planning a settlement in some part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, when death surprised him. He had been educated and died in the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. “It is a pity (said the queen of France, when she heard of his death) that they cannot say a single De profundis (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> for the dead) for a man who has made us sing so many Te Deums.” All France lamented his death. By his will, which is dated at Paris, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1, 1748, he directed that his body should be buried in quicklime: “that nothing (says he) may remain of me in this world but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of me among my friends.” These orders, however, were not complied with; for his body was embalmed, put into a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, which was inclosed in another of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and this covered with one of wood, bound about with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. His heart was put into a silver gilt box, and his entrails into another coffin. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. was at the charge of his funeral. By his order his corpse was interred with great pomp and splendour in the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Thomas, at Strasburg, on the 8th February 1751. The marechal was a man of ordinary stature, of a robust <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and extraordinary strength. To an aspect, noble, warlike, and mild, he joined the excellent qualities of the heart. Affable in his manners, and disposed to sympathize with the unfortunate, his generosity sometimes carried him beyond the limits of his fortune. On his death-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> he reviewed the errors of his life with remorse, and expressed much <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>. The best edition of his Reveries was printed at Paris 1757, in two vols 4to. It was compared with the greatest attention with the original manuscript in the king's library. It is accompanied with many designs exactly engraved, and a Life of the Author. The Life of Marechal Saxe was written by M. d'Espagnac, two vols 12mo. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is written in the panegyrical style. The author is, however, impartial enough to remark, that in the three battles upon which the reputation of Marechal Saxe is founded, he engaged in the most favourable circumstances. “Never did a general (says he) stand in a more advantageous situation. Honoured with the confidence of the king, he was not restrained in any of his projects. He always commanded a numerous army: his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were steady, and his officers possessed great merit.”

SAXIFRAGA

Pages 552-552

Saxifrage, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dendaria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SAXO-GRAMMATICUS

Pages 552-553

descended from an illustrious Danish (a) family, was born about the middle of the 12th century. Stephens, in his edition of Saxo-Grammaticus, printed at Soroe, indubitably proves, that he must have been alive in 1156, but cannot ascertain the exact <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his birth. See Stephens's Prolegomena to the Notes on Saxo-Grammaticus, p. 8, to 24; also Holberg, vol. i. p. 269; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Antiqui, vol. i. p. 4. On account of his uncommon learning, Saxo was distinguished by the name of Grammaticus. He was provost of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Roskild, and warmly patronized by the learned and warlike Absalon, the celebrated archbishop of Lunden, at whose instigation he wrote the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. His epitaph, a dry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> in bad Latin verses, gives no account of the era of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened, according to Stephens, in 1204. His history, consisting of 16 books, begins from the earliest account of the Danish annals, and concludes with the year 1186. According to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of an accurate writer, the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, which relates to the origin of the Danes, and the reigns of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings, is full of fables; but the eight last books, and particularly those which regard the events of his own times, deserve the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. He wrote in Latin; (a) Some authors have erroneously conjectured from his name Saxo, that he was born in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; but Saxe was no uncommon appellation among the ancient Danes. See Olaus Wormius Monumenta Danica, p. 186, and Stephens's Prolegomena, p. 10. Latin; the style, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider the barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he flourished, is in general extremely elegant, but rather too poetical for history. Mallet, in his *Histoire de Danemark*, vol. i. p. 182, says, "that Sperling, a writer of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> erudition, has proved, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the assertions of Stephens and others, that Saxo-Grammaticus was secretary to Absalon; and that the Saxo provost of Roskild, was another person, and lived earlier."

SAXONY

Pages 553-555

the name of two circles of the German empire, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and a dutchy of the same. The lower circle is bounded to the south by the circle of Upper Saxony, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the dutchy of Sleswick, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and the Baltic; to the west, by the circle of Westphalia and the North <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and to the east by the circle of Upper Saxony. The states belonging to it are the dukes and princes of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> and Bremen, Zell, Grubenhangen, Calenburg, Wolfenbuttle, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a>, Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Gustro, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUCKSTADT">Gluckstadt</a>, Holstein-Gottorf, Hildesheim, Saxe-Lawenburg; the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>; the principalities of Schwerin, Ratzeburg, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANKENBURG">Blankenburg</a>, Ranzau; the imperial cities of Lubeck, Gotzlar, Muhlhausen, Nordhausen, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, and Bremen. The dukes of Bremen and Magdeburg are alternately directors and summoning princes; but, ever since the year 1682, the diets which used generally to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a> have been discontinued. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the empire, which, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the empire in 1681, was settled at 40,000 men, this circle was to furnish 1322 horsemen and 2707 foot; and of the 300,000 florins granted to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> in 1707, its quota was 31,271 florins; both which assessments are the same with those of Upper Saxony, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, Swabia, and Westphalia. The inhabitants of this circle are almost all Lutherans. The circle of Upper Saxony is bounded by that of Franconia, the Upper Rhine, and Lower Saxony; and also by the Baltic sea, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and contains the following states; viz. the electors of Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, Saxe-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, Saxe-Eisenach, Saxe-Cobourg, Saxe-Gotha, Saxe-Altenburg, Saxe-Querfurt, the Hither and Farther Pomerania, Camin, Anhalt, Quiddelnburg, Gernrode, Walkenried, Schwarzburg, Sondershausen, Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, Mansfeld, Stolberg, Barby, the counts of Reussen, and the counts of Schonberg. No diets have been held in this circle since the year 1683. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony has always been the sole summoning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of it. Most of the inhabitants profess the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. When the whole empire furnishes 40,000 men, the quota of this circle was 1322 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 2707 foot. Of the 300,000 florins granted by the empire in 1707, it contributed only 31,271 florins, 28 krutitzers, being rated no higher than those of Westphalia, Lower Saxony, Swabia, and Burgundy, though it is much larger. Agreeable to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and regulation in 1654, this circle was to nominate only two assessors of the chamber-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Saxony was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a kingdom by Bonaparte in 1806, and still retains the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Previous to the overthrow of the French power in 1814, it consisted of the dutchy of Saxony, the greatest part of the margravate of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, a part of Vogtland, and the northern half of the landgraviate of Thuringia. The Lusatias also, and a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Henneberg, belong to it, though no part of this circle; but by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> in 1814, one half of the territory, and two-fifths of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> were given to Prussia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the kingdom of Saxony is in general exceeding rich and fruitful, yielding corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> in abundance, together with hops, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, aniseed, wild saffron, wood; and in some places woad, wine, coals, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, clay, terra sigillata, fuller's-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, fine shiver, various sorts of beautiful marble, serpentine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and almost all the different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sulphur also, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, sand, and free-stone, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, turf, cinnabar, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, arsenic, cobalt, and other minerals, are found in it. This country, besides the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, contains likewise valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. In 1790, the produce of the mines was estimated at 2,000,000 crowns. The country abounds in many places with horned cattle, sheep, horses, and venison. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> by which it is watered are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, the Schwarze-Elster, the Mulde, the Saale, the Unstrut, the Weiße-Elster, and the Pleisse. These rivers, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and rivulets, abound in fish; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Elster are found beautiful pearls. The kingdom is extremely well cultivated and inhabited. The population, in 1802, was estimated at 2,150,000; but by the cession in 1814, it is reduced to 1,200,000. The superficial extent of the kingdom is now about 7200 English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles; before the cessions, it was about 15,200. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> diets here consist of three classes. The first is composed of the prelates, the counts, and lords, and the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Leipsic and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a>. To the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> belong the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in general, immediate or mediate, that is, such as stand immediately under the fief <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> or the aulic judicatories, and such as are immediately under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMAN">amman</a>. The third class is formed of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in general. The general provincial diets are ordinarily held every six years; but there are others called selection diets, which are convened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> every two years. We would here observe, that not only these diets, but those in most of the other states of Germany, are at present extremely insignificant and unimportant, retaining little more than the shadow of their former power and privileges; for even the petty princes, though they depend upon their more potent neighbours, and must be careful not to give them any umbrage, are almost as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in their respective territories as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior himself. As to religion, it was in this country that the reformation took its rise in the 16th century, to which it hath ever since adhered, according to the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>.* The two late electors, when they embraced <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> in order to qualify themselves to be elected kings of Poland, gave the most solemn assurances to their people, that they would inviolably maintain the established religion and its professors in the full and free enjoyment of all their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, privileges, and prerogatives whatsoever, in regard to churches, worship, ceremonies, usages, universities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, benefices, incomes, profits, jurisdictions, and immunities. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family still continue <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman catholics</a>, though they have lost the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Saxony, crown of Poland, for which they at first embraced Popery. With respect to ecclesiastical matters, the country is divided into parishes, and these again into spiritual inspections and consistories, all subordinate to the ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and upper consistory of Dresden, in which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and Leipsic the Calvinists and Roman Catholics enjoy the free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religion. Learning flourishes in this kingdom; in which, besides the free schools and gymnasia in most of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns, is the celebrated university of Leipsic, in which are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> for the liberal arts and the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and in the town are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> and printers of the greatest eminence. A great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are also carried on in this country. The principal are those of fine and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, thread, fine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fine glasses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>; porcelain, equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; iron, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wares; manufactures of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; gloves, caps, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>; in which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions mentioned above, together with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, an important foreign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is carried on. Leipsic is one of the most industrious places. In 1800 it had eight manufactories of wax-cloth, eight of velvet and other silk stuffs, two of silk-stockings, two of painted paper; two extensive and excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a>-foundries, fifteen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> establishments, besides others of tobacco, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, &c. But the mining district round Freyberg is the most industrious of the whole kingdom. Here, besides the extensive establishments for the amalgamation and purification of silver, there are foundries of cannon and bells, several manufactures of gold and silver lace, of woollen cloth, of cotton yarn, &c. At <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMNITZ">Chemnitz</a>, there were, in 1793, 1626 weavers, and twelve establishments for printing cotton. Before the abolition of the electorate, the titles of the elector of Saxony were, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony, Juliers, Cleve, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>; as also of Engern and Westphalia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-marshal and elector of the Holy Roman empire, landgrave in Thuringia, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Meissen, and of Upper and Lower Lusatia, burgrave of Magdeburg, princely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Henneberg, count of La Mark, Ravensberg, Barby, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANAU">Hanau</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Ravenstein. Among the electors he was reckoned the sixth, as great marshal of the empire, of which he was also <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, during an interregnum, in all places not subject to the vicariate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine of the Rhine. He was moreover sole director of the circle; and in the vacancy of the see of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> claims the directorium at the diet of the empire. His matricular assessment, on account of the electorate, was 1984 florins, besides what he paid for other districts and territories. To the chamber-courts he contributed, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, the sum of 1545 rix-dollars, together with 83 rix-dollars and 62 kruitzers on account of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>. In this kingdom, subordinate to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, are various colleges for the departments of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, foreign affairs, the finances, fiefs, mines, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and ecclesiastical affairs, together with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tribunals and courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, to which appeals <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the inferior. The revenues of the king of Saxony amounted to about 900,000l. in 1816. They arise from the ordinary and extraordinary subsidies of the states; his own demesnes, consisting of several bailiwics; the impost on beer, and the fine porcelain of the country; tents of corn, fruit, wine, &c.; his own silver mines, Saxony, and the tenths of those that belong to individuals. The kingdom, however, is at present deeply in debt. The regular troops amount to 12,000 men, exclusive of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of the ban, the arriere-ban, and the body of miners and hunters, who are obliged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war to bear arms. The whole kingdom is divided into circles. Saxony was raised to the rank of a kingdom by Bonaparte in 1806. In the following year, Prussia was compelled to cede to Saxony the district of Cottbus, and at the same time four-fifths of her Polish territories were disunited from her, and erected into a principality, under the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>, and the sovereignty given to the King of Saxony. The duchy was afterwards enlarged by cessions from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject to the king of Saxony till 1814, when it was transferred to Russia. The country of Saxony is remarkable for being the mother of the present English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but concerning the Saxons themselves, previous to that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we have very few particulars. The Saxons (says Mr Whitaker) have been derived by our historians from very different parts of the globe; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the north of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the forests of Germany. And their appellation has been equally referred to very different causes; the name of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> progenitor, the plundering disposition of their Asiatic fathers, and the short hooked weapons of their warriors. But the real origin of the Saxons, and the genuine derivation of their name, seem clearly to be these. In the earlier period of the Gallic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the Celtæ of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> crossed the Rhine in considerable numbers, and planted various colonies in the regions beyond it. Thus the Volcae Tectosages settled on one side of the Hercynian forest and about the banks of the Neckar; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a> upon another and about the Rhine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>; the Boii beyond both; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENONES">Senones</a> in the heart of Germany. Thus also we see the Treviri, the Norvii, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SUEVI">Suevi</a>, and the Marcomanni, the Quadi, the Venedi, and others, in that country; all plainly betrayed to be Gallic nations by the Gallic appellations which they bear, and all together possessing the greatest part of it. And, even as late as the conclusion of the first century, we find one nation on the eastern side of this great continent actually speaking the language of Gaul, and another upon the northern using a dialect nearly related to the British. But as all the various tribes of the Germans are considered by Strabo to be γαλάται, or genuine Gauls in their origin; so those particularly that lived immediately beyond the Rhine, and are asserted by Tacitus to be indubitably native Germans, are expressly denominated γαλάται, or Gauls, by Diodorus, and as expressly declared by Dio to have been distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> appellation of Celte from the earlier period. And the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> line of nations, which extended along the ocean, and reached to the borders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, was all known to the learned in the days of Diodorus, by the same significant appellation of γαλάται, or Gauls. Of these the most noted were the Si Cambri and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>; the former being seated near the channel of the Rhine, and the latter inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. And the denominations of both declare their original original; and show them to have been derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock of the Celtæ, and to be of the same Celtic kindred with the Cimbri of our own Sommersetshire, and the Cymbri or Cambrians of our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The Cimbri are accordingly denominated Celtæ by Strabo and Appian. And they are equally asserted to be Gauls by Diodorus; to be the descendants of that nation which sacked the city of Rome, plundered the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, and subdued a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and some of Asia. Immediately to the south of these were the Saxons, extending from the isthmus of the Chersonesus to the current of the Elbe. And they were equally Celtic in their origin as their neighbours. They were denominated Ambrones as well as Saxons; and, as such, are included by Tacitus under the general appellation of Cimbri, and comprehended in Plutarch under the equal one of Celtæ-Scythæ. And the name of Ambrones appears particularly to have been Gallic; being common to the Saxons beyond the Elbe, and the Ligurians in Cisalpine Gaul; as both found to their surprise, on the irruption of the former into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with the Cimbri. And, what is equally surprising, and has been equally unnoticed by the critics, the Welsh distinguish England by the name of Loegr or Liguria, even to the present moment. In that irruption these Saxons, Ambrons, or Ligurians, composed a body of more than 30,000 men, and were principally concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> to pieces the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> armies of Manlius and Caprio. Nor is the appellation of Saxons less Celtic than the other. It was originally the same with the Belgic Suessiones of Gaul; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that tribe being now intitled Soisson by the French, and the name of the Saxons pronounced Saisen by the Welsh, Sason by the Scotch, and Sasenach or Saxenach by the Irish. And the Suessiones or Saxones of Gaul derived their own appellation from the position of their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> on a river, the stream at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a> being now denominated the Aisne, and formerly the Axon; Uesson or Axon importing only waters or a river, and S-uesson or S-ax-on on the waters or the river. The Suessiones, therefore, are actually denominated the Uessiones by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; and the Saxones are actually intitled the Axones by Lucan. These, with their brethren and allies the Cimbri, having been more formidable enemies to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, than the Samnites, Carthaginians, Spaniards, Gauls, or Parthians, in the second century applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and became nearly as terrible by sea. They soon made themselves known to the inhabitants of the British isles by their piracies in the northern channels, and were denominated by them Lochlyn or Lochlynoch; lucd-lyn signifying the people of the wave, and the d being quiescent in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>. They took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORKNEY_ISLANDS">Orkney <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, which were then merely large shoals of sand, uncovered with wood, and overgrown with rushes; and they landed in the north of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and ravaged the country. Before the middle of the third century they made a second <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the latter, disembarked a considerable body of men, and designed the absolute subjection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Before the conclusion of it, they carried their naval operations to the south, infested the British channel with their little vessels, and made frequent descents upon the coasts. And in the fourth and fifth centuries, acting in conjunction with the Picts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a> and the Scots of Ireland, they ravaged all the eastern and south-eastern shores of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, began the formal conquest of the country, and finally settled their victorious soldiery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>.

SCABIOSA

Pages 555-555

SCABIOUS; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, Aggregatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCABRITA

Pages 555-555

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SCÆVOLA, C. MUCIUS, a young Roman of illustrious birth, is particularly celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for a brave but unsuccessful attempt upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Porsea <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Heturria, about the year before Christ 504. See the article Rome, No 71. SCÆVOLA, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandria class. See BOTANY Index.

SCAFFOLD

Pages 555-555

also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised in the manner of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, for the more commodious viewing any show <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>: it is also used for a stage raised in some public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the execution of criminals. SCALA-nova, anciently Neapolis, called by the Turks Konshadase, is situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on the slope of a hill, the houses rising one above another, intermixed with minarets and tall slender cypresses. "A street, through which we rode (says Dr Chandler†), was hung with goat skins exposed to dry, dyed of a most lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. At one of the fountains is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> used as a cistern. The port was filled with small craft. Before it is an old fortress on a rock or islet frequented by gulls and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-mews. By the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-side is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and good khan, at which we passed a night on our return. This place belonged once to the Ephesians, who exchanged it with the Samians for a town in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>."

SCALADO

Pages 555-555
or SCALLADE, in the art of war, a furious assault made on the wall or rampart of a city, or other fortified place, by means of ladders, without carrying on works in form, to secure the men.

SCALD-CREAM

Pages 555-556

sometimes also called Clouted-cream; a curious method of preparing cream for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, almost peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Dr Hales, in Philosophical Transactions volume xlix. p. 342, 1755, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. gives some account of the method of preparing this delicate and luxurious article; other writers also speak of it. With an elucidation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, we shall nearly quote Mr Feltham's account from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, volume lxi. part ii. It is there observed, that the purpose of making scald-cream is far superior butter than can be procured from the usual raw cream, being preferable for flavour and keeping; to which those accustomed are so partial, as seldom to eat any other. As leaden cisterns would not answer for scalding cream, the dairies dairies mostly adopt <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> pans, which hold from three to five gallons, for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and that which is put into those pans one morning, stands till the next, when, without disturbing it, it is set over (on a trivet) a steady brisk wood fire, devoid of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, where it is to remain from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to fifteen minutes, according to the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in it: the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of removing it from the fire must be particularly attended to, and is, when the surface begins to wrinkle or to gather in a little, showing signs of being near the agitation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, which it must by no means do; it is then instantly to be taken off, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a> until the next morning, when the fine cream is thrown up, and may be taken for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or for butter, into which it is now soon converted by stirring it with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Some know when to remove it from the fire by sounding the pan with the finger, it being then less sonorous; but this can only be acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Dr Hales observes, that this method of preparing milk takes off the ill <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which it sometimes acquires from the cows feeding on turnips, cabbage, &c.

SCALDS

Pages 556-556

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of literature, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of the northern countries to their poets; in whose writings their history is recorded.

SCALE

Pages 556-556

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a line divided into equal parts, placed at the bottom of a map <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> draught, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to all the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, or all the distances and places of the map.

SCALENE

Pages 556-556
or SCALENOUS TRIANGLE, scalenum, in Geometry, a triangle whose sides and angles are unequal. See Geometry.

SCALIGER

Pages 556-557

Julius Caesar, a learned critic, poet, physician, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at the castle of Ripa, in the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in 1484; and is said to have been descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> princes of Verona, though this is not mentioned in the letters of naturalization he obtained in France in 1528. He learned the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin tongue in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and in his 12th year was presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, who made him one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. He served that emperor 17 years, and gave Scaliger signal proofs of his valour and conduct in several expeditions. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> in April 1512, in which he had the misfortune to lose his father Benedict Scaliger, and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Titus; on which his mother died with grief: when being reduced to necessitous circumstances, he entered into the order of the Franciscans, and applied himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; but soon after, changing his mind with respect to his becoming a monk, he took arms again, and served in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a physician persuaded him to study physic, which he did at his leisure hours, and also learned Greek; and at last the gout determined him, at 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to abandon a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He soon after settled at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a>, where he married, and began to apply himself seriously to his studies. He learned first the French tongue, which he spoke perfectly in three months: and then made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the Gascon, Italian, Spanish, German, Hungarian, and Slavonian: but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object of his studies was polite literature. Meanwhile, he supported his family by the practice of physic. He did not publish any of his works till he was 47 years of age; when he soon gained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> name in the republic of letters. He had a graceful person, and so strong a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, even in his old age, that he dictated to his son 200 verses which he had composed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> before, and retained without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. He was so charitable, that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was as it were an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and sick; and he had such an aversion to lying, that he would have no correspondence with those who were given to that vice; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he had much vanity, and a satirical spirit, which created him many enemies. He died of a retention of urine in 1558. He wrote in Latin, 1. A Treatise on the Art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. 2. Exercitations against Cardan: which works are much esteemed. 3. Commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Animals, and on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. 4. Some Treatises on Physic. 5. Letters, Orations, Poems, and other works, in Latin. Scaliger, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Justus, one of the most learned critics and writers of his time. He was the son of the former, and was born at Agen in France in 1540. He studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Bordeaux; after which his father took him under his own care, and employed him in transcribing his poems; by which means he obtained such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for poetry, that before he was 17 years old he wrote a tragedy upon the subject of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a>, in which he introduced all the poetical ornaments of style and sentiment. His father dying in 1558, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> the year following, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to apply himself to the Greek tongue. For this purpose he for two months attended the lectures of Turnebus; but finding that in the usual course he should be a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time in gaining his point, he shut himself up in his closet, and by constant application for two years gained a perfect knowledge of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. After which he applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, which he learned by himself with great facility. He made no less progress in the sciences; and his writings procured him the reputation of one of the greatest men of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other age. He embraced the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at 22 years of age. In 1563, he attached himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Casteignier de la Roch Pozay, whom he attended in several journeys; and in 1593, was invited to accept of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of honorary professor. professor of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, which he complied with. He died of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1609. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; was never married; and was so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> a student, that he often spent whole days in his study without eating; and though his circumstances were always very narrow, he constantly refused the presents that were offered him. He published many works; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Notes on Seneca's Tragedies, on Varro, Ausonius, Pompeius Festus, &c. 2. His Latin Poems. 3. A Treatise de Emendatione Temporum. 4. Eusebius's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, with Notes. 5. Canones Isagogeici; and many other works. The collections entitled Scaligeriana, were collected from his conversations by one of his friends; and being ranged into alphabetical order, were published by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius. SCALLOP. See Ostrea, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the Highlands of Scotland, the great scallop shell is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for skimming <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. In old times, it had a more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> place; being admitted into the halls of heroes, and was the cup of their festivity when the tribe assembled in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of their chieftain.

SCALPEL

Pages 557-557

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> used in anatomical dissections and operations in surgery.

SCALPER

Pages 557-557
or SCALPING-IRON, a surgeon's instrument used for scraping foul carious bones.

SCALPING

Pages 557-557

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, in practice among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> warriors, of taking off the tops of the scalps of the enemies' skulls with their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on. They preserve them as trophies of their victories, and are rewarded by their chiefs according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scalps they bring in.

SCALPRA DENTALIA

Pages 557-557

instruments used by surgeons to take off those <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, livid, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> crusts which adhere to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and not only loosen and destroy them, but taint the breath.

SCAMMONY

Pages 557-557

a concreted vegetable juice of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of convolvulus, partly of the resin, and partly of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> kind. See CONVOLVULUS, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCANDALUM MAGNATUM

Pages 557-557

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a defamatory speech <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the injury of a person of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; for which a writ that bears the same name is granted for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of damages.

SCANDERBEG

Pages 557-557

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of George Castriot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, dependent on the Ottoman empire. He was delivered up with his three elder brothers as hostages, by their father, to Amurath II. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Turks, who poisoned his brothers, but spared him on account of his youth, being likewise pleased with his juvenile <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and amiable person. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he became one of the most renowned generals of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and revolting from Amurath, he joined Hunniade Corvin, a most formidable enemy to the Ottoman power. He defeated the sultan's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, took Amurath's secretary prisoner, obliged him to sign and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> an order to the governor of Croia, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Albania, to deliver up the citadel and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> to the bearer of that order, in the name of the sultan. With this forged order he repaired to Croia; and thus recovered the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> and maintained the independency of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the numerous armies of Amurath and his successor Mahomed II who was obliged to make peace with this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in 1461. He then went to the assistance of Ferdinand of Arragon, at the request of Pope Pius II. Scanderbeg and by his assistance Ferdinand gained a complete victory over his enemy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Anjou. Scanderbeg died in 1467. SCANDEROON. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRETTA">Alexandretta</a>.

SCANDINAVIA

Pages 557-558

a general name for the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, anciently under the dominion of one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The inhabitants of these countries, in former times, were excessively addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. From their earliest years they applied themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, and accustomed themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, fatigue, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. Even the very sports of youth and childhood were dangerous. They consisted in taking frightful leaps, climbing up the steepest rocks, fighting naked with offensive weapons, wrestling with the utmost fury; so that it was usual to see them grown up to be robust men, and terrible in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 15. At this early age the young men became their own masters; which they did by receiving a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, a buckler, and a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed at some public meeting. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> men of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> named the youth in public; after which he was obliged to provide for his own subsistence, and was either now to live by hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by joining in some incursion against the enemy. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> care was taken to prevent the young men from too early connexions with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and indeed they could have no hope to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the affection of the fair, but in proportion to the courage and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> they had shown in their military exercises. Accordingly, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> song, we find Bartholin, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Norway, extremely surprised that his mistress should prove unkind, as he could perform eight different exercises. The children were generally born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>; and being inured from their infancy to behold nothing but arms, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, and slaughter, they imbibed the cruel disposition of their fathers, and when they broke forth upon other nations, behaved rather like furies than like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creatures. The laws of this people, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, resembled those of the ancient Lacedemonians. They knew no virtue but bravery, and no vice but cowardice. The greatest penalties were inflicted on such as fled from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The laws of the ancient Danes declared such persons infamous, and excluded them from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Among the Germans, cowards were sometimes suffocated in mud; after which they were covered over with hurdles, to show, says Tacitus, that though the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of crimes should be public, there are certain degrees of cowardice and infamy which ought to be buried in oblivion. Frotho king of Denmark enacted, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that whoever solicited an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> ought upon all occasions to attack one enemy, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> two, to retire only one step back from three, and never to make an actual retreat till assaulted by four. The rules of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> themselves were adapted and warped to these prejudices. War was looked upon as a real <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of justice, and force was thought to be an incontestable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> over the weak, and a visible mark that God had intended them to be subject to the strong. They had no doubt but that the intentions of the Deity had been to establish the same dependence among men that takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among inferior creatures; and, setting out from this principle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inequality among men, they had from thence inferred that the weak had no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to what they could not defend. This maxim was adopted with such rigour, that the name of divine judgment was given not only to the judicatory combat, but to conflicts and battles of all sorts; victory being, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, the only certain mark by which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> enables us to distinguish those whom it has appointed to command others.—Lastly, Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, by annexing eternal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to the military virtues, gave the utmost possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of vigour to that propensity which these people had for war, and to their contempt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, of which we shall now give some instances. We are informed that Harold, surnamed Blaatand, or Blue-tooth, a king of Denmark, who lived in the beginning of the ninth century, had founded on the coasts of Pomerania a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> named Julin or Jomsburg. To this place he sent a colony of young Danes, bestowing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> on a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> called Palnatoko. In this colony it was forbidden to mention the word fear, even in the most imminent dangers. No citizen of Jomsburg was to yield to any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of enemies however great. The sight of inevitable death was not to be taken as an excuse for showing the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>. And this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> really appears to have eradicated from the minds of most of the youths bred up under him, all traces of that sentiment so natural and so universal, which makes men think on their destruction with horror. Nothing can show this better than a single fact in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which deserves to have place here for its singularity. Some of them having made an irruption into the territories of a powerful Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, named Haquin, were overcome in spite of the obstinacy of their resistance; and the most distinguished among them being made prisoners, were, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of those times, condemned to death. The news of this, far from afflicting them, was on the contrary received with joy. The first who was led to punishment was content to say, without changing countenance, and without expressing the least sign of fear, "Why should not the same happen to me as did to my father? He died, and so must I." A warrior, named Thorchill, who was to cut off the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, having asked him what he felt at the sight of death, he answered, "that he remembered too well the laws of Jomsburg to utter any words that denoted fear." The third, in reply to the same question, said, "he rejoiced to die with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; and that he preferred such a death to an infamous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> like that of Thorchill's." The fourth made an answer much longer and more extraordinary. "I suffer with a good heart; and the present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> is to me very agreeable. I only beg of you (added he, addressing himself to Thorchill) to be very quick in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off my head; for it is a question often debated by us at Jomsburg, whether one retains any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> after being beheaded. I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore grasp this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> in my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, after my head is cut off, I strike it towards you, it will show I have not lost all sense; if I let it drop, it will be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary. Make haste therefore, and decide the dispute." Thorchill, adds the historian, cut off his head in a most expeditious manner; but the knife, as might be expected, dropt from his hand. The fifth showed the same tranquillity, and died rallying and jeering his enemies. The sixth begged of Thorchill, that he might not be led to punishment like a sheep; "Strike the blow in my face (said he), I will sit still without shrinking; and take notice whether I once wink my eyes, or betray one sign of fear in my countenance; for we inhabitants of Jomsburg are used to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> ourselves in trials of this sort, so as to meet the stroke of death without once moving." He kept his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> before all the spectators, and received the blow without betraying the least sign of fear, or so much as winking with his eyes. The seventh, says the historian, was a very beautiful young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in the flower of his age. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, as fine as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, floated in curls and ringlets on his shoulders. Thorchill asked him, what he thought of death? "I receive it willingly (said he), since I have fulfilled the greatest duty of life, and have seen all those put to death whom I would not survive. I only beg of you one favour, not to let my hair be touched by a slave, or stained with my blood." Neither was this intrepidity peculiar to the inhabitants of Jomsburg; it was the general character of all the Scandinavians, of which we shall only give this further instance. A warrior, having been thrown upon his back in wrestling with his enemy, and the latter finding himself without his arms, the vanquished person promised to wait, without changing his posture, till his antagonist fetched a sword to kill him; and he faithfully kept his word.—To die with his arms in his hand was the ardent wish of every free man; and the pleasing idea which they had of this kind of death led them to dread such as proceeded from old age and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. The history of ancient Scandinavia is full of instances of this way of thinking. The warriors who found themselves lingering in disease, often availed themselves of their few remaining moments to shake off life, by a way that they supposed to be more glorious. Some of them would be carried into a field of battle, that they might die in the engagement. Others slew themselves: many procured this melancholy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to be performed by their friends, who considered it as a most sacred duty. "There is, on a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, (says the author of an old Iceland <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>,) a rock so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that no animal can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the top and live. Here men betake themselves when they are afflicted and unhappy. From this place all our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, even without waiting for sickness, have departed into Eden. It is useless, therefore, to give ourselves up to groans and complaints, or to put our relations to needless expenses, since we can easily follow the example of our fathers, who have all gone by the way of this rock."—When all these methods failed, and at last when Christianity had banished such barbarous practices, the disconsolate heroes consoled themselves by putting on complete armour, as soon as they found their end approaching.

SCANDIX

Pages 558-558

Shepherd's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Venus Comb, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCANNING

Pages 558-558

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, the measuring of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> by feet, in order to see whether <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not the quantities be duly observed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used in Greek and Latin verses. Thus an hexameter verse is scanned by resolving it into six feet; a pentameter, by resolving it into five feet, &c.

SCANTLING

Pages 558-558

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, size, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> standard, by which the dimensions, &c. of things are to be determined. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is particularly applied to the dimen-

SCANTO

Pages 558-559
or SPAVENTO, a sudden impression of horror upon the mind and body. It is extremely dreaded by the inhabitants of Sicily; and the wild ideas of the vulgar part of the inhabitants respecting it are almost incredible, and their dread of a sudden shock is no less surprising. There is scarce a symptom, disorder, or accident, they do not think may befall the human frame in consequence of the scanto. They are persuaded that a man who has been frightened only by a dog, a viper, a scorpion, or any other creature, which he has an antipathy to, will soon be seized with the same pains he would really feel, had he been torn with their teeth, or wounded with their venomous sting; and that nothing can remove these nervous imaginary pangs but a strong dose of dilena, a species of cantharides found in Sicily.

SCAPE-GOAT

Pages 559-559

in the Jewish antiquities, the goat which was set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>. For the ceremonies on this occasion, see Levit. xvi. 5, 6, &c. Some say, that a piece of scarlet cloth, in form of a tongue, was tied on the forehead of the scapegoat. Hoff. Lex. Univ. in voc. Lingua. Many have been the disputes among the interpreters concerning the meaning of the word scape-goat; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of azazel, for which scape-goat is put in our version of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. Spencer is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that azazel is a proper name, signifying the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> or evil daemon. See his reasons in his book De leg. Hebr. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>. Dissert. viii. Among other things, he observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews used to substitute the name Samaël for Azazel; and many of them have ventured to affirm, that at the feast of expiation they were obliged to offer a gift to Samaël to obtain his favour. Thus also the goat, sent into the wilderness to Azazel, was understood to be a gift or oblation. Some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> have been of the same opinion. But Spencer thinks that the genuine reasons of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> were, 1. That the goat loaded with the sins of the people, and sent to Azazel, might be a symbolical representation of the miserable condition of sinners. 2. God sent the goat thus loaded to the evil daemons, to show that they were impure, thereby to deter the people from any conversation or familiarity with them. 3. That the goat sent to Azazel, sufficiently expiating all evils, the Israelites might the more willingly abstain from the expiatory sacrifices of the Gentiles.

SCAPEMENT

Pages 559-559

in clock-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for the manner of communicating the impulse of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>. The ordinary scapements consist of the swing-wheel and pallets only; but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> improvements have added other levers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> detents, chiefly for the purposes of diminishing friction, or for detaching the pendulum from the pressure of the wheels during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its vibration. See WATCH-work.

SCAPULA

Pages 559-559

in Anatomy, the shoulder, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shoulder-bone. Scapula, John, the reputed author of a Greek lexicon, studied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>. His name is recorded in the annals of literature, neither on account of his talents nor learning, nor virtuous industry, but for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of disingenuity and fraud which he committed against an eminent literary character of the 16th century. Being employed by Henry Stephens as a corrector to his press while he was publishing his Thesaurus linguae Graecae, Scapula extracted those words and explications which he reckoned most useful, comprised them in one volume, and published them as an original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, with his own name. The compilation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of the Thesaurus had cost Stephens immense labour and expense; but it was so much admired by those learned men to whom he had shown it, and seemed to be of such essential importance to the acquisition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that he reasonably hoped his labour would be crowned with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he had expended would be repaid by a rapid and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>.
