But before his work came abroad, Scapula's abridgement appeared; which, from its size and price, was quickly purchased, while the Thesaurus itself lay neglected in the author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, a bankruptcy on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Stephens, while he who had occasioned it was enjoying the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his treachery. Scapula's Lexicon was first printed in 1570, in 4to. It was afterwards enlarged, and published in folio. It has gone through several editions, while the valuable work of Stephens has never been reprinted. Its success is, however, not owing to its superior merit, but to its price and more commodious size. Stephens charges the author with omitting a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. He accuses him of misunderstanding and perverting his meaning; and of tracing out absurd and trifling etymologies, which he himself had been careful to avoid. He composed the following epigram on Scapula. Quidam exterruit me capulo tenus abdidit ense Äeger eram à Scapulis, sanus et huc redeo. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Busby, so much celebrated for his knowledge of the Greek language, and his success in teaching it, would never permit his scholars at Westminster school to make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Scapula.

SCAPULAR

Pages 559-559
or Scapulery, a part of the habit of several religious orders in the church of Rome, worn over the gown as a badge of peculiar veneration for the Blessed Virgin. It consists of two narrow slips or breadths of cloth covering the back and the breast, and hanging down to the feet.—The devotees of the scapulary celebrate its festival on the 10th of July. SCARABÆUS, the Beetle, a genus of insects of the coleoptera order. See ENTOMOLOGY Index.

SCARBOROUGH

Pages 559-560

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, seated on a steep rock, near which are such craggy cliffs that it is almost inaccessible on every side. On the top of this rock is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> green plain, with two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> springing out of the rock. It is greatly frequented on account of its mineral waters called the Scarborough-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>; on which account it is much improved in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the buildings. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> was under the cliff, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in 1737, and the water was lost; but in clearing away the ruins in order to rebuild the wharf, it was recovered, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> joy of the town. The waters of Scarborough are chalybeate and purging. The two wells are both impregnated with the same principles, in different proportions; though the purging well is the most most celebrated, and the water of this is usually called the Scarborough water. When these waters are poured out of one glass into another, they throw up a number of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> bubbles; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are shaken for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a phial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> stopped, and the phial be suddenly opened before the commotion ceases, they displace an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> vapour, with an audible noise, which shows that they abound in fixed air. At the fountain they have a brisk, pungent chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the purging water tastes bitterish, which is not usually the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the chalybeate one. They lose their chalybeate virtues by exposure and by keeping; but the purging water the soonest. They both putrefy by keeping; but in time recover their sweetness. Four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five half pints of the purging water drank within an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, give two or three easy motions, and raise the spirits. The like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the chalybeate purges less, but exhilarates more, and passes off chiefly by urine. These waters have been found beneficial in hectic fevers, weaknesses of the stomach, and indigestion; in relaxations of the system; in nervous, hysteric, and hypochondriacal disorders; in the green sickness, scurvy, rheumatism, and asthmatic complaints; in gleets, the fluor albus, and other preternatural evacuations; and in habitual costiveness. Here are assemblies and balls as at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade, has a very good harbour, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> in 1811, 7067. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54° 18'. N. Lat. 0° 3'.

SCARDONA

Pages 560-560

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, seated on the eastern banks of the river Cherca, with a bishop's see. It has been taken and retaken several times by the Turks and Venetians; and these last ruined the fortifications and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings in 1537; but they have been since put in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. "No vestiges (says Fortis) now remain visible of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where the states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBURNIA">Liburnia</a> held their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> in the times of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. I however transcribed these two beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, which were discovered some years ago, and are preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the reverend canon Mercati. It is to be hoped, that, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Scardona continues increasing, new lands <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be broken up, and consequently more frequent discoveries made of the precious monuments of antiquity. And it is to be wished, that the few men of letters, who have a share in the regulation of this reviving city, may bestow some particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on that article, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> memorials of their ancient and illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which once held so eminent a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the Liburnian cities, may not be lost, nor carried away. It is almost a shame, that only six legible inscriptions actually exist at Scardona; and that all the others, since many more certainly must have been dug up there, are either miserably broken, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lost, or transported to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where they lose the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their merit. Roman coins are very frequently found about Scardona, and several valuable ones were shown to me by that hospitable prelate Monsignor Trevisani, bishop and father of the rising settlement. One of the principal gentlemen of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was so kind as to give me several sepulchral lamps, which are marked by the name of Fortis, and by the elegant form of the letters appear to be of the best times. The repeated devastations to which Scardona has been exposed, have left it no traces of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. It is now, however, beginning to rise again, and many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a> and Bosnia have settled there, on account of the convenient situation for trade with the upper provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. But the city has no fortifications, notwithstanding the assertion of P. Farkati to the contrary." E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 25'. N. Lat. 43° 55'.

SCARIFICATION

Pages 560-560

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of making several incisions in the skin by means of lances <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other instruments, particularly the cupping <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. See Surgery.

SCARLET

Pages 560-560

a beautiful bright <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours, minium mixed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> produces a good scarlet: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a flower in a print is to be painted a scarlet colour, the lights as well as the shades should be covered with minium, and the shaded parts finished with carmine, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce an admirable scarlet. SCARLET-Fever. See Medicine Index.

SCARP

Pages 560-560

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the scarf which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> commanders wear for ornament. It is borne somewhat like a battoon sinister, but is broader than it, and is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> out to the edges of the field, whereas the battoon is cut off at each end.

SCARPANTO

Pages 560-560

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, and one of the Sporades, lying to the south-west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of that of Candia. It is about 22 miles in length and 8 in breadth; and there are several <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It abounds in cattle and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, quarries of marble, with several good harbours. The Turks are masters of it, but the inhabitants are Greeks.

SCARPE

Pages 560-560

a river of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, which has its source near Aubigny in Artois, where it washes <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>; after which it runs on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> and Hainault, passing by St Amand, and a little after falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>.

SCARRON

Pages 560-562

Paul, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> writer, was the son of a counsellor in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> about the end of the year 1610, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the beginning of the succeeding year. His father marrying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he was compelled to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24 he visited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he freely indulged in licentious pleasures. After his return to Paris he persisted in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of dissipation till a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and painful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> convinced him that his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was almost worn out. At length when engaged in a party of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> at the age of 27, he lost the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of those legs which danced so gracefully, and of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> which could paint and play on the lute with so much elegance. In the year 1638 he was attending the carnival at Mons, of which he was a canon. Having dressed himself one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, his singular appearance excited the curiosity of the children of the town. They followed him in multitudes, and he was obliged to take shelter in a marsh. This wet and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> situation produced a numbness which totally deprived him of the use of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>; but notwithstanding this misfortune he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> gay and cheerful. He took up his residence at Paris, and by his pleasant humour soon attracted to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> all the men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The loss of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was followed by the loss of his fortune. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father he entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> with his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He pleaded the cause in a ludicrous manner, though his whole fortune depended on the decision. He accordingly lost the cause. Made- moiselle de Hautefort, compassionating his misfortunes, procured for him an audience of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. The poet requested to have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a> to her majesty. The queen smiled, and Scarron considered the smile as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to his new office. He therefore assumed the title of Scarron, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of God, unworthy valetudinarian to the queen. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine gave him a pension of 500 crowns; but that minister having received disdainfully the dedication of his Typhon, the poet immediately wrote a Mazarinade, and the pension was withdrawn. He then attached himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Condé, and celebrated his victories. He at length formed the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of marrying, and was accordingly, in 1651, married to Madeleine d'Aubigné (afterwards the famous Madame de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAINTENON">Maintenon</a>), who was then only 16 years of age. "At that time (says Voltaire) it was considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> acquisition for her to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> for a husband a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who was disfigured by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, impotent, and very little enriched by fortune." When Scarron was questioned about the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he said he acknowledged to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> invincible eyes, a very beautiful shape, two fine hands, and a large portion of wit. The notary demanded what dowry he would give her? Immediately replied Scarron, "The names of the wives of kings die with them, but the name of Scarron's wife shall live for ever." She restrained by her <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> his indecent buffooneries, and the good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> which had formerly resorted to his house were not less frequent in their visits. Scarron now became a new man. He became more decent in his manners and conversation; and his gaiety, when tempered with moderation, was still more agreeable. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, he lived with so little economy, that his income was soon reduced to a small annuity and his marquisate of Quinet. By the marquisate of Quinet, he meant the revenue he derived from his publications, which were printed by one Quinet. He was accustomed to talk to his superiors with great freedom in his jocular style. In the dedication to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Japhet d'Armenie, he thus addresses the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. "I shall endeavour to persuade your majesty, that you would do yourself no injury were you to do me a small favour; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> I should become more gay: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I should become more gay, I should write sprightly comedies; and if I should write sprightly comedies, your majesty would be amused, and thus your <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> would not be lost. All this appears so evident, that I should certainly be convinced of it if I were as great a king as I am now a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> unfortunate man." Though Scarron wrote comedies, he had neither time nor <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the rules and models of dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Horace, Plautus and Terence, would have frightened him; and perhaps he did not know that there was ever such a person as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> an open path before him, and he followed it. It was the fashion of the times to pillage the Spanish writers. Scarron was acquainted with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and he found it easier to use the materials which were already prepared, than to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> his brain in inventing a subject; a restraint to which a genius like his could not easily submit. As he borrowed liberally from the Spanish writers, a dramatic piece did not cost him much labour. His labour consisted not in making his comic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> talk humorously, but in keeping up serious characters; for the serious was a foreign language to him. The great success of his Jodellet Maître was a vast allurement to him. The comedians who acted it eagerly requested more of his productions. They were written without much toil, and they procured him large sums. They served to amuse him. If it be necessary to give more reasons for Scarron's readiness to engage in these works, abundance may be had. He dedicated his books to his sister's greyhound bitch; and when she failed him, he dedicated them to a certain Monseigneur, whom he praised higher, but did not much esteem. When the office of historiographer became vacant, he solicited for it without success. At length Fouquet gave him a pension of 1600 livres. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> queen of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> having come to Paris, was anxious to see Scarron. "I permit you (said she to Scarron) to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with me. The queen of France has made you her valetudinarian, and I create you my Roland." Scarron did not long enjoy that title: he was seized with so violent a hiccup, that every person thought he would have expired. "If I recover (he said), I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make a fine satire on the hiccup." His gaiety did not forsake him to the last. Within a few minutes of his death, when his domestics were shedding tears about him, "My good friends (says he), I shall never make you weep so much for me as I have made you laugh." <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before expiring, he said, "I could never believe before that it is so easy to laugh at death." He died on the 14th of October 1660, in the 51st year of his age. His works have been collected and published by Bruxen de la Martinière, in 10 vols 12mo, 1737. There are, 1. The Eneid travestied, in 8 books. It was afterwards continued by Moreau de Brasey. 2. Typhon, or the Gigantomachia. 3. Many comedies; as Jodellet, or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">Valet</a>; Jodellet cuffed; Don Japhet d'Armenie; The Ridiculous Heir; Every Man his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>; The Foolish Marquis; The Scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>; The False Appearance; The Prince Corsaire, a tragi-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. Besides these, he wrote other pieces in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. 4. His Comic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">Romance</a> in prose, which is the only one of his works that deserves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It is written with much purity and gaiety, and has contributed not a little to the improvement of the French language. Scarron had great pleasure in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> his works to his friends as he composed them: he called it trying his works. Segrais and another of his friends coming to him one day, "Take a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> (says Scarron to them) and sit <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, that I may examine my Comic Romance." When he observed the company laugh, "Very well (said he), my book will be well received since it makes persons of such delicate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> laugh." Nor was he deceived. His Romance had a prodigious run. It was the only one of his works that Böileau could submit to read. 5. Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOVELS">Novels</a> translated into French. 6. A volume of Letters. 7. Poems; consisting of Songs, Epistles, Stanzas, Odes, and Epigrams. The whole collection abounds with sprightliness and gaiety. Scarron can raise a laugh in the most serious subjects; but his sallies are rather those of a buffoon than the effusions of ingenuity and taste. He is continually falling into the mean and the obscene. If we should make any excep- tion in favour of some of his comedies, of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his Eneid travestied, and his Comic Romance, we must acknowledge that all the rest of his works are only fit to be read by footmen and buffoons. It has been said that he was the most eminent man in his age for burlesque. This might make him an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> to those who choose to laugh away their time; but as he has left nothing that can instruct posterity, he has but little title to posthumous fame.

SCENE

Pages 562-563

in its primary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denoted a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where dramatic pieces and other public shows were exhibited; for it does not appear that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets were at all acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way of changing the scenes in the different parts of the play, in order to raise the idea of the persons represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> being in different places. The original scene for acting of plays was as simple as the representations themselves: it consisted only of a plain plot of ground proper for the occasion, which was in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> shaded by the neighbouring trees, whose branches were made to meet together, and their vacancies supplied with boards, sticks, and the like; and to complete the shelter, these were sometimes covered with skins, and sometimes with only the branches of other trees newly cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and full of leaves. Afterwards more <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> scenes, or scenaical representations, were introduced, and paintings used instead of the objects themselves. Scenes were then of three sorts; tragic, comic, and satiric. The tragic scene represented stately magnificent edifices, with decorations of pillars, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and other things suitable to the palaces of kings: the comic exhibited private houses with balconies and windows, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> buildings: and the satiric was the representation of groves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, dens, and other rural appearances; and these decorations either turned on pivots, or slid along grooves as those in our <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>. To keep <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, the scene should never be shifted from place to place in the course of the play: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were pretty severe in this respect, particularly Terence, in some of whose plays the scene never shifts at all, but the whole is transacted at the door of some old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, whither with inimitable art he occasionally brings the actors. The French are pretty strict with respect to this rule; but the English pay very little regard to it. Scene is also a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a dramatic poem. Thus plays are divided into acts, and acts are again subdivided into scenes; in which sense the scene is properly the persons present at or concerned in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> on the stage at such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; whenever, therefore, a new <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> appears, or an old one disappears, the action is changed into other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and therefore a new scene then commences. It is one of the laws of the stage, that the scenes be well connected; that is, that one succeed another in such a manner as that the stage be never quite empty till the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. Scenography, (from the Greek σκηνή, scene, and γραφή, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>), in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, a representation of a body on a perspective <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; or a description thereof in all its dimensions, such as it appears to the eye. See Perspective. Sceptic, οἰκετικός, from οἰκετεύομαι, "I consider, look about, or deliberate," properly signifies considerative and inquisitive, or one who is always weighing reasons on one side and the other, without ever deciding between them. It is chiefly applied to an ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers founded by Pyrrho (see Pyrrho), who, according to Laertius, had various other denominations. From their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> they were called Pyrrhonians; from the distinguishing tenets or characteristic of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> they derived the name of Aporetic, from ἀπορεῖν, "to doubt;" from their suspension and hesitation they were called ephetic, from ἐπιστάναι, "to stay or keep back:" and lastly, they were called zetetic, or seekers, from their never getting beyond the search of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. That the sceptical philosophy is absurd, can admit of no dispute in the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and that many of the followers of Pyrrho carried it to the most ridiculous height, is no less true. But we cannot believe that he himself was so extravagantly sceptical as has sometimes been asserted, when we reflect on the particulars of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which are still preserved, and the respectful manner in which we find him mentioned by his contemporaries and writers of the first name who flourished soon after him. The truth, as far as at this distance of time it can be discovered, seems to be, that he learned from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a> to deny the real existence of all qualities in bodies, except those which are essential to primary atoms, and that he referred every thing else to the perceptions of the mind produced by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, in other words, to appearance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. All knowledge of course appeared to him to depend on the falacious report of the senses, and consequently to be uncertain; and in this notion he was confirmed by the general spirit of the Eleatic school in which he was educated. He was further confirmed in his scepticism by the subtleties of the Dialectic school in which he had been instructed by the son of Stilpo; choosing to overturn the cavils of sophistry by recurring to the doctrine of universal uncertainty, and thus breaking the knot which he could not unloose. For being naturally and habitually inclined to consider invincible tranquillity as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end of all philosophy, he was easily led to despise the dissensions of the dogmatists, and to infer from their endless disputes, the uncertainty of the questions on which they debated; controversy, as it has often happened to others, becoming also with respect to him the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of scepticism. Pyrrho's doctrines, however new and extraordinary, were not totally disregarded. He was attended by several scholars, and succeeded by several followers, who preserved the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his notions. The most eminent of his followers was Timon (see Timon), in whom the public succession of professors in the Pyrrhonic school terminated. In the time of Cicero it was almost extinct, having suffered much from the jealousy of the dogmatists, and from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> aversion in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind to acknowledge total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, or to be left in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> darkness. The disciples of Timon, however, still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to profess scepticism, and their notions were embraced privately at least by many others. The school itself was afterwards revived by Ptolemaeus a Cyrenaean, and was continued by Enesidemus a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of Cicero, who wrote a treatise on the principles of the Pyrrhonic philosophy, the heads of which are preserved by Plotius. From this time it was continued through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of preceptors of little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> to Sextus Empiricus, who also gave a summary of the sceptical doctrine. A system of philosophy thus founded on doubt, and clouded with uncertainty, could neither teach tenets of any importance, nor prescribe a certain rule of conduct; and accordingly we find that the followers of scepticism were guided entirely by chance. As they could form no certain judgment respecting good and evil, they accidentally learned the folly of eagerly pursuing any apparent good, or of avoiding any apparent evil; and their minds of course settled into a state of undisturbed tranquillity, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> postulate of their system. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the sceptics we find ten distinct topics of argument urged in support of the doctrine of uncertainty, with this precaution, however, that nothing could be positively asserted either concerning their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or their force. These arguments chiefly respect objects of sense: they place all knowledge in appearance: and, as the same things appear very different to different people, it is impossible to say which appearance most truly expresses their real nature. They likewise say, that our judgment is liable to uncertainty from the circumstance of frequent or rare occurrence, and that mankind are continually led into different conceptions concerning the same thing by means of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, fabulous tales, and established opinions. On all these accounts, they think every human judgment is liable to uncertainty; and, concerning any thing, they can only assert, that it seems to be, not that it is what it seems. This doubtful reasoning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> reasoning it may be called, the sceptics extended to all the sciences, in which they discovered nothing true, or which could be absolutely asserted. In all nature, in physics, morals, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, they found contradictory opinions, and inexplicable or incomprehensible phenomena. In physics, the appearances they thought might be deceitful; and respecting the nature of God and the duties of morality, men were, in their opinion, equally ignorant and uncertain. To overturn the sophistical arguments of these sceptical reasoners, would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, if their reasoning were worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a>. Indeed, the great principle is sufficiently, though shortly refuted by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, in these words. "When you say all things are incomprehensible (says he), do you comprehend or conceive that they are thus incomprehensible, or do you not? If you do, then something is comprehensible; if you do not, there is no reason we should believe you, since you do not comprehend your own assertion." But scepticism has not been confined entirely to the ancients and to the followers of Pyrrho. Numerous sceptics have arisen also in modern times, varying in their principles, manners, and character, as chance, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, vanity, weakness, or indolence, prompted them. The great object, however, which they seem to have in view, is to overturn, or at least to weaken, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and testimony; though some of them have even attempted to show, that the axioms of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> are uncertain, and its demonstrations inconclusive. This last attempt has not indeed been often made; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> aim of Mr Hume's philosophical writings is to introduce doubts into every branch of physics, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, ethics, and theology. It is needless to give a specimen of his reasonings in support of modern scepticism. The most important of them have been noticed elsewhere (see MIRACLE, METAPHYSICS, and PHILOSOPHY, No. 41); and such of our readers as have any relish for speculations of that nature can be no strangers to his essays, or to the able confutations of them by the Doctors Reid, Campbell, Gregory, and Beattie, who have likewise exposed the weakness of the sceptical reasonings of Des Cartes, Malbranche, and other philosophers of great fame in the same school.

SCEPTICISM

Pages 563-563

the doctrines and opinions of the sceptics. See the preceding article.

SCEPTRE

Pages 563-563

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a>, borne on solemn occasions by Kings, as a badge of their command and authority. Nicod derives the word from the Greek σκῆπτρον, which he says originally signified "a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>," which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings usually bore as a badge of their authority; that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> being in very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration among the heathens. But σκῆπτρον does not properly signify a javelin, but a staff to rest upon, from σκέπτομαι, ἵνα ἐπιστήσω, "I lean upon." Accordingly, in the simplicity of the earlier ages of the world, the sceptres of kings were no other than <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> walking-staves: and Ovid, in speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, describes him as resting on his sceptre (Met. i. ver. 178.) The sceptre is an ensign of royalty of greater antiquity than the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. The Greek tragic and other poets put sceptres in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the most ancient kings they ever introduce. Justin observes, that the sceptre, in its original, was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTA">hasta</a>, or spear. He adds, that, in the most remote antiquity, men adored the hastae or sceptres as immortal gods; and that it was upon this account, that, even in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they still furnished the gods with sceptres.—<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>'s sceptre is his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>. Tarquin the Elder was the first who assumed the sceptre among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Le Gendre tells us, that, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the French kings, the sceptre was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> rod, almost always of the same height with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> who bore it, and crooked at one end like a crozier. Frequently instead of a sceptre, kings are seen on medals with a palm in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. See REGALIA. SCHÆFFERIA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioica class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those that are doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHAFFHAUSEN

Pages 563-564

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and owes its origin to the interruption of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of that river by the cataract at Lauffen. It was at one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> an imperial town, and admitted a member member of the Helvetic confederacy in 1501; and its territory forms the 12th canton in point of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The inhabitants of this town are computed at 6000, but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of citizens <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> burgesses is about 1600. From these were elected 85 members, who formed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, or little council of 25, being entrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>; and the great council finally deciding all appeals, and regulating the more important concerns of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Though a frontier town, it has no garrison, and the fortifications are weak; but it once had a famous wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Rhine, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of one Ulric Grubenman, a carpenter. The sides and top of it were covered; and it was a kind of hanging bridge; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> was nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and not carried, as usual, over the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, but let into the middle of it, and there suspended. This curious bridge was burnt by the French, when they evacuated Schaffhausen, after being defeated by the Austrians, April 13, 1799. Schaffhausen is 22 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, and 39 east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 41' E. Lat. 47° 39' N.

SCHALBEA

Pages 564-564

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHEDULE

Pages 564-564

a scroll of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, annexed to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, lease, or other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>; containing an inventory of goods, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> omitted in the body of the deed. The word is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of the Latin scheda, or Greek σχέδιον, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or piece of paper.

SCHEELE

Pages 564-566
CHARLES WILLIAM, was born on the 19th of December 1742, at Stralsund, where his father kept a shop. When he was very young, he received the usual instructions of a private school; and was afterwards advanced to an academy. At a very early age he showed a strong desire to follow the profession of an apothecary, and his father suffered him to gratify his inclinations. With Mr Bauch, an apothecary at Gottenburg, he passed his apprenticeship, which was completed in six years. He remained, however, some time longer at that place, and it was there that he so excellently laid the first foundations of his knowledge. Among the various books which he read, that treated of chemical subjects, Kunkell's Laboratory seems to have been his favourite. He used to repeat many of the experiments contained in that work privately in the night, when the rest of the family had retired to rest. A friend of Scheele's had remarked the progress which he had made in chemistry, and had asked him by what inducements he had been at first led to study a science in which he had gained such knowledge? Scheele returned the following answer: "The first cause, my friend, arose from yourself. Nearly at the beginning of my apprenticeship you advised me to read Neuman's Chemistry, from the perusal of which I became eager to make experiments myself; and I remember very well how I mixed together, in a conserve-glass, oil of cloves, and fuming acid of nitre, which immediately took fire. I see also still before my eyes an unlucky experiment which I made with pyrophorus. Circumstances of this kind did but the more inflame my desire to repeat experiments." After Scheele's departure from Gottenburg, in the year 1765, he obtained a place with Kalstrom, an apothecary at Malmo. Two years afterwards he went from thence to Stockholm, and managed the shop of Mr Scharenberg. In 1773, he changed this appointment for another at Upsal, under Mr Loock. Here he was fortunately situated; as, from his acquaintance with learned men, and from having free access to the university laboratory, he had opportunities of increasing his knowledge. At this place also he happily commenced the friendship which subsisted between him and Bergman. During his residence at this place, his Royal Highness Prince Henry of Prussia, accompanied by the Duke of Suedermania, visited Upsal, and chose this opportunity to see the academical laboratory. Scheele was accordingly appointed by the university to exhibit some chemical experiments to them. This office he undertook, and showed some of the most curious processes in chemistry. The two princes asked him many questions, and expressed their approbation of the answers which he returned to them. The duke asked him what countryman he was, and seemed to be much pleased when Scheele informed him that he was born at Stralsund. At their departure they told the professor, who was present, that they should esteem it a favour if he would permit the young man to have free access to the laboratory, as often as he chose to make experiments. In the year 1777 Scheele was appointed by the Medical College to be apothecary at Koping. It was at that place that he soon showed the world how great a man he was, and that no place or situation could confine his abilities. When he was at Stockholm he showed his acuteness as a chemist, as he discovered there the new and wonderful acid contained in the fluor spar. It has been confidently asserted, that Scheele was the first who discovered the nature of the aerial acid; and that whilst he was at Upsal he made many experiments to prove its properties. This circumstance might probably have furnished Bergman with the means of treating this subject more fully. At the same place he began the series of excellent experiments on that remarkable mineral substance, manganese; from which investigation he was led to make the very valuable and interesting discovery of oxymuriatic acid. At the same time he examined the properties of ponderous earth. At Koping he finished his dissertation on Air and Fire; a work which the celebrated Bergman most warmly recommended in the friendly preface which he wrote for it. The theory which Scheele endeavours to prove in this treatise is, that fire consists of pure air and phlogiston. According to more recent opinions (if inflammable air be phlogiston), water is composed of these two principles. Of these opinions we may say, in the words of Cicero, "Opiniones tam variae sunt tamque inter se dissidentes ut alterum profecto fieri posset, ut earum nulla, alterum certe, non potest ut plus una, vera sit." The author's merit in this work, exclusive of the encomiums of Bergman, was sufficient to obtain the approbation of the public; as the ingenuity displayed in treating so delicate a subject, and the many new and valuable observations (A) which are dispersed through the treatise, justly (A) Scheele mentions in this work, in a cursory way, the decomposition of common salt by the calx of lead. Mr Turner, justly entitled the author to that fame which his book procured him. It was spread abroad through every country, became soon out of print, was reprinted, and translated into many languages. The English translation is enriched with the notes of that accurate and truly philosophic genius Richard Kirwan, Esq. Scheele now diligently employed himself in contributing to the Transactions of the Academy at Stockholm. He first pointed out a new way to prepare the salt of benzoin. In the same year he discovered that arsenic, freed in a particular manner from phlogiston, partakes of all the properties of an acid, and has its peculiar affinities to other substances. In a Dissertation on Flint, Clay, and Alum, he clearly overturned Beattie's opinion of the identity of the siliceous and argillaceous earths. He published an Analysis of the Human Calculus. He showed also a mode of preparing mercurius dulcis in the humid way, and improved the process of making the powder of Algaroth. He analyzed the mineral substance called molybdena or flexible black lead. He discovered a beautiful green pigment. He showed us how to decompose the air of the atmosphere. He discovered that some neutral salts are decomposed by lime and iron. He decomposed plumbago, or the common black lead. He observed, with peculiar ingenuity, an acid in milk, which decomposes acetated alkali; and in his experiments on the sugar of milk, he discovered another acid, different in some respects from the above-mentioned acids and the common acid of sugar. He accomplished the decomposition of tungsten, the component parts of which were before unknown, and found in it a peculiar metallic acid united to lime. He published an excellent dissertation on the different sorts of ether. He found out an easy way to preserve vinegar for many years. His investigation of the colouring matter in Prussian blue, the means he employed to separate it, and his discovery that alkali, sal ammoniac, and charcoal, mixed together, will produce it, are strong marks of his penetration and genius. He found out a peculiar sweet matter in expressed oils, after they have been boiled with litharge and water. He showed how the acid of lemons may be obtained in crystals. He found the white powder in rhubarb, which Model thought to be selenite, and which amounts to one-seventh of the weight of the root, to be calcareous earth, united to the acid of sorrel. This suggested to him the examination of the acid of sorrel. He precipitated acetate of lead with it, and decomposed the precipitate thus obtained by the vitriolic acid; and by this process he obtained the common acid of sugar; and by slowly dropping a solution of fixed alkali into a solution of the acid of sugar, he regenerated the acid of sorrel.—From his examination of the acids contained in fruits and berries, he found not one species of acid alone, viz. the acid of lemon, but another also, which he denominates the malaceous or malic acid, from its being found in the greatest quantity in apples. By the decomposition of Bergman's new metal (siderrite) he showed the truth of Meyer's and Klaproth's conjecture concerning it. He boiled the calx of siderrite with alkali of tartar, and precipitated nitrate of mercury by the middle salt which he obtained by this operation; the calx of mercury which was precipitated was found to be united to the acid of phosphorus; so that he demonstrates that this calx was phosphorated iron. He found also, that the native Prussian blue contained the same acid. He discovered by the same means, that the perlate acid, as it was called, was not an acid sui generis, but the phosphoric united to a small quantity of the mineral alkali. He suggested an improvement in the process for obtaining magnesia from Epsom salt; he advises the adding of an equal weight of common salt to the Epsom salt, so that an equal weight of Glauber's salt may be obtained; but this will not succeed unless in the cold of winter. These are the valuable discoveries of this great philosopher, which are to be found in the Transactions of the Royal Society at Stockholm. Most of his essays have been published in French by Madame Picardet, and Mons. Morveau of Dijon. Dr Beddoes also has made a very valuable present to his countrymen of an English translation of a greater part of Scheele's dissertations, to which he has added some useful and ingenious notes. The following discoveries of Scheele are not, we believe, published with the rest. He showed what that substance is, which has been generally called 'the earth of the fluor spar.' It is not produced unless the fluor acid meet with siliceous earth. It appears from Scheele's experiments to be a triple salt, consisting of flint, acid of fluor, and fixed alkali. Scheele proved also, that the fluor acid may be produced without any addition of the vitriolic or any mineral acid: The fluor is melted with fixed alkali, and the fluorated alkali is decomposed by acetated lead. If the precipitate be mixed with charcoal dust, and exposed in a retort to a strong heat, the lead will be revived, and the acid of fluor, which was united to it, will pass into the receiver possessed of all its usual properties. This seems to be an ingenious and unanswerable proof of its existence. He observed, that no pyrophorus can be made unless an alkali be present; and the reason why it can be prepared from alum and coal is, that the common alum always contains a little alkali, which is added in order to make it crystallize; for if this be separated from it, no pyrophorus can be procured from it. His last dissertation was his very valuable observations on the acid of the gall-nut. Ehrhart, one of Scheele's most intimate friends, asserts, that he was the discoverer of both of the acids of sugar and tartar. We are also indebted to him for that masterpiece of chemical decomposition, the separation of the acid of phosphorus from bones. This appears --- Turner, a gentleman who happily unites the skill of the manufacturer with the knowledge of the philosophic chemist, has also the merit of this discovery, as he observed the same fact, without having been indebted to Scheele's hint on the subject. Mr Turner has done more; he has converted this discovery to some use in the arts; he produces mineral alkali for sale, arising from the decomposition; and from the lead which is united to the marine acid he forms the beautiful pigment called the patent yellow. pears from a letter which Scheele wrote to Gahn, who has generally had the reputation of this great discovery. This acid, which is so curious in the eye of the chemist, begins to draw the attention of the physician. It was first used in medicine, united to the mineral alkali, by the ingenious Dr Pearson. The value of this addition to the materia medica cannot be better evinced than from the increase of the demand for it, and the quantity of it which is now prepared and sold in London. We may stamp the character of Scheele as a philosopher from his many and important discoveries. What concerns him as a man we are informed of by his friends, who affirm, that his moral character was irreproachable. From his outward appearance, you would not at first sight have judged him to be a man of extraordinary abilities; but there was a quickness in his eye, which, to an accurate observer, would point out the penetration of his mind. He mixed but little with the crowd of common acquaintance; for this he had neither time nor inclination, as, when his profession permitted him, he was for the most part employed in his experimental inquiries. But he had a soul for friendship; nor could even his philosophical pursuits withhold him from truly enjoying the society of those whom he could esteem and love. Before he adopted any opinion, or a particular theory, he considered it with the greatest attention; but when once his sentiments were fixed, he adhered to them, and defended them with resolution. Not but that he was ingenuous enough to suffer himself to be convinced by weighty objections; as he has shown that he was open to conviction. His chemical apparatus was neither neat nor convenient; his laboratory was small and confined; nor was he particular in regard to the vessels which he employed in his experiments, as often the first phial which came to hand was placed in his sand heat; so that we may justly wonder how such discoveries, and such elegant experiments, could have been made under such unfavourable circumstances. He understood none of the modern languages except the German and Swedish; so that he had not the advantage of being benefited by the early intelligence of discoveries made by foreigners, but was forced to wait till the intelligence was conveyed to him in the slow and uncertain channel of translation. The important services which Scheele did to ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy entitled him to universal reputation; and he obtained it: his name was well known by all Europe; and he was member of several learned academies and philosophical societies. It was often wished that he would quit his retirement at Koping, and move in a larger sphere. It was suggested to him, that a place might be procured in England, which might afford him a good income and more leisure; and, indeed, latterly an offer was made to him of an annuity of 300l. if he would settle in this country. But death, alas! put an end to this project. For half a year before this melancholy event, his health had been declining, and he himself was sensible that he would not recover. On the 19th of May 1786, he was confined to his bed; on the 21st he bequeathed all of which he was possessed to his wife (who was the widow of his predecessor at Koping, and whom he had lately married); and on the same day he departed this life. So the world lost, in less than two years, Bergman and Scheele, of whom Sweden may justly boast; two philosophers, who were beloved and lamented by all their contemporaries, and whose memory posterity will never cease most gratefully to revere.

SCHELDE

Pages 566-566

a river which rises on the confines of Picardy, and runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by Cambrey, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIENNES">Valenciennes</a>, Tourmay, Oudenarde, &c. and receiving the Lis at Ghent, runs east by Dendermond, and then north to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>: below which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> it divides into two branches, one called the Wester-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>, which separates <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> near Flushing; and the other called the Ooster-Scheldt, which runs by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-zoom, and afterwards between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> Beveland and Schowen, and a little below falls in the sea.

SCHEME

Pages 566-566

a draught <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> representation of any geometrical or astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, or problem, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> sensible to the eye; or of the celestial bodies in their proper places for any moment; otherwise called a diagram.

SCHEMNITZ

Pages 566-566

a town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, with three castles. It is famous for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, as also for hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. Near it is a rock of a shining blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> mixed with green, and some spots of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 0. N. Lat. 48. 40.

SCHERARDIA

Pages 566-566

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SCHETLAND. See Shetland.

SCHEUCHZERIA

Pages 566-566

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the fifth order, Tripetalotidea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHIECHS

Pages 566-566
or Schech, among the Arabs, is a name applied to their nobles. "Among the Bedouins," says Niebuhr, "it belongs to every noble, whether of the highest or the lowest order. Their nobles are very numerous, and compose in a manner the whole nation: the plebeians are invariably actuated and guided by the scheichs, who superintend and direct in every transaction. The scheichs, and their subjects, are born to the life of shepherds and soldiers. The greater tribes rear many camels, which they either sell to their neighbours, or employ them in the carriage of goods, or in military expeditions. The petty tribes keep flocks of sheep. Among those tribes which apply to agriculture, the scheichs live always in tents, and leave the culture of their grounds to their subjects, whose dwellings are wretched huts. Scheichs always ride on horses or dromedaries, inspecting the conduct of their subjects, visiting their friends, or hunting. Traversing the desert, where the horizon is wide as on the ocean, they perceive travellers at a distance. As travellers are seldom to be met with in those wild tracts, they easily discover such as pass that way, and are tempted to pillage them when they find their own party the strongest."

SCHIRAS

Pages 566-567
or Schiraz, a large and famous town of Persia, capital of Farsistan, is three miles in length from east to west, but not so much in breadth. It is seated at the north-west end of a spacious plain surrounded with very high hills, under one of which the town stands. The houses are built of bricks dried in the sun; the roofs are flat and terraced. There are 15 handsome mosques, tiled with stones of a bluish green colour, and lined within with black polished marble. There are many large and beautiful gardens, surrounded with walls 14 feet high, and four thick. They contain various kinds of very fine trees, with fruits almost of every kind, besides various beautiful flowers. The wines of Schiras are not only the best in Persia, but, as some think, in the whole world. The women are much addicted to gallantry, and Schiras is called an earthly paradise by some. The ruins of the famous Persepolis are 30 miles to the north-east of this place. E. Long. 56° 0'. N. Lat. 29° 36'.

SCHISM

Pages 567-567

(from the Greek, σχίσμα, cliff, fissure), in its general acceptation signifies <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> separation; but is chiefly used in speaking of separations happening from diversity of opinions among people of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Thus we say the schism of the ten tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the schism of the Persians from the Turks and other Mahometans, &c. Among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authors, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> schism of the West is that which happened in the times of Clement VII. and Urban VI. which divided the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> for 40 or 50 years, and was at length ended by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Martin V. at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. The Romanists <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 34 schisms in their church. —They bestow the name English schism on the reformation of religion in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Those of the church of England apply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> schism to the separation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">presbyterians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">independents</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">anabaptists</a>, for a further reformation.

SCHISTUS

Pages 567-567

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a name given to several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, as argillaceous, siliceous, bituminous, schistus, &c. See Mineralogy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHMIEDELIA

Pages 567-567

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHNEIDER

Pages 566-566

CHRISTOPHER, a German mathematician, astronomer, and Jesuit, eminent for being the first who discovered spots on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, was born at Schwaben in the territory of Middelheim in 1575. He first discovered spots on the sun's disk in 1611, and made observations on these phenomena at Rome, until at length reducing them to order, he published them in one volume folio in 1630. He wrote also some smaller things relating to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and died in 1660.

SCHOENOBATES

Pages 567-567

(from the Greek, σχενός, a rope; and βάνος, I walk), a name which the Greeks gave to their rope-dancers: by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called funambuli. See Rope-dancer and Funambulus. The schœnobates were slaves whose masters made <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of them, by entertaining the people with their feats of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Mercavialis de arte gymnastica. lib. iii. gives us five figures of schœnobates engraven after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>.

SCHOENUS

Pages 567-567

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 3d order, Calamariae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SCHOLASTIC

Pages 567-567

something belonging to the school. See School. Scholastic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of divinity which clears and discusses questions by reason and arguments; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, opposed to positive divinity, which is founded on the authority of fathers, councils, &c. The school-divinity is now fallen into contempt; and is scarce regarded Scholastic anywhere but in some of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, where they are still by their charters obliged to teach it.

SCHOLIAST

Pages 567-567
or Commentator, a grammarian who writes scholia, that is, notes, glosses, &c. upon ancient authors who have written in the learned languages. See the next article.

SCHOLIUM

Pages 567-567

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, annotation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remark, occasionally made on some passage, proposition, or the like. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is much used in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, where, after demonstrating a proposition, it is customary to point out how it might be done some other way, or to give some advice or precaution in order to prevent mistakes, or add some particular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> or application thereof.

SCHOMBERG

Pages 567-568

Frederick-Armand <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of, a distinguished officer, sprung from an illustrious family in Germany, and the son of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Schomberg by an English lady, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, was born in 1608. He was initiated into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> under Frederick-Henry <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and afterwards served under his son William II. of Orange, who highly esteemed him. He then repaired to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, where his reputation was so well known, that he obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Gravelines, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FURNES">Furnes</a>, and the surrounding countries. He was reckoned inferior to no general in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> except Mareschal Turenne and the prince of Condé; men of such exalted eminence that it was no disgrace to acknowledge their superiority. The French court thinking it necessary to diminish the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, sent Schomberg to the assistance of the Portuguese, who were engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> respecting the succession to their throne.—Schomberg's military talents gave a turn to the war in favour of his allies. The court of Spain was obliged to solicit for peace in 1668, and to acknowledge the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> heirs to the throne of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. For his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> services he was created Count Mentola in Portugal; and a pension of 5000l. was bestowed upon him, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> to his heirs. In 1673 he came over to England to command the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but the English at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being disgusted with the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, Schomberg was suspected of coming over with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to corrupt the army, and bring it under French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. He therefore found it necessary to return to France, which he soon left, and went to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1676, he forced the prince of Orange to raise the siege of Maestricht; and it is said he was then raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Mareschal of France. But the French Dictionnaire Historique, whose information on a point of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> ought to be authentic, says, that he was invested with this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> the same year in which he took the fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELLEGARDE">Bellegarde</a> from the Spaniards while serving in Portugal. Upon the revocation of the edict of Nantes, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> commenced against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, Schomberg, who was of that persuasion, requested leave to retire into his own country. This request was refused; but he was permitted to take refuge in Portugal, where he had reason to expect he would be kindly received on account of past services. But the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> zeal of the Portuguese, though it did not prevent them from accepting assistance from a heretic when their kingdom... Schomberg's kingdom was threatened with subversion, could not permit them to give him shelter when he came for protection. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a> interfered, and obliged the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to send him away. He then went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> by the way of England. Having accepted an invitation from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, he was invested with the government of Ducal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and appointed commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the elector's forces. When the prince of Orange sailed to England to take possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> which his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> James II. had abdicated, Schomberg obtained permission from the elector of Brandenburg to accompany him. He is supposed to have been the author of an ingenious stratagem which the prince employed after his arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to discover the sentiments of the people respecting the revolution. The stratagem was, to spread an alarm over the country that the Irish were approaching with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. When the prince was established on the throne of England, Schomberg was appointed commander in chief of the forces, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the ordnance. In April 1689 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>, and naturalized by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in May following was created a baron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, marquis, and duke of the kingdom of England, by the name and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Teys, earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRENTFORD">Brentford</a>, marquis of Harwich, and duke of Schomberg. The House of Commons voted to him 100,000l. as a reward for his services. Of this he only received a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; but after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> a pension of 5000l. a year was bestowed upon his son. In August 1689 he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to reduce that kingdom to obedience.
